Subject:  DEA Suspension of Cardinal License
Attach:

Although the most recent DEA suspension involves Cardinal location in Swedesboro NJ, clearly the same action taken at Cardinal in Lakeland FL and Cardinal in Washington state are related to suspicious order monitoring.


DEA Suspends Cardinal Health License
Friday December 7, 10:00 am ET

DEA Suspends Controlled-Substance License of Another Cardinal Health Distribution Center

DUBLIN, Ohio (AP) -- The government has suspended the medical products and services company's license to distribute controlled substances from its Lakeland, Fla., distribution center effective Dec. 10, the company said Friday.

ADVERTISEMENT
<http://us.ard.yahoo.com/SIG=12ff9sspl/M=617048.11403091.12110175.1383221/D=fin/S=8988914:LREC/Y=YAHOO/EXP=1197592389/A=5054844/R=0/SIG=1224cq05r/*http://www.pplweb.com/investors/ppl+performs/ad+-+megawatts+out/>
 <http://us.bc.yahoo.com/b?P=2Vc3lESOxCYHPQAcQQj.uQHGktZncEdhsyUAAmHQ&T=1drgg9n30%2fX%3d1197585189%2fE%3d8988914%2fR%3dfin%2fK%3d5%2fV%3d2.1%2fW%3dH%2fY%3dYAHOO%2fF%3d1283064936%2fH%--%2fQ%3d-1%2fS%3d1%2fJ%3dB8C28E44&U=13bp14v6s%2fN%3dNYCKAtG_RuQ-%2fC%3d617048.11403091.12110175.1383221%2fD%3dLREC%2fB%3d5054844>
The suspension follows a similar action announced last week against Cardinal's Washington state distribution center amid an investigation of a customer's online sales of the prescription painkiller hydrocodone, commonly known by the brand name Vicodin.

That suspension went into effect Monday after a U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration order said Cardinal's distribution center in Auburn, Wash., supplied the drug to a pharmacy that allegedly dispensed excessive amounts based on illegitimate prescriptions from Internet pharmacies.

Cardinal spokesman Jim Mazzola on Friday said the Florida center's suspension is related to the same matter. The company is working with the DEA to resolve the issue and is taking steps that guard against distribution to pharmacies "engaged in diversion," he added.

Subject: RE: Request Advice on Customer Order for Material to Prepare Reference Standard
Karen,

Last year (2008) I dispensed 63.5 grams of Codeine Phosphate reference standard for the analytical support of our
manufacturing of the bulk here in St. Louis and all the dosage forms in Hobart. So far this year (2009) I have dispensed 13


   grams. Last year Sherryl Ruder shipped one order for 200 milligrams to an external customer and had no internal requests for
Codeine Phosphate.

If I were to subdivide 1000 grams, that would last us almost 16 years at the rate that we used it in 2008. I must say that our
reference standard use is increasing, so that 1000 grams may only last maybe 10 years. That still is a very long time to store a
qualified reference. I also know that storing any controlled substance that long invites opportunities for diversion. So that
generally should be discouraged.

We use the manufacturing registration for our operation. When it is shipped to Hobart  it goes out under our manufacturing
registration and is transferred to Hobart's Analytical registration via their form 222.

It seems to me that if the customer is "manufacturing" a reference standard, it should be received into their manufacturing
registration. When it goes to their client to be used in the lab, that is when it should be transferred to analytical lab registration.

Ted
From: Harper, Karen
Sent: Friday, May 15, 2009 8:07 AM
To: Myrick, Ted
Cc: Pokorny, Camille M; Ratliff, Bill; Hunter, Dave
Subject: Request Advice on Customer Order for Material to Prepare Reference Standard
Ted
Controlled Substance Compliance and Security are working with Customer Service to determine the validity of a customer order
for 1 kg of Codeine Phosphate, within the scope of our Suspicious Order Monitoring Program.
Customer states their intended use is to "prepare a reference standard for a client who will use the material for testing activities".

Our concerns are:
The 1 kg quantity seems too large, does this exceed the quantity of API we would normally use internally to prepare reference
standards?
Does the intended use differ from the activity that you and Sherryl perform? Within Mallinckrodt, we use DEA Manufacturing
registration for the work you do in "making" ARS compounds, customer is requesting the material on an Analytical Lab DEA
registration.
Our regulatory interpretation is that use of Analytical Lab DEA registration is reserved for an entity that actually performs tests
on the material (example:
Gateway Medical Research obtains material on Analytical Lab DEA registration to perform clinical trial work)

Please comment and thank you.

To: Harper, Karen; Mannino, Tony; Ratliff, Bill; Hunter, Dave; Pokorny, Camille M
Subject: RE: Request Advice on Customer Order for Material to Prepare Reference Standard



Karen,
 
Last year (2008) I dispensed 63.5 grams of Codeine Phosphate reference standard for the analytical support of our manufacturing of the bulk here in St. Louis and all the dosage forms in Hobart. So far this year (2009) I have dispensed 13 grams. Last year Sherryl Ruder shipped one order for 200 milligrams to an external customer and had no internal requests for Codeine Phosphate.
 
If I were to subdivide 1000 grams, that would last us almost 16 years at the rate that we used it in 2008. I must say that our reference standard use is increasing, so that 1000 grams may only last maybe 10 years. That still is a very long time to store a qualified reference. I also know that storing any controlled substance that long invites opportunities for diversion. So that generally should be discouraged.
 
We use the manufacturing registration for our operation. When it is shipped to Hobart it goes out under our manufacturing registration and is transferred to Hobart's Analytical registration via their form 222.
 
It seems to me that if the customer is "manufacturing" a reference standard, it should be received into their manufacturing registration. When it goes to their client to be used in the lab, that is when it should be transferred to analytical lab registration.
 
Ted

Sent: Friday, May 15, 2009 8:07 AM
To: Myrick, Ted
Cc: Pokorny, Camille M; Ratliff, Bill; Hunter, Dave
Subject: Request Advice on Customer Order for Material to Prepare Reference Standard



Ted
Controlled Substance Compliance and Security are working with Customer Service to determine the validity of a customer order for 1 kg of Codeine Phosphate, within the scope of our Suspicious Order Monitoring Program.
Customer states their intended use is to "prepare a reference standard for a client who will use the material for testing activities".
 
Our concerns are:
The 1 kg quantity seems too large, does this exceed the quantity of API we would normally use internally to prepare reference standards?
Does the intended use differ from the activity that you and Sherryl perform?  Within Mallinckrodt, we use DEA Manufacturing registration for the work you do in "making" ARS compounds, customer is requesting the material on an Analytical Lab DEA registration.
Our regulatory interpretation is that use of Analytical Lab DEA registration is reserved for an entity that actually performs tests on the material (example:
Gateway Medical Research obtains material on Analytical Lab DEA registration to perform clinical trial work)
 
Please comment and thank you.

To: Harper, Karen
Subject: Mallinckrodt Agrees To Pay $35 Million Settlement for Failure To Report Suspicious Orders of Pharmaceutical Drugs and for Recordkeeping Violations



 

 
{banner}

 


  FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE


 


  Contact: DEA Public Affairs


 


  (202) 307-7977


 


 


Press Release

 
 
 

Mallinckrodt Agrees To Pay $35 Million Settlement for Failure To Report Suspicious Orders of Pharmaceutical Drugs and for Recordkeeping Violations

 

JULY 11 - (Washington, D.C.)   Mallinckrodt LLC, a pharmaceutical manufacturer and one of the largest manufacturers of generic oxycodone, agreed to pay $35 million to settle allegations that it violated certain provisions of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) that are subject to civil penalties, Attorney General Jeff Sessions of the Justice Department and Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg of theDrug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced today.

 

This is the first settlement of its magnitude with a manufacturer of pharmaceuticals resolving nationwide claims that the company did not meet its obligations to detect and notify DEA of suspicious orders of controlled substances such as oxycodone, the abuse of which is part of the current opioid epidemic. These suspicious order monitoring requirements exist to prevent excessive sales of controlled substances, like oxycodone in Florida and elsewhere. The settlement also addressed violations in the company s manufacturing batch records at its plant in Hobart, New York. Both sets of alleged violations impact accountability for controlled substances, and the compliance terms going forward are designed to help protect against diversion of these substances at critical links in the controlled substance supply chain. 

 

 In the midst of one of the worst drug abuse crises in American history, the Department of Justice has the responsibility to ensure that our drug laws are being enforced and to protect the American people,  said Attorney General Sessions.  Part of that mission is holding drug manufacturers accountable for their actions. Mallinckrodt s actions and omissions formed a link in the chain of supply that resulted in millions of oxycodone pills being sold on the street.  Thanks to the hard work of our attorneys and law enforcement, Mallinckrodt has agreed to do everything they can to help us identify suspicious orders in the future. And as a result of today's settlement, we are sending a clear message to drug companies:  This Department of Justice will hold you accountable for your legal obligations, and we will enforce our laws. I believe that will prevent drug abuse, prevent new addictions from starting, and ultimately save lives. 

 

 Manufacturers and distributors have a crucial responsibility to ensure that controlled substances do not get into the wrong hands,  said DEA Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg.  When they violate their legal obligations, we will hold them accountable. 

 

The government alleged that Mallinckrodt failed to design and implement an effective system to detect and report  suspicious orders  for controlled substances   orders that are unusual in their frequency, size, or other patterns. From 2008 until 2011, the U.S. alleged, Mallinckrodt supplied distributors, and the distributors then supplied various U.S. pharmacies and pain clinics, an increasingly excessive quantity of oxycodone pills without notifying DEA of these suspicious orders. Through its investigation, the government learned that manufacturers of pharmaceuticals offer discounts, known as  chargebacks,  based on sales to certain downstream customers.  Distributors provide information on the downstream customer purchases to obtain the discount.  The groundbreaking nature of the settlement involves requiring a manufacturer to utilize chargeback and similar data to monitor and report to DEA suspicious sales of its oxycodone at the next level in the supply chain, typically sales from distributors to independent and small chain pharmacy and pain clinic customers.

   

The government also alleged that Mallinckrodt violated record keeping requirements at its manufacturing facility in upstate New York. Among other things, these violations created discrepancies between the actual number of tablets manufactured in a batch and the number of tablets Mallinckrodt reported on its records. Accurate reconciliation of records at the manufacturing stage is a critical first step in ensuring that controlled substances are accounted for properly through the supply chain.

 

In addition to the significant monetary penalty, this settlement includes a groundbreaking parallel agreement with the DEA, as a result of which the company will analyze data it collects on orders from customers down the supply chain to identify suspicious sales. The resolution advances the DEA s position that controlled substance manufacturers need to go beyond  know your customer  to use otherwise available company data to  know your customer s customer  to protect these potentially dangerous pharmaceuticals from getting into the wrong hands. DEA s Memorandum of Agreement with Mallinckrodt also sets forth specific procedures it will undertake to ensure the accuracy of batch records and protect loss of raw product in the manufacturing process.

 

By entering into these agreements, elements of which Mallinckrodt is already implementing, the company is becoming part of the solution to this public health epidemic.

 

This lengthy investigation was led by DEA s Detroit Field Division on the suspicious order issues and the New York Field Division on the manufacturing record keeping issues.

 

U.S. Attorneys  Offices for the Eastern District of Michigan and the Northern District of New York, along with DEA Office of Chief Counsel and Diversion Control Division, led the civil settlement negotiations. The Criminal Division s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Section (NDDS) also coordinated and assisted in negotiating the settlement.

MALLINCKRODT AGREES TO PAY RECORD $35 MILLION SETTLEMENT FOR FAILURE TO REPORT SUSPICIOUS ORDERS OF PHARMACEUTICAL DRUGS AND FOR RECORDKEEPING VIOLATIONS

 

WASHINGTON – Mallinckrodt LLC, a pharmaceutical manufacturer and one of the largest manufacturers of generic oxycodone, agreed to pay $35 million to settle allegations that it violated certain provisions of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) that are subject to civil penalties, Attorney General Jeff Sessions of the Justice Department and Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced today.

 

This is the first settlement of its magnitude with a manufacturer of pharmaceuticals resolving nationwide claims that the company did not meet its obligations to detect and notify DEA of suspicious orders of controlled substances such as oxycodone, the abuse of which is part of the current opioid epidemic. These suspicious order monitoring requirements exist to prevent excessive sales of controlled substances, like oxycodone in Florida and elsewhere. The settlement also addressed violations in the company’s manufacturing batch records at its plant in Hobart, New York. Both sets of alleged violations impact accountability for controlled substances, and the compliance terms going forward are designed to help protect against diversion of these substances at critical links in the controlled substance supply chain.

 

            “In the midst of one of the worst drug abuse crises in American history, the Department of Justice has the responsibility to ensure that our drug laws are being enforced and to protect the American people,” said Attorney General Sessions. “Part of that mission is holding drug manufacturers accountable for their actions. Mallinckrodt’s actions and omissions formed a link in the chain of supply that resulted in millions of oxycodone pills being sold on the street.  Thanks to the hard work of our attorneys and law enforcement, Mallinckrodt has agreed to do everything they can to help us identify suspicious orders in the future. And as a result of today's settlement, we are sending a clear message to drug companies: this Department of Justice will hold you accountable for your legal obligations and we will enforce our laws. I believe that will prevent drug abuse, prevent new addictions from starting, and ultimately save lives.”

 

“Manufacturers and distributors have a crucial responsibility to ensure that controlled substances do not get into the wrong hands,” said DEA Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg. “When they violate their legal obligations, we will hold them accountable.”

 

The government alleged that Mallinckrodt failed to design and implement an effective system to detect and report “suspicious orders” for controlled substances – orders that are unusual in their frequency, size, or other patterns. From 2008 until 2011, the U.S. alleged, Mallinckrodt supplied distributors, and the distributors then supplied various U.S. pharmacies and pain clinics, an increasingly excessive quantity of oxycodone pills without notifying DEA of these suspicious orders. Through its investigation, the government learned that manufacturers of pharmaceuticals offer discounts, known as “chargebacks,” based on sales to certain downstream customers.  Distributors provide information on the downstream customer purchases to obtain the discount.  The groundbreaking nature of the settlement involves requiring a manufacturer to utilize chargeback and similar data to monitor and report to DEA suspicious sales of its oxycodone at the next level in the supply chain, typically sales from distributors to independent and small chain pharmacy and pain clinic customers.

 

The government also alleged that Mallinckrodt violated record keeping requirements at its manufacturing facility in upstate New York. Among other things, these violations created discrepancies between the actual number of tablets manufactured in a batch and the number of tablets Mallinckrodt reported on its records. Accurate reconciliation of records at the manufacturing stage is a critical first step in ensuring that controlled substances are accounted for properly through the supply chain.

 

In addition to the significant monetary penalty, this settlement includes a groundbreaking parallel agreement with the DEA, as a result of which the company will analyze data it collects on orders from customers down the supply chain to identify suspicious sales. The resolution advances the DEA’s position that controlled substance manufacturers need to go beyond “know your customer” to use otherwise available company data to “know your customer’s customer” to protect these potentially dangerous pharmaceuticals from getting into the wrong hands. DEA’s Memorandum of Agreement with Mallinckrodt also sets forth specific procedures it will undertake to ensure the accuracy of batch records and protect loss of raw product in the manufacturing process.

 

By entering into these agreements, elements of which Mallinckrodt is already implementing, the company is becoming part of the solution to this public health epidemic.

 

This lengthy investigation was led by DEA’s Detroit Field Division on the suspicious order issues and the New York Field Division on the manufacturing record keeping issues.

 

U.S. Attorneys’ Offices for the Eastern District of Michigan and the Northern District of New York, along with DEA Office of Chief Counsel and Diversion Control Division, led the civil settlement negotiations. The Criminal Division’s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Section (NDDS) also coordinated and assisted in negotiating the settlement.

Feds raid a pair of pain clinics in city

By KATE HOWARD
Publication: Florida Times-Union (Jacksonville)
Date: {LexisNexis: 20100730}Friday, July 30 2010





{ID_Web_horizontal_sml_white}{ID_Web_horizontal_sml_white}



You are viewing page 1
 




Nearly all of the patients at a North Jacksonville pain clinic raided Thursday were prescribed the same remedy: the highly addictive pain killer oxycodone, the anti-anxiety medicine Xanax and a muscle relaxer called Soma. And the unassuming clinic, tucked away in a West 48th Street strip mall, did a staggering business.

Florida Department of Health records show that 611,000 oxycodone pills were dispensed by Duval Wellness Center in April and May alone.

The clinic and its owner, 78-year-old osteopathic physician Donald W. Hall, were issued a cease and desist order Wednesday by the health department.

About 10 a.m. Thursday, FBI and DEA agents and Jacksonville police burst into the clinic and First Coast Pain and Urgent Care on Normandy Boulevard, also owned by Hall.

No charges have been brought and no arrests were made in the months-old investigation, federal officials said.

The targeted businesses are among a growing number of pain management clinics registered in Jacksonville - with the number jumping from less than 50 in March to about 60 today.

"Pill mills" have been largely viewed as a South Florida problem. But as crackdowns and moratoriums on the pain clinics grew more intense in Broward County and nearby towns, many clinic owners opened shop farther north.

Steve Cole, spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office, said the Jacksonville investigation focused on the two clinics.

"We've had similar investigations like this throughout the Middle District of Florida, looking into pain clinics that may be dispensing prescription drugs illegally," he said. "Florida has had a problem with that. So we obviously are looking in all the major cities to see if and where there are problems."

FBI spokesman Jeff Westcott said he couldn't reveal any details about the investigation or the dozen search warrants executed Thursday.

About 99 percent of the 8,000 prescriptions issued by Duval Wellness in April and May were identical: oxycodone, Xanax and Soma, according to the health department. The state inspected the facility's medical records in early June and also found that they had been operating as a pain clinic without state authorization.

Hall, who has been practicing medicine for 40 years, couldn't be reached for comment.

A neighbor of Hall's, Pat Collins, said she saw lots of police activity at Hall's Lake City home early Thursday.

"He lives down the street and the police have been at his house all morning," Collins said.

Hall was disciplined by the state medical board once, in 1985, for dispensing dextroamphetamines for weight loss even though it wasn't approved for that use. He was reprimanded and ordered to pay a $1,000 fine.

Duval Wellness, at North Main and West 48th, opened in March but quickly became a mecca for out-of-state people seeking pain pills. Times-Union reporters who visited the location multiple times since April saw dozens of cars from Tennessee, Kentucky, Ohio and other states routinely lining the parking lot. Armed security guards patrolled the entrance to the clinic.

Children and parents crossed paths with the customers on a daily basis. A day care is located across the plaza from the clinic, and North Shore Elementary School is a short walk away.

At First Coast Pain and Urgent Care, the strip center parking lot was also filled with out-of-state plates, with people often waiting in their cars with the windows down until they were called in for their appointment.

As DEA agents carried out boxes filled with files Thursday, a man who identified himself as a patient walked up with his 2 p.m. appointment card to see what was going on.

He refused to give his name but said he thought the clinic with the blacked-out windows was on the up-and-up. He said he was a patient at S&P Medical in 2007, when the Jacksonville clinic was closed for illegally prescribing narcotics to patients without medical need.

He said he thought those doctors were over-prescribing but that the doctors at First Coast Pain required all his medical records and counseled him about the addictive nature of Roxicodone, the fast-acting pain killer he was prescribed.

"It looked to me like they were running legit," he said.

First Coast Pain has not been issued a closure order from the state, and Department of Health officials present during the raid Thursday were only gathering information, the agency said.

Records show that First Coast Pain is registered with the state as a pain clinic.

Times-Union writer Bridget Murphy contributed to this report.

Subject: RE: EDI 867 Transmissions - Cardinal request 

All, 

Here is my understanding of the requirements of TIRF REMS: 

a) The new requirements go into effect March 12, 2012. 

b) McKesson was hired to create a database showing which entities (distributors, retailers, 
physicians, patients) have completed the requirements to be eligible to handle / write scripts, etc for 
the Fentanyl oral product. (McKesson will bill us for this service). 

c) As of that date, Mallinckrodt's responsibility will be to ensure any customer ordering the product 
directly from us has met the requirements to distribute the product. Therefore, we must access the 
website and verify the customer's eligibility prior to shipping the product. 

d) The distributor (and retailer) must then verify (again by accessing the website) their customer's 
eligibility before forwarding the product. 

e) There does not appear to be any requirement to capture number of units shipped to any location. 
Therefore, there would be no need for us to capture EDI 867 (sales tracings) data from any distributor. 
(Note: an EDI 867 is reporting from a wholesaler / distributor providing all units they shipped to all 
customers, regardless of price charged. Currently, Pharma does not include this data in our systems, 
however, other business units do include it. If a decision was made to include within the Pharma data, 
several downstream implications would need to be considered, including, sales comp, government reporting 
and Suspicious order Monitoring), not to mention the incremental customers that would be required to be 
added). 

If I have the facts correct above, can Kathy Weiss or Debbie Digby reach out to Cardinal and ask why they 
believe we need to receive the EDI 867? 

Thanks, 
Carol

News Release [printer-friendly version]
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
June 10, 2011
Contact: Rich Isaacson
Number: (313) 234-4310
Cincinnati Pharmaceutical Supplier's DEA License Suspended
Keysource Medical distributed 48 million doses of oxycodone products to Florida pharm acies
JUN 10 - DETROIT- Robert L. Corso, Special Agent in Charge of the Detroit Field Division, Drug  Enforcement
Administration (DEA) announced today the immediate suspension of the federal controlled substance Registration of
Keysource Medical, a wholesale supplier of pharmaceuticals.
Keysource Medical, based in Cincinnati, Ohio, has been the subject of a DEA investigation that alleges the company was
selling large quantities of controlled substances to pharmacies, primarily in Florida. The investigation has revealed that
several of Keysource Medical's largest purchasers of oxycodone were engaged in schemes to dispense controlled
substances based on prescriptions that were written for other than legitimate medical  purposes. The investigation
revealed that Keystone Medical distributed approximately 48 million dosage units of oxycodone products to customers in
Florida over a two year time between November of 2008 and November of 2010.
 Pharmaceutical companies have a responsibility to ensure that the drugs they sell don't end up in the hands of drug
traffickers or businesses that are conducting their business illegally,  said Corso.  Prescription drug abuse in Florida,
southern Ohio and northern Kentucky has risen to epidemic proportions, and Keysource Medical, should have known
based on the large, frequent quantities, that their customers were diverting oxycodone into arenas that were not
legitimate. This action is another reminder that the DEA is working hard to hold accountable those companies who
choose to operate outside the law.
DEA's action suspends Keysource Medical's DEA Certificate of Registration in accordance with an Immediate
Suspension Order and pursuant to Sections 303 and 304 of the Controlled Substances Act, Title 21, Sections 823 and
824. The DEA's investigation of Keysource Medical has determined that the continued registration of this company
constitutes an imminent danger to public health and safety.
Keysource Medical received written notice of the factual and legal basis for this action. In addition, Keysource Medical
will be given an opportunity for an administrative hearing within the next 60 days. After the hearing, the DEA Deputy
Administrator will make a final decision on whether Keysource Medical's registration should be permanently revoked.
This decision will be published in the Federal Register.
Oxycodone is the generic name of an addictive prescription painkiller that is classified under federal narcotics laws as a
Schedule II controlled substance. Oxycodone is typically legally prescribed to combat  acute, severe pain for legitimate
medical purposes.

DEA Announces “Groundbreaking” Guidance that is Inconsistent with the Settlement they are Announcing – Time at Last for Rulemaking?

 

By John A. Gilbert, Jr. –

On July 11, 2017, the Department of Justice and the Drug Enforcement Administration (“DEA”) announced that Mallinckrodt LLC, a pharmaceutical manufacturer, agreed to pay $35 million to settle allegations related to the adequacy of its efforts to detect and inform DEA of suspicious orders of controlled substances.  Although DEA has reached similar settlements with distributors and pharmacy chains (see, e.g., here), this is the first settlement of its kind with an opioid manufacturer.  DOJ’s press release states that the settlement reflects manufacturers’ obligation to monitor orders not only from their own customers, but also between distributors and pharmacies and clinics downstream in the distribution chain.  However, this statement appears  inconsistent with the language in the settlement document, marks a stark shift in the prevailing understanding of manufacturers’ suspicious order monitoring obligations and raises serious questions about the legal basis and workability of such a requirement.

For years, DEA has been criticized for failure to provide guidance on the suspicious order monitoring regulation, 21 C.F.R. § 1301.74(b).  The language in that section has remained unchanged since its enactment in 1971 and while DEA issued informal guidance letters to certain industry groups in 2006, 2007 and 2012,  DEA’s interpretation of that regulation has evolved significantly beyond that guidance.  More important, a fundamental deficiency in the regulation is that it fails to recognize the differences between manufacturers and distributors, including the level of data available to each concerning sales between distributors and pharmacies.  Thus, the lack of a clear regulation has continued to hinder industry’s ability to meet DEA’s expectations.

Unfortunately for industry, in the last several years, DEA has set forth its evolving view of the regulation primarily in presentations at conferences, through Memoranda of Agreement (“MOAs”) related to enforcement actions and in the Southwood and, more recently, the Masters decisions. (see, e.g., here and here).  While this approach has allowed DEA to avoid the notice and comment rulemaking requirement under the Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”), it has also left industry with little clarity about their obligations around the reporting of suspicious orders. A critical element of notice and comment rulemaking is for an agency to solicit important industry input on the impact of potential rulemaking, with the ultimate goal being effective and clear regulations.  Such clarity would result in a more secure supply chain for controlled substances, which would better serve the public interest as the U.S. continues to struggle with the issue of opioid diversion and abuse.

The press release concerning the Mallinckrodt settlement, which purported to set out “groundbreaking” new rules, is another example of DEA establishing a new standard while avoiding notice and comment rulemaking. 

The problem revolves around DEA’s discussion of chargebacks (which are a common pharmaceutical pricing feature), for the first time, and a critical discrepancy between the language set forth in the government’s press release and the obligation outlined in the MOA with Mallinckrodt.  (In general, a chargeback is a payment made by a manufacturer to a distributor to make the distributor whole when it sells the manufacturer’s product at a price below a specified rate. After a distributor sells a manufacturer’s product to the pharmacy, for example, it requests a chargeback from the manufacturer and to support that request for payment, the distributor identifies the product, volume and the pharmacy to which it sold the product.) In its press release, the government stated that, “[t]he groundbreaking nature of the settlement involves requiring a manufacturer to utilize chargeback and similar data to monitor and report to DEA suspicious sales of its oxycodone at the next level in the supply chain, typically sales from distributors to independent and small chain pharmacy and pain clinic customers.” (emphasis added). This appears to set forth DEA’s position that manufacturers must review chargebacks and report the underlying sales from the distributor to downstream pharmacies as suspicious orders.

However, we have reviewed Mallinckrodt’s MOA and it does not require reporting downstream transactions as suspicious orders.  Rather, the MOA provides that Mallinckrodt review chargeback data and alert DEA of pharmacies (not orders) that may be concerning.   The clear focus of the language is a reporting of pharmacies as a condition of the MOA, not the reporting of chargebacks as suspicious orders under 21 CFR 1301.74(b). Note, as of this writing, the MOA has not been posted to the government’s websites.

As an initial matter, it is not clear that DEA can create such a new requirement by announcing it in a press release. First, nothing in the language of 21 C.F.R. § 1301.74(b) suggests that a manufacturer must review orders between two downstream third parties and report them as suspicious. Second, we could find no prior public statement from DEA that a manufacturer must report such third party transactions as suspicious under 21 C.F.R. § 1301.74(b). Finally, if this really is “groundbreaking” – to use the government’s own word – surely such a change should warrant notice and comment rulemaking.

Moreover, there is no indication manufacturers’ attempts to monitor downstream transactions would be productive. It appears instead that manufacturers will be expected to second guess distributors’ decisions to fill orders from pharmacies (well after those sales have been completed), even though the manufacturers have far less information than the distributors have about those pharmacies. Distributors often have longstanding relationships with their pharmacy customers and sophisticated monitoring programs to evaluate pharmacy orders.  In contrast, a manufacturer can only see – after the fact – the manufacturer’s products a distributor sells to a pharmacy and for which the distributor submits a chargeback request. With such limited visibility, a simple and perfectly legitimate switch by a pharmacy from one manufacturer’s product to another’s, for example, could look like a suspicious “increase” in the distributor’s sales to that pharmacy. 

DEA’s position raises many additional practical questions. If the manufacturer and distributor disagree about which orders are suspicious, will DEA hold manufacturers’ reports of suspicious orders against the distributor, even if the distributor is better positioned to assess those orders?  How many orders that appear “suspicious” to a manufacturer can be filled by a distributor before the manufacturer must stop selling to that distributor?  And how should a manufacturer structure a program designed to monitor distributor sales to tens of thousands of pharmacies with which the manufacturer has no contact?

Manufacturers will likely be struggling with these issues for years to come. That ongoing confusion and its negative impact on the security of the supply chain emphasizes, once again, the need for DEA to make clear the obligations of manufacturers through notice and comment rulemaking on this critical issue, especially as the country continues to struggle with the problem of opioid diversion and abuse.

		From: Spaulding, Eileen L.
		Sent: March 12, 2009 1:16 PM
		To: 'White, Heather R.'
		Subject: Suspicious Order Monitoring Processes


		Hi Heather,

		I just wanted to take a moment and let you know of some situations that we have had recently with one of our customers, AmerisourceBergen in Orlando FL.  Due to the shortage of Oxycodone in the market, Mallinckrodt is being extra sensitive to possible diversion issues that may occur.

		Within the past week AmerisourceBergen Orlando has contacted us twice regarding suspicious orders that they have received regarding Oxycodone shipments.  Attached are e-mails for your review of us being notified by AmerisourceBergen Orlando that they have received as suspicious call about an upcoming Oxycodone shipment and what we are doing to ensure the safety and security of our shipments when we are made aware of such a circumstance.

		Basically as part of our suspicious order monitoring process when notified by the customer that they have an indication of a possible diversion issue, we are "walking" the shipment through the transportation system and monitoring it through senior FedEx security at each touch point to ensure adequate delivery to our customer.

		Notes:  On the 1st e-mail last dated 3/5/09 confirming receipt of shipment where the customer says "not the Oxycodone 30", we did not ship Oxycodone 30 as it is currently backordered, only the Oxycodone/Acetaminophen 5/325mg Tablets were shipped.  On the 2nd e-mail originally dated 3/6/09 in which AmerisourceBergen is stating that a consumer advised them that they obtained their phone number from the Manufacturer, Mallinckrodt never supplies any customer information to anyone over the phone (other than law enforcement inquiries regulated through our Legal Department).

		This is just an FYI for you to know what Mallinckrodt is doing on our end of the supply chain.

		Regards,

Subject: DEA Dialog 07/20/10 - Suspicious Order Monitoring and Harvard Drug License Suspension

<< File: Harvard Drug DEA License Suspension 06_15_10.doc >>
Tom,

Per the previous communication below, Mallinckrodt customer Harvard Drug's CII distribution license for their Livonia, MI,
location was suspended last month (DEA press release attached).
Based upon the parameters established within our Suspicious Order Monitoring system, Harvard had not met or
exceeded the excessive quantity calculation for Oxycodone sales.

Yesterday, DEA visited the St. Louis Site at our request to inspect Building 5 Annex for the OTFC project expansion.
The DEA Diversion Group Supervisor accompanied two Diversion Investigators for the visit and the Supervisor requested
an impromptu meeting after the Building 5 inspection.

Meeting Notes

The meeting began with an assurance that this information is an FYI to Mallinckrodt and not an adverse action.

The Diversion Group Supervisor explained that he attended a DEA training for Diversion Unit personnel last week in


   Washington, DC. Agenda for the meeting included an array of topics including ARCOS, Quota, DEA222 Forms, and
Suspicious Order Monitoring.
During the Suspicious Order Monitoring segment, the DEA suspension of Harvard Drug CII distribution license was
reviewed as a current event. Mallinckrodt was named within the forum as a supplier of  Harvard Drug. Although the
statement was qualified in that Harvard had multiple suppliers, Mallinckrodt was the only supplier company named.
Within that session, DEA announced a "new direction" initiative whereby enforcement action will be aimed at all entities
within the supply chain, including manufacturing registrants. The expectation is becoming that suppliers have not only an
obligation to know their customers but an additional responsibility to know their customers. DEA now has information that
indicates, as enforcement activity directed at pain clinics in Florida as it relates to the diversion of Oxycodone 15 and 30
mg is escalated; the pain clinics are re-establishing their businesses in Georgia, Ohio, Texas.

I spoke to DEA about the attributes of our Suspicious Order Monitoring Program and our ongoing commitment to comply
with the regulations. Further, I indicated that we have visits scheduled within the next two weeks with two Mallinckrodt
Wholesaler/Distributor customers to collaborate on Suspicious Order Monitoring processes and systems.

At the conclusion of the brief meeting (1/2 hour in duration), DEA again assured me that Mallinckrodt is not being
targeted for DEA action but the information being provided for us to take under advisement.

Action Plan

Yesterday afternoon, I attended a Suspicious Order Monitoring meeting I had previously scheduled with Marketing,
Trade Relations, and Customer Service. The team believes the Suspicious Order Monitoring Program can be further
enhanced by analyzing chargeback data for indirect customers and direct sales information available within existing
systems. Use of various analytics will provide a more in-depth review of controlled substance sales by market segment,
etc., that can be used to supplement the existing program.

A meeting will be scheduled ASAP next week to reconvene and expand the Suspicious Order Monitoring Team. The
group will be led by Controlled Substance Compliance and include representatives from  Security, Marketing, Trade
Relations, Customer Service, Customer Data Integrity, Medical Affairs/REMS.

===========
I will continue to keep you informed.

Thank you,

Karen Harper
Mallinckrodt/Covidien Pharmaceuticals
Senior Manager, Controlled Substance Compliance
Global Logistics Group

Subject: Oxycodone Sales in Florida - Summary

As many of you have probably heard, Harvard Drug's license to handle controlled substances was
suspended this week. The predominate reason for the suspension was the sale of Oxycodone in the
state of Florida. Please see the attached article for additional information and details.

http://www.freep.com/article/20100616/NEWS06/6160364/1322/DEA-suspends-license-
of-Livonia-distributor

Additionally, it came to our attention that Sunrise Wholesaler's DEA license was suspended pending further
investigation. Although the official reason for the suspension has not been named, we  are under the
impression that it is also due to the sale of Oxycodone in the state of Florida.

The two wholesaler/distributor license suspensions led us to do a more in-depth analysis of Covidien's
Oxycodone sales in the state of Florida. We specifically focused on doctors' offices and pain clinics. It
appears that Harvard and Sunrise were the dominate players in this market with over 50% of their total
sales coming from this market. HD Smith, Keysource and McKesson Onestop are next with  only 3% to their
total sales coming from doctors' offices and pain clinics:

<< OLE Object: Picture (Metafile) >>

Karen Harper and team (internal Covidien investigators) will be working closely with the DEA regarding their
investigation of the distribution of Oxycodone in Florida and we will keep you apprised of further happenings.

A special thanks goes out to Vic Borelli, who was instrumental in notifying us of the  Harvard situation and
providing us with continuous news updates. Thank you for bringing to our attention.

If anyone has additional questions regarding their specific account, please fee free to reach out to me or to

Press Release
 
 
  MCKESSON AGREES TO PAY RECORD $150 MILLION SETTLEMENT FOR FAILURE TO REPORT SUSPICIOUS ORDERS OF PHARMACEUTICAL DRUGS
 
JAN 17 - (Washington, DC) – McKesson Corporation (McKesson), one of the nation’s largest distributors of pharmaceutical drugs, agreed to pay a record $150 million civil penalty for alleged violations of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA), the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced today.
 
The nationwide settlement requires McKesson to suspend sales of controlled substances from distribution centers in Colorado, Ohio, Michigan and Florida for multiple years. The staged suspensions are among the most severe sanctions ever agreed to by a DEA-registered distributor. The settlement also imposes new and enhanced compliance obligations on McKesson’s distribution system.
 
In 2008, McKesson agreed to a $13.25 million civil penalty and administrative agreement for similar violations. In this case, the government alleged again that McKesson failed to design and implement an effective system to detect and report “suspicious orders” for controlled substances distributed to its independent and small chain pharmacy customers– i.e. orders that are unusual in their frequency, size, or other patterns. From 2008 until 2013, McKesson supplied various U.S. pharmacies an increasing amount of oxycodone and hydrocodone pills, frequently misused products that are part of the current opioid epidemic.
 
The government’s investigation developed evidence that even after designing a compliance program after the 2008 settlement, McKesson did not fully implement or adhere to its own program. In Colorado, for example, McKesson processed more than 1.6 million orders for controlled substances from June 2008 through May 2013, but reported just 16 orders as suspicious, all connected to one instance related to a recently terminated customer. 
 
"This groundbreaking resolution is tough and appropriate and underscores our commitment to hold accountable all DEA registrants, including those who distribute controlled substances," said DEA Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg.  "DEA is committed to fighting the opioid epidemic with all of the tools at our disposal."
 
In addition to the monetary penalties and suspensions, the government and McKesson agreed to enhanced compliance terms for the next five years. Among other things, McKesson has agreed to specific, rigorous staffing and organizational improvements; periodic auditing; and stipulated financial penalties for failing to adhere to the compliance terms. Critically, the settlement will require McKesson to engage an independent monitor to assess compliance – the first independent monitor of its kind in a CSA civil penalty settlement.
 
This was a multi-district investigation that involved the following DEA Field Divisions:  Boston Field Division, Chicago Field Division, Denver Field Division, Detroit Field Division, Miami Field Division, New Jersey Field Division, San Francisco Field Division, St. Louis Field Division, and Washington Division Office. The following U.S. Attorneys’ Offices participated in the case: Central District of California, Eastern District of California, District of Colorado, Middle District of Florida, Eastern District of Kentucky, Northern District of Illinois, District of Massachusetts, Eastern District of Michigan, District of Nebraska, District of New Jersey, Northern District of West Virginia, and Western District of Wisconsin.
 
U.S. Attorneys’ Offices for the District of Colorado and the Northern District of West Virginia, along with DEA’s Office of Chief Counsel and its Diversion Control Division, led the civil settlement negotiations.  DEA’s Denver, Detroit and Miami Field Divisions and its Washington Division Office led the administrative and civil investigation. The U.S. Department of Justice Criminal Division’s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Section (NDDS) also coordinated and assisted in negotiating certain portions of the settlement. Assistant United States Attorneys Amanda Rocque (Colorado) and Alan McGonigal (NDWV) represented the United States in the civil penalty investigations and negotiations.  Associate Chief Counsel Lee Reeves and Senior Attorneys Dedra Curteman, Dana Hill and Krista Tongring represented DEA in the investigations and negotiations. Trial Attorneys Harry Matz and Kirtland Marsh were involved for NDDS.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
FRIDAY, MAY 2, 2008
WWW.USDOJ.GOV
OPA
(202) 514-2007
TDD (202) 514-1888
McKesson Corporation Agrees to Pay More than $13 Million to Settle Claims
that it Failed to Report Suspicious Sales of Prescription Medications
WASHINGTON - McKesson Corp., one of the nation's largest distributors of
pharmaceutical drugs, has agreed to settle allegations that it violated
federal reporting provisions relating to its handling of certain
prescription medications regulated by the Drug Enforcement Administration
(DEA).  Under the agreement between the company and six U.S. Attorney's
Offices, McKesson has agreed to pay $13,250,000 in civil penalties for
alleged violations of its obligations under the Controlled Substances
Act.
McKesson Corp., which operates 30 DEA-registered distribution facilities,
failed to report to DEA suspicious sales of controlled substance
pharmaceuticals it made to pharmacies that filled orders from illegal
"Internet pharmacies" that sell drugs online to customers who do not have
a legal prescription. McKesson also failed to report suspicious orders of
controlled substances that it received from other pharmacies and clinics
even though the orders were unusually large. Every DEA registrant is
required to report to DEA any suspicious orders or the theft or
significant loss of controlled substances.
"The abuse of prescription medications is a significant and growing
problem, and there is an erroneous perception among our youth that the
recreational use of these powerful medications is somehow safer than the
abuse of illegal drugs such as cocaine, meth, and heroin," said Deputy
Attorney General Mark Filip. "Today's settlement makes clear that the
Department of Justice is committed to doing its part to curtail illegal
access to these dangerous drugs."
Three McKesson distribution centers received and filled hundreds of
suspicious orders placed by pharmacies participating in illicit Internet
schemes, but failed to report the orders to DEA. They did so even after a
Sept.1, 2005, meeting at which DEA officials met with and warned McKesson
officials about excessive sales of their products to pharmacies filling
illegal online prescriptions. The pharmacies filled purported online
"prescriptions" for hydrocodone (contained in drugs such as Vicodin), but
the prescriptions were issued outside the normal course of professional
practice and not for a legitimate medical purpose. The United States
Attorneys allege that the orders that McKesson received from these
pharmacies were unusually large, unusually frequent, and/or deviated
substantially from the normal pattern. As a result, millions of dosage
units of controlled substances were diverted from legitimate channels of
distribution.
"By failing to report suspicious orders for controlled substances that it
received from rogue Internet pharmacies, the McKesson Corporation fueled
the explosive prescription drug abuse problem we have in this country,"
said DEA Acting Administrator Michele M. Leonhart. "This civil penalty
demonstrates the strong action DEA is taking to cut off the drug supply to
pharmacies engaged in Internet diversion schemes."
The Controlled Substances Act is the primary federal law regulating the
flow of controlled substances into the marketplace for medical purposes. 
Among other requirements, the Act requires that distributors register with
DEA to sell controlled substances to retail pharmacies and report to DEA
suspicious orders or the theft or significant loss of controlled
substances.  The Act authorizes the imposition of up to a $10,000 civil
penalty for each violation of the reporting requirement.
       The civil penalty will be collected by the U.S. Attorney's Office
in each of the following districts, in the amounts indicated:
Middle District of Florida $7,456,000 District of Maryland $2,000,000
District of Colorado $1,000,000 Southern District of Texas $2,000,000
District of Utah $ 544,000 Eastern District of California $ 250,000
The settlement agreement is neither an admission of liability by McKesson
nor a concession by the United States that its claims are not well
founded.

This case was handled by trial attorneys from the following U.S.
Attorneys' Offices: Middle District of Florida, District of Maryland,
District of Colorado, Southern District of Texas, District of Utah and
Eastern District of California. Additional assistance was provided by the
Criminal Division?s Narcotics and Dangerous Drug Section. Investigatory
assistance was provided by the DEA.

Press Release
	
  
MCKESSON AGREES TO PAY RECORD $150 MILLION SETTLEMENT FOR FAILURE TO REPORT SUSPICIOUS ORDERS OF PHARMACEUTICAL DRUGS
 
JAN 17 - (Washington, DC)   McKesson Corporation (McKesson), one of the nation s largest distributors of pharmaceutical drugs, agreed to pay a record $150 million civil penalty for alleged violations of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA), the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced today.
 
The nationwide settlement requires McKesson to suspend sales of controlled substances from distribution centers in Colorado, Ohio, Michigan and Florida for multiple years. The staged suspensions are among the most severe sanctions ever agreed to by a DEA-registered distributor. The settlement also imposes new and enhanced compliance obligations on McKesson s distribution system.
 
In 2008, McKesson agreed to a $13.25 million civil penalty and administrative agreement for similar violations. In this case, the government alleged again that McKesson failed to design and implement an effective system to detect and report  suspicious orders  for controlled substances distributed to its independent and small chain pharmacy customers  i.e. orders that are unusual in their frequency, size, or other patterns. From 2008 until 2013, McKesson supplied various U.S. pharmacies an increasing amount of oxycodone and hydrocodone pills, frequently misused products that are part of the current opioid epidemic.
 
The government s investigation developed evidence that even after designing a compliance program after the 2008 settlement, McKesson did not fully implement or adhere to its own program. In Colorado, for example, McKesson processed more than 1.6 million orders for controlled substances from June 2008 through May 2013, but reported just 16 orders as suspicious, all connected to one instance related to a recently terminated customer. 
 
"This groundbreaking resolution is tough and appropriate and underscores our commitment to hold accountable all DEA registrants, including those who distribute controlled substances," said DEA Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg.  "DEA is committed to fighting the opioid epidemic with all of the tools at our disposal."
 
In addition to the monetary penalties and suspensions, the government and McKesson agreed to enhanced compliance terms for the next five years. Among other things, McKesson has agreed to specific, rigorous staffing and organizational improvements; periodic auditing; and stipulated financial penalties for failing to adhere to the compliance terms. Critically, the settlement will require McKesson to engage an independent monitor to assess compliance   the first independent monitor of its kind in a CSA civil penalty settlement.
 
This was a multi-district investigation that involved the following DEA Field Divisions:  Boston Field Division, Chicago Field Division, Denver Field Division, Detroit Field Division, Miami Field Division, New Jersey Field Division, San Francisco Field Division, St. Louis Field Division, and Washington Division Office. The following U.S. Attorneys  Offices participated in the case: Central District of California, Eastern District of California, District of Colorado, Middle District of Florida, Eastern District of Kentucky, Northern District of Illinois, District of Massachusetts, Eastern District of Michigan, District of Nebraska, District of New Jersey, Northern District of West Virginia, and Western District of Wisconsin.
 
U.S. Attorneys  Offices for the District of Colorado and the Northern District of West Virginia, along with DEA s Office of Chief Counsel and its Diversion Control Division, led the civil settlement negotiations.  DEA s Denver, Detroit and Miami Field Divisions and its Washington Division Office led the administrative and civil investigation. The U.S. Department of Justice Criminal Division s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Section (NDDS) also coordinated and assisted in negotiating certain portions of the settlement. Assistant United States Attorneys Amanda Rocque (Colorado) and Alan McGonigal (NDWV) represented the United States in the civil penalty investigations and negotiations.  Associate Chief Counsel Lee Reeves and Senior Attorneys Dedra Curteman, Dana Hill and Krista Tongring represented DEA in the investigations and negotiations. Trial Attorneys Harry Matz and Kirtland Marsh were involved for NDDS.

From: HDMA Weekly Digest <digest@hdmanet.org>

{HDMA Weekly Digest: A Newsletter for HDMA Members} 
{A Newsletter for HDMA Members} August 13, 2013 
  

 
   
In This Issue   
  Kerlikowske to Leave ONDCP, Nominated as Commissioner of Customs and Border Protection

 CMS Releases Responses to FAQ on the Open Payments Act and Holds Conference Call for Physicians 

   Distribution Center Challenge Update: AmerisourceBergen Hosts Alabama State Senator Jimmy Holley (R-31)

 {corner}  
{divider}

Kerlikowske to Leave ONDCP, Nominated as Commissioner of Customs and Border Protection

President Obama recently nominated the current director of the Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP), R. Gil Kerlikowske, as Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection. If he is confirmed by the Senate, President Obama will nominate a new director of the ONDCP, who will coordinate drug-control activities and related funding across the federal government.

For more information, contact Allison Tuszynski.
{top of page}

Reminder: DEA Hosting October Conference for Distributors

As reported in last week's Weekly Digest, the DEA is hosting a Distributor Conference on October 22 at the Gaylord National Resort and Convention Center in National Harbor, Md. Due to space limitations, this DEA-organized conference invites two representatives from each distributor registrant to attend on a first-come, first-served basis.

An agenda is not yet available, but DEA intends to address such topics as drug and chemical trends, Automation of Reports and Consolidated Orders System (ARCOS) reporting, record-keeping requirements, and "suspicious orders" reporting.

If you plan to attend, register directly with the DEA. Further information and directions for online registration can be found through their website, or by contacting DEA directly at ODLL@usdoj.gov.

For more information, contact Anita Ducca.
{top of page}

CMS Releases Responses to FAQ on the Open Payments Act and Holds Conference Call for Physicians

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) released responses to additional "Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)" last week. In response to FAQ 8980, CMS addresses the question of how distributors should report information in the "Product Indicator" data element. CMS stated that:

"Distributors that are considered applicable manufacturers because they hold title to a covered drug, device, biological or medical supply may report 'None' in the Product Indicator indicating that the payment or other transfer of value was not associated with any covered drugs, device, biological or medical supply if the payment or other transfer of value was related to the distributors full line of products, rather than any specific covered products."

Additionally, CMS hosted an August 8 conference call entitled, "Policy Updates on Payments and the Physician Resource Toolkit," which provided additional information for physicians on the Open Payments Act. View the PowerPoint presentation from the call; the audio recording and written transcript of the call will be posted here when available.

For more information, contact Kristen Freitas.
{top of page}

Distribution Center Challenge Update: AmerisourceBergen Hosts Alabama State Senator Jimmy Holley (R-31)


 
From Left: AmerisourceBergen's Dave Leverette, President, Oncology Supply, and Julie Eddy, Director, State Government Affairs; and State Senator Jimmy Holley (R-31). 

Alabama State Senator Jimmy Holley (R-31) visited AmerisourceBergen's Oncology Supply Center in Dothan, Ala., on July 18. AmerisourceBergen staff discussed a number of issues with the senator, including the challenges facing community oncology, Medicare reimbursement, compounding pharmacies and managed care systems. Senator Holley owns a compounding pharmacy with his son, who is a pharmacist in the community.

For more information on the Distribution Center Challenge, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

{top of page}

Learn Best Practices for Navigating Corporate Acquisitions and Divestitures at HDMA's Upcoming "Trade Management Seminar"

Geared toward individuals responsible for trade relations or account and vendor management, HDMA's "Trade Management Seminar" — September 23–24 at The Umstead Hotel in Cary, N.C. — will provide the opportunity to hear perspectives on building effective connections between distributors and manufacturers, solving key everyday problems and anticipating changes that may affect your company or one of your trading partners.

On Tuesday, September 24, Steve Noetzel, Director, Trade Accounts, Johnson & Johnson HealthCare Systems Inc.; and Dianne Pfahl, Vice President, Industry and Manufacturer Relations, Cardinal Health, Inc., will lead a session on, "The Angst of Acquisition." This session will present how product and corporate acquisitions or divestitures impact the supply chain, outline best practices for smooth transitions and but explore how to navigate these changes.

The full agenda is available through the HDMA website. For registration information, contact HDMA's Meetings & Conferences Department at (703) 885-0278.

From: Ratliff, Bill
To: Harper, Karen; Spaulding, Eileen L.; Nikolaus, Richard P

Sent: Thu Jun 04 07:57:09 2009
Subject: RE: DEA Audit prep
Karen/Rich/Eileen, when I spoke with Mike Moye, retired DEA Diversion Executive, he advised that audits were now going to be
conducted every three years as opposed to five. In addition, he advised that the 1801, Diversion Investigators would always start
the audit, but there has been new direction given by DEA Washington, D.C. that if they find any issues of non-compliance, they
are to call in the DEA 1811 Special Agents for a full "criminal audit." According to Mike this is a "radical" change from past
practice. Please carefully consider what he is saying. According to Mike, DEA believes the audits have not been as thorough as
they should be and they are going to be going beyond what they normally check. Please  ensure you do not have any Schedule
ll's stored improperly in reject areas. I strongly recommend going through the plant and carefully reviewing all storage issues to
ensure everything is in order. There is very little time left.

Bill Ratliff
Director of Security
Covidien

bill.ratliff@covidien.com

From: Harper, Karen
Sent: Thursday, June 04, 2009 7:39 AM
To: Spaulding, Eileen L.; Nikolaus, Richard P
Cc: Ratliff, Bill
Subject: RE: DEA Audit prep
Good, thank you.

Regarding Suspicious Order Monitoring Program, we were not able to roll out the New Customer Account Set-up and Ongoing
Monitoring of Existing Customer Accounts due to extensive feedback received from CSRs  in the training on the yes/no checklist.
I have another meeting this morning with Cathy Stewart and Jim Rausch to re-visit the  content.
I still have a next step to forward the program to you for inclusion in the book, my hope is to have the Customer Account portion
mentioned above finalized within the next week so that the procedure sent to you is final.
Remaining procedure that will be sent is still "draft" awaiting ASR completion and that is how we monitor specific orders for
unusual frequency, size, type.

Another note related to DEA audit prep:
Have you or Rich conducted the Audit Preparedness meeting with those that may be called in to speak to the investigators?
I am concerned that we are running out of time to determine target audience and get the training done. Also, we discussed
possible delivering a high level training to all employees containing information such as "don't speculate if you don't know the
answer, keep the answers as brief as possible and use a yes/no reply without embellishment whenever possible".

From: Spaulding, Eileen L.
Sent: June 03, 2009 3:40 PM
To: Harper, Karen
Subject: DEA Audit prep
Karen,

Just wanted to update you that Rich and I held a meeting today with Aaron Nickolette, Reid Cameron, Deb Gula and Carrie to
develop a path forward on how to best conduct the physical count when the DEA conducts their audit.

We brought the group up to speed as far as we could as to what to expect.

We realize that it's difficult to determine what products the DEA will audit but we believe we have a idea on how to proceed
and how best to get the controlled substances counted in a efficient manner. We have  also solicited other departments to
ensure availability in manpower such as warehousing to be able to get the material pu lled quickly to expedite the counting
process.

In addition we decided to have the cycle counters reconcile the Oxy, Methadone and Hydrocodone products prior to the audit
to check and make sure we don't have any issues reconciling and to also allow us a point that should something not reconcile
we would have a starting point to go from to try and detect the error.

MIAMI NEWS


September 14, 2012
Contact: Public Information Officer
Number: 954-660-4602
DEA Serves a Suspension Order on Walgreens Distribution Center in Jupiter, Florida

SEP 14 (MIAMI) - Mark R. Trouville, Special Agent in Charge of the Miami Field Division, Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), announced today the issuance of an Immediate Suspension Order (ISO) at Walgreens Distribution Center located at 15998 Walgreens Drive, Jupiter, Florida ("Walgreens Jupiter"). An ISO is served pursuant to Section 303 and 304 of the Controlled Substances Act, Title 21 U.S.C.   823 and 824 when a DEA-registered business or individual ("registrant") constitutes an imminent danger to the public safety and suspends a registrant's ability to handle or distribute a controlled substance such as oxycodone, hydrocodone and others pending a judicial proceeding.

DEA Special Agent in Charge Mark R. Trouville said, "The diversion of pharmaceutical controlled substances is a great concern for the DEA. All DEA Registrants have an obligation to ensure that medications are getting into the hands of legitimate patients, and when they choose to look the other way patients suffer and drug dealers prosper. The Miami Field Division will continue to investigate all those who contribute to this intolerable situation and deal with them accordingly."

The Walgreens Jupiter is one of twelve distribution centers owned and operated by the Walgreens Corporation in Deerfield, Illinois, which is also the parent company to more than 7800 Walgreens retail pharmacies in the United States. The Walgreens Jupiter distributes controlled substances exclusively to its own Walgreens pharmacies located on the east coast of the United States, including the state of Florida.

Since 2009, Walgreens Jupiter has been the single largest distributor of oxycodone products in Florida. At about the same time as the abuse of prescription drugs became an epidemic in Florida, Walgreens' Florida retail pharmacies, supplied by Walgreens Jupiter, commanded an increasingly large percentage of the oxycodone business. In 2010, only three Walgreens retail pharmacies were in the top 100 purchasers of oxycodone within Florida. In 2011, 38 Walgreens pharmacies made the top 100 and six were in the top 10. Through May 2012, 52 Walgreens pharmacies are in the top 100 oxycodone purchasers, eight in the top 15 and five in the top 10. According to DEA records, in 2011, Walgreens operated 7862 retail pharmacies in the U.S. and 16 of the top 25 largest oxycodone purchasers by Walgreens retail pharmacies, including the top six purchasers, were in Florida and supplied by the Jupiter Distribution Center. In 2011, the average pharmacy in the U.S. ordered approximately 73,000 oxycodone dosage units. The following table shows these six stores and their yearly oxycodone purchases for 2009 through 2011:

Oxycodone is a Schedule II controlled substance which is highly addictive and known to be highly abused and diverted in the state of Florida. According to the 2010 Florida Medical Examiner's Commission Drug Report, the drug that caused the most deaths in the state of Florida for 2010 was oxycodone (1,516 deaths).

On April 4, 2012, the DEA Miami Field Division served an Administrative Inspection Warrant (AIW) on Walgreens Jupiter and its top six retail pharmacies in Florida. These administrative actions were to determine if these Walgreens' maintained a system in place that detects and reports suspicious orders to the DEA to prevent the diversion of control substances as governed by federal laws and the Control Substance Act relating to the proper distribution of control substances.

Based on the ongoing investigation and the evidence gathered from the AIW, the ISO against Walgreens Jupiter, alleges that this distribution center failed to maintain effective controls against the diversion of controlled substances into other than legitimate medical, scientific, and industrial channels, in violation of 21 U.S.C.   823(b)(1) and (e)(1). Furthermore, it alleges that Walgreens Jupiter failed to conduct due diligence to ensure that the controlled substances were not diverted into other than legitimate channels.

Today's action only applies to Walgreens Jupiter Distribution Center and only suspends the distribution of controlled substances in Schedule II to Schedule V and will not affect non-controlled pharmaceutical drugs.

The Walgreen's Corporation will be given an opportunity for an administrative hearing to determine whether the DEA Certificate of Registration at the Walgreen's Jupiter Distribution Center location should be revoked. The final decision will be published in the Federal Register.

I have no doubt that we could help move dabblers up the adoption curve with this program and that is a potential strategy but the current strategy and list of prescribers provided by the brand team is very prescriptive and needs the support of the sales force to realize the ROI.

> Cc: Harrell, Jamie; Terifay, Terry W; Novak, Rod P; Webb, Kevin J; Lierman, Jennifer A; Patterson, Mike E; Wessler, Michael; Rausch, Ryan; Wickline, Ronald P; Swartz, Betty Jean (BJ); Jones, Jason D
> Subject: Competitive Update - Vimovo and Duexis
> 
> Field Sales Force-
> 
> There have been a few recent changes in the NSAID market. The PENNSAID Brand Team wanted to provide you with an update so you are knowledgeable about our competition and what your customers may be hearing.
> 
> Vimovo 
> The FDA recently issued a class wide warning for all Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) for bone fracture. There is evidence to suggest that chronic PPI use is associated with osteoporosis related fractures of the hip, wrist, and spine. The warning cautions that PPIs should be taken at the lowest dose for shortest duration possible to reduce this risk. Vimovo contains esomeprazole (a PPI) and as a result a warning on bone fracture has recently been placed in the Vimovo PI. Also, since Vimovo has esomeprazole in combination with naproxen (an NSAID), and is indicated for 2 tablets daily in the treatment of chronic conditions. Please see the top of page 11 of the attached Vimovo PI for more information on this new warning.
> 
> Additionally, as a result of containing esomeprazole, Vimovo has another warning. This additional warning is for hypomagnesemia, or low magnesium levels, seen with chronic use of PPIs. Serious adverse events that can result from hypomagnesemia include  arrhythmias and seizures. Please see the top of page 12 of the attached Vimovo PI for more information on this warning.
> 
> While Vimovo does an effective job of reducing GI risk from taking oral naproxen alone, it has not been shown to reduce other risks associated with NSAIDs such as abnormal liver function tests, cardiovascular risks, or renal risks, and introduces other risks associated with PPIs.  As a reminder, while PENNSAID is an NSAID and carries the same black box warning, as a topical it produces < 1% of the peak plasma concentration compared to oral NSAIDs.  In addition, topical NSAIDs carry neither the bone fracture or hypomagnesemia warnings, even with chronic use.
> 
> Duexis 
> 
> Late last week, Horizon Pharmaceuticals announced the licensure of Duexis, a combination NSAID containing ibuprofen and famotidine (a histamine H2-receptor antagonist). You may be more familiar with famotidine from its brand name, Pepcid .
> 
> 
> 
> While Duexis is the combination of two products that are both currently available over the counter, the precise dose (800 mg ibuprofen and 26.6 mg famotidine) is not available over the counter in one pill.  In addition, the product is dosed TID. Please see the attached Duexis PI for more information.
> 
> Because Duexis contains an H-2 antagonist as opposed to a PPI, it does not contain the bone fracture or hypomagnesemia warnings. But similar to the PPI in Vimovo, the H-2 antagonist in Duexis only addresses the GI adverse events; not any of the other NSAID associated risks such as abnormal liver function tests, cardiovascular risks, or renal risks.
> 
> Going Forward
> These two market changes are certainly interesting, but they should not change your approach to PENNSAID. Do not let this distract you from the messaging you learned at the National Sales Meeting.  Our message and strategy are strong   for some high risk patients as identified by the physician who cannot tolerate an oral NSAID, some of these patients may have limited treatment options (even with a combination oral NSAID), PENNSAID may be a viable treatment option. As a result, the STRATEGY, LOGIC, and MESSAGE you learned in Dallas are still your best option!
>

{*}       Keep the momemtum in your current territory.  We must focus on the products in our bag today.

{*}       Encourage appropriate dose conversion and titration

Melissa Falcone and Stacy Chick

Hello everyone,

 

We have just heard that Ontario is considering to list Methadose on June 1st with a possible roll-out of 30 days before delisting the compounded product. The date is still tentative as Ontario is going through some political changes, but we are hopeful that it will be met.

 

By chance, the Ontario Pharmacists Association is holding its annual meeting (June 19th-June 21st), ie during this transition period. OPA could collaborate with Mallinckrodt in order to have a lunch and learn about the transition from compounded methadone to Methadose – we were thinking about having Dr Beth Sproule for this event: she is the leading individual who took part in the guidelines update for the introduction of Methadose in Ontario.

 

OPA would need some financial support from Mallinckrodt to host this event – about $15,000. It would be a unique opportunity to reach a large number of pharmacists and educate them on how to use Methadose according to the new guidelines. It would also be a great opportunity for Medical Affairs to connect with KOLs in Ontario. Unfortunately, this event was unplanned and Marketing does not have the budget to support it.

 

Please let me know if Medical Affairs would be able to provide the required financial support – we could then coordinate with OPA and KOLs.

 

 

There is also another opportunity in British Columbia, where the transition took place in February. London Drugs (largest pharmacy chain in BC) will hold its annual conference in June – we could support a speaker presentation on Saturday May 31st, given by a doctor specialist who will discuss MMT in BC. They allow 45 minutes for the presentation including a 5 minute question and answer period. Attendance is approximately 180 staff London Drugs pharmacists, coming from Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. London Drugs covers all expenses for the staff. Due to the costs of this event, they charge $ 3,500 to participate to the company. The vendor pays the speaker honorarium and also finds the speaker.

Team,
