From: "Goddard, Matthew S" <Matthew.Goddard@covidien.com<mailto:Matthew.Goddard@covidien.com>>
Date: August 30, 2011 11:00:49 PM EDT
To: "Dean, Todd E" <Todd.Dean@covidien.com<mailto:Todd.Dean@covidien.com>>
Subject: Success
Todd,

I just wanted to share a success that I had today with a Doctor.  It has the potential to boost my sales through the roof and I am excited to see where this relationship can go.

I had a lunch today with Dr. John Demarco of Palmetto Orthopaedics.  The practice has 4 physicians and they have 2 offices in the Charleston area.  He is the #1 Voltaren Gel writer in my territory.  He has a total market basket of 644 and 333 of them are Voltaren Gel......... 52% market share.  2 of the other physicians are also in my top 6 writers of Voltaren Gel.  They each have a market share of 59% and 20% respectively with V Gel.  So, as you can see, a huge opportunity for Pennsaid in this practice, especially since between the 3 of them they have written a grand total of......wait for it....... 8!!!! 8 scripts out of 1700.  C'mon man!!!

Back to my lunch, I went in with a "sponge approach", played the new card,  and just wanted to learn as much as I could about his practice and his state of mind.  I asked a lot of questions about topicals, why Voltaren Gel, what's the difference between a Pennsaid patient and a VG patient, what pharmacy they refer to,  etc.  I got a lot of information from him and his staff and then I switched roles and told  him and his staff that they must have questions for me and then I let them ask me questions.  It worked great.

I spent 45 minutes with him, his staff, and his assistant and answered every question they had.

*         Dosing - didn't understand how easy it was; didn't know how to write it;

*         Didn't really know why he wrote VGel- it was first, but no real loyalty is what he said; didn't even know VGel reps names

*         Samples are huge - no samples=no scripts; Co-pay cards, knee models, patient ed., they wanted it all

*         Has never seen study about Physical function being measured

*         Didn't know about lotions, suntan lotion, insect repellent, etc. and no use with VGel; never been told that;

*         Formulary and pharmacy questions; price questions; Medicare Part D;

I then ended the call with one question and said what can I do to become a resource and earn more of your business?  He said just keep him in the loop, remind him of Pennsaid dosing, work with Danielle on samples and managed care questions and he will use Pennsaid.  He also said that he will talk with the other MD's about Pennsaid and recommend that they try it as well.   I gave him my card with my cell and email, told him he can call me with anything and then he gave me his cell number as well.

In closing, this was a great day and I definitely feel like I sold something today.  I'm going to stay in front of this office and follow up with him on Tuesday next week to see how things have progressed and what else I can do.  I've been doing this for a long time and I know not everyday is going to be this way, but man it felt good to have a possible score with this physician and office.

Hope this helps and I'll talk with you soon.

Thanks,

Matt Goddard
Covidien Specialty Pharmaceuticals
Field Sales Specialist
Charleston, SC

Subject: FW: NDA 21217 S-004 Labeling Information Request 09jul12

Mike,

Per the new LAO REMS harmonized label, and in regards to the upcoming speaker programs, I want to ensure we are compliant with the new black box language for all LAOs in our content development. Please see the highlighted section in the new BB warning below, and we can discuss at an upcoming meeting.

HIGHLIGHTS OF PRESCRIBING INFORMATION
These highlights do not include all the information needed to use
EXALGO  safely and effectively. See full prescribing information
for EXALGO.
EXALGO (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets,
for oral use, CII
Initial U.S. Approval: 1984
WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL, LIFE-THREATENING
RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE
See full prescribing information for complete boxed warning.
? EXALGO contains hydromorphone, a Schedule II controlled
substance. Monitor for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction
during EXALGO therapy. (5.1, 9)
? Fatal respiratory depression may occur, with highest risk at
initiation and with dose increases; instruct patients on
proper administration of EXALGO tablets to reduce risk.
EXALGO is for use in opioid-tolerant patients only. Crushing,
dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and
absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone. (5.2)
? Accidental ingestion of EXALGO can result in fatal overdose
of hydromorphone, especially in children. (5.3)


Thanks.

jtp

Subject: FW: NDA 21217 S-004 Labeling Information Request 09jul12

Dear All,
Please find attached approval letter for Exalgo class REMS.  Yes!!

In addition, please find recommendation from DMEPA for the Exalgo bottle labels, in conjunction with the review of the 32mg but also requested to be implemented at next printing for the 8, 12 and 16mg bottle labels.  We will need to respond to FDA as to whether we intend to comply with their request to revise all the bottle labels for Exalgo.

Since DMEPA recommendations for labeling changes will be required for Exalgo 32mg, it makes sense to make the change for all the strengths, even though the current bottle labels were included in the class REMS approval issued today.

Look like FDA is requesting only the bolding of the statement  Swallow tablets whole. Do not break, crush or chew tablet  but no other changes for the 32mg and also requested for the other strengths at next printing.

Kind regards,
Linda

From: Walker, Diana [mailto:Diana.Walker@fda.hhs.gov]
Sent: Monday, July 09, 2012 9:46 AM
To: Noa, Linda
Subject: NDA 21217 S-004 Labeling Information Request 09jul12


Dear Linda,

I have received the following comment from the Division of Medication Errors Prevention and Analysis (DMEPA) concerning your proposed carton and container labels for Exalgo S-004.  Please respond to the following comment/recommendation regarding your container label:

Postmarketing review identified 3 domestic cases where patients reported cutting their Exalgo tablets in half and experienced adverse events including
respiratory arrest. Due to the potential severity of the outcome from cutting Exalgo tablets, we recommend bolding or highlighting the statement  Swallow tablets whole. Do not break, crush or chew tablet  on the side panel by utilizing a different color font such as red. Also, consider revising this statement in a similar manner on the 8 mg, 12 mg and 16 mg container labels at the next printing.


Please note that labeling comments for your proposed Package Insert label for this supplement are still in progress and will be sent at a later date.

Kind regards,

Diana

Mark,

Thanks for your note!
I received many positive comments back from the managers yesterday about your presentation at the meeting and it really hit the mark. I would suggest some emphasis on the year the SP team is having.  This team has really pulled through the numbers and doubled down their efforts with the additional training on the launch for 32mg and our two new products. 

As for your 2nd set of thoughts (I wanted to make sure I had the rough numbers before I sent you a response)-


Base demand plan coming in at 		~$32MM
32mg launch August 15th 			~$2.1MM
CNS 40% Price Increase				~$200K

Exalgo 5% Price Increase all SKUs		~$200k

The 40%CNS price increase does not yield as much as one would think based on 75+% of the business being Govt and we don't realize the PI due to CPI penalty. 

The $400k yielded by the PI on Brands is due to the short (6 week) runway.
					
An important note for the July Financial Forecast was the Pennsaid dollar sales out run-rate used for the calculation from the months of April -June.  These data  do not take into account the re-introduction of Voltaren Gel to the market and TRx demand impact.  Our sales out run rate was strong during the April-June period as the Demand TRx data started to transition back to the original forecast.  This had positive impact during Q3 with Pennsaid exceeding our Financial Forecast, but not our TRx forecast.  Now we are seeing market transition back to VG resulting in Wholesalers reconciling their inventories positions.  This is the majority of the issue with the July sales for Brands.

We will be working with Finance to put these data sets into the upside/downside list for Monday.

To sum it up simply, we need to be BALANCED, have FOCUS, and make calls with FREQUENCY.  Let's take a closer look at each of those:



*         BALANCE:

o    With 4 products in our bag, we need to "Balance" our time in the field very carefully.

o    We received our product weighting, and Exalgo remains our Flagship product in all territories throughout the district.

o    While Exalgo is key to our success, we can't maximize our IC plan, Contest dollars or sales force ranking without successfully promoting the NSAID basket and SDP.

o    The "Call Planner" will help you to balance your time and allocate your call capacity throughout the month. We will review this document together on each field visit. *         FOCUS:

o    It is very important that we focus our time and resources on our most important customers who can provide the biggest return on our investment.

o    Plan "focused" dinner/lunch programs planned around hyper targets. You will get more out of this valuable resource.  Get those programs scheduled ASAP!!!

o    Focus your field time on the top decile physicians within each market basket.

o    Use IMS to identify top prescribing physicians who accept plans where our products are covered

o    Deliver a calculated message based upon a solid pre-call plan.  What are we going to say to move the customer during this call?  What are we going to ask for as a result of the interaction?

o    Use the new "Pre-Call Planning" document to help develop a goal for each call.

*         FREQUENCY:

o    Frequency of calls on your top prescribers/targets drives results!!!!

o    Our top prescribers should be seen at least once per week. (or at the very least 3 times per month)

o    When we are in the office 3+ times in a month, hyper targets prescribe twice the amount of EXALGO than when we are there 2 times/month.  This is evidence that your efforts make a difference!

o    Frequency with top targets in all three market baskets is key to our success. Market research shows that one call per month does nothing.



We cannot afford to waste any calls.  We need to challenge our customers' perceptions of hydromorphone, challenge them to identify a patient for EXALGO, challenge the coverage perceptions and how they are dosing EXALGO.  We need to sell with passion, enthusiasm, and confidence in all of our calls whether it's selling Exalgo, Sumavel DosePro, Pennsaid, and/or Duexis!!  Remember, these products can change patients' lives for the better!  We need to challenge our customers to ask their migraine patients......."How are you really doing?" Does their current therapy relieve all of their headache types? What about the wake up or the throw up headaches?  Sumavel DosePro can significantly help these patients.  We need to hypertarget our prescribers for Duexis and get those prescriptions written.  We need to maintain and increase our Pennsaid business by targeting managed care plans where we have the access via IMS and selling on our Simon data comparing Pennsaid to oral diclofenac.



Q2 will be a defining quarter for this business and for each of you.  We need to show what we are made of and put our mark on FY13 during this quarter and showing why we are designating ourselves as the Southern Heat. Jay, Connie and Gavin,

Below is a message I have drafted to send out on behalf of the National Accounts Team to the DM's. The goal is to provide some practical suggestions on HOW utilizing the Top 5 Plan Lists can help shape targeting and messaging so that we are calling on the offices that have the least managed care barriers. My intention was to send this out to the DM's, and then it would be up to their discretion on whether or not they would send out to their teams. It is certainly not the position of the NA Team to provide or replace direction from the sales leadership team. As we ride with representatives in the field, many of us have observed that this data is currently not being utilized. I was hoping an exercise like this would guide reps to think strategically how managed care impacts their messaging and ultimately their success. Gaining familiarity with this data, will also help address the concern of "rep confidence" when talking about managed care.

Please review and let me know if you would like me to send this message out to your DM's, or feel free to offer up any modifications or suggestions. If you would like the message to come from the RD's, we can do that as well.

Thank you. I look forward to hearing back from you.
Krista




DM's, 

Below is an exercise that I've borrowed from Denise Davies. Thank you Denise! She has used this with success with several of her representatives. The Top 5 Plan List is a great data source, however means nothing if the representative does not apply it to their pre-call planning and routing. This is a simple to follow worksheet that will help your reps identify those offices where managed care opportunities are most favorable and lead the physician down the path of least resistance. Obviously as managed care improves over time, this "HIT LIST" could be modified. 

Keep in mind, this is just a suggestion from your National Accounts Team. It is certainly up to each DM whether they want to implement this tool or not.



Instructions:

Use the attached sheet to create your top 25 HIT LIST. 25 Pennsaid Targets and 25 Exalgo Targets.
Use the Top 5 Managed Care Plan List to sort the top plans in each office.

                        - Use the Anti Arthritic List for the Pennsaid Exercise
                        - Use the Pain List for the Exalgo Exercise

Identify 25 offices who have decent volume of our competitor products, good rep access and favorable managed care (BCBS, Tricare, Humana, Aetna to name just a few)
List those top 25 physicians on the attached spreadsheet along with their VG (or ER Opiod) volume and up to 3 favorable plans they accept.
Use your fingertip formulary sheets and copay reduction cards on every call in these offices.

LET'S SKATE WHERE THE PUCK IS!!

From: Voorhis, Joanna <joanna.voorhis@gsw-w.com>

Cc: Gunn, Edward <EGunn@gsw-w.com>
Sent: Thu Nov 11 10:52:57 2010
Subject: 1st Interview
Good Morning!  Just wanted to give you a little feedback from our first interview.  I captured their initial reactions to the concepts, quotes, etc. below.  Showing the sales aid first seems to be working well and this doctor got every concept pretty amazing.   Will keep you updated.

 

Respondent #1  (Rank:  Pitfalls, Good Day, Challenges)

 

Doctor not familiar with EXALGO at all.

 

Pitfalls

SA:  Sees it as a bomb on the front cover.  Informs him of the 24 hour benefit overall.  "It's a ticking time bomb going down and the inside is a pill with a timer representing of the technology built into the pill."

Ad1/2:  "As the day wears on and the person does the stuff they need to do, there is a chance without 24 hour relief, there might be problems in activities." 

Overall:  All about activity of daily living and being able to continue on without having to stop.  Seeing the adlobs helps him to lock in the idea of daily activity help for 24 hours, when paired with the sales aid.  This is talking about extended, 24 hour relief.

 

Challenges (5): 

SA/Adlobs:  Idea is it is a challenge to do a lot of activities for a patient.  Using a medication to overcome that challenge is the message.  

Overall:  I don't get the 24 hour relief message right away.  I get the challenge of going to the mailbox and the office.

 

Good Day  (5-"I like the idea of being able to go through good and bad days without the extra burden of pain problems"):

SA-A busy person that has a filled schedule of doing unpleasant things.  This can be a good day, even though it's a bad day because they don't have other relief issues.  It doesn't talk about the chronic pain much, so it could be confusing why it's a good day (just only having seen the Sales Aid without the adlob imagery).

Adlobs:  "It's saying, you can make a good thing out of bad situations.  This is a concept of something unpleasant and someone having fun out of it, making good out of bad.  The concept is a little "over the top", I have never had a tornado at a picnic and not run, and you might think someone was a little crazy for this.  The cartoon display is fine and it could seem too realistic if not in cartoon form.

Overall:  With the unpleasantness of the overall day, it can still be a good day. "this is correct, they will get 24 hour relief with this medication and can spend time with the mother-in-law".

After a few internal complications, under the direction of Jackie Kim in Medical Affairs, we are back on an accelerated track to meeting our goal of having 100 qualified and trained speakers for both Pennsaid and Exalgo. However, all of these speakers will not be immediately available at launch. The goal of Medical Affairs is that we will have approximately 50 speakers for each product, ready to be utilized immediately after launch.
 
Given this slight delay, we have a cross functional team working together internally to best address your most immediate needs for speaker programs. We have several different approaches being considered that we think will help your district level efforts. The first approach will be to arrange pre-established programs in our major metropolitan areas, utilizing the expertise of The Selva Group, the vendor who is currently managing speaker bureau logistics. These programs will have an assigned speaker with invitations that can be delivered by multiple representatives to help populate a program for 20-25 healthcare professionals. Your representatives will not need to worry about any of the logistics except for ensuring a strong audience. Jackie is working with Selva to establish a method in which they will handle all program-related expenses, including the necessary compliance reporting documents.   
 
Another initiative will be based on your ability to determine speaker opportunities for what I call "pre-planned" groups. We know that certain groups of physicians, PAs, NPs, and various city or regional medical associations have regular monthly or quarterly meetings with an audience of 25-50 clinicians in attendance. When the audience is appropriate for our product and the group is looking for a speaker, we can take advantage of this type of group meeting  without burdening our representatives to build an audience. In this case the vendor might only need to coordinate the payment to the speaker, but Jackie and her team can customize the approach to meet your needs.
 
Maximizing our speakers early will help us with our launch success and having larger venues delivers our message to more potential prescribers faster. As more speakers get trained we will be better positioned to address the individual territory level programs. While we will still be able to handle a select number of individual territory requests at launch, our internal capabilities will not be at full speed until late May.
 
The direction that you should take from this message is to start identifying "pre-planned" group meeting opportunities now. Where the audience is appropriate and the speaker need exists, we will make every effort to get you a qualified and recognized speaker. Through your Regional Directors we will begin to identify the best "metropolitan markets" for a speaker program that can be coordinated by our national vendor, but you will be responsible for generating the audience. We will work with you closely to coordinate preferred dates and or restaurant locations.
 
That's it for now, more details will be available at the managers meeting and of course, if you have any questions at all, please contact your Regional Director or Jackie Kim in Medical Affairs. We are dedicated to your launch success and know that your success is our success. We will do everything possible to help you and your district have a positive experience with these speaker programs.  
 
Ron Wickline

Tom

There were several changes that were made to the Q3 plan as it relates to XARTEMIS XR payout and Exalgo promotion.  The changes for each product are listed below. 

 

To cultivate Sales Specialist engagement and improve our XXR performance, the payout structure was modified as follows in regards to the XXR contribution to plan payout:

 

1.       Pay the higher of 3Q14 SICP XXR attainment (based on the original Q3 territory goals) or $1,500 stipend payout  -- the 4Q14 SICP Plan is designed to reward those who generated XXR prescribers and prescriptions in 3Q14

Sorry for the delayed response. I conducted interviews this afternoon then flew up to Atlanta this evening.

I hear a number of things as I talk to DMs and work in the field. I can put together a more formal response, but here are some items in no particular order:


1.    A certain degree of disruption with the realignment   some more than others. I tend to forget about that but the DMs quickly remind me that reps are still learning some new targets   again, some more than others. That will show when we see numbers for frequency.

2.    While most reps are able to get access with most targets, getting access at our desired frequency can be a challenge especially where lunch appointments are a requirement.

3.    Overall regulatory climate for opioids is deteriorating. I know we don t want to acknowledge that, but I hear it more and more when I work with reps. It s not always in the form of new legislation. In Louisiana, for example, it is a new investigator for the LA Board of Medical Examiners. Here is a quote from Jerry from his latest report to me on this   Apparently she is  heavily against the prescribing of opioids and believes that all pain patients should be treated with NSAIDs , injections and physical therapy. She has gone head to head with many of my physicians arguing that there are no studies demonstrating opioids as being effective in managing long term chronic pain. She utilizes intimidation going into their offices sometimes monthly  combing  thru their files and forcing them to document their discussions sending them back to her in what she calls a  memorial  of their discussion. She has recently informed two of my physicians that they can only write one opioid for a patient. The physicians say that she cannot legally do this but at the same time they do not want her back in their office next month. One of my physicians had a patient controlled on 32 mg of Exalgo with hydrocodone for breakthrough. When he told her that he could now only prescribe one of the two she chose hydrocodone.  Just seems that the environment for opioids is getting more hostile. If we were bigger, we d have a corporate initiative to combat this.

4.    The item above would also include additional step-edits, quantity limits, and more denials on PAs. I m hearing that but don t have a lot of specifics to back it up. I ll ask the DMs.

5.    I m hearing that reps feel  spread thin . I push back because I don t buy it. As Gavin said this morning, if you do the math on targets for each product and time invested, we should be able to sell four products. Where I will give some ground is that perhaps there is less time to protect the script as that sometimes requires a lot of legwork (and time).

6.    Can t ignore the obvious some reps have much better selling skills than others.

7.    Still hearing way too many discussions in which the starting dose is far too low. A setup to fail.

8.    Coming off of a good FY12, the decrease in bonus is a topic of discussion. That s where we come back with the money available through the contests.


Bill

Hi team,

 

Below please find this week s monitoring report for EXALGO; this report includes coverage from Friday, March 26, to Friday, April 2, 2010.

 

This week, CombinatoRx announced that they will be focusing their efforts on the research and development of new therapies in the pain management and inflammation sector following recent product advancements and a profitable fourth quarter. EXALGO was mentioned as one of the reasons the company is expected to see a continued increase in profitability this year. The announcement was covered by the Boston Business Journal and picked up by Mass High Tech.

 

Also of importance this week, Pain Management News reported on a review published in the most recent edition of the Cochrane Library that found that for certain carefully-selected patients with non-cancer related pain, opioids may offer long-term, clinically significant pain relief with low risk for addiction, abuse or other serious side effects. However, authors of the study caution that more research is needed to determine long-term health risks as well as which patients might be best suited for opioid therapy.

 

Additionally this week, Psychiatry Update ran an article on the school of thought that prescribing less  likeable  opioids will help curb dependence in patients with chronic pain.

 

Also, the American Society of Anesthesiologists released new guidelines for chronic pain, which will appear in the April issue of Anesthesiology.

 

Finally, Pain Medicine News reported on two preliminary studies conducted by researchers at the University of Chicago that showed that some opioid therapies may trigger the growth and migration of cancer cells. According to the article, however, a modification in opioid treatment may help patients avoid the spreading of cancerous cell in their bodies.

 

Attached please find the full-text coverage. As always, please let us know if you have any questions.

 

Thanks,

Jenny

Subject: EXALGO Monitoring Report -- Week of 5/21



 

Hi team,

 

Below please find this week s monitoring report for EXALGO; this report includes coverage from Friday, May 14, to Friday, May 21, 2010.

 

This week, RecoveryView.com published an editorial about EXALGO, citing its concerns for the potential abuse and misuse of the medication. The article begins by highlighting the evolution in pain management from Oxycontin, a 12-hour formula for pain management, to EXALGO, which is taken every 24 hours. The reporter s concerns with the drug is that opiate-na ve patients are at high-risk for overdosing on EXALGO, and that there may be a greater possibility for people to divert the drug for illegal sale. The reporter did have hope that, with proper patient and prescriber education, the drug will be used to effectively treat opioid-tolerant patients who suffer from moderate to severe chronic pain.

 

Of other interest this week: A conversation about EXALGO was posted on the CafePharma forum titled,  Five reasons why EXALGO ER is a failure.  The forum post highlighted the top-five reasons one member felt EXALGO was not going to be successful, including the price of the medication and the potential risks involved with taking EXALGO. One person replied to the forum claiming to be a representative from Covidien, accusing the person who began the discussion of being an employee of a competitor.

 

The Los Angeles Times wrote a blog post this week about an essay published in the past issue of the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA). From: Webb, Kevin J [Webb, Kevin J]

To: Nosco, Dennis L; Estes, Penny L 
CC: Novak, Rod P 
Subject: RE: Unacceptable Delay in Table Top Panels 

Thanks Dennis. "Release" was in relation to allowing the vendor begin production of the panels. And I agree, nothing 
was going to ship to the reps until all of the documents, including the memo was approved. 

Regarding the memo, since it hasn't gone out yet, we can re-word it state that PENNSAID and EXALGO panels can NOT 
be interchanged. 

Lastly, I was not aware of your request that the bottom of the panels state 'panel 1 of _' . We did this for Tofranil- 
PM. Since the disk has not been released, perhaps we can still add this to the very bottom. 

Kevin 


    From: Nosco, Dennis L 
    Sent: Friday, July 23, 2010 1:26 PM 
    To: Webb, Kevin J; Estes, Penny L 
    Cc: Novak, Rod P 
    Subject: RE: Unacceptable Delay in Table Top Panels 

    Kevin, 

    I share your concern. 

    When we are talking about "release" are we talking about DDMAC submission? If that is it we should have been 
    able to submit to DDMAC, if the need was indicated as urgent, when all the submission documents were made 
    available to Penny by Marketing. If the DDMAC submission was held up and we could have done it faster then 
    how we all can improve that needs to be discussed and fixed. 

    If we are talking about "release" as the ability to have these panels manufactured and shipped to the sales force, 
    I, again, share your concern. Once we approve a piece it should be able to be manufactured. If that didn't 
    happen for some reason I apologize. The intent was that the approved table top graphics could not be USED by 
    the sales force until the memo was finalized, NOT that the pieces could not be printed. 

    If we are talking about "release" as the ability of the sales force to use a piece then there are two 
    components. The one that comes into play most often is DDMAC submission, which we have discussed 
    above. Unless implementation guides or memos are required, the sales force can use a piece, from our 
    perspective, the day after submission to DDMAC. If a memo is required to go along with the piece, all that is 
    necessary is that the memo be approved by PARC and sent to the sales force before the piece is 
    used. This approval is almost ALWAYS done on the fly, either electronically or as an unscheduled review 
    sandwiched into an already full meeting, very similar to what we did with the PENNSAID journal ad that we 
    received, I think, on Tuesday and that we approved at yesterday's packed meeting. 

    Kevin, we only ask for a memo when absolutely necessary but, frankly, our interpretation of the information we 
    were getting led us to believe there was flexibility in how the sales force could use a piece that we approved as 
    one contiguous unit. ..and we wanted some training (in the form of a memo) on how this graphic was to be 
    used. In fact, from our conversation today, that flexibility DOES exist as reps could, very easily, put the panels 
    together in any order and might only use one or two panels instead of the required 3 panels (giving us less than 
    required fair balance). Heck, the way I read Julie's memo, it was even theoretically possible, without some 
    instruction, that EXALGO and PENNSAID panels could accidentally be used together. 

    All this is with the backdrop of repeated Marketing pushback when I have asked for the simple language to be 
    placed on all panels of a multiple panel display: "Panel _ of. Only to be used in order and with the other 



                                                MNKOI 0004023123 

panels". I have seen this done a number of times in this industry at meetings where companies wanted to make 
sure that their materials were used as approved. As we did not have that we chose the fastest route: electronic 
review of a memo that explained how to use the pieces that we reviewed AND approved to be used in a particular 
way. The approval of this memo took place in about 90 minutes this morning, based on Penny's original e- 
mail. The approval of the memo was never intended to be an impediment to manufacturing the panels. It was 
always intended to be a required element of the training on how to properly use these pieces before they were 
used by the sales force. 

As I told you this morning, some of the need for the original discussion on this issue was due to PARC not 
completely understanding this table top graphic format and that a physical mockup might have been more

Thanks, Hugh.


As Mario certainly knows, Exalgo will likely serve as an excellent reference for "market performance" of an otherwise highly-abusable opioid. Hydromorphone, embedded in PEO, demonstrated it was difficult at best for abusers to circumvent. As such, despite high payloads of "dilaudid" per tablet, Exalgo has witnessed quite low abuse rates, and much negative sentiment within the abuser forums.


In fact, the FDA refused to approve the 32mg dosage form until they witnessed the performance of the 8, 12 and 16mg dosages once commercially available. It was primarily based on the low-abuse profile of those strengths that supported the safety of the approval of the 32mg dosage.


I believe MNK's history of good stewardship along with the low abuse rate of Exalgo should be considered in decisions related to XXR. And by the way, Exalgo has about 200mg PEO per tablet, XXR has 322mg PEO per tablet.


Fingers crossed.

Southeast Region Sales Team,

Thanks to all of you who responded to the request for EXALGO successes and best practices. Our District Manager representing the region on the EXALGO Field Advisory Council, Jerry Robinson, has pulled together a few gems in the message below. PLEASE take the time to read this and hopefully find some ideas that may help you in expanding your EXALGO business.

At our POA meeting in April, I showed you that our weekly script count had grown from around 600/week in early January to over 1,000/week by the end of March. Well, another three months have passed since that meeting and we are still hovering around 1,000/week. We need to move EXALGO up in our success algorithm!

Here's to a great selling week.

Bill

                                                                                                                                [Final-REVISED-2.0-Logo-DK-blue.png]

        [cid:image003.jpg@01CD5DBB.97694AE0]




Southeast Region:

As we enter the final quarter of 2012 we can all look back at the hard work we have put into selling Exalgo and are really beginning to see our "fair share" of successes.  Let's not forget we still have one quarter left to expand on these successes.  I wanted to take a moment of your time to share some of these successes with everyone and highlight the hard work, persistence, thinking outside the box and never give mentality demonstrated within the Southeast Region.  Because, after all, you need all the above to be successful in selling Exalgo.

We have a great message with Exalgo and utilizing the OROS more often can help differentiate ourselves from the competition.  Chris Clark utilizes the INSPIRE message very well below and is now being used in other Districts as well:

"One thing I have found effective, especially with PCP's, is relating the combination of hydromorphone and OROS to become Exalgo with the experience they had with Ritalin and its abuse as a QID drug and its combination with OROS to become Concerta. I tell them that this changed the ADHD landscape forever and the fact that they don't call Concerta -> Ritalin ER  -( I must give Chris Clark credit here) - ... I emphasize using the PK values located in the MSA of Dilaudid and Exalgo that OROS is innovative in the pain market and that Exalgo is NOT Dilaudid ER. I ask them which PK profile do they want their chronic opioid tolerant pain patients on long term."

It's an understatement to say persistence and  a never give up mentality are needed to sell Exalgo.  These two qualities are critical for Covidien Representatives.  Lisa Wimberly and Nikki Ziegenhirt provide some great examples of this in their successes below.  It's not too hard to wonder why they are ranked numbers 4 and 10 on the April Rank Report respectively.  Keep up the nice efforts!

"I had spoken to you before about Dr. Vilasuso, who  I've been calling on for over a year now and never could get him to commit to trying Exalgo.  He has always been hesitant about hydromorphone and its potency.  I was able to use the new PK data in the Master Sales Aid to get into a great discussion with him on our last call. I specifically  showed him the PK chart with the IR hydromorphone in comparison to the different strengths for Exalgo.  I truly believe that this changed the way he viewed Exalgo and told me he was going to put his first patient on it.  We went over the dosing and conversion chart, in order to ensure the patient would receive the correct dose.  I went to his office to follow up with him and he informed that the patient was stable with 32mg of Exalgo  and she was doing great.  He followed the dosing and titration properly JHe is excited about the results and is looking to convert several new patients."

"I have recently had success with a specialty that I originally thought didn't have much potential.  As I was looking over my Leap Frog and IMS data, I noticed that quite a few of my Internal Med/Family Practice physicians were writing more long-acting pain meds than I had realized.  When we first launched Exalgo I would present it if it was part of the call plan but I didn't really feel they had a strong need for a medication like Exalgo (my mistake).  To be honest,  I didn't sell it with as much passion as I did when talking to a pain physician.  I have since realized that many internal med/family practice physicians do have a strong need for Exalgo with their patient population.  Many of these physicians treat people who have had chronic pain for years but aren't complicated cases.  Due to their close relationship, both the patient and physician are more comfortable not referring out .  These types of patients are ideal for Exalgo since they are well-known, compliant , stable patients.  Since I have opened my eyes to this missed opportunity and targeted them with the same enthusiasm as my pain physicians I have had many successes.  I currently have 5 internal/primary care physicians writing Exalgo on a regular basis.  I have 2 more that I think will start prescribing Exalgo within the next few weeks.  Several scripts a month from 5 or 6 physicians can really make a difference at the end of the quarter!!!  I thought you might want to pass this on because maybe others in our district have been overlooking these "diamonds" like I had."

And finally, thinking outside the box leads to new ideas for everyone to stay in front of our competition.  Kim McCoy provide a great example for National Pain Awareness Month (which is September).  So, let our planning begin!!


"Here is an idea.  Since September is National Pain Awareness month, (I know it's July but some offices get booked up quickly)  Make those lunches all about Cares Alliance and focused on the patients, physicians and staff.  Bring in the patient cards and resource portfolio,  order the kits early from smart source and show how we want to partner with them.   Discuss challenges they may be facing.  I have heard from staff many issues including:  Lack of patient information, reimbursement issues, how to overcome QL issues, etc.  This is also a good time to get EEIFs out.  Really  go all out for the offices,  use our Exalgo lunch kits and really make it an event.  We will be remembered and since Oct - Dec can be tough months why not do something to differentiate ourselves and give Exalgo a little more top of mind awareness as well."



Thanks to everyone for sharing their successes with Exalgo.  Your hard work is starting to pay off and we are beginning set some new highs with the brand.  Keep up the nice efforts!!

  A two-day, joint meeting of FDA's Anesthetic and Life Support Drugs and Drug Safety and Risk Management 
  advisory committees will consider the design of post-marketing studies for Purdue Pharma's Oxycontin and 
  King Pharmaceuticals' Embeda to determine if their product-specific properties intended to discourage misuse 
  and abuse are effective. 

  Both Oxycontin (oxycodone hydrochloride controlled-release) and Embeda (morphine sulfate extended-release 
  with a sequestered naltrexone hydrochloride inner core) are approved for management of moderate to severe 
  pain when a continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extensive period. 

  The post-marketing studies are intended to be epidemiological or observational trials to assess the drugs' known 
  serious risks as well as whether their abuse deterrent properties "actually result in a decrease" of abuse and 
  misuse as well as curtailing their potential consequences - addiction, overdose and death, according to FDA. 

  FDA is happy to see the development of potentially safer opioids, but the agency has been loathe to give the 
  products a claim for abuse deterrence, since simply engineering the pills not to be enjoyed doesn't prove they 
  will work that way, and a controlled trial couldn't ethically have misuse as a endpoint. 

  The advisory committee meeting, set for Oct. 21 and Oct. 22 in Gaithersburg, Md., is a signal, though, that the 
  agency may consider allowing different kinds of data to support risk reduction language in the label. 

  Getting The Message Out With A REMS 
  Having an abuse reduction claim or even just robust data in labeling would be a great benefit for either product, 
  particularly as the agency may be pushing all sponsors to shift their promotional efforts to a risk and education 
  message as part of a potential class-wide Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy for long-acting and extended- 
  release opioids. 

  In July, the agency issued a proposed REMS for long-acting opioids, to consist of a MedGuide, requirements 
  for drug sponsors to provide prescriber education, requirements for educational sheets to be offered to patients, 
  and a program and timetable for assessing the plan's effectiveness ('FDA's Guide To Mitigating Risks Of Long- 
  Acting Opioids,' The Pink Sheet, July 5, 2010). 

  But the Anesthetic and Life Support Drugs and Drug Safety and Risk Management advisory committees voted 
  against approval of the FDA proposal by 10-25 on July 22. Panel members cited concerns that prescriber 
  participation in the educational programs would be voluntary rather than mandatory. 

  The panel also considered an industry proposal for an opioids REMS during that meeting, suggesting that if 
  prescriber education be mandatory, implementation be through either a third-party industry-wide registry or a 
  Drug Enforcement Administration registry that would require approval by Congress. Industry participants 
  indicated they probably would prefer the latter option ('If Opioid REMS Mandates Prescriber Training, Firms 
  May Ask DEA For Help,' The Pink Sheet, Aug. 2, 2010).

13:16 ET 6/20/11 [StreetAccount] PFE Preview of upcoming FDA decision on Pfizer/Pain Therapeutic's Remoxy (abuse-resistant formulation oxycodone) for moderate to severe pain ($20.20 -$0.06)

The PDUFA date for PFE/PTIE's class 2 NDA resubmission for Remoxy <https://www.streetaccount.com/biotech_search_productname.aspx?product_id=6018&searchtype=drug_names>  (extended release, abuse-resistant formulation oxycodone) for moderate to severe pain is 23-June. StreetAccount notes that the Street is generally expecting a delay to approval (Complete Response Letter) based on 3-May guidance provided by Pfizer. 

*	Background: 

	*	This FDA decision follows a December 2008 Complete Response Letter (CRL) and December 2010 resubmission, deemed a complete, class 2 filing in January. The CRL requested no new clinical trials, and sought additional non-clinical, later determined to be six-month stability data. The sponsor also took steps to strengthen the resubmission by completing a likeability study (positive topline results reported 25-Apr) and a pharmacokinetic trial in volunteers. 
	*	On May 16, 2011, the FDA met with members of the Industry Working Group (IWG) and other sponsors of Long Acting and Extended Release opioid drugs. The purpose of the meeting was to discuss the next steps in implementing A Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) for these products through a single shared system. 

		*	According to the FDA.gov website: "We continue to work on the Medication Guide Template and expect to be able to provide it by June 24, 2011." 

			*	StreetAccount notes that this is coincidentally one day after Pfizer's 23-Jun PDUFA date. 

*	Approval issues: 

	*	Recall that Pfizer warned, on its Q1 earnings call on May 3, that it was working to address a specific issue in the manufacturing section of the Remoxy application, as well as to understand any potential implications of FDA's recent class-wide REMS announcement for extended release opioids. Pfizer stated that these issues could delay the timing of approval or the launch of REMOXY. 

*	Leveraged: 

	*	Pfizer (PFE), via its $3.6B acquisition of King Pharmaceuticals, has worldwide commercialization rights, ex-Australia and New Zealand. 
	*	Pain Therapeutics (PTIE) is entitled to receive a 20% royalty except for the first $1B in cumulative net sales, which royalty is set at 15%; outside the US, the royalty rate is flat 10%. 
	*	Durect Corporation (DRRX) is entitled to a royalty of 6-11.5% of sales, paid by PFE and through PTIE supplemental to the royalty above, for the use of its Oradur technology. 

*	Competition: 

	*	Branded Extended Release Opioid Products listed by the FDA include JNJ's Duragesic and Exalgo (the latter with COV), ENDP's Opana ER, several privately-owned, as well as King Pharmaceuticals' (now part of Pfizer) Avinza and Embeda. 
	*	StreetAccount notes that ACUR/PFE's Oxecta (formerly Acurox), approved on 17-Jun, is an immediate release opioid (as opposed to extended release). 

*	Recent sell-side research, commentary: 

	*	BOAML noted on 16-May the Remoxy PDUFA as one of several potentially positive catalysts for shares for PFE. 
	*	UBS noted on 4-May that a "manufacturing delay seems likely", echoing management's remarks but notably more focused on the former warning versus the REMS-specific warning. 
	*	Wells Fargo noted on 3-May management's expectation for delay, due to the two issues mentioned above. 
	*	Goldman Sachs on 3-May projected revenues 2011-2016 of $22M, $85M, $228M, $358M, $441M and $475M. 
	*	Oppenheimer noted on 21-April in an ENDP note the potential approval of Remoxy as a competing drug to the Opana franchise. 
	*	Jefferies noted on 13-April in an ENDP note that Endo's Opana should be in "excellent shape with managed care (even with Remoxy entry)". 

Shares of PTIE are trading +4.1% to $8.99 ahead of the FDA decision, and in sympathy to Friday's FDA approval of ACUR's Oxecta, +24%.

Wed Sep 23, 2009 4:00pm EDT
* Agency expected to decide on approval by Nov. 22
WASHINGTON, Sept 23 (Reuters) - A U.S. panel of medical experts backed Neuromed Pharmaceuticals Inc and
Covidien's (COV.N) plan to limit potential abuse with their powerful, once-a-day painkiller Exalgo, saying the drug
was very effective but could easily be misused.
Neuromed, which is expected to finalize its merger with CombinatoRx (CRXX.O) later this year, is seeking U.S.
Food and Drug Administration approval of its opioid drug for patients who no longer get relief with other similar
medications.
Neuromed sold the drug's U.S. rights to Covidien in June.
Company officials told the FDA advisory panel that they aimed to curb abuse by educating patients and having
them sign an agreement. It also would require doctors and pharmacists to register to dispense the drug, among
other efforts.
FDA's panelists largely agreed Exalgo could help patients feel better and was more convenient. But they said the
company needed to closely watch how the drug was used.
Panel chairman Dr. Jeffrey Kirsch, head of anesthesiology at Oregon Health and Science University, said the
panel felt Exalgo was "highly efficacious" but very prone to crushing and other methods of abuse compared to
other opioid painkillers.
"On the spectrum of abuse, I think it's toward the top," he said.
The FDA will weigh the panel's comments before making a decision on approval, expected by Nov. 22. (Reporting
by Susan Heavey; Editing by Tim Dobbyn)

Subject:        FDA Letter-draft content

Draft Content,


Exalgo REMS - Voluntary ETASUs-Development Methodology and Organization

1) Developmental and Continuous Improvement Methodologies

A) After being informed by the agency that the REMS for Exalgo would consist of a MG, Communications Plan and voluntary ETASUs COV/Mallon implemented a evidence based approach, RxFMEA,( failure mode and effects analysis) to define the details of the REMS. This approach is based on a detailed proactive assessment of the medication use and care delivery process related to Exalgo. The RxFMEA application identified specific points where the process could fail

( failure modes). All failures were scored to identify the most hazardous, and the underlying causes were identified.

B) Specific tools were then selected and designed to mitigate the risks of failure. Tools are both educational and enabling in nature and are targeted for use by prescribers, patients, pharmacists and prescriber office staff. Built in redundancy of tools assures at least 2 different stakeholders are targeted for the most hazardous points of failure to ensure more comprehensive risk reduction.

C) Previously invalidated tools are being tested with key stakeholders using a variety of testing methodologies. Revisions will be made based on the testing. Some previously validated tools are being used as is.

D)Continuous improvement will take place via the required and additional voluntary periodic tool assessments and additional RxFMEA analyses at regular intervals post launch. This will likely result in additions, deletions or modifications

to the tools

2) Required REMS Elements-Medication Guide(MG) and Communication Plan(CP)

A) The following required elements will be implemented in the following manner:

1) MGs will be available with Exalgo as part of it's packaging. Specifically, 6 MGs will accompany each bottle of 100 tablets shipped to whosalers and pharmacies. The MG will also:  1)  be contained in the CP, 2) available on 2 Covidien websites( product and safety), 3) carried by sales representatives calling on physicians and retail pharmacies 4) available via a telephone request and a direct mail request system.

2) The CP will consist of the following required elements: Intro letter, PI,MG, Prescriber Brochure and a BRC to request educational and enabling tools. Packages will be direct mailed to the following:

1) all retail and hospital pharmacies ( approx 70,000 recipients)
2) prescribers in our sales rep call plan( approx 13,500 recipients-deciles 5 to 10 of prescribers of LAOs)
3) additional prescribers not in our sales rep call plan( approx 47,000 recipients-deciles 3 and 4 of prescribers of LAOs)

4) relevant Professional Associations( approv 50 recipients)

3) Soon after commercial launch the CP will be repeated to the above audiences.

3) Voluntary Elements to Assure Safe Use( ETASU) -Safe Use Tools

A) The following tools were identified, are being developed and will be provided by Covidien free to charge to stakeholders.

 16 prescriber/office tools
 6 pharmacy tools
 7 patient and caregiver tools

Examples:

1) a non promotional safe use initiative website which will contain information on responsible prescribing, educational information and materials, and downloadable tools.

2) a Clinical Management Brochure which expands on the prescriber brochure and reinforces key safety,

3) a Urine Drug Screen Monograph and primer to assist prescribers in deterring patient opioid naïveté and or compliance.

4) A Patient/Prescriber Medication Agreement( PPMA) to improve physician/patient counseling and appropriate use.

5) a paper dosing diary and 24 hr countdown electronic dosing reminder to help ensure only one dose/day is taken by patients on Exalgo,

6) the APS Clinical Guidelines for Pain Management, Responsible Opioid Prescribing- A Physician's Guide by Scott Fishman to provide educational reference material,

7) the BPI, NRS and ORT to provide prescribers with easy access to validated patient and pain assessment tools.

8) Referral letters in a template format that a PCP could adapt to refer a patient to a pain specialist or a pain specialist could adapt to refer a patient to an addiction specialist.

9) An in- person and Web based training program on responsible opioid prescribing.

10) a patient brochure focused on safe storage, handling and potential disposal of opioids to assist in minimizing theft, misuse or any access by children.

Note: Based on our recent discussions the content of relevant tools will be modified to focus more attention on the safety aspects of higher doses and higher strength tablets.

B) Voluntary Elements to Assure Safe Use( ETASU) -Safe Use Tools-Distribution

1) Prescribers in the 13,500 audience will receive all the prescriber tools at launch via direct mail.
2) Covidien will distribute the prescriber tools to any prescriber once we become aware of Rx activity( see below).

C) Rx Activity Monitoring and Interventions

1) Rx Databases available to Covidien will enable the identification of a prescriber of Exalgo within 21 days after the prescription is dispensed to a patient.

2) If this prescriber is not within  the audience that has received our MG,CP and ETAUS their identification will trigger this to be sent.

3) it will trigger a personal call from a trained Covdien representative to advise the prescriber on the key safety information, available tools, programs, and the potential scheduling of further safety related training or activities.

4) calls and follow-up activities will be triaged to focus on the least experienced physicians prescribing the highest doses first.

D) Assessments and Continuous Improvement

1) The FDA required 6 month, 12 month and annually thereafter assessments will be performed in a robust manner with respect to sample size and stakeholder segment and reported to the agency.

2) Additional market research of tool use and effectiveness are planned in the first 2 years of commercial activity to help ensure a complete picture of tool effectiveness.

3) Covidien will convene a external Safety Advisory Board( SAB) of experts in the field of opioid prescribing, addiction and diversion. This board will meet at least twice yearly to review the data relative to Exalgo utilization, diversion, tool use, and advise Covidien on the need for additional programs related to safe use.

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

Here is a press release from Medscape, reporting from the American Association of Pain Management Meeting.


http://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/711149?sssdmh=dm1.546688&src=nldne&uac=126123BR

Medscape Conference Coverage, based on selected sessions at the:

American Association of Pain Management (AAPM) 20th annual clinical meeting

This coverage is not sanctioned by, nor a part of, the American Association of Pain Management.

Extended-Release Hydromorphone Shows Safety, Efficacy for Sustained Pain Control
Nancy A. Melville
October 22, 2009 (Phoenix, Arizona)   An extended-release form of the opioid drug hydromorphone (Exalgo, Neuromed Pharmaceuticals) provides effective and safe therapy for chronic moderate to severe lower back pain, according to a phase 3 study presented here at the American Association of Pain Management 20th annual clinical meeting.
Although similar in efficacy to the opioid morphine, hydromorphone offers an advantage in the treatment of pain in the elderly and patients with problems with renal clearance of drugs because it lacks the active metabolites that are present in morphine, said Douglas Gourlay, MD, director of the Pain and Chemical Dependency Division, Wasser Pain Centre, Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto, Ontario.
"Morphine is often considered a poor choice for the elderly or people who are renally impaired because of the active metabolites, but hydromorphone offers an advantage, in that it's a relatively clean molecule, so it's often preferred," said Dr. Gourlay, who was not involved in the study. "It's a potent opioid with nice, clean kinetics."
The double-blind study involved 268 patients with mild to severe lower back pain who were randomized into 2 groups of 134 patients each to receive either extended release hydromorphone or placebo for 12 weeks. The patients recorded pain intensity scores on an 11-point Likert Numeric Rating Scale. Results were presented at the meeting by Arifulla Khan, MD, medical director and principal investigator of Northwest Clinical Research Center in Bellevue, Washington.
The results showed significant improvements in changes in mean pain intensity scores from baseline to week 12 between the hydromorphone group (median, 0.2) and the placebo group (median, 1.6; P < .0001).
Adverse events reported by the hydromorphone group were similar to those of other oral opioids, including drug withdrawal syndrome (7.5%), constipation (6%), nausea (3%), and headache (3%).
An extended-release hydromorphone product made its way to the American marketplace briefly under the name Palladone, but the product was voluntarily withdrawn in 2005 by maker Purdue Pharma after a US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory issued a warning of potentially fatal adverse effects related to dose dumping when combined with alcohol.
Joanna Schooler, a spokesperson for Neuromed, said that data provided to the FDA indicate that Exalgo is not subject to dose dumping.
"In vitro studies have shown that alcohol in various concentrations does not alter the extended-release properties or pharmacokinetic profile of Exalgo," she said.
The benefits of a controlled-release formulation of hydromorphone are 2-fold; it offers improved steady pain control and serves as a deterrent for abuse, Dr. Gourlay noted.
"There is clearly a population of patients who struggle with withdrawal-mediated pain resulting from the waxing and waning of drug levels from medication taken over the course of a 24-hour period, and the ultimate effect is that their pain is amplified," he said.
"The idea with the controlled release is to not only reduce the tendency toward multiple doses required throughout the day, but also to give increased stability and have a lower incidence of that withdrawal-mediated pain."
The steady delivery of the drug also eliminates the highs and lows that make the drug susceptible to abuse.
"Drugs that rapidly cross over the blood brain barrier and that peak quickly and fall off quickly tend to be drugs with higher abuse liability, so the theoretical advantage of a controlled-release delivery system is that the reward associated with taking the drug is less intense and will hopefully have a lower abuse liability," he said.
The study received funding from Neuromed Pharmaceuticals. Dr. Gourlay has disclosed no relevant financial relationships.
American Association of Pain Management (AAPM) 20th annual clinical meeting: Poster abstract 2. Presented October 9, 2009.

The FDA has approved the EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) 32 mg tablet for use in
appropriate opioid-tolerant chronic pain patients. With the
addition of the 32 mg tablet, along with the already approved
8, 12, and 16 mg tablets, you now have greater dosing flexibility.

Learn more about EXALGO.



The features of the added EXALGO 32 mg tablet include:

 

 Dosing flexibility. EXALGO 32 mg complements the already approved 8, 12, and 16 mg tablets.1

 
 

 Proven efficacy. EXALGO 32 mg was the median effective dose in the pivotal trial.*2

 
 

 Robust patient exposure. EXALGO 32 mg has been thoroughly tested in 14 clinical trials conducted in 2474 patients, with 1483 of these patients exposed to a dose of 32 mg or greater.3

 

* Mean effective dose was 37.8 mg.1

Additional EXALGO information available.

P.S. Learn about proper dosing and titration with
once-daily EXALGO.

REFERENCES: 1. EXALGO  Prescribing Information. 2. Hale M, Khan A, Kutch M, Li S. Once-daily OROS hydromorphone ER compared with placebo in opioid-tolerant patients with chronic low back pain. Curr Med Res Opin. 2010;26(6):1505-1518. 3. Data on file. Mallinckrodt Inc.



800-778-7898 | www.EXALGO.com

COVIDIEN, COVIDIEN with logo and Covidien logo are U.S. and internationally
registered trademarks of Covidien AG.
EXALGO is a registered trademark of Mallinckrodt LLC.
  2012 Mallinckrodt LLC, a Covidien company.  MK20158 September 2012



To ensure that you receive future email from EXALGO, add us to your address book.
If you no longer wish to receive email from EXALGO, unsubscribe now.

 

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

 


 

 

 EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications

 
 

 EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.

 
 

 EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.

 
 

 Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.

 
 

 Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.

 
 

 Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.

 
 

 Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.

 
 

 Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.

 
 

 Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.

 
 

 Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

 

See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information and Medication Guide.

INDICATION
EXALGO is an extended-release oral formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION
[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15839Covidien(Exalgo)PH_LG/wv4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_06t.jpg][http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15839Covidien(Exalgo)PH_LG/wv4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_06m.jpg]

[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15839Covidien(Exalgo)PH_LG/wv4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_07.jpg]


WARNING: POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE, IMPORTANCE OF
PROPER PATIENT SELECTION AND LIMITATIONS OF USE

Potential for Abuse
EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid analgesics. EXALGO can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. These risks should be considered when administering, prescribing, or dispensing EXALGO in situations where the healthcare professional is concerned about increased risk of misuse, abuse, or diversion. Schedule II opioid substances which include hydromorphone, morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, oxymorphone and methadone have the highest potential for abuse and risk of fatal overdose due to respiratory depression.

Proper Patient Selection
EXALGO is an extended-release formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients when a continuous around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extended period of time. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.
EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only.
Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.
Accidental consumption of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

Limitations of Use
EXALGO is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain.
EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic.
EXALGO tablets are to be swallowed whole and are not to be broken, chewed, dissolved, crushed or injected. Taking broken, chewed, dissolved or crushed EXALGO or its contents leads to rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.




[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15839Covidien(Exalgo)PH_LG/wv4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08t.jpg][http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15839Covidien(Exalgo)PH_LG/wv4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08m.jpg]



*


EXALGO is also contraindicated in patients who:
- need management of mild pain or pain not expected
  to persist
- have significant impaired respiratory function including
  those with acute or severe bronchial asthma or hypercarbia
- have or are suspected to have paralytic ileus
- have narrowed or obstructed gastrointestinal tract
  including those from previous surgery or "blind loops"
  in the GI tract
- have known hypersensitivity to any components including
  hydromorphone hydrochloride and sulfites


*


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


*


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


*


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison's disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


*


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


*


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


*


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible
to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


*


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO
