Subject: Important Corporate Marketing Update: Launch Plans - Specialty Pharmaceuticals
Importance: High



 

Hello API, Brands and Generics marketing leaders,

 

Many of you have seen much of our Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals marketing launch plan in pieces to date, and many have contributed as we have asked for your support and guidance on meeting local needs along the way. Pat Hastings, Brand Manager, and I thank you for your collaboration and valuable contributions.

 

As we are now less than two very short weeks away from the official launch, it is important to share with you the detailed plan and tools you will receive to aid our efforts to effectively launch the new company brand, and promote broad awareness of and engagement with Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals. Please share this information broadly among your marketing and sales leadership teams so they are aware of the launch plans. The files are not to be shared externally prior to spin. (The text from this email is also contained in an attached file.)

 

Here is the comprehensive plan specifically applicable to the three Specialty Pharmaceuticals  businesses:

 

-       Corporate Brochure: Developed in English and translated into a number of other languages; copies of the brochure will be distributed each business based on numbers provided, including translations as requested for the API business. Each employee worldwide will also receive a copy of the brochure.

o    The first samples of the printed brochure have been received, and it looks great. Distribution of the English version will begin this week, with the translated versions sent out sometime next week.

o    An electronic version of the brochure has been developed, which can be used on iPads or iPhones, or emailed if desired (2MB file). The English version of the file will be shared next week with instructions for how to use on Apple devices. We can convert the other languages to similar electronic versions as needed.

 

-       Corporate Ad: For your businesses, the corporate ad will be utilized at the corporate level on a number of pain management web sites and print publications as chosen by your teams. Full placement details will be provided later this week.

o    All ad placements will begin on July 1 and run through December, 2013.

o    A sample of the digital ad that will be used is attached. (To view it, save the zip file to your desktop, extract the swf file further to your desktop, and open with Internet Explorer.)

o    The print ad, which has a bit more text, as well as the digital ad is available as desired for use commercially if desired beyond the placements we re making at the corporate level. The general ad is attached. Please contact Pat Hastings or me with artwork requests.

o    Other ad placements are also being implemented for the Global Medical Imaging business.

o    Work is also underway with your teams related to convention sponsorships as part of the corporate launch plan.

 

-       Customer Direct Mail/E-Mailer: The print version of this tool is a variation on the corporate print ad, with additional text added specific to each business. The e-mailer will likely be a variation of the digital ad. 

o    The print file is attached. Note there are three variations on the back side of the card, one for each of your businesses where the products are reflected in the closing paragraph. (This has had PARC approval.)

o    The Brands business will be using the print version only (details provided to you separately on printing/timing); Generics will use e-mailer for most customers with exception of Addiction Treatment, where print version will be used. API will have the option of either.

o    Customer letters will also be made available for use announcing the spin. (API already has theirs.)

 

-       Corporate Web Site : A fantastic new web site has been developed and will launch on June 30 as the most readily and frequently accessed face of the new company. Annie Haarmann, Digital and Social Media Manager, has led this effort with strong collaboration across all businesses.

o    There are two sections of the site    corporate  content and product content. There is a deliberate and distinct separation of the two sections; visitors will be alerted by a brief pop-up message that they are leaving corporate content and going to a promotional area of the site if they click on any product categories.

o    Note all micro-sites of any kind (e.g. EXALGO) have also been rebranded; those rebranded sites will go live at spin as well.

 

-       Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals Story Presentation: A PowerPoint presentation is in development for use at or near separation that will incorporate elements from the corporate brochure, financial data and other elements deemed appropriate.

 

-       Business Cards, Stationery, Name Tags: Last Friday the announcement was made that Smart Source was chosen as the U.S. source for these materials. There have admittedly been a few glitches in the process, but we have worked through them and you and your teams should be fully able to place orders through Smart Source now.

 

-       Company Launch Press Release: On Monday morning, July 1, a press release will be issued announcing the completed separation of Covidien and Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals. The release will be distributed via international wire services.

o    If any of you have specific trade publications that you would like to have the release sent to, please send your lists to Diane or to me, including contact names and email addresses, and we will compile a list to provide to Lynn Phillips, Media Relations Manager.

o    As a reminder, all media inquiries must be directed to Lynn.

 

Additional General Promotional Plans

-       Mark Trudeau external launch video is being produced and will appear on the new web site (linked from our YouTube page)

-       NYSE Bell-Ringing/Ads: On Monday morning (US time), Mark Trudeau and others will ring the opening bell on the New York Stock Exchange. As part of that event package, we have corporate banners that will appear outside the Exchange, along with billboards and other advertising in the New York City area

-       Billboards: In the St. Louis area, there will be strategically placed billboards in three spots around the area, as well as ad placements in Lambert St. Louis International Airport.

-       Newspaper ads have been placed for opening day or soon thereafter in St. Louis and other cities where we have a manufacturing presence.

-       Facility signage is being replaced to reflect the new brand at all sites around the world, with the majority being completed by spin.

-       Social Media: Our initial steps into these waters will begin with YouTube and Linked In, with additional avenues being explored further into the future. More details about the process to utilize social media for commercial purposes will be shared in mid-July

 

Pat and I will be working closely with each team to distribute the materials noted above, and you will be kept informed as they become available.

 

In addition, a separate message will be sent related to the official launch of www.mpbranding.com which is expected in the next couple of days, so stay tuned for that.

 

If anyone has questions about any of the information provided above, please let me know. Contact Pat or me with any brand-related questions or further needs.  It s an intense, exciting time to be part of Mallinckrodt as we prepare for the next stage in our evolution as a company and the launch of Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals!

 

Thanks,
Nancy

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information<http://lists.jobson.com/t?r=4&c=36701&l=8583&ctl=54D84:733B4C71B177CE915389A685CD760E63&> and Medication Guide<http://lists.jobson.com/t?r=4&c=36701&l=8583&ctl=54D85:733B4C71B177CE915389A685CD760E63&>.

Subject: Family Practice News: Stratify Patients for Opioid Misuse and Abuse Risk

Hi JoAnna,

We wanted to be sure you saw this article published in Family Practice News, which highlights a presentation from Dr. Webster at the AMA House of Delegates Interim meeting. In his discussion he stressed the importance of clarifying misuse versus abuse, and further examining patients motives and stratifying based on risk. Dr. Webster specifically states "The potency of a pharmacologic substance and how fast it works are important, as those factors help determine how much dopamine is released, and thus, the amount of reward the patient feels," which falls in line with EXALGO's slow, steady release.

Please let us know if you have any questions.

[Logo]<http://www.familypracticenews.com/home.html>
Stratify Patients for Opioid Misuse and Abuse Risk
By: ALICIA AULT, Family Practice News Digital Network<mailto:a.ault@elsevier.com>
12/05/11
________________________________
FROM THE AMERICAN MEDICAL ASSOCIATION HOUSE OF DELEGATES INTERIM MEETING
________________________________
NEW ORLEANS - Do you know which of your patients is likely to misuse or abuse opioid medications?
They can be stratified according to risk, but many physicians don't know how or don't take the time to do so, according to Dr. Lynn R. Webster, medical director of Lifetree Clinical Research in Salt Lake City and director at large for the American Academy of Pain Medicine.
It is important to try to prevent misuse or abuse, given that overdoses and deaths from prescription drugs are on the rise, said Dr. Webster at the American Medical Association House of Delegates Interim meeting.
According to the National Institute on Drug Abuse<http://www.nida.nih.gov/infofacts/hospitalvisits.html>, emergency department visits involving nonmedical use of pharmaceuticals (either alone or in combination with another drug) increased 98% between 2004 and 2009, from 627,291 visits to 1.2 million visits. There was an 83% rise in emergency department visits involving adverse reactions to pharmaceuticals between 2005 and 2009, from 1.3 million to 2.3 million visits.
Opioids were the most frequently cited in those ED visits, accounting for about 50% of nonmedical use. Psychotherapeutic agents accounted for a third of the nonmedical use. According to the National Institute on Drug Abuse, the three most frequently cited drugs in those visits were hydrocodone (alone or in combination), accounting for 104,490 visits; oxycodone (alone or in combination), for 175,949 visits; and methadone, for 70,637 visits.
To properly assess and treat patients, physicians should understand and agree upon terminology, said Dr. Webster. Patients may "misuse" prescriptions if they are not taking them as directed. They aren't seeking a high, they may just have undertreated pain, he said.
Abuse is the willful self-administration of a drug to get high. Addiction is a medical condition with complex genetic, psychosocial, and environmental factors that influence its development and manifestations. Addicts may have impaired control over drug use, compulsive use, or continued use despite harm.
"You don't just put someone on an opioid and think you've done your job."
Pseudoaddiction results from undertreatment of pain, and may resolve with proper therapy. Patients in this state may manifest behavior that is misidentified as drug-seeking, according to Dr. Webster.
Even with chronic pain, "people prescribed opioids over a long period of time are going to have aberrant behavior," said Dr. Webster, noting that "it's not a small problem." In research he conducted, up to 40% of patients in his chronic pain practice had aberrant behavior within a year of starting treatment.
But, he said, "only a small percent have the disease of addiction."
To prevent misuse and abuse, it's important to understand patients' motives, he said. Nonmedical users may have been prescribed pain medications, but they move on to recreational use and then, often, abuse.
Medical users generally are pain patients who are seeking more pain relief and end up misusing the drugs. They also may become abusers. In all, 40%-60% have other chronic conditions for which opioids provide relief, such as anxiety, said Dr. Webster. That use is obviously not appropriate, but it can only be prevented if physicians fully assess pain patients.
There is a constellation of risk factors that help determine potential for misuse and abuse, according to Dr. Webster.
The potency of a pharmacologic substance and how fast it works are important, as those factors help determine how much dopamine is released, and thus, the amount of reward the patient feels, said Dr. Webster. If the drug is readily available, that also determines its attractiveness.
One-fifth of the overall population is at risk for addiction. There is no on/off switch, but a continuum of risk, he explained. Biological, psychiatric, and social factors all play a role in where patients fall on that continuum. Age, gender, family history, cigarette smoking, pain severity and duration, and sleep disorders are all risk factors. Patients with a history of a psychiatric disorder, being sexual abused, or substance use disorder also are at higher risk. "We must assess mental health," said Dr. Webster, noting that patients with anxiety, depression, traumatic brain injury, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder are at risk for self-medicating and overdose.
A history of legal problems and motor vehicle accidents, or poor family support and unemployment also are predictors, Dr. Webster said.
Aberrant behaviors are directly related to the duration and the intensity of pain. Patients who cannot completely eliminate their pain may resort to taking more medication, which they will see as less of a wrong than the pain itself, he said.
Physicians generally have not done a good job at evaluating these risks, and selecting and managing patients according to these factors. But how patients are managed can help determine whether they end up in the emergency room, "or going to a substance abuse treatment center or the morgue," he said.
There are tools that can be used to screen patients for risk. Among those are the Screener and Opioid Assessment for Patients With Pain (SOAPP); the Opioid Risk Tool (ORT); the Diagnosis, Intractability, Risk Efficacy (DIRE) test; and the Current Opioid Misuse Measure (COMM), which is used for patients already taking opioids.

[http://www.familypracticenews.com/uploads/RTEmagicC_2bh694wv_85390.graphic.im.jpg.jpg]

These tests all are simple and take only 1 to 10 minutes to administer. They can be given by any physician, including primary care physicians, he said.
Once all the factors are taken into account, patients can be stratified according to risk. Lower-risk patients - those with moderate pain and no personal or family history of substance use disorders - can be managed by primary care physicians. Those at moderate risk may need the addition of a pain specialist. The higher-risk patients will need consultations with mental health professionals and pain physicians.
Monitoring higher-risk patients may require urine drug testing and prescription monitoring programs. Pharmacists should be kept in the loop to see whether patients are shopping around. Family and friends can be invaluable sources to help identify risky behaviors.
Physicians need to do a better job of titrating opioids and determining proper dosing. Many patients have died at initiation of opioid therapy, or from rotating from one drug to another, he said. Patients should not be allowed to determine how much of a long-acting medication they can take.
So how do doctors mitigate risk? The first order of business is to treat the pain. "Uncontrolled pain, untreated pain, I believe is the number one reason for aberrant behavior," said Dr. Webster. Physicians cannot eliminate all pain, however, so education also is crucial.
Physicians also have a duty to monitor pain patients. "You don't just put someone on an opioid and think you've done your job," said Dr. Webster. A doctor would not stop managing a diabetic; pain patients need long-term management, he said.
Dr. Webster reported having no relevant conflicts of interest.

dosing strength; tablets should be swallowed whole.

INDICATION
EXALGO is an extended-release oral formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION
[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_06t.jpg][http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_06m.jpg]

[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_07.jpg]


WARNING: POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE, IMPORTANCE OF
PROPER PATIENT SELECTION AND LIMITATIONS OF USE

Potential for Abuse
EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid analgesics. EXALGO can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. These risks should be considered when administering, prescribing, or dispensing EXALGO in situations where the healthcare professional is concerned about increased risk of misuse, abuse, or diversion. Schedule II opioid substances which include hydromorphone, morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, oxymorphone and methadone have the highest potential for abuse and risk of fatal overdose due to respiratory depression.

Proper Patient Selection
EXALGO is an extended-release formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients when a continuous around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extended period of time. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.
EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only.
Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.
Accidental consumption of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

Limitations of Use
EXALGO is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain.
EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic.
EXALGO tablets are to be swallowed whole and are not to be broken, chewed, dissolved, crushed or injected. Taking broken, chewed, dissolved or crushed EXALGO or its contents leads to rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.




[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08t.jpg][http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08m.jpg]



*


EXALGO is also contraindicated in patients who:
- need management of mild pain or pain not expected
  to persist
- have significant impaired respiratory function including
  those with acute or severe bronchial asthma or hypercarbia
- have or are suspected to have paralytic ileus
- have narrowed or obstructed gastrointestinal tract
  including those from previous surgery or "blind loops"
  in the GI tract
- have known hypersensitivity to any components including
  hydromorphone hydrochloride and sulfites


*


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


*


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


*


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison's disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


*


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


*


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


*


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible
to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


*


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO

Subject: FDA Request - Exalgo Safety Analysis - Allergic Reactions - Sodium Metabisulfite

Commercial colleagues,

I want to make you aware of a recent FDA request for an analysis of the available data (Clinical development and post marketing) for the incidence of allergic reactions (Anaphylaxis, Anaphylactoid, Urticaria, Angioedema, etc.) associated with Exalgo. They have indicated they believe this is attributable to an excipient, Sodium Metabisulfite (See agency letter of request below). This is an important request, and could have significant impact on Exalgo, up to and including labeling change or even reformulation. It is my understanding that sodium metabisulfite is a component of the HM active ingredient rather than the OROS technology (Phil, please correct if I am mistaken). We are working with the agency to identify the appropriate analysis methodology and when they agree, we will conduct the review of data and provide the requested information.

John,

Do we know the potential implication of a request for reformulation with a API source of HM that does not contain sodium metabisulfite? Has a measure of this nature been discussed with our manufacturing partner?

Thanks.

jtp


Please refer to your New Drug Application (NDA) submitted under section 505(b) of the Federal
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) for EXALGO (hydromorphone HCl) 8-, 12-, and 16-mg
Extended-Release Tablets.
We also refer to your Periodic Safety Update Reports for Exalgo, received March 8 and June 30,
2011. These reports described cases of anaphylactic shock and pharyngeal edema/urticaria. A
preliminary search of the Adverse Events Reporting System (AERS) also identified cases
suggesting allergic reactions.
Given the occurrence of these cases, and the sodium metabisulfite component in the Exalgo
formulation, we request the following:
Review the Exalgo clinical development program, as well as your postmarket safety surveillance
system, to comprehensively describe cases of allergic reactions and hypersensitivity reactions
that have occurred with Exalgo exposure. This assessment should also include a review of the
medical literature to identify any published cases.
* Provide the proposed search strategy to identify cases to the Division for review prior to
conducting the evaluation.
* The description of the cases from the clinical development program should include a
section with narrative summaries for cases leading to discontinuation and a section with
narrative summaries for cases that qualified as serious adverse events. All cases should be
summarized in tabular form by preferred term, giving the number of cases and incidence
for each treatment arm. Please present data from randomized controlled trials separately
from open label trials.
* Describe separately the experience in the postmarket period. Each case should be
summarized in a narrative summary.

letter.

Abuse Potential
EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Life-threatening Respiratory Depression
Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.
Accidental Exposure
Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone. 


CONTRAINDICATIONS 
   EXALGO is contraindicated in: 
  - Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant. 
  - Patients with significant respiratory depression 
  - Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or in the absence of resuscitative equipment 
  - Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus 
  - Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction 
  - Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications 
   EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer. 
   EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist. 
   Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery. 
   Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO. 
   Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment. 
   Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO. 
   Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness. Post marketing events include hypersensitivity reactions, angioedema and urticaria. 
   Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention. 
   Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO. 
See Full Prescribing Information and Medication Guide.

I think it would be a good study. We have to assume that Exalgo data published after early 2013 has little to no value because of IP issues.

 

From: Rod Hughes [mailto:rhughes@synchronyhc.com]
Sent: Friday, June 03, 2011 6:15 AM
To: Neuman, Herbert R
Cc: Morelli, Art ; Patrick, Jeffrey
Subject: Phase IV Study on Conversion of EX



 

I know we have been thinking a good deal about REMS and CARES but I wanted to suggest a Phase IV study that I think would be very important for EXALGO.


I believe that this study could be used to communicate the ideal dosing strategy and could perhaps lead to a potential label change with regard to the 50% reduction in calculated dose.


 


Randomize subjects into three conversion groups


                A. Converting from other long-acting/ER opioid without reduction in starting dose (ie, like nearly every EXALGO study but two)


                B. 25% reduction in starting dose (ie, like 301 and 302)


                C. 50% reduction in starting dose (ie, never been tested and may be associated with significant 


For each of the groups titration would occur (if necessary) in the same manner


 


We would have to discuss what to do about supplemental medication. The advantage of the study would be to test the conversion and titration according to the label which, as you know, includes no supplemental medication. 


 


Primary Outcome Measure:


Percentage of patients who achieve a stable dose of EXALGO 


                This can be stratified by previous opioid therapy and dose


 


Secondary Outcome Measures:


·         Duration of time and number of titration steps required to titrate patients to a stable dose of EXALGO 

o    Overall

o    Stratified by conversion group

o    Stratified by prior opioid therapy

·         Measures of opioid withdrawal syndrome COWS/SOWS

o    Overall

o    Stratified according to conversion group

o    Stratified according to prior opioid dose

·         Morphine equivalent of stable dose

o    Overall 

o    Stratified by conversion group

o    Stratified by prior opioid therapy

·         Change from baseline in the NRS, and measures of Brief Pain Inventory 

·         Use of supplemental analgesics

·         Adverse events (treatment emergent)

o    It would be especially important to assess symptoms associated with potential withdrawal and symptoms associated with potential over dosage (eg, sedation)

·         Number of patients at various risk level as assessed by the investigator (low, moderate, high - according to SOAPP or ORT)

o    including prior/current concerns with prescription opioid misuse, abuse and/or diversion 

·         Number of patients with aberrant behaviors (Current Opioid Misuse Measure [COMM®] score ≥ 9)

·         Number of patients with abnormal urine drug screening results 

The latter assessments would be done to document a low incidence of aberrant behaviors

Colleagues,

I wanted to share with you a new initiative that Anthony Lassiter and I feel is crucial to moving forward as an independent pharmaceutical company.

That initiative is the creation of a Label Review Committee (LRC).  This committee would be responsible for three major areas:


1)     Driving changes to labels (i.e., package inserts) globally (and, in some cases, regionally) based on new information and/or requests from either internal (e.g., from our Signal Action Committee or other internal sources like the CCSI working group (see below)) or external (e.g., FDA or O-US regulatory agencies) sources.

2)     Approving company core safety information (sometimes referred to as CCDS or CCSI) documents.  These documents, common throughout the pharmaceutical industry but lacking for all but a couple (Optimark and Optiray) of our products, contain the core safety concepts that the company feels should appear in all labels, globally, for a product.   These documents are currently being generated by our relatively newly-formed CCSI working group.  The first one will be ready for approval by the second week in May at the latest.

3)     Helping to ensure alignment of labels (globally) to CCSI content.  This includes aiding, if requested, in addressing questions from local regulatory personnel and/or local regulatory agencies as variations are filed to account for changes due to CCSI content.

Anthony and I have talked through this and we believe that the membership of this committee should be:

Regulatory/Global Labeling: Dennis Nosco, chairperson
Pharmacovigilance: Anthony Lassiter
Legal: Joe Wuestner
Commercial: (business head of area, either Imaging or Specialty Pharma)
Scientific Affairs: Alfredo Bozzini

This committee could also include ad hoc members from other areas (e.g., Regulatory Strategy and CMC Regulatory, PK, Clinical Studies) as their special expertise is needed.

By this e-mail I am asking if all of you would either (a) agree to be on this committee or (b) designate someone from your area to be the representative on this committee.

Once I get agreement as to membership I will call our first meeting.  The timing of formation of this committee is crucial as we have our first new CCSI document that is about ready to be submitted to the LRC for review.  In addition, we have a company initiative regarding EXALGO labeling and inclusion of abuse deterrent safety language that will require this committee's input on language and help on getting these changes implemented globally)

As timing is short to get this committee operational please get back to me AND Anthony with any questions you have.  I would like to set up our first meeting for sometime in the next 3 weeks.

Thanks,

I thought that he was sending out a " smokescreen" until someone else brought it up..Today a PA called me due to a patient's XR script having to be switched due to the patient's concern over the same issue.. On our coupons and literature there is a very pronounced disclaimer regarding risk of abuse, death etc.. This is language that patient's and HCPs are familiar with regarding opioids.. What is articulated a little different that " put off" the physician and now patient is the language regarding how death can occur even if taken as prescribed and after other medicines basically are not adequate.. I understand what this means as someone can obviously die even if taking as prescribed due to various other variables.. Also I and most HCPs understand that an acute opioid is generally written after or when an NSAID etc will not suffice. The language though is strung together in a way though that HCPs have not seen with other opioids.. As for the patient the PA and physician "broke it all down" for them but the death even if taken as prescribed scared them.. I looked at all opioid leave behinds/ coupons as well as Zohydro's warnings and disclaimers and could not find anything like. They were all similar to Exalgo which breaks down for ex why risk of death or abuse.. I am just curious and would like feedback if this comes up again as to why our wording is a little different.. Although  it is saying the same thing as others it is in a more succinct and different manner that can be perceived as, " I risk dying if taking this even as prescribed and it should be last resort". My HCP thought that the language made him appear more liable if someone abuses etc and at a detriment if ever sued because it states clearly that can die and use other medicines first. I get it but what is the reason that our language is "different".. ? I know that they have " tightened" up on opioid labeling but again ours is unique.Sorry if provided too much info. Hopefully it makes sense.. Thanks so much!

Rachel

Why stock the 32 mg tablet?

 

 EXALGO 32 mg was the median effective dose in the pivotal trial.*1

 
 

 You may already be distributing multiple 16 mg tablets to patients.

 
*

 Mean effective dose was 37.8 mg.2

 

EXALGO TABLET STRENGTHS2

Tablets shown are not actual size.

START STOCKING EXALGO 32 MG TODAY!

REFERENCES: 1. Hale M, Khan A, Kutch M, Li S. Once-daily OROS hydromorphone ER compared with placebo in opioid-tolerant patients with chronic low back pain. Curr Med Res Opin. 2010;26(6):1505-1518.
2. EXALGO  Prescribing Information.

800-778-7898 | www.EXALGO.com

COVIDIEN, COVIDIEN with logo and Covidien logo are U.S. and internationally
registered trademarks of Covidien AG.
EXALGO is a registered trademark of Mallinckrodt LLC.
  2012 Mallinckrodt LLC, a Covidien company.  MK20164 September 2012

To ensure that you receive future email from EXALGO, add us to your address book.
If you no longer wish to receive email from EXALGO, unsubscribe now.

 INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

 

 

 EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications



 
 

 EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.



 
 

 EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.



 
 

 Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.



 
 

 Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.



 
 

 Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.



 
 

 Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.



 
 

 Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.



 
 

 Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.



 
 

 Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


 

See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information and Medication Guide.

Please join us for an important event!

 
THURSDAY, OCTOBER 18, 2012
Two Live Broadcasts
7:30 PM EST | 9:30 PM EST

 
 

You are invited to participate in the upcoming National
Broadcast Event "Important Considerations in Customizing
Pain Management: Patient Selection and Dosing Strategies."
The expert faculty panel will cover the following information:

 

 Establish a rationale for choosing a long-acting
extended-release opioid

 
 

 Define proper patient selection

 
 

 Explore dosing conversion and titration strategies

 
 

 Improve prescriber-patient communication to help
facilitate successful treatment outcomes

 

PROGRAM DETAILS



 See the Program Chair, Michael Brennan, MD, describe the importance of this educational event.

 


 
Important: At the conclusion of the video, you will be
directed to the Registration website. If you are in the
Eastern or Central time zones please use NEbroadcast for
your invitation code. If you live in the Mountain or Pacific time zones, please use WTbroadcast for your invitation code.
If you are unable to make it to a meeting site, you also can
view the event from your home computer.

 

This interactive program will be broadcast to 60 venues
throughout the United States on Thursday, October 18th,
and will include a complimentary dinner at each venue.
The first live broadcast begins at 7:30 PM EST; a second live
broadcast will begin at 9:30 PM EST.

SEATING IS LIMITED REGISTER TODAY!

RSVP today using one of the following methods:

1.

 Online at: www.HLXBroadcast.com. If you are in the
Eastern or Central time zones please use NEbroadcast for
your invitation code. If you live in the Mountain or Pacific
time zones, please use WTbroadcast for your invitation code.

 
2.

 Call: 800-111-0467.

 
3.

 Contact your Mallinckrodt sales representative for more
information.

 

This event is promotional; there are no certified continuing medical education credits approved for this presentation. Covidien proudly adheres to the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers Association Code for Interactions with Healthcare Professionals. Attendance must be limited strictly to healthcare professionals. Spouses and other guests cannot be accommodated. Thank You.

Expert Faculty Panel

Michael Brennan, MD (Program Chair)
The Pain Center of Fairfield
Fairfield, CT

Charles E. Argoff, MD, PhD
Albany Medical College
Albany Medical Center
Albany, NY

Joseph Shurman, MD
Scripps Memorial Hospital
San Diego, CA

In addition to a live Question and Answer session with the
nationally recognized faculty, there will be robust post-event discussion at each venue led by a local faculty speaker.

 


800-778-7898 | www.EXALGO.com

COVIDIEN, COVIDIEN with logo and Covidien logo are U.S. and internationally registered trademarks of Covidien AG. EXALGO is a registered trademark of Mallinckrodt LLC.
  2012 Mallinckrodt LLC, a Covidien company.  MK20185 October 2012

 INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION,
and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase.
Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

 

 

 EXALGO is contraindicated in:

- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 
 

 EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.



 
 

 EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.

 
 

 Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.

 
 

 Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.

 
 

 Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.

 
 

 Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.

 
 

 Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.

 
 

 Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.

 
 

 Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


 

See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information and Medication Guide.

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

		To: #MKG - Pharma Field Sales
		Cc: Harrell, Jamie; Novak, Rod P; Webb, Kevin J; Grelle, Edward G; Patterson, Mike E; Kast, Mike; Lierman, Jennifer A; Albonico, Lisa A; Rausch, Ryan; Crandall, Margaret A
		Subject: Oxecta
		

		Field Sales Force -

		As a follow up to the voicemail message I left last week, below is some additional information relative to the newest entrant in the pain space -Oxecta.

		On June 20th, Pfizer Inc. and Acura Pharmaceuticals Inc. announced the marketing approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) of OXECTA (oxycodone HCl, USP) Tablets CII. OXECTA is an immediate-release oral formulation of oxycodone HCl indicated for the management of acute and chronic moderate to severe pain where the use of an opioid analgesic is appropriate.

		Oxecta is available in two dosing strengths 5mg and 7.5mg of oxycodone HCl.  Currently, generic oxycodone immediate release tablets are available in 5mg, 10mg, 15mg, 20mg and 30mg strengths.  The recommended dosing interval for Oxecta is every 4 to 6 hours, similar to other immediate release oxycodone products.  The Oxecta label does indicate it is not amenable to crushing and dissolution; however, it also states the product may be abused by crushing, chewing, snorting or injecting the product.  

		Also, caution is advised when initiating oxycodone treatment, including Oxecta, in patients currently taking or discontinuing CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers.  
		Remember unlike Exalgo or hydromorphone, oxycodone is metabolized through the CYP450 system.

		Oxecta peak plasma concentrations occur on average within 1.2 to 1.4 hours of the first dose.  Thereafter, oxycodone concentrations fall with an average terminal half-life ranging between 3-4 hours.  Oxecta is bioequivalent with other oxycodone immediate-release tablets with no differences identified in the time to peak exposure (tMax) and terminal elimination half-life (T ½) of oxycodone between administration of Oxecta and the other oxycodone immediate-release tablets.  

		In a double-blind, active-comparator, crossover study in 40 non-dependent recreational opioid users, "drug liking" responses and single-dose safety of crushed OXECTA tablets were compared with Other crushed immediate-release Oxycodone tablets when subjects self-administered the drug intranasally.  The presence of sequence effects resulted in questionable reliability of the second period data. First period data demonstrated small numeric differences in the median and mean drug liking scores, lower in response to OXECTA than immediate-release oxycodone. Thirty percent of subjects exposed to OXECTA responded that they would not take the drug again compared to 5% of subjects exposed to immediate-release oxycodone. Study subjects self-administering OXECTA reported a higher incidence of nasopharyngeal and facial adverse events and a decreased ability to completely insufflate two crushed tablets within a fixed time period (21 of 40 subjects). The clinical significance of the difference in drug liking and difference in response to taking the drug again reported in this study has not yet been established.

		There is no evidence that OXECTA has a reduced abuse liability compared to immediate-release oxycodone.
		
		In conclusion, Oxecta is another immediate release oxycodone product, with a minimal range of doses.  While it may appear to have physical properties unique to immediate release oxycodone products, it has no approved claims pertaining to tamper resistance or abuse deterrence.  

		It is critical you continue to message to the unique benefits of hydromorphone, as well as the showcase how the OROS technology has transformed the hydromorphone in Exalgo.  Remember if a patient is unable to tolerate a generic oxycodone product, why would a physician select Oxecta as the next choice?  In fact, arguably Exalgo would be the most logical selection for these opioid tolerant chronic pain patients.  It is more potent, the moiety or active ingredient is dissimilar to oxycodone (unlike another oxycodone product or oxymorphone) and it has good product access, especially given the new co pay card and some of our recent Managed Care wins. 

		As important, our competitive advantage is the physician has you as a resource for Exalgo! 
		
		If you have any questions regarding the product, please do not hesitate to contact me.

		Take care and good selling.

INDICATION
EXALGO is an extended-release oral formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

Potential for Abuse
EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid analgesics. EXALGO can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. These risks should be considered when administering, prescribing, or dispensing EXALGO in situations where the healthcare professional is concerned about increased risk of misuse, abuse, or diversion. Schedule II opioid substances which include hydromorphone, morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, oxymorphone and methadone have the highest potential for abuse and risk of fatal overdose due to respiratory depression.

Proper Patient Selection
EXALGO is an extended-release formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients when a continuous around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extended period of time. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.
EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only.
Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.
Accidental consumption of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

EXALGO is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain.
EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic.
EXALGO tablets are to be swallowed whole and are not to be broken, chewed, dissolved, crushed or injected. Taking broken, chewed, dissolved or crushed EXALGO or its contents leads to rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.




[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08t.jpg][http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08m.jpg]

- have narrowed or obstructed gastrointestinal tract

- have known hypersensitivity to any components including
  hydromorphone hydrochloride and sulfites

Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


*

May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:

- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

FDA approves abuse-deterrent labeling for reformulated OxyContin
Agency will not approve generics to original OxyContin
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved updated labeling for Purdue Pharma L.P.'s
reformulated OxyContin (oxycodone hydrochloride controlled-release) tablets. The new labeling indicates
that the product has physical and chemical properties that are expected to make abuse via injection
difficult and to reduce abuse via the intranasal route (snorting).
Additionally, because original OxyContin provides the same therapeutic benefits as reformulated
OxyContin, but poses an increased potential for certain types of abuse, the FDA has determined that the
benefits of original OxyContin no longer outweigh its risks and that original OxyContin was withdrawn
from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness. Accordingly, the agency will not accept or approve any
abbreviated new drug applications (generics) that rely upon the approval of original OxyContin.
The FDA approved the original formulation of OxyContin in Dec. 1995. The product was abused, often
following manipulation intended to defeat its extended -release properties. Such manipulation causes the
drug to be released more rapidly, which increases the risk of serious adverse events, including overdose
and death. In April 2010, the FDA approved a reformulated version of OxyContin, which was designed to be
more difficult to manipulate for purposes of misuse or abuse. Purdue stopped shipping original OxyContin
to pharmacies in August 2010.
"The development of abuse-deterrent opioid analgesics is a public health priority for the FDA," said
Douglas Throckmorton, M.D., deputy director for regulatory programs in the FDA's Center for Drug
Evaluation and Research. "While both original and reformulated OxyContin are subject to abuse and misuse,
the FDA has determined that reformulated OxyContin can be expected to make abuse by injection difficult
and expected to reduce abuse by snorting compared to original OxyContin."
The FDA has determined that the reformulated product has abuse-deterrent properties. The tablet is more
difficult to crush, break, or dissolve. It also forms a viscous hydrogel and cannot be easily prepared
for injection. The agency has determined that the physical and chemical properties of the reformulated
product are expected to make the product difficult to inject and to reduce abuse via snorting. However,
abuse of OxyContin by these routes, as well as the oral route, is still possible. The reformulated
product also may reduce incidents of therapeutic misuse, such as crushing the product to sprinkle it onto
food or to administer it through a gastric tube. When FDA finds that a new formulation has abuse
deterrent properties, the agency has the authority to require generics to have abuse-deterrent properties
also
The agency review of this issue included an analysis of the following:

MNKOI 0000602185

 Citizen petitions requesting that the agency determine whether original oxyContin was
voluntarily withdrawn from sale for reasons other than safety or effectiveness;
comments submitted to the public dockets associated with these petitions;
Information concerning original and reformulated oxyContin and the withdrawal of original
oxyContin;
clinical data, peer-reviewed literature, and other information concerning postmarketing adverse
events associated with original oxyContin, reformulated oxyContin, and other extended -release oxycodone
products.
Postmarketing assessments of the impact of reformulated oxyContin on abuse are ongoing, and the FDA will
update its evaluation of the effects of reformulated oxyContin on abuse as new data become available.
The FDA, together with other public health agencies, continues to encourage the development of abusedeterrent formulations of opioids and believes that such products will help reduce prescription drug
abuse. At the same time, the FDA remains committed to ensuring that patients with pain have appropriate
access to °plaid analgesics.

Estimate Changes

 
Mallinckrodt plc

 
We maintain our SELL rating and $34PT, which we arrive at via two valuation methods: a 7.1x multiple on our 2013 EBITDA estimate of $382 million, and a P/E multiple (11.6x our CY13 EPS estimate of $2.92). We believe MNK s current premium valuation is NOT warranted, as we think F 14 sales and earnings are likely to fall as a result of increased competition within its pharmaceutical segment. Key products (generic Concerta and Exalgo) are expected to face competition, likely leading to a fall in sales and profits beginning in the first quarter of F 14. While the Company updated its F 13 financial guidance to reflect sales growth of 8-10% (from 7-11%), with specialty pharma segment sales growth of 22-25% (from 21-25%), and medical imaging sales declines of -5 to -8% (from -3 to -7%). We believe F 14 financial guidance (expected to be announced by the end of October) could be far less robust. In F 14, we expect sales declines for generic Concerta and branded Exalgo, as generic competition enters. In addition, with the Company preparing for a potential approval and launch of MNK-795 (an extended-release hydrocodone / acetaminophen combo product with abuse deterrent technology for the relief of acute, moderate to severe pain), we believe SG&A costs are likely to increase. On last Friday s call, management indicated its plans to expand its current 200-person sales force by 50-100%. As a result, we have increased our annual SG&A cost estimates by ~$45 million/year.

 

Lowering F 13-F 16 EPS forecasts to $2.89, $2.27, $2.50, and $2.75, from $3.18, $2.61, $2.73, and $2.87, respectively. We have increased our F 14-F 16 revenue forecasts to reflect a greater contribution from its two new drug pipeline products, MNK-795 and MNK-155, both abuse deterrent formulations of acetaminophen containing combination pain products. Combined, our new F 13-F 15 estimates include sales of $25 million, $120 million, and $200 million, up from $10 million, $60 million, and $80 million, respectively. While MNK-795 was recently granted a priority review, we believe much is riding on the Company s ability to garner an abuse-deterrent label. While management indicated on its call that it feels it has done all of the necessary pre-clinical and clinical work to garner such a label, we believe the FDA s decision here is an upcoming binary event, which could have a significant impact on MNK s share price.

 

Investment Summary   SELL/$34PT. We maintain our SELL rating and $34PT, which we arrive at via two valuation methods, a 7.1x multiple on our 2013 EBITDA est. of $382 million, and a P/E multiple (11.6x our CY13 EPS estimate of $2.92). MNK shares currently trade at 15.5x our new CY13 EPS estimate of $2.92, and 19.9x our new CY14 EPS estimate of $2.28. On average, we believe MNK shares are trading at a 58% premium to its peers on a forward P/E multiple basis. Based on our expectations for MNK to face additional competition on several of its key pharmaceutical products (generic Concerta, and Exalgo) in the second half of 2013, we believe F 14 revenue could fall approximately (4.6%) vs. F 13, with EPS dropping to $2.27 (21% YOY) in F 14. With F 14 expected to be a transition year, we believe MNK shares could drop 25% from current levels.
