Roge,

 

There will be two phases to complete the Generics separation 1) 12-31 plan (Accounting changes), and 2) Generics Alignment Project (update contracts, licenses, registrations, complete the separation, etc.)

 

12-31 Plan:

 

This phase is designed to separate the financials by Jan 1.

 

The name of the new Generics legal entity will be SpecGx LLC.  It should be formed this week, but it will not be operational from an accounting standpoint until December 31, 2016.  Similar to Mallinckrodt APAP LLC, the new entity will not be  operationalized  for the outside world.  For example, even though fixed assets do not legally transfer to the new entity, we will account for the fixed assets as if they have transferred.  Following is additional information regarding the upcoming changes related to this new legal entity.

 

Effective December 31, 2016, Mallinckrodt LLC will be assigned JDE company 00003, which was assigned to Mallinckrodt Enterprises LLC through December 30, 2016, and journal entries will be prepared to move the appropriate general ledger balances from JDE company 00008 accounts to JDE company 00003 accounts, which will include the December 30, 2016 equity balances of JDE company 00008.  There is no historical data conversion.  For employees affected by this change (Corporate, Shared Services, etc.), their cost centers will begin with "003" instead of "008" or  157  effective December 31.  To the extent possible, we will keep the remaining 9 digits of the cost centers the same.  A detailed review of balance sheet accounts will be conducted to support the movement between JDE general ledger companies (there is no actual movement of assets or liabilities between legal entities).  Mallinckrodt LLC non-Generics businesses will also remain in Mallinckrodt LLC, and I believe these currently are XARTEMIS (MNK-795/155) and Fluorite.  AAIs will be changed for the Mallinckrodt LLC activity that is moving to JDE company 00003 effective December 31, 2016.

 

A new legal entity (SpecGx LLC) will be formed to include the Generics business plus specific Specialty Brands products (Gablofen, CNS non-promoted, Roxicodone and Exalgo), and it will include facilities at St. Louis Plant, Webster Groves and Hobart (Greenville and Raleigh API are included in Mallinckrodt APAP LLC for accounting).  SpecGx LLC will commence accounting operations effective December 31, 2016, which is the first day of the January fiscal period.  SpecGx LLC will be assigned JDE company 00008 effective December 31, 2016, and this will alleviate the need to make many system changes for this new legal entity.  The appropriate equity balances will be recorded in JDE company 00008 for SpecGx LLC effective December 31, 2016 (e.g., common stock, additional paid in capital). 

 

We will assign the existing Mallinckrodt LLC disbursement and lockbox bank accounts to the new legal entity (SpecGx LLC) and set up new disbursement and lockbox bank accounts for Mallinckrodt LLC no later than April 1, 2017 in time for the SAP conversion.  We will continue to use the existing Mallinckrodt LLC disbursement and lockbox bank accounts until the new bank accounts are set up for Mallinckrodt LLC.

 

Generics Alignment Project

 

This project will begin after the  kick off  on December 5 and will continue well into 2017.  The most significant parts of this phase include:

1)      Identification and assessment of all impacted contracts, including updates and approvals if required

Congressman Hal Rogers (R-Ky.), Chairman of the House Appropriations Committee, held a
September 20 briefing featuring findings from a new white paper entitled, "Prescription Drug Monitoring
Programs: An Assessment of the Evidence of Best Practices."
The white paper finds that PDMPs are an "underutilized resource" in the overall effort to address
prescription drug abuse. The report provides background information on the establishment of PDMPs,
a framework to measure effectiveness, describes best practices and proposes research into additional
practices to properly determine effectiveness to enhance PDMP use in addressing prescription drug
abuse. The report, authored by Brandeis University's Prescription Drug Monitoring Program Center of
Excellence, and sponsored by the Pew Charitable Trust, makes a number of recommendations,

CMS Releases Supplemental Guidance on Drug Utilization Reviews in
Medicare Part D
On August 31, CMS released additional supplemental guidance to Part D plan sponsors related to
improving drug utilization reviews (DURs) to understand and comply with the opioid overutilization
policy for Medicare Part D in 2013. More specifically, the 2013 Medicare Part D Call Letter requires
plan sponsors to comply with drug utilization management requirements to prevent overuse of opioids,
and in particular, CMS' guidance focuses observations from case management pilots, modifications
from the agency's previous memo and analysis of the morphine equivalent dose in Medicare Part D
Program.
For more information, contact Allison Wilms.

consumer protection issues. Originally, comments on the questions included in the notice were due

allow DEA registrants to "know their customer" and compare that activity to a bank's obligation to report $10,000 transactions to
law enforcement for detection of money laundering while having the ability  to detect multiple transactions at $9,999.

 On-site visits for all controlled substance customers
 Close scrutiny of small, independent pharmacies
 Close scrutiny of pain management clinics

{DEA Announces New Ways for the Public to Dispose of Unused Controlled Substances}DEA Announces New Ways for the Public to Dispose of Unused Controlled Substances

By Shannon O'Boye on September 8, 2014 Posted in Drug Policy

{Description: http://deachronicles.quarles.com/files/2014/09/Prescription_bottle_DEA_Blog-108x150.gif}Beginning next month, consumers will have an easier time getting rid of unused painkillers and other addictive drugs, which DEA hopes will discourage people from flushing the drugs down the toilet, throwing them in the garage, or leaving them, forgotten, in their medicine cabinets. The new disposal methods include allowing people to drop off unwanted pills at pharmacies, some hospitals and long-term care facilities, and police stations.

DEA s Final Rule, which implements the Secure and Responsible Drug Disposal Act of 2010 ( the Disposal Act ) by expanding the options to collect controlled substances back from ultimate users, is expected to be released tomorrow and will take effect on October 9. The disposal methods include take-back events, mail-back programs, and drop-off locations.

The new regulations:

allow authorized retail pharmacies; hospitals and clinics with on-site pharmacies; manufacturers; distributors; reverse distributors; and narcotic treatment programs (NTPs), to place collection receptacles inside their establishments and to permit people to mail back unwanted controlled substance mediations;
expand the authority of authorized pharmacies and hospitals/clinics to place collection receptacles inside long-term care facilities; and
allow law enforcement agencies to place collection receptacles inside their stations, conduct drug take-back events, and administer mail-back programs. (Note that law enforcement agencies are not required to use collection receptacles that meet all of the specifications in the rule.)

DEA registrants that want to become controlled substances  collectors  will need authorization from the Agency to keep secure containers at their locations for controlled substances drop off or to conduct mail-back programs. A registrant may seek to modify its DEA registration to become a collector by making a written request by mail or online. Retail pharmacies and hospitals/clinics that become collectors will be allowed to put collection receptacles inside long-term care facilities for those facilities  residents.

For security reasons, collection receptacles must be securely fastened to a permanent structure. In addition, as a general rule, the collection receptacles must be placed in the immediate proximity of a designated area where controlled substances are stored and where an employee is present. Hospitals/clinics, which would have difficulty meeting that requirement, must place receptacles in locations that are regularly monitored by employees and are not in the proximity of any area where emergency or urgent care is provided.

Collection receptacles must be accessible to the public because only the ultimate users of the drugs are authorized to place the controlled substances in a receptacle. Pharmacy and hospital staff cannot take the drugs and put them into a container.

Registrants that choose to conduct mail-back programs must be able to destroy returned packages on site. And registrants must provide customers with mail-back packages. They can charge for the packaging, or provide the packaging for free.

The new rule permits controlled substances collected through take-back events, mail-back programs, and collection receptacles to be comingled with non-controlled substances.

Other highlights of the Rule:

Methods of Destruction:

DEA is not requiring a specific method of destruction for controlled substances that are collected. Registrants are free to develop their own methods of destruction so long as, in the end, the drug is  non-retrievable , which means the condition or state to which a controlled substance must be rendered following a process that permanently alters the controlled substance s physical or chemical condition or state through irreversible means and thereby renders the controlled substance unavailable and unusable for all practical purposes. See 21 C.F.R.   1300.05(b). Once a controlled substance is  non-retrievable,  it is not longer subject to DEA requirements.

Long-Term Care Facilities:

In addition to allowing retail pharmacies and hospitals/clinics with on-site pharmacies to place collection receptacles in LTCFs for residents, DEA is also implementing special security requirements for these collection receptacles to encourage their use.

First, DEA is permitting sealed inner liners that have been removed from collection receptacles to be stored at LTCFs for up to three business days in a securely-locked, substantially constructed cabinet or in a securely-locked room with controlled access until the liners can be transferred for destruction. However, DEA is encouraging authorized collectors to schedule inner liner removals on the same day that medications are delivered, if possible, to make storage of sealed inner liners unnecessary.

It is also important to note that collectors cannot transfer sealed inner liners from LTCFs to their registered locations (i.e., the pharmacy or hospital/clinic). DEA is concerned that pharmacy or hospital/clinic employees transporting large quantities of controlled substances pose a security risk. Therefore, collectors must deliver sealed inner liners to a reverse distributor or a distributor by common or contract carrier or by reverse distributor or distributor pick-up at the LTCF.

Second, collectors will be allowed to have one of its employees and a supervisory level employee of the LTCF (e.g., a charge nurse, supervisor, or similar employee) install, remove, store, or transfer inner liners, or the collector can have two of its own employees do the work.

DEA hopes that these modifications will result in expanded safe and secure disposal options for LTCF residents.

DEA Registrant Disposal:

DEA has modified DEA Form 41 and is requiring that the form to be used to record the destruction of controlled substances that remain in the closed system of distribution and to account for the destruction of controlled substances collected from consumers and other non-registrants pursuant to the Disposal Act.

Reverse Distributors:

DEA added a definition of  reverse distribute,  revised the definition of  reverse distributor , and clarified that the security, inventory, and recordkeeping requirements for controlled substance destruction apply to some entities that reverse distribute even if they are not required to register as reverse distributors.

In addition, DEA has extended the time that a registrant that reverse distributes has to destroy controlled substances to 30 days, from the proposed 14 days.

Distributors may acquire controlled substances from collectors for the purpose of destruction, as a coincident activity to distribution.

The rules are intended to expand the options available to safely and securely dispose of potentially dangerous prescription medications on a routine basis. Beginning in 2010, DEA has sponsored eight National Prescription Drug Take-Back events around the country that resulted in the collection of more than 4.1 millions pounds (over 2,100 tons) of medication at over 6,000 locations.

         Risk of $0M   $20M

         Generics risk of $1M-$7M vs. the July LE for 2017.

o   IDA Foundation order for Vietnam Methadose was cancelled $3M. 

o   Grunenthal has not been willing to pull forward Hydro APAP and Methadone orders for Columbia $2M.  Unless we are able to work something out, the timing would be pushed out from November 2017 to May 2018.

o   Sinopharm Oxy APAP for China was in the July LE at $2M in August.  They have since doubled the order to $4M for shipment in September.  Risk remains as timing of securing import/export permits prior to our legal entity change will be very tight. 

         API risk of $14M vs. the July LE.

o   Import/export permit processing timing in a number of geographies $11M.

o   FMA (Foreign Manufacturer Accreditation) update timing in Japan $3M. 

 

2.       The range of potential implications of the latest DEA answer (re-registration need)   you can include into the above, but call out separately please. Please call out deviation from July LE

         Open   Waiting for feedback from Mark. 

 

3.       The latest estimate on generic Concerta revenue this year, and rationale for any change. Please call out potential deviation from July LE as well.

         Risk of $0M - $15M due to competitive launches and potential FDA actions. 

         QBR scenarios are still valid.

         July YTD Net Sales of $47M.

         July LE reflected the high case of $68M. 

         However, our current outlook is closer to the base case of $65M. 

         Timing of Osmotica and Impax launches could present further risk.  However, Osmotica has taken 600 kg of API to date. 

         Low case which reflected earlier launches from Osmotica and Impax was at $52M.   

 

4.       As per my email from yesterday: commentary on our July Gx revenue numbers / recovery chances. George, I can show you my data from the screenshot I received   so you know what I was referring to.

         July Sales are projected to be $5M below the July LE in Generics with three primary drivers:

o   Concerta is down $2M we lost the Rite-Aid Business (~20% of our Concerta sales) and McKesson is adjusting their inventory levels accordingly. 

o   Shelf Stock Adjustments related to the Econdisc for pricing changes under their RFP $0.7M and Walmart for pricing changes related to ClarusONE portfolio offer $0.8M.

o   Post Audit Claims for Shelf Stock Adjustments from Walgreens $1.1M and Walmart $0.7M.  These claims are corrections for historical periods (2015 Walgreens and 2016 Walmart) that resulted from routine detailed audits of transactional data performed by our customers.

 

5.       Anything we would change on guidance/LE? Still within the 13-16% range?

         Consider raising the upper limit of the range to 17%

         Low end of current guidance is our July LE which reflects a 13% decline.

         2016 Net Sales base is $981M vs. July LE of $850M.

         The above downside risks total $40M including the $5M miss in the current July sales projection.  This would put us at $810M or a decline of 17%.

Frank

From: mcaverly@us.imshealth.com [mailto:mcaverly@us.imshealth.com]
Sent: Tuesday, September 27, 2016 3:41 PM
To: Harper, Karen
Subject: RE: CONFIDENTIAL MALLINCKRODT INQUIRY: Transfer of a Product Line Within the Mallinckrodt Portfolio to Another DEA Registrant



 

Hi Karen.  Sale or transfer of one or more controlled substance product lines from Hobart would not invoke 1301.52 if Hobart continues manufacturing of other controlled substance products.  The only issue you should explore is a modification of the existing DEA registration should the product transfer result in a discontinuance of a specific Schedule(s).  For example, if Hobart will no longer manufacture any Schedule II products after the transfer you should consider modifying the existing DEA registration and drop Schedule II.  Other actions, such as returning unused quota to DEA, should also be performed.  

 

DEA will require a modification request be made in writing to the local DEA office if in the middle of a registration cycle.  At renewal, you can just not check that box for the applicable Schedule.

 

Thanks,

Mark

 

From: Harper, Karen [mailto:Karen.Harper@mallinckrodt.com]
Sent: Tuesday, September 27, 2016 4:10 PM
To: Mark CAVERLY <mcaverly@us.imshealth.com>
Subject: CONFIDENTIAL MALLINCKRODT INQUIRY: Transfer of a Product Line Within the Mallinckrodt Portfolio to Another DEA Registrant



 

Mark,

Mallinckrodt is evaluating the possibility of transferring a segment of existing business (methadose liquid and methadone tablet) to a third party DEA registrant.

At such time of potential transfer, Mallinckrodt Hobart will discontinue manufacture of this product line but continue production of other controlled substances.

 

Mallinckrodt will retain its existing DEA Manufacturer Certificate of Registration at the Hobart facility for other products, so there is technically no termination of registration, no transfer of registration, no distribution upon discontinuance of business (except the exit of a segment of the business).

 

Don and I have been asked to explore the regulatory requirements around such a move.

Would the provisions of  1301.52 apply in this circumstance?                             

OR would the transaction simply be a distribution of product?

 

MODIFICATION, TRANSFER AND TERMINATION OF REGISTRATION
 1301.52 Termination of registration; transfer of registration; distribution upon discontinuance of business.

(d) Any registrant desiring to discontinue business activities altogether or with respect to controlled substance (by transferring such business activities to another person) shall submit in person or by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, to the Special Agent in Charge in his/her area, at least 14 days in advance of the date of the proposed transfer (unless the Special Agent in Charge waives this time limitation in individual instances), the following information:
(1) The name, address, registration number, and authorized business activity of the registrant discontinuing the business (registrant-transferor);
(2) The name, address, registration number, and authorized business activity of the person acquiring the business (registrant-transferee);
(3) Whether the business activities will be continued at the location registered by the person discontinuing business, or moved to another location (if the latter, the address of the new location should be listed);
(4) Whether the registrant-transferor has a quota to manufacture or procure any controlled substance listed in Schedule I or II (if so, the basic class or class of the substance should be indicated); and
(5) The date on which the transfer of controlled substances will occur.
(e) Unless the registrant-transferor is informed by the Special Agent in Charge, before the date on which the transfer was stated to occur, that the transfer may not occur, the registrant-transferor may distribute (without being registered to distribute) controlled substances in his/her possession to the registrant-transferee in accordance with the following:
(1) On the date of transfer of the controlled substances, a complete inventory of all controlled substances being transferred shall be taken in accordance with Sec. 1304.11 of this chapter. This inventory shall serve as the final inventory of the registrant-transferor and the initial inventory of the registrant-transferee, and a copy of the inventory shall be included in the records of each person. It shall not be necessary to file a copy of the inventory with the Administration unless requested by the Special Agent in Charge. Transfers of any substances listed in Schedule I or II shall require the use of order forms in accordance with part 1305 of this chapter.
(2) On the date of transfer of the controlled substances, all records required to be kept by the registrant-transferor with reference to the controlled substances being transferred, under part 1304 of this chapter, shall be transferred to the registrant-transferee. Responsibility for the accuracy of records prior to the date of transfer remains with the transferor, but responsibility for custody and maintenance shall be upon the transferee.
(3) In the case of registrants required to make reports pursuant to part 1304 of this chapter, a report marked "Final" will be prepared and submitted by the registrant-transferor showing the disposition of all the controlled substances for which a report is required; no additional report will be required from him, if no further transactions involving controlled substances are consummated by him. The initial report of the registrant-transferee shall account for transactions beginning with the day next succeeding the date of discontinuance or transfer of business by the transferor-registrant and the substances transferred to him shall be reported as receipts in his/her initial report.

  Sun Pharmaceuticals and Caraco overview (November 2011) 
  INS NSP data is attached to the email for your review 


  1. API - In November 2008 Sun Pharmaceuticals acquired 100% ownership of chattem chemicals, Inc 
  from Elcat, Inc. chattem was a narcotic importer for methamphetamine, phenylacetone, raw opium and 
  concentrate poppy straw. They are licensed by the DEA to manufacture schedule 1 to 5 controlled 
  substances. For the year ending 2008, chattem was estimated to have sales of USD 26 million. In a 
  recent company earnings release, sun called out an 8% increase in the API facility revenue as well as 
  bringing 5 new API products on-line in 2011. company press releases state that the cranbury' NJ 
  manufacturing facility (the old Able Labs) sources its API from the chattem API plant for controlled 
  substances. 



  Z. DOSAGE MANUFACTURING - In 2005 Sun Pharmaceuticals acquired the site in cranbury, NJ (the old 
  Able Labs that was in Bankruptcy court} which was authorized to manufacture finished dosage forms for 
  controlled substances. This is named by sun as their only site in the us authorized to manufacture 
  finished dosage forms of controlled substances. Products manufactured at the cranbury' NJ plant include 
  HYCD-APAP, Promethazine and oxycodone. There are at least two other controlled substances 
  manufactured there - I believe these may be codeine APAP and ADHD medications. 



  In August 2010, Sun received an FDA warning letter for the Cranbury facility; the FDA reinspected in 
  June 2011 and a press release in September 2011 stated all issues had been resolved. In reviewing the 
  483 associated with the warning letter, there were citations involving gemfibrozil, promethazine, 
  oxycodone (broken tablets and repackaging quality issues) as well as one mention of stability data issues 
  for certain lots of HYCD-APAP from I2/08-12/09. 



  a. I noted per the INS NSP data that oxycodone HCL shipments out began in August 2011 and escalated 
  in September of 2011; the October 2011 data shows shipment of 2.8 million tablets for all three strengths 
  (~2.0 million were the 30 mg). They are shipping 5 mg, 15 mg and 30 mg strengths. It appears to have 
  taken them about 3 months to get back up to near pre-interruption capacity. sun pharma mentioned in some 
  of their documents that they would be bringing back products a few at a time and that ramp-up to full 
  capacity would happen slowly. 



  b. I also noted that there was a similar ramp-up of Codeine-Promethazine in the September-October 
  timeframe in the INS NSP data. 



  c. Finally, INS NSP data shipments of the HYCD-APAP 5-325 strength have begun as of October 2011 
  (220,000 tablets). The other strengths (7.5-325, I0-325 and 10-660) have not yet begun shipping as of 
  October 2011 NSP data. My estimate is that they will be back up to full capacity by the end of January 
  for HYCD-APAP with all 325 mg strengths. I question whether they will bother with the I0-660 as the 
  volume was not significant prior to interruption. 



  3. CARACO - Caraco (now a wholly owned subsidiary of sun Pharmaceuticals) distributes controlled 
  substances for sun Pharmaceuticals including HYCD APAP, Promethazine and Roxicodone (oxycodone HCL). 
  They also have their own manufacturing facility which is currently under consent decree and is not 
  manufacturing. The only pain-related product manufactured in the Detroit facility was Tramadol (not a 
  controlled substance). several publically available news articles implied that certain AmoAs were being 
  transferred to the Cranbury Facility in order that they might continue shipping products; specifically 
  10-12 Amoxs. In looking at the INS data there are certain products that have not dropped off in the NSP

New York State EDI Report Requirements

 http://www.nyhealth.gov/professionals/narcotic/facilities/2010-01_distributor_controlled_substances_letter.htm

Users Manual

http://www.nyhealth.gov/professionals/narcotic/facilities/2009-12-15_manual_manufacturers_distributers.htm

 

Manufacturers and distributors located within New York State must transmit information from all controlled substances sales. Manufacturers and distributors located outside of New York State must transmit information only from controlled substances sales to DEA registrants located within New York State. Reverse distributors must transmit information from the return of controlled substances from DEA registrants located within New York State. See applicable 'sales transaction' codes in Section VIII.

 

Manufacturers and distributors that use a third-party to distribute all controlled substances are exempt from the requirement to report controlled substance sales. Such exemption is contingent upon approval by the NYSDOH.

 

The transaction code '7' must be transmitted in months where no sales of controlled substances occur.

 

Transfers of controlled substances between licensees authorized to distribute controlled substances are not required to be reported


 

What I get from this is a monthly ARCOS-like report  is required for all St. Louis sales to New York except distributor sales to Hobart (sales to other distributors are exempted).  Only codes S and R are reported.  (with V, X, 7 manual records added).

Cannon Ave., has been prohibited from dispensing drugs classified as controlled dangerous substances following allegations that he filled thousands of prescriptions for Oxycodone, OxyContin, methadone and other powerful painkillers written by two physicians whose licenses were subsequently suspended. (By Ric Dugan, Staff Photographer)

 
By DON AINES
 
dona@herald-mail.com
 
7:12 p.m. EDT, March 17, 2011
hm-pharmacist-can-no-longer-dispense-controlled-dangerous-substances-20110317 
A Hagerstown pharmacist has been prohibited from dispensing drugs classified as controlled dangerous substances following allegations that he filled thousands of prescriptions for Oxycodone, OxyContin, methadone and other powerful painkillers written by two physicians whose licenses were subsequently suspended.

The Maryland Board of Pharmacy voted on Dec. 22, 2010, to summarily suspend the license of David Russo, owner of Russo's Rx at 25 N. Cannon Ave.

"There has since been a consent agreement by which my license has been restored, but I cannot dispense controlled dangerous substances," Russo said Tuesday. However, Russo said he can dispense other prescribed medications. 



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Get the information you need fast. Sign up for our Breaking News alerts today. 
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


No formal charges have been filed against him, and an evidentiary hearing will be scheduled during which he will present a defense to the allegations made by investigators with the pharmacy board, Russo said.

"We hope to have it resolved at that point," Russo said. He deferred specific questions to his attorney, but issued the following statement:

"Russo's Rx has always endorsed the American Academy of Pain Management's Patient Bill of Rights to insure access to medications prescribed for the treatment of chronic pain. We also do our best due diligence in the performance of our corresponding responsibility to mitigate abuse and diversion of controlled dangerous substances. We look forward to a hearing and the chance to defend ourselves."

"Certainly, Mr. Russo did fill prescriptions written by those two doctors and others," said his attorney, Richard Karceski of Towson, Md. "Every prescription written was legitimate .... There were no forgeries."

The investigative findings accompanying the suspension order cited Russo for "dispensing inappropriately large amounts of CDS prescribed by doctors known to engage in suspicious subscribing patterns."

The prescriptions were written in 2009 and 2010 by Dr. Nicola M. Tauraso, of Frederick, Md., and Silviu Ziscovici, of Rockville, Md., according to the investigative findings. 

The Maryland Board of Physicians summarily suspended Tauraso's license on Aug. 12, 2010, and Ziscovici's on Dec. 1, 2010, the report said.

Their licenses were suspended for prescribing high doses and large quantities of painkillers to mostly young people "who appeared healthy and did not appear to be in chronic pain or terminally ill," the Board of Pharmacy report alleged.

"It's not Dr. Russo's decision what to prescribe or how much," Karceski said. Those decisions were up to Tauraso and Ziscovici, both pain-management physicians, he said.



DEA investigated

Investigators from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration met with Russo in January 2010 and questioned him about prescriptions written by the two doctors, Karceski said. 

Russo provided them with copies of the requested prescriptions, he said. 

Russo did not know what the investigation was about at that time and asked the DEA investigators if he should stop filling prescriptions from Ziscovici and Tauraso, Karceski said. The investigators told him he could continue to fill those prescriptions, he said.

Russo told inspectors he filled prescriptions for Tauraso's patients from Washington County, the report said. However, investigators alleged that Russo filled prescriptions for Tauraso's and Ziscovici's patients from other counties and states.

The telephone number for Tauraso's clinic was not in service, and there was no answer at the number for Ziscovici's practice.

 A Board of Physicians spokeswoman said Friday that the licenses of Tauraso and Ziscovici were still suspended.

Cc: Rees, Dale J; Levy, JoAnne; Harper, Karen; Novak, Rod P; Freebury, Jennifer
Subject: Exalgo and Pennsaid Product Launch



Exalgo Strategy:

Shipments to customers

          Ship and invoice minimum of 1 case of each strength of exalgo on March 31.  We may be able to ship more depending upon timing as follows: regulatory approval, inventory arrives in Hobart; approvals, quality release, order allocation (sales/marketing).

 

Pennsaid Strategy:

Shipments to customers assuming regulatory approval

          Ship and invoice all orders on 03/31.  This requires sales/marketing, planning, and customer service to complete all allocations on 03/30.

 

 

Exalgo Receipts from Puerto Rico Shipment 03/29

          We will ship FedEx Custom Critical from Puerto Rico on Monday 03/29 for arrival and receipt on Tuesday 03/30 at approx 10 AM.

          Quality will need to QA release the product ASAP on 03/30 (as appropriate).

          Once released by QA, Sales/Marketing will work with Planning to allocate (items are on manual allocation) inventory to all outstanding orders as appropriate.  (A 222 must be on file in Customer Service for each order).

          On 3/30-03/31 Hobart DC will pick pack orders for all orders that have been allocated inventory from sales/marketing.

          On 03/31 Hobart DC will ship all picked/packed orders

 

We will make at least two additional FedEx Express shipments from Puerto Rico 03/30, 03/31, and possibly an additional 04/01 shipment.  The multiple shipment strategy allows us to spread and minimize shipment risk.  As these are received into Hobart and the inventory is released and allocated they will be picked, packed and shipped.  The cutoff time for allocation to occur (assuming inventory availability, 222 receipt, etc) is 2:30 eastern time for shipment that day.  We will ship all product that is allocated per planning/sales and marketing.

 

 

Exalgo Contingency Plan from Puerto Rico

If there are any delays or potential delays due to weather that may impact the FedEx Custom Critical Shipment from Puerto Rico to Hobart on 03/29, we will enact our contingency plan.

          We will ship on a FedEx charter flight on 03/30 arriving on the evening of 3/30. 

          Quality will need to QA release the product within as appropriate on 03/30.

          ASAP on the morning of 03/31-- Sales/Marketing will work with Planning to allocate (items are on manual allocation) inventory to all outstanding orders as appropriate.  (A 222 must be on file in Customer Service for each order).  We may be limited to shipping only the minimum of 1 case each strength in this contingency scenario.

          Additional inventory is scheduled to arrive on 04/01.  Sales/Marketing and Planning can begin manually releasing orders and as inventory is QA released; pick slips will drop and the DC will pick pack and ship orders.  Cutoff time is 2:30 eastern time.

 

We will make at least two additional FedEx Express shipments from Puerto Rico 03/30, 03/31, and possibly an additional 04/01 shipment.  The multiple shipment strategy allows us to spread and minimize shipment risk.  As these are received into Hobart and the inventory is allocated they will be picked, packed and shipped.  The cutoff time for allocation to occur (assuming inventory availability, 222 receipt, etc) is 2:30 eastern time for shipment that day.  We will ship all product that is allocated per planning/sales and marketing.  The goal is maximize allocation and shipment of product on 04/01.

 

Exalgo--Another Possibility:

Steve Fluhr is working with Janssen to determine if we can ship  analysis in-transit.   This would enable transportation to Hobart to occur as early as 03/26 arriving on Sat. 

 

 

Action Items:

 

Dave Kratcha 

          Follow up with Jason Jones on customer/item/quantities.  Goal is to identify one customer for both Pennsaid and Exalgo just in case the final prior approval supplement is not approved until 3/31.  Open awaiting customer P.O.  Scott Parker working to get POs from Rochester Drug Cooperative. 

          Must ensure we have hard copy of customer 222 in hand for Exalgo shipments to customers. Open

          Dave will also work with PDIG to ensure launch date can be easily changed if necessary.  Open   PDIG is ready to make any required changes on short notice. 

          Document process flow for communication and subsequent manual allocation of orders.  Open

          Coordinate with QA to ensure product is released. Open    

          Work with Eileen Spaulding and Jerilynn to ensure our 222 arrives at supplier by March 25.  Complete  

 

Jim Champion 

          Work with Hobart DC to establish procedures to stage orders, as identified by Dave K and Jason J., in advance of approval.  Again this assumes an approval date or product availability date of 3/31.  Complete

          Jim will also work with IS to ensure invoicing program runs on 3/31 for the orders associated with Pennsaid/Exalgo shipment.  Complete

          If Exalgo is shipped from PR on 03/26, Jim will ensure Hobart receiving is available to receive and put away product on 03/27. Complete

          Coordinate transportation with Cathy Gidcumb for outbound shipments to customers as required. Complete

 

Jerilynn Carroll/Steve Fluhr 

          We were expecting daily updates on the status of Exalgo inventory availability and estimated ship date and quantities from PR to all on copy of this email To date we have received no communication on the inventory status.  Open

          While we have received the official address of the location in Puerto Rico We have not received a local contact name (at the PR warehouse). Open

          Determine feasibility of shipping product from Puerto Rico  analysis in transit  on 03/26 for arrival on 03/27. Open

 

Cathy Gidcumb 

          Determining other options for inbound shipments from PR on Sat. or Sun.  Cathy is continuing to work these options a firm shipment quantity is required to finalize. Complete

          Investigate charter service Given the potential dollars involved we may opt to charter a plane.  Cathy has a last resort contingency plan established with FedEx to utilize a charter service. Complete

          Identify Spanish speaking resources as necessary. Complete

          Finalize FedEx labeling requirements and Janssen capabilities. Open awaiting Janssen contact name.

 

Eileen Spaulding

          Supply NY state license as requested.  Open She needs a contact to whom she will supply the information.

          Send 222 form to Victor Baez at Janssen.  Complete 03/22

          Confirm receipt of 222 with Victor Baez. Open

 

Steve Horner

          Ensure invoicing occurs on 03/31 for a minimum of 1 case of pennsaid and 1 case of each strength of Exalgo.  Rose to notify when ship confirmation is complete.  Open

 

Key Dates:

The Opioid Abuse Deterrence Act and DOJ Initiatives: Just What the Doctor Ordered?

Posted: 07 Dec 2017 08:48 PM PST

By John A. Gilbert & Larry K. Houck  

 For Americans under the age of 50, drug overdoses are now the leading cause of death.  DOJ, Attorney General Jeff Sessions Delivers Remarks Announcing New Tools to Combat the Opioid Crisis (Nov. 29, 2017) (here).   With evidence suggesting that nearly 80 percent of individuals addicted to heroin started out on opioid pain relievers, the link is clear that opioid prescriptions are driving this epidemic.   Rep. Mark Meadows, Opioid Abuse Deterrence, Research and Recovery Act (here).  These statements by government officials, one representing the Trump Administration, the other from Congress, provide a sobering picture of the nationwide opioid abuse epidemic and form the basis for two new actions designed to stem the opioid crisis.  On November 29, 2017, Congressman Mark Meadows (R-NC) introduced H.R. 4482, the Opioid Abuse Deterrence, Research, and Recovery Act of 2017.  On the same day, Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced several Department of Justice ( DOJ ) and Drug Enforcement Administration ( DEA ) efforts also aimed at addressing the crisis.

Opioid Abuse Deterrence, Research, and Recovery Act of 2017

The Opioid Abuse Deterrence, Research and Recovery Act ( the Act ) would amend the Federal Controlled Substances Act ( CSA ) to require DEA-registered and state-licensed practitioners authorized to prescribe schedule II or III controlled substances to submit a  certification  to DEA that they will not prescribe a schedule II or III opioid  for the initial treatment of acute pain  unless the prescribed quantity is for less than seven days or falls within a State-established prescription limit.  Acute pain  is defined as  pain with abrupt onset and caused by an injury or other process that is diagnostically determined to have minimal risk of escalating in intensity.    Acute pain  under the Act does not include chronic pain, pain treated as part of cancer care, hospice, end-of-life care, or palliative care.

Under the Act, the certification would not prevent practitioners from prescribing opioids approved by FDA for opioid use disorder treatment; for immediate, post-operative pain relief; or for longer than seven days if prescribing is consistent  with a clear medical standard of care,  provided that the practitioner documents the prescription in the patient s medical record and consults the State electronic health record system or prescription drug monitoring program.

The legislation would also require the FDA Commissioner to continue working with stakeholders and encouraging the development of abuse-deterrent opioids. In addition, to understand what led to the opioid crisis, the Act requires the Comptroller General to submit a report to Congress within two years on the health care policy changes that may have contributed to the increase in opioid overdoses and deaths.  The report must include:

A review of the federal health care-related legislative, administrative, and judicial decisions that affected access to pharmaceutical pain management strategies;
An analysis of the financial and non-financial costs and benefits of reversing or revising such decisions;
An analysis of the differences between State prescription drug monitoring programs;
 An analysis of the impacts of State and Federal prescribing limitations on patient medical outcomes; and
An analysis of the costs of using abuse-deterrent opioids compared to non-abuse-deterrent opioids.

Finally, the Act would require the FDA Commissioner to conduct a study on the feasibility of replacing the prescribing limits in the bill  with evidence-based clinical guidelines,  including a limitation  on the first opioid prescription for patients for an acute pain diagnosis  and  the incorporation into routine medical visits of evidence-based screening tools [to monitor] the misuse of opioids and other controlled substances. 

HPM Comments

We have long believed that effectively addressing the opioid epidemic requires focus on the physicians, doctors, dentists, and other practitioners who are the gatekeepers of public access to controlled substances. It is clear that overprescribing or inappropriate prescribing of controlled substances has been a significant cause in creating and sustaining the opioid abuse crisis.

The Act was clearly drafted with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention s ( CDC s ) Guidelines for Prescribing Opioids for Chronic Pain in mind. While the CDC guidelines voluntarily limit opioid prescribing for chronic pain, the Act limits only the first or initial prescription of schedule II or III opioids to treat acute pain to seven days unless the practitioner fulfills requirements to prescribe for a longer period.  In fact, the Act does not reference prescribing for chronic pain.  Both the Act and the CDC guidelines focus on a theme that we believe is a significant contributor to the opioid abuse problem, that is, overprescribing or inappropriate prescribing of controlled substances.  However, the mechanics of having a prescriber provide a  certification  to DEA is problematic.  There are no details on how prescribers would  certify  (e.g., during the application or renewal process).  More importantly, the Act does not address the regulatory effect of certifying or, even more significantly, failure to comply with the certification.  It also fails to address whether practitioners will self-certify or obtain certification for submission from an official or unofficial organization.  It is worth noting that the CSA and DEA regulations related to sales of pseudoephedrine, provide for a certification by retail sellers that they will not sell in amounts greater than allowed under the CSA.  21 U.S.C.   830(e)(1)(A)(vii); 21 C.F.R.    1314.35-.42, 1314.101-.103.  Regardless, the Act s requirements will make practitioners more carefully consider issuing a first opioid prescription for longer than seven days.  The inescapable downside is that some overly cautious practitioners may decline to issue necessary prescriptions to legitimate patients for longer than a week if they do not want to adhere to the requirements to do so or from fear that they will appear on DEA s radar.

We believe that mandatory training and education for practitioners is more critical and an alternative would be to require that all practitioners who intend to be registered with DEA to prescribe Schedule II controlled substances should certify that they have received such training.

DOJ and DEA Initiatives

Attorney General Sessions announced several initiatives including a restructuring of DEA Field Offices to focus on the opioid abuse problem. The Attorney General announced that DOJ was awarding $12 million to law enforcement agencies in states hit hard by illegal prescription opioid, heroin, and methamphetamine activity.  DOJ awarded $7 million through its Anti-Heroin Task Force Program to investigate heroin and illegal opioid distribution in states with high per capita levels of treatment admissions for heroin and other opioids, and $5 million through the Anti-Methamphetamine Program to states that have  demonstrated numerous seizures of precursor chemicals, finished methamphetamine, laboratories, and laboratory dump seizures.  DOJ, Attorney General Sessions and Acting DEA Administrator Patterson Announce New Tools to Address Opioid Crisis (Nov. 29, 2017) (here).

Attorney General Sessions also announced the formation of a new DEA Louisville Field Division. This new office will strengthen DEA investigation and enforcement efforts under a single Special Agent in Charge in Kentucky, Tennessee, and West Virginia.  The geographic area served by the new Louisville Field Division was previously distributed among the Detroit, Atlanta, and Washington, D.C., Field Divisions.  The Attorney General anticipates that consolidating Kentucky, Tennessee, and West Virginia within a single jurisdiction  will produce more effective investigations on heroin, fentanyl, and prescription opioid trafficking, all of which have a significant impact on the region.  Id.

Lastly, the Attorney General directed every U.S. Attorney to designate an Opioid Coordinator for their district by December 15th. The Attorney General s memo to all U.S. Attorneys instructed that Opioid Coordinators will be responsible for:

Facilitating intake of cases involving prescription opioids, heroin, and fentanyl;
Convening a task force of federal, state, local, and tribal law agencies to identify opioid cases for federal prosecution, facilitate interdiction efforts, and tailor their district s response to the needs of their communities;
Advising and training Assistant United States Attorneys on prosecuting opioid offenses;
Maintaining statistics on opioid prosecutions; and
Developing and evaluating the strategy to combat the opioid epidemic.

HPM Comments  

The creation of a new DEA Field Office focuses on several states particularly hard hit by the opiate abuse problem. Thus, it makes sense that DEA would consolidate resources to narrow the geographic scope to address these issues.  DEA drug investigations are better coordinated and more efficient when conducted within a single Field Division rather than multiple jurisdictions.  It also seems to us that the creation of an Opioid Coordinator should result in a more focused approach by U.S. Attorney offices to the opioid problem.  We note that in August 2017 the Attorney General had announced the formation of the Opioid Fraud and Abuse Detection Unit, which is a pilot program funding 12 prosecutors nationwide to focus on investigating and prosecuting health care fraud related to prescription opioids. Thus, DOJ/DEA is devoting significant resources to the fight against opioid abuse, which will likely result in more criminal, civil and administrative actions.

Subject: Published Op-Ed in today's St. Louis Post-Dispatch



Good morning:

 

Today’s St. Louis Post-Dispatch – as noted – features our Opinion Editorial, submitted by Mark on behalf of the company. Attached shows how the article appears in print. We also attach a PDF of the online article, and include the link and text below. This will also be included in our morning daily news clips report.

 

Link: http://www.stltoday.com/news/opinion/mallinckrodt-helps-address-opioid-misuse-diversion/article_0b0e8c93-3349-575a-948f-241e6a53a463.html

 

Text

 

Opinion

Mallinckrodt helps address opioid misuse, diversion

{http://www.stltoday.com/news/opinion/columns/the-platform/editorial-the-mallinckrodt-connection-to-america-s-opioid-epidemic/article_cac8edcf-dd6c-5628-beb3-141d1352a352.html}The Post-Dispatch editorial “The Mallinckrodt connection” (April 10) overlooks Mallinckrodt’s efforts to ensure responsible use of its medications and the complexity of the broader issue. As a Missouri-founded company celebrating 150 years in this state, we believe the editorial board criticized Mallinckrodt without, perhaps, fully understanding this complicated issue and all the facts.

As a publicly traded company, Mallinckrodt routinely discloses information affecting the company, such as the agreement in principle reached with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency and U.S. Attorneys’ Offices to settle the previously disclosed investigations of the company’s monitoring programs for controlled substances.

The disclosure of the $35 million settlement was in no way meant to downplay the seriousness of the opioid epidemic. Mallinckrodt recognizes that prescription drug abuse is one of the St. Louis region’s — and the nation’s — greatest health and safety concerns, with devastating societal and emotional effects as well as an economic burden on the healthcare system.

Mallinckrodt’s medications are approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and Mallinckrodt supplies its controlled substance products to legitimate national and regional distributors that are registered with the DEA. Mallinckrodt has long had processes in place to monitor its distributor customers, as the law requires. Mallinckrodt has limited ability to monitor downstream sales at the pharmacy level, where diversion has historically occurred, but it has also been a leader among manufacturers in helping distributors better monitor their pharmacy customers.

Although the company has reached an agreement in principle with the government, it does not agree with government allegations that it violated the law in connection with its suspicious order monitoring program. In discussions with the government, the company has responded to unfounded claims and successfully refuted factual inaccuracies in the government’s allegations. In fact, Mallinckrodt has been and is a leader in developing and sharing best practices related to its innovative suspicious order monitoring program, which we believe exceeds DEA requirements.

Prescription drugs are designed to heal, not harm. Mallinckrodt is dedicated to providing safe and effective medications for the treatment of patients with chronic and acute pain. In addition to helping those patients, Mallinckrodt is equally committed to working with patient groups, policymakers, law enforcement and industry to address the complex issues of opioid misuse and diversion.

Mallinckrodt has invested millions of dollars in its comprehensive program to address opioid abuse and misuse. For years, Mallinckrodt has been a vocal advocate for a prescription drug monitoring program in Missouri to help doctors identify potential opioid misuse. The company also purchased and donated more than 1.5 million drug deactivation pouches distributed in our communities and across the U.S. so that families can safely dispose of unused medication.

Mallinckrodt regularly works with law enforcement to help prevent diversion, including by providing no-cost placebo tablets of Mallinckrodt opioids to officers and prosecutors for use in law enforcement operations; attacking drug theft through tracking devices in selected Mallinckrodt drug bottles; and contributing testimony on behalf of prosecution in drug diversion cases. We helped to found the Anti-Diversion Industry Working Group, a collective of leading manufacturers and distributors of pharmaceutical controlled substances coming together to collaborate and share best practices with the purpose of exceeding DEA obligations for opioid anti-diversion programs.

The opioid epidemic is a complex and confounding problem, and no one policy initiative or program will solve it. We commend the Post-Dispatch for its focus on this issue and its support of prescription drug monitoring in the state. However, to truly make an impact on opioid abuse, all stakeholders must better understand the various interrelated causes and contributors to the problem, and work together to address all of them in a comprehensive, thoughtful manner. We continue to work to be part of the solution.

Mark Trudeau is chief executive officer and president of Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals.

[RxNews] Mandatory Prescriber Training

The issue of mandatory training for opioid prescribers is again in the news after a joint meeting last week of the
FDA's Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee and its Anesthetic and Analgesic Drug
Products Advisory Committee once again recommended it. This suggestion was first raised by these committees
in July 2010 when they were discussing whether a proposed REMS that FDA had put forward then was an
appropriate approach to the problem of opioid abuse.
The vote in 2010 was 25 to ten, with the majority saying that the FDA's proposal was insufficient. In discussing
the vote, the notion of training opioid prescribers was suggested. Dr. John Jenkins, Director, Office of New
Drugs, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, agreed with the panelists but said that prescriber training — as
a REMS requirement — would require congressional action.
Dr. Jenkins indicated that the DEA, being the only federal agency authorized to register prescribers of
controlled substances, might be able to require such training as a condition for new or continued prescriber
registration.
The Controlled Substances Act gives the Attorney General broad authorization "to promulgate rules and
regulations and to charge reasonable fees relating to the registration and control of the manufacture,
distribution, and dispensing of controlled substances." [21 USC 821] Assuming that the Attorney General
could, by rulemaking, add training to the list of conditions already required for DEA registration, the larger
question remains as to whether such training would have the desired effect of reducing the abuse of opioids.
Thus far, there has been no "needs assessment" showing, for example, that the problem of opioid abuse results
from a lack of training on the part of prescribers. While it stands to reason that some infrequent prescribers of
opioids might benefit from specialized training, many regular prescribers of opioids probably already know as
much as they need to know about these drugs and the patients using them. For them, the benefits of mandatory
training would be marginal at best.
We can expect to hear more about this recommendation in the coming months. Training, after all, is the plain
vanilla universal solution for just about any problem and generates little opposition. In this regard, whether it
will have much of an effect in reducing opioid abuse remains unknown.
John Coleman

Dakota Drug's Ted Scherr Named HDMA Chairman

Ted Scherr, President/CEO of Dakota Drug, Inc., was elected as Chairman of HDMA's Board of Directors at the fifth Annual Board & Membership Meeting in Laguna Beach, Calif. Scherr assumes the chairmanship from David Neu, President, AmerisourceBergen Drug Corporation, who was elected to the position in October 2012 and remains a member of the HDMA Board and Executive Committee.

Two additional Board members also were announced at the meeting. Jon Giacomin, President, U.S. Pharmaceutical Distribution, Cardinal Health, Inc., will replace Michael Kaufmann, Chief Executive Officer, Pharmaceutical Segment, Cardinal Health, Inc., on the Board and Executive Committee. Mr. Kaufmann served on the Board and Executive Committee since 2008. Timothy Booth, President/COO, Metro Medical Supply, Inc., was named to the Board in June.

"It was truly an honor to work closely with Dave as Chairman, and Mike as a member of the Executive Committee, during their tenures," said HDMA President and CEO John M. Gray, in a statement. "Ted, Jon and Tim all bring fresh perspectives to our organization, and I look forward to working with them and the entire Board of Directors to ensure that HDMA continues to deliver value to our members and the industry."

A complete listing of the HDMA Board is available here. For more information, contact Anne Johnson.

{top of page}

Registration Now Open for HDMA's 2015 Distribution Management Conference and Expo

Registration for the 2015 Distribution Management Conference and Expo is now open, with early bird rates available through December 15. Early registration ensures saving up to $800 on conference registration fees for this annual event.

Slated to take place March 8–11 at the JW Marriott Orlando Grande Lakes, the event will provide attendees with a forum to engage in discussions on topics ranging from reverse logistics and disposal to traceability and licensure. With nearly 500 attendees present each year, the Conference and Expo is HDMA's largest supply chain education event.

Sessions for the 2015 conference include:

"Big Data: a Revolution That Will Change How We Live, Work and Think," a presentation by Viktor Mayer-Schönberger, bestselling Author of Delete and Big Data and expert on the networked economy;
"Achieving the Impossible," words from Ben Saunders, the world record-breaking polar explorer and endurance athlete;
"What's In, What's Out, What's Ahead: 2015 Healthcare Marketplace Trends," a presentation by Doug Long of IMS Health, Inc.; and,
"Washington From a Different Angle," with Katty Kay, Author and Lead Anchor of BBC World News America.

For early bird registration information, visit the conference website. Contact HDMA's Meetings & Conferences Department at (703) 885-0278 for registration questions. For program questions, contact Jo-Anne Torres.

{top of page}

FDA Announces "Know Your Source" Campaign to Educate Prescribers on Rogue Distributors

FDA announced a new campaign called "Know Your Source" aimed at advising healthcare professionals and practice administrators to purchase prescription drugs only from wholesale drug distributors licensed in their states to protect patients from unsafe or ineffective drugs. The campaign website includes tips to identify rogue distributors, flyers and a map of state licensing authorities for prescribers to verify that wholesale drug distributors are licensed in their states.

For more information, contact Allison Tuszynski.

{top of page}

Register for "Contracts and Chargebacks Seminar: Perspectives on Process Improvement" — October 15–16

Less than three weeks remain to register for HDMA's "Contracts and Chargebacks Seminar: Perspectives on Process Improvement." Taking place on October 15–16 in Wilmington, Del., the seminar will bring together professionals in the contracts and chargebacks sector to discuss current industry processes and challenges.

Agenda topics include:

"The 340B Landscape — Driving Program Integrity and Compliance in the 340B Program" with: Stephanie Trunk, Legal Counsel, Arent Fox LLP;
Marijo Bustos, Supervisor, Chargebacks, Fresenius Kabi, USA;
BJ Centers, Senior Director, Operations & Distribution Apexus/Prime Vendor Program; and,
Dr. Andrew L. Wilson, PharmD, Vice President, 340B Solutions, McKesson Corporation.


"EDI Q-and-A" with: Gail Jones, Business Analyst, Pharma Contract Administration, McKesson Corporation; and,
Susan Lowe, Principal, LoMac Consulting.


A "Managing Change with Team Building" presentation led by EJ Johnson, Director of Talent Development, AmerisourceBergen Corporation.
"Interactive Roundtables," offering an opportunity to discuss the 340B Refund Process (from both the manufacturer and distributor perspective); credit and rebills; and other topics.

The agenda also features distributor hosted roundtables, with table hosts and facilitators from AmerisourceBergen Corporation, H.D. Smith and McKesson Corporation.

As a reminder, the deadline to make reservations at the Hotel du Pont at the special HDMA group rate is tomorrow, Wednesday, October 1. For details, visit the seminar website.

Visit the seminar website for more information on the agenda. For registration questions, contact HDMA's Meetings & Conferences Department at (703) 885-0278. For program questions, contact Jo-Anne Torres.

{top of page}

Registration Continues for the Center's November 12–13 Specialty Seminar

Registration is under way for the Center for Healthcare Supply Chain Research's annual educational event, the Specialty Pharmaceutical Supply Chain Issues and Trends Seminar — taking place on November 12–13 at the Renaissance Arlington Capital View Hotel in Arlington, Va.

Program highlights include:

The potential impact of the Affordable Care Act (ACA) on the pharmaceutical supply chain, including changes in benefit design, the delivery system and involvement of consumers with Dan Mendelson, CEO & Founder, Avalere Health LLC.
An overview of what is in the pharmaceutical pipeline by disease state and drug characteristics with Ray Tancredi, RPh, MBC, CSP, Vice President, Specialty Pharmacy Development, Walgreens.
A panel discussion on cost-containment measures and how the supply chain will be impacted.
A new research study from the Center addressing learning opportunities from Europe in the commercialization of biosimilars and the market potential for biosimilars in the U.S., with insights provided by: Tom Moore, Marketing Director, US Value & Access, Amgen, Inc.;
Rich Tremonte, Vice President, Global Generic Pharmaceuticals, AmerisourceBergen Corporation;
Murielle Thinard-McLane, Vice President, Generics, McKesson Specialty Health;
Ray Tancredi, RPh, MBC, CSP, of Walgreens; and,
Bruce A. Feinberg, Vice President & Chief Medical Officer, Cardinal Health Specialty Solutions, Clinical Pathways, Cardinal Health Inc.


A dialogue facilitated by IMS' Vice President, Industry Relations, Doug Long on launching new specialty pharmaceuticals with: Chris Doerr, Senior Director, Trade Operations, TEVA Pharmaceuticals USA;
Thomas Doyle, Executive Vice President, Commercial Solutions, H. D. Smith Specialty Solutions; and,
Gayle Johnston, President, CuraScript Specialty Distribution, an Express Scripts Company.


A presentation on the potential impact of Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) on the supply chain with Peter Weissberg, Associate Director, Client Strategist, Xcenda®, AmerisourceBergen.
A discussion by Michael Werner, Partner, Holland & Knight, to spotlight issues and insights relating to medical ethics in America and their effect on the supply chain.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
Date: June 15, 2010
Contact: Rich Isaacson
Number: (313) 234-4310

Michigan Pharmaceutical Supplier S Dea License Suspended
-Harvard Drug Group, LLC distributed 13 million doses of Oxy from 2008-2010

JUN 15 -- (Detroit, MI)   Robert L. Corso, Special Agent in Charge of the Detroit Field Division, Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced today the Immediate Suspension of the Federal Controlled Substance Registration of Harvard Drug Group, LLC.

Harvard Drug Group, LLC, based in Livonia, Michigan, has been the subject of a DEA investigation that alleges the company was selling large quantities of controlled substances to pharmacies, primarily in Florida. The investigation has revealed that several of Harvard s largest purchasers of oxycodone were engaged in schemes to dispense controlled substances based on prescriptions that were written for other than legitimate medical purposes. The investigation revealed that Harvard Drug Group, LLC, distributed over 13 million dosage units of oxycodone products to customers in the two year time frame between March 2008 and March 2010.

Robert L. Corso, stated,  Pharmaceutical companies have a responsibility to ensure that the drugs they sell don t end up in the hands of drug traffickers or businesses that are conducting their business illegally. Harvard Drug Group, LLC, should have known, based on the large, frequent quantities, that their customers were diverting oxycodone into arenas that were not legitimate. Today s action sends the message that the DEA is working hard to hold accountable those companies that are operating in a manner outside of federal law.

DEA s action suspends Harvard Drug Group, LLC s DEA Certificate of Registration in accordance with an Immediate Suspension Order and pursuant to Sections 303 and 304 of the Controlled Substances Act, Title 21, Sections 823 and 824. The DEA s investigation of Harvard Drug Group, LLC, has determined that the continued registration of this company constitutes an imminent danger to public health and safety.

Harvard Drug Group, LLC. received written notice of the factual and legal basis for this action. In addition, Harvard Drug Group, LLC will be given an opportunity for an administrative hearing within the next 60 days. After the hearing, the DEA Deputy Administrator will make a final decision on whether Harvard Drug Group, LLC registration should be permanently revoked. This decision will be published in the Federal Register.

Oxycodone is the generic name of an addictive prescription painkiller that is classified under federal narcotics laws as a Schedule II controlled substance. Oxycodone is typically legally prescribed to combat acute, severe pain for legitimate medical purposes. Accordingly, these prescriptions are usually for a modest number of pills to be taken over a short period of time.

This is an ongoing investigation. Please forward any questions to DEA Detroit Public Information Officer Rich Isaacson at (313) 234-4310.

SPOKANE, Wash. -- The Drug Enforcement Administration has suspended the license of a North Spokane pharmacy,
leaving their customers scrambling to find other pharmacies to fill their prescriptions.
The Bates Pharmacy has been in Spokane since 1942 and competes with larger corporate stores with good customer
service and home deliveries. However, according to company officials, last November the DEA did an audit on Bates and
found problems with the way it handles controlled substances.
For example, the pharmacy was letting its customers return unused portions of their prescriptions and then destroying
them at the waste-to-energy plant.

 Bates officials say the DEA also felt the pharmacy needed to better protect its controlled substances from theft,
particularly during deliveries. Bates says it tightened up security but on Friday the DEA showed up again and seized all
of the narcotics in their inventory.
The pharmacy says, "in spite of our efforts and good faith, the DEA has suspended our license to dispense controlled
substances. We are surprised by this action."
Bates customers are surprised too as now hundreds of them need to find a new pharmacy to fill their narcotic
prescriptions and Bates is trying to help saying, "we are working with local pharmacies to ensure the needs of our
patients are met and they have access to critical medications."
DEA officials said Wednesday they couldn't discuss anything about their enforcement action at Bates Pharmacy as their
case remains under investigation.
Bates officials say they are not suspected of black market sales or allowing drugs to fall into the wrong hands. Bates
continues to fill non-narcotic prescriptions and selling other medical supplies.

Let’s step back here.

 

Bruce is working the ASR for single sided H transactions where the registration number is improperly captured.

 

The ARCOS reporting is likely taking the data straight from the very files which have the bad data as a result of this issue.

 

Once this issue is resolved, the ARCOS reports can be run to verify the correct registration number appears. If this is still an issue, a new ASR can be kicked off.

 

On a side note, there is a State ARCOS report ASR that is in progress. Not sure how this is related.

Eileen,

 

Yes, this is a known problem in BPCS.  BPCS switched from the U transaction to the H transaction to receive inter-company shipments.  However the single sided H transaction has never worked in ARCOS or DEA Annual. 

 

ASR516327 - BPCS-ST/HB-(ASR MFG00605) Re-supply order receipts not picking up correct DEA registration (Bruce Barker)

Subject: Psychiatric Times Article
From: "Phillips, Lynn" <lynn.phillips@covidien.com>
Date: Wed, 29 Jun 2011 09:10:53 -0500
To: "Neuman, Herbert R" <herbert.neuman@covidien.com>,
    "Morelli, Art" <art.morelli@covidien.com>,
    "Mills, Sherice R" <sherice.mills@covidien.com>,
    "Walker, Preston" <preston.walker@covidien.com>,
    "Wang, Jennie L" <jia.wang@covidien.com>
Cc: "Littlejohn, Stephen E" <stephen.littlejohn@covidien.com>,
    "Schooler, JoAnna S" <joanna.schooler@covidien.com>,
    "Stauder, Nancy R" <nancy.stauder@covidien.com>


All-

Attached is an article that is running in the current issue of Psychiatric Times, which discusses our Exalgo REMS program as it relates to the new FDA guidelines.

 

 

WASHINGTON REPORT 

Obama Drug Misuse Strategy Targets Physician Education

By Stephen Barlas | June 28, 2011


-----

{http://www.psychiatrictimes.com/image/image_gallery?img_id=1891382&t=1309284867966}The new federal government effort to limit unnecessary prescriptions of opioids has at least 2 prongs that will affect psychiatrists. The first is the FDA dictate that manufacturers of the drugs develop risk evaluation and mitigation strategies (REMS) for their individual products, which include methadone and buprenorphine. REMS are dictated when the FDA has worries about a drug s adverse effects or other risks, such as diversion, with the latter being the main driver. One component of REMS is a physician education program, which the manufacturer offers to a physician but which the physician may volunteer to take. However, the FDA wants the companies to establish and meet targets for voluntary physician participation.

The potentially more important prong is the announcement by the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy that it will work with Congress to pass new legislation requiring all physicians with Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) registrations to undergo mandatory education on the use of long-acting and extended-release opioids.

 It is important for all clinicians to recognize that we share a major professional responsibility to ensure that opioids and other abusable medications are prescribed only for appropriate indications, that patients are followed closely, and that both patients and their families understand the risks associated with these drugs,  said John Renner, MD, chair of the American Psychiatric Association s (APA) Council on Addiction Psychiatry.  This plan recognizes that public education and, specifically, patient and clinician education are critical to this new approach. 

However, the APA s Council on Addiction Psychiatry has not recommended nor has the APA Board of Trustees adopted a policy that addresses this federal initiative or the need for the  extra  mandatory education for psychiatrists. One APA staffer, speaking about all the recommendations in the Obama strategy (formerly called Epidemic: Responding to America s Prescription Drug Crisis) said,  It is a big document, and we would probably express some reservations to some of the stuff in there. 

Concerns about unnecessary opioid prescriptions and their diversion were at the center of the Obama administration strategy released on April 19. At a press conference that day, Gil Kerlikowske, Director of the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy; Howard Koh, MD, Assistant Secretary for Health, US Department of Health and Human Services; Margaret A. Hamburg, MD, FDA Commissioner; and Michele M. Leonhart of the DEA released the Obama administration s comprehensive action plan (ie, Epidemic). It focuses on several key areas, including:

  Supporting the expansion of state-based prescription drug monitoring programs

  Recommending more convenient and environmentally responsible disposal methods to remove unused medications from the home

  Supporting education for patients and health care providers

  Reducing the prevalence of pill mills and doctor shopping through enforcement efforts

One strand of the enhanced physician education effort will emerge from the FDA requirement that all long-acting and extended-release opioids have REMS. These products are methadone (Dolophine), morphine (MS Contin, Kadian, Avinza, Embeda, Oramorph), oxycodone (OxyContin), hydromorphone (Exalgo), transdermal fentanyl (Duragesic), transdermal buprenorphine (Butrans), and oxymorphone (Opana ER). Companies must produce these REMS for FDA approval within 120 days, and they are expected to go into effect in early 2012.

In the REMS, manufacturers must describe their goals for the percentage of prescribers who complete the program at specified times. The FDA expects manufacturers of the class of long-acting and extended-release opioids to work together to provide the educational materials as part of a class-wide, single shared system to reduce the burden of the REMS on the health care system.

Although the FDA imposed the REMS requirement on the entire class of opioids, it had previously demanded REMS from certain manufacturers. One of those is Mallinckrodt, a subsidiary of Covidien, which markets Exalgo (hydromorphone HCl).

Lynn Phillips, manager of media relations for Covidien Pharmaceuticals, says the FDA asked for and approved REMS for Exalgo extended-release tablets when the drug was introduced in 2010. The REMS materials for Exalgo are posted on a Covidien Web site (www.exalgorems.com) and include the prescribing guide, medication guide for patients, a package insert, and an Exalgo Essential Information Form to test a physician s understanding of the material. Additional educational materials and enabling tools that are not specific to Exalgo or any other specific product are available through www.caresalliance.org, also sponsored by Covidien. It includes a current opioid misuse measure, numeric rating scale, opioid clinical management checklist, and pain management and documentation tool.

A physician voluntarily decides whether to complete the Exalgo online Essential Information form. According to Phillips,  Over a third of the prescriptions written for the product are written by prescribers who have studied the educational materials for Exalgo and completed the training verification form.  Phillips declined to say what percentage of Exalgo prescribers are psychiatrists. She added that the REMS Covidien has produced for Exalgo  is generally consistent  with the REMS the FDA is now dictating for the entire class of opioids.

The FDA said it would not require mandatory physician education as part of the REMS education program because the agency is concerned that such a system would be overly burdensome on the health care system and could negatively affect access to these necessary medications. The FDA will, however, work with other agencies, chiefly the DEA, to develop legislation that Congress would pass. That legislation would require physicians to complete some sort of opioid prescribing education test to obtain a DEA license to prescribe controlled substances.

Erica Chabot, spokeswoman for the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has the lead role on DEA issues, said no legislation had been sent up there yet by the Obama administration  but we will be speaking with the administration about its ideas and proposals,  she added.

Customer operates using a Retail Pharmacy DEA Registration.

Mallinckrodt interpretation of the regulations is as follows:

Retail Pharmacy
Compounds medications to fit the unique needs of the patient, as authorized by a prescription from physician.
The medications must be dispensed directly to a patient and not sent to the physician.
DEA does not  require  quota issuance for acquisitions by Retail Pharmacy registrants, distributions of CI and CII require
DEA 222 order forms.
Note: The Mallinckrodt business model does not include direct sales to Retail Pharmacy registrants.

Compounding Pharmacy
Compounds medications to fit the unique needs of the patient, as authorized by a prescription from physician.
Compounding pharmacy does not dispense medication to the patient but may send it directly to the prescribing physician
for office administration.
DEA requires Compounding Pharmacy registrants to be licensed within the category of Manufacturing registrants.
Manufacturing registrants require quota  for acquisitions of CI and CII controlled substances, distributions of CI and CII
require DEA 222 order forms.
Note: The Mallinckrodt business model accommodates sales to Compounding Pharmacy/Manufacturing registrants,
upon proof of current DEA registration license, provided they certify in writing that  the firm has available Procurement
Quota issued by DEA, adequate to cover the quantity of the specific sale.
