Subject: FW: Concern from Sovereign Pharmaceuticals for the Codeine Phosphate impurity reference standard.
From: "harper, karen"
Date: Tue, 29 Apr 2008 19:45:41 +0000
To: "ratliff, bill"
Cc: "kegg, christie l"


Bill,
Christie will be conducting a discrepancy investigation to determine how a shipping error occurred on a reference standard put up in Bldg 96.
A CII product was ordered and the bottle labeled correctly for the product that should have shipped, however, a CI material was put into the bottle.
 
Karen Harper
Manager, DEA Compliance
Covidien
Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals
3600 North Second Street
St. Louis, MO 63147
 
office phone (314) 654-1868
24/7 access (314) 654-1600
 


-----
From: Lewis, Mary
Sent: April 21, 2008 8:35 AM
To: Harper, Karen
Subject: FW: Concern from Sovereign Pharmaceuticals for the Codeine Phosphate impurity reference standard.



 


-----
From: Fay, Dave
Sent: April 10, 2008 1:01 PM
To: Lewis, Mary
Cc: Palmer, Tom; Wisneski, Sandy; Ruder, Sherryl; Longenecker, Jacob; Vaught, Marilyn N
Subject: RE: Concern from Sovereign Pharmaceuticals for the Codeine Phosphate impurity reference standard.



Mary,
 
There's no value to us in having the codeine N-oxide returned.  Sovereign can just keep it.
 
Thanks for your assistance,
Dave


-----
From: Lewis, Mary
Sent: Thursday, April 10, 2008 11:56 AM
To: Fay, Dave; Ruder, Sherryl; Longenecker, Jacob; Vaught, Marilyn N
Cc: Palmer, Tom; Wisneski, Sandy; Lewis, Mary
Subject: RE: Concern from Sovereign Pharmaceuticals for the Codeine Phosphate impurity reference standard.



All,
 
I pulled the 222 form and the good news is that Sovereign is registered to accept schedule I material - that was my main concern. 
 
a) Will Sovereign keep the codeine-n-oxide that we shipped by mistake, or return it?
b) I will work with Marilyn and/or Sovereign DEA contact to decide how to correct the paperwork.
c) I can make an ARCOS transaction to correct what was actually shipped, but I would like to discuss with Sovereign, so we are in agreement on how to correct the paper trail, and handling it the same way on both ends.
 
Mary


-----
From: Fay, Dave
Sent: April 10, 2008 10:39 AM
To: Ruder, Sherryl; Longenecker, Jacob; Lewis, Mary; Vaught, Marilyn N
Cc: Palmer, Tom; Wisneski, Sandy
Subject: RE: Concern from Sovereign Pharmaceuticals for the Codeine Phosphate impurity reference standard.



Sherryl has confirmed that 50 mg of Codeine N-Oxide was errantly packaged and shipped to Sovereign Pharmaceuticals in place of their order for 50 mg of Codeine Methyl Ether (order 637358, 10/30/2007).  Sherryl will be packaging a replacement of 50 mg of Codeine Methyl Ether, and I believe Marilyn will be placing the order which should be free of charge.
 
Mary:  It seems we shipped 50 mg of a Schedule 1 (codeine N-oxide) but the paperwork, Form 222, etc. indicates we shipped 50 mg of a Schedule 2 (codeine methyl ether).  What if anything needs to be done about this?
 
Jake:  Do you want to call Zhongsheng Deng at Sovereign, or do you want me to?  He expects to hear from someone today.
 

Regards,
Dave


-----
From: Ruder, Sherryl
Sent: Thursday, April 10, 2008 8:46 AM
To: Fay, Dave; Vaught, Marilyn N
Cc: Longenecker, Jacob
Subject: RE: Concern from Sovereign Pharmaceuticals for the Codeine Phosphate impurity reference standard.



Yes that is exactly what happened. I apologize. Marilyn will you please set up an order to ship for the codeine methyl ether?


-----
From: Fay, Dave
Sent: Wednesday, April 09, 2008 4:09 PM
To: Ruder, Sherryl
Cc: Vaught, Marilyn N; Longenecker, Jacob
Subject: RE: Concern from Sovereign Pharmaceuticals for the Codeine Phosphate impurity reference standard.



Sherryl,
 
Is it possible Code 1565 was inadvertently used to fill an order for Code 1545?  Please investigate?
 
If we discover we shipped the wrong stuff, let's ship them the correct material free of charge.
 
Dave


-----
From: Ruder, Sherryl
Sent: Wednesday, April 09, 2008 12:29 PM
To: Fay, Dave
Subject: FW: Concern from Sovereign Pharmaceuticals for the Codeine Phosphate impurity reference standard.



Dave: I found the order we sent to them:
 
637358

 10/30/2007

 1545 L11937

 Codeine Methyl Ether

 0.050

 Sovereign

 10/30/2007

 $792.00

 


 
I looked up the HPLC for this lot and another L lot that we have. Both LC chromatograms show the N-Oxide peak at 11.2-11.4 minutes and the CME peak is at 16.4 for the lot we sent to Sovereign and 14.6 for the other L lot. They seem to separate fine with our method.
 
Sherryl


-----
From: Vaught, Marilyn N
Sent: Wednesday, April 09, 2008 11:37 AM
To: Fay, Dave
Cc: Ruder, Sherryl; Palmer, Tom; Longenecker, Jacob
Subject: FW: Concern from Sovereign Pharmaceuticals for the Codeine Phosphate impurity reference standard.



Hi Dave - see below.  Can you help with this or tell me who can?
Thanks,
 
Marilyn
 


-----
From: Zhongsheng Deng [mailto:zdeng@sovpharm.com]
Sent: Wednesday, April 09, 2008 11:22 AM
To: Vaught, Marilyn N; Vaught, Marilyn N
Cc: Kathleen Parker
Subject: Concern from Sovereign Pharmaceuticals for the Codeine Phosphate impurity reference standard.



 

Hi Marilyn,

 

We have one concern of the Codeine Methyl Ether (product code: 1545) reference standard that we ordered before from Mallinckradt for the impurity of Codeine Phosphate, it shows up as the same retention time as that of Codeine N-Oxide reference standard which we ordered from USP. 

 

I already spent some time (about two weeks) on this trying to find out what’s wrong with my system or my sample preparations since we have good relationship with Mallinckradt for so many years and this type of issue didn’t happen before.  But no matter what I checked (checked with manufactures’ method or other methods), the Codeine Methyl Ether peak still shows the same retention time as that of Codeine N-Oxide USP standard (I don’t think we can question USP reference standard at this time).   When checked with the Mallinckrodt’s method (method found in DMF of codeine phosphate), all other impurities show comparable results with the document recorded in the DMF (the same order of the retention times for all the impurities of codeine phosphate such as Morphine comes out first, followed by 10-Hydroxycodeine, Codeine-N-Oxide, Codeine, Norcodeine and Codeinone) except the Codeine Methyl Ether.   We would like to address this issue ASAP.   Would you please help us to approach this?

 

Thank you very much.

 

Zhongsheng Deng, Ph.D.

Senior Analytical Scientist

Research & Development Department

Sovereign Pharmaceuticals, LTD.

7590 Sand Street

Fort Worth, TX 76118

Phone: 817-616-0984 (o); 817-590-1607(Lab.)

www.sovpharm.com

E-mail: zdeng@sovpharm.com

text:
From:  Ratliff, Bill <Bill.Ratliff@Covidien.com>
Sent:  Friday, March 20, 2009 7:23 PM
To:  Paul.D.Kleissle@usdoj.gov
Cc:  Harper, Karen <Karen.Harper@Covidien.com>; Hunter, Dave <Dave.Hunter@Covidien.com>
Subject:  Suspicious Order Report
Attach:  1102_001.pdf

Pete as part of the Suspicious Order Monitoring Program, information was provided to Karen and me regarding the below listed order. They are a new customer and this is the first order they placed with our company. The salesman has been ill, but still takes orders and has not been to the customers business address as required. Please see his quote below in blue. This may well be a legitimate customer that is just getting started, but they can not be located on the internet under their company name or under "compounding pharmacies." They have a suite in an industrial park North of the University of California at San Diego (see attachment).


Southern California Compounding Company
Mark Badria, Pharmacist
11120 Roselle Street Suite H
San Diego CA 92121
DEA Registration FS1137997
Requesting 50 grams of Fentanyl Citrate


They also made contact regarding setting up another customer account in the company name of Innovative requesting 5-10 grams of Fentanyl Base for Innovative. They passed their credit check showing they have done business with: McKesson Medical; Pacific Surgical Institute; and Analytical Research Laboratories. I spoke with our fentanyl company expert and he believed the order could be considered an excessive amount. With the limited information provided and the amount of product they are requesting this seemed to be suspicious and the order has been placed on hold.

Please let me know if you need anything. We plan to have someone actually go to the business to talk with the occupants and to have a conference call next week to determine their target application unless you advise to the contrary.


"Bill, I have someone that perhaps can go look into Innovative. Should have been a red flag to me when the e-mail address was simply Innovative through some phone company, and best contact was a cell number. They do claim to be currently buying Fentanyl (for a separate requirement) from either B&B or Medisca, but I'll see what I can learn. Tom"


Bill Ratliff
Director of Security
Covidien
314-654-8112
24 hours 314-654-1600
bill.ratliff@covidien.com

Approved.  Letter in the mail.

 

From: Harper, Karen [mailto:Karen.Harper@Covidien.com]
Sent: Thursday, February 04, 2010 2:14 PM
To: Collier, Scott
Subject: Request for Temporary Storage of CII Material at Webster Groves Tech Center Vault



 

Scott,


 


Per our conversation, Mallinckrodt requests DEA permission to temporarily store Methadose (Methadone HCl) Liquid that is manufactured at Mallinckrodt Hobart - Manufacturing DEA Registration RM0231821 at the Mallinckrodt Webster Groves Tech Center - Manufacturing DEA Registration RM0324602.  50 pallets of material will be stored at Webster pending validation of the temperature and humidity controls in the Hobart vault that currently houses the material.  Mallinckrodt plans on storing the Methadose (Methadone HCl) Liquid at a DEA approved CII Webster Groves vault for a period of not more than 6 months.  At such time that the Hobart vault temperature and humidity controls are validated or, as other CII storage space at Hobart becomes available, the material will be returned to the original Hobart manufacturing site prior to further distribution.


 


Please reference previous similar DEA authorization dated March 18, 2009 (correspondence attached).  Note that Mallinckrodt has not had the need to temporarily store Fentanyl Transmucosal at Webster as previously requested. 


 


Given that both Mallinckrodt Hobart and Mallinckrodt Webster Groves are properly registered as Manufacturers, Mallinckrodt assumes that no further registrations or procurement quota would be required if DEA authorizes the temporary storage at Webster.  Further, Mallinckrodt will move the material via a DEA 222 form from/to each respective site's DEA manufacturing registration number.

[Federal Register: April 13, 2011 (Volume 76, Number 71)] [Notices] [Page 20710] From the Federal Register Online via GPO Access [wais.access.gpo.gov] [DOCID:fr13ap11-127] ----------------------------------------------------------------------- DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE Drug Enforcement Administration [OMB Number 1117-0010] Agency Information Collection Activities: Proposed Collection; Comments Requested: U.S. Official Order Forms for Schedule I and II Controlled Substances (Accountable Forms); Order Form Requisition DEA Form 222, 222a, Controlled Substances Order System ACTION: 60-Day Notice of Information Collection Under Review. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- The Department of Justice (DOJ), Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), will be submitting the following information collection request to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. The proposed information collection is published to obtain comments from the public and affected agencies. Comments are encouraged and will be accepted until June 13, 2011. This process is conducted in accordance with 5 CFR 1320.10. If you have comments, especially on the estimated public burden or associated response time, suggestions, or need a copy of the proposed information collection instrument with instructions or additional information, please contact Cathy A. Gallagher, Acting Chief, Liaison and Policy Section, Office of Diversion Control, Drug Enforcement Administration, 8701 Morrissette Drive, Springfield, VA 22152; (202) 307-7297. Written comments concerning this information collection should be sent to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, Office of Management and Budget, Attn: DOJ Desk Officer. The best way to ensure your comments are received is to e-mail them to oira_ submission@omb.eop.gov or fax them to 202-395-7285. All comments should reference the 8 digit OMB number for the collection or the title of the collection. If you have questions concerning the collection, please call Cathy A. Gallagher at 202-307-7297 or the DOJ Desk Officer at 202- 395-3176. Written comments and suggestions from the public and affected agencies concerning the proposed collection of information are encouraged. Your comments should address one or more of the following four points: Evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility; Evaluate the accuracy of the agencies estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used; Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology, e.g., permitting electronic submission of responses. Overview of information collection 1117-0010: (1) Type of Information Collection: Extension of a currently approved collection. (2) Title of the Form/Collection: U.S. Official Order Forms for Schedule I and II Controlled Substances (Accountable Forms); Order Form Requisition. (3) Agency form number, if any, and the applicable component of the Department of Justice sponsoring the collection: Form Number: DEA Forms 222 and 222a. Component: Office of Diversion Control, Drug Enforcement Administration, Department of Justice. (4) Affected public who will be asked or required to respond, as well as a brief abstract: Primary: Business or other for-profit. Other: Not-for-profit; State, local, or tribal government. Abstract: DEA-222 is used to transfer or purchase Schedule I and II controlled substances and data are needed to provide an audit of transfer and purchase. DEA-222a Requisition Form is used to obtain the DEA-222 Order Form. Persons may also digitally sign and transmit orders for controlled substances electronically, using a digital certificate. Orders for Schedule I and II controlled substances are archived and transmitted to DEA. (5) An estimate of the total number of respondents and the amount of time estimated for an average respondent to respond: DEA estimates that 109,632 registrants participate in this information collection, taking an estimated 17.33 hours per registrant annually. (6) An estimate of the total public burden (in hours) associated with the collection: It is estimated that there are 1,898,970 annual burden hours associated with this collection. If additional information is required contact: Lynn Murray, Department Clearance Officer, Policy and Planning Staff, Justice Management Division, U.S. Department of Justice, Two Constitution Square, 145 N Street, NE., Room 2E-808, Washington, DC 20530. Dated: April 7, 2011. Lynn Murray, Department Clearance Officer, PRA, U.S. Department of Justice. [FR Doc. 2011-8748 Filed 4-12-11; 8:45 am] BILLING CODE 4410-09-P

CVS probed in alleged loss of painkillers

CVS Caremark Corp. could face as much as $29 million in fines for allegedly losing track of hydrocodone pills at four California stores. They may have been sold on the black market.

CVS Caremark Corp. could face as much as $29 million in fines for allegedly losing track of prescription painkillers at four of its California stores, from which authorities said thousands of pills may have been sold on the black market. Doug Kolk reports

By David Lazarus

March 10, 2014, 7:25 p.m.

{CVS Caremark Corporation}CVS Caremark Corp. could face as much as $29 million in fines for allegedly losing track of prescription painkillers at four of its California stores, from which authorities said thousands of pills may have been sold on the black market.

Officials at the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration and the California Board of Pharmacy told me Monday that more than 37,000 pills were apparently taken from CVS stores in Modesto, Fairfield, Dixon and Turlock.

Meanwhile, CVS pharmacists in Southern California said they've been instructed by the drugstore chain to get their paperwork in order so that no other prescription meds are found to be missing.

David Lazarus

{Description:}Photo: 

Have a consumer question? Ask Laz

Casey Rettig, a special agent in the DEA's San Francisco office, said warrants were served on the four California CVS stores last May. She declined to comment further because the agency's investigation is still open.

Virginia Herold, executive officer of the state Board of Pharmacy, which licenses and oversees all drugstores in California, said each of the missing pills   all painkillers, such as {Vicodin (drug)} Vicodin   could have a street value of as much as $10.

Lauren Horwood, a spokeswoman for the U.S. attorney's office in Sacramento, said CVS faces 2,973 possible violations of the federal Controlled Substances Act for alleged discrepancies between the company's records and its inventory of prescription drugs.

The maximum fine for these violations could be $29 million, she said.

Horwood said CVS has yet to respond to a letter sent last month by her office. The letter outlines the alleged violations and seeks more information from the company.

Officials, requesting anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter, described the loss of painkillers as a big problem throughout the pharmacy business.

In some cases, the drugs have gone missing because pharmacists "self-medicate," they said. But in most cases, the officials said, lower-level pharmacy workers, such as technicians, have made off with the drugs and then sold them to others.

Such thefts typically come to light after pharmacies perform routine inspections of their inventory. They're required by law to report any missing meds within 14 days of discovery.

According to formerly sealed affidavits submitted as part of the DEA's application for search warrants, an investigator for the agency, Brian Glaudel, said the Sacramento district office became aware in late 2012 of losses of numerous {Hydrocodone (drug)} hydrocodone tablets from CVS stores in the region.

Hydrocodone is a narcotic painkiller sold under various brand names, including Vicodin and Norco.

The pending investigations stem from a case involving a CVS store in Rocklin, northeast of Sacramento.

Glaudel said CVS notified officials in December 2012 that a pharmacy worker in the Rocklin store was seen hiding a bottle of hydrocodone in her pants.

The worker subsequently admitted to CVS managers that she had stolen more than 20,000 hydrocodone tablets, Glaudel said.

The worker was arrested and charged with embezzlement, he said. It's unclear whether the stolen hydrocodone was recovered in the Rocklin case.

Glaudel said DEA investigators went over records for other CVS stores in the area and found more than 16,000 hydrocodone tablets missing from the Turlock store, 11,000 from the Fairfield store and almost 5,000 each from the Modesto and Dixon stores.

Michael DeAngelis, a CVS spokesman, said the investigations are aimed at "assuring compliance with state and federal requirements for administrative record keeping related to invoices and inventory for controlled substances."

DEA to scrutinize hospital pharmacists for opioid monitoring

Julia Talsma, Content Channel Director

Publish Date: SEP 03,2014
When it comes to preventing opioid abuse and misuse, hospital pharmacists are under the same pressures as those in the community setting.

Both groups have the legal duty to ensure that prescriptions for controlled substances are for legitimate medical needs, and both are required to have procedures in place to minimize the risk of employee theft or diversion, according to a report published online in the American Journal of Health-System Pharmacy.

Labels, orders, and treatment

One area where it is important for pharmacists to keep current is that of labeling standards for opioids, as they are subject to change. For example, in September 2013, FDA issued new labeling for long-acting and extended-release opioids, requiring that these drugs be used only for severe pain by patients needing continuous daily treatment over the long term and for whom alternative treatments are not adequate.

In addition, ?Health-system pharmacists must remain vigilant for questionable orders of prescriptions. As individuals who abuse drugs find it more difficult to obtain opioids from retail pharmacies, they may turn to emergency departments and outpatient pharmacies to obtain these medications,? wrote Daniel J. Cobaugh, PharmD, vice president of ASHP Research and Education Foundation, Bethesda, Md., and his colleagues in their article, ?The opioid abuse and misuse epidemic: Implications for pharmacists in hospitals and health systems,? scheduled for publication in the September 15 issue.

Related news: Higher rates of hospitalization seen in opioid prescribing by multiple providers

Record-keeping requirements are extremely important in hospital pharmacies, and policies should be in place to ensure that orders and prescriptions are complete and accurate. Pharmacists working in the hospital setting should also be aware of the restrictions on opioids for maintenance or detoxification of drug-addicted patients.

?The basic rule is that only an opioid treatment program registered with DEA is permitted to use an opioid drug to maintain or detoxify an opioid-addicted individual,? the authors wrote. ?However, hospital staff is permitted to provide opioid maintenance or detoxification therapy to a patient as an incidental adjunct to medical or surgical treatment of conditions other than addiction, thereby allowing a hospitalized addicted person to avoid the risk of withdrawal while being treated for some other condition.

In addition, hospital staff can provide opioids to an addicted patient with intractable pain, such as the case of a cancer patient who has become addicted to these medications.


Prevention of drug diversion

Policies and procedures should be in place to prevent or minimize the risk of hospital staff theft or diversion of opioids.

The risk of diversion is particularly problematic in the case of prefilled syringes or single-use vials of controlled substances when the physician orders a smaller dose than the syringe or vial contains.

?A nurse could carry an empty sterile vial in a pocket and, instead of destroying excess drug, inject it into the vial; this pattern could be repeated several times throughout the shift,? diverting a large amount of a controlled substance that could be hard to trace, Cobaugh and colleagues wrote.

Directors of pharmacy should be aware of these risks and institute policies and procedures to minimize the potential of employee theft or diversion of these drugs, the authors said.

Overall, pharmacists working within a health system can play a vital role in identifying opioid toxicity and in preventing inappropriate prescribing of these controlled substances and diversion of these painkillers.

Hi MK, hope you're well.  We are getting ready to "go live" with an opioid policy statement that will be used externally - in particular with policy makers.  


Can you take a look at the one component below, particularly as it relates to pdmp, and suggest an edit that would reflect what we discussed a few weeks back re: public payers (especially medicaid / managed care plans) having some metrics around data utilization to track fraud / abuse / aberrant prescribing. Enhanced Regulatory Standards and Data Usage to Prevent Diversion: Mallinckrodt believes that there are opportunities for the US Government to improve understanding of the prescription drug abuse problem and to clarify the manner in which manufacturers can assist the DEA in identifying suspicious orders. A substantial portion of the recent increase in drug overdose deaths is attributable to the increased availability of illicit manufactured opioids, which the CDC does not distinguish from opioid medications manufactured under the authority of the FDA and under DEA-established quotas. We call on the appropriate agencies to clearly define and appropriately classify the scope of the opioid overdose epidemic and provide clear guidance regarding industry supply chain management, namely:

?            DEA should clarify Suspicious Order Monitoring guidance, particularly the scope of responsibility for each component of the supply chain from manufacturer through dispenser

?            CDC should identify, surveil and quantify opioid drug use and overdose data by bifurcating illegal counterfeit opioids from legitimate pharmaceutical-grade opioid medications

?            State policymakers should continue to enhance Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs (PDMP), which remain a critical tool in the fight against prescription drug abuse. While all 50 states now have a PDMP in place, there remains a patchwork of approaches which could be optimized. As such, we call for:

  Greater policy coordination around PDMPs for interoperability and real-time, consistent data

  Increased federal funding and coordination with respect to interoperability of state PDMPs




?            Linking mandatory training/use of PDMPs by prescribers to state licensure and/or DEA registration

?            Requiring prescribers of Schedule II drugs to affirm in the patient record and PDMP that they screened for abuse, deemed the patient low risk, & provided appropriate counseling

?            Review PDMP data when starting opioid therapy for chronic pain and periodically during opioid therapy for chronic pain, ranging from every prescription to every 3 months (CDC guidelines)

Gary,

Hydrocodone is mid-level complex.  It has only one input - Codeine - and one output - 1582 hydrocodone bitartrate.  It is a good example of straight-line production with short recycles.

Morphine has everything you mentioned below, but has 2 quotas, raw materials from 3 countries, 5 charging points, 7 isolated intermediates, multiple assay intermediate (M&C), and besides 2 sales products is converted to 6 other synthetic products.  Also after it is converted, there are derivative streams which come back into inventory and need their own WIP.

Opium/CPS receipts are simple, but they have multiple assays and 19 year-end reports.

Maybe Morphine and Opium/CPS should be added as Extra Complex!

John Leonard and I talked and if you have not picked a complex item, you may want to use Hydrocodone.

Hydrocodone Alkaloid (6282) gets made from Codeine.
There are waste streams from the process that contain Hydrocodone Alkaloid and affect Quota.
Hydrocodone Alkaloid has a recycle stream that goes to another process that gets converted to another product 3959 (Recovered Hydrocodone Alkaloid).

A portion of this gets reprocessed back into 3959 because the impurities are too high to process forward.  This process is done in Building 235 and 6&7.

Hydrocodone Alkaloid is converted to Hydrocodone Bitartrate which has a conversion factor to adjust it back to Alkaloid.

There is also a recycle stream from this which goes back to be recovered as Hydrocodone Alkaloid Code 3959.

There may also be other items that I am missing.

Thanks

Gary

Ginger / all,

This is the crux of the issue to me, coming in new to the conversation.  Without knowing the history of prior conversations with Cardinal, I was wondering why (and if) we felt that the Force Majeure language in the contract would not apply to Quota situations.  Because the contract explicitly says "any event beyond reasonable control of Supplier that directly impacts Supplier's ability to manufacture and/or ship".  It gives some examples but states "including, without limitation", so I didn't see why Quota should be excluded simply because wasn't explicitly mentioned.  Also, this interpretation of Force Majeure is certainly not unique to this contract.  The basic definition  of Force Majeure include 1) an event or effect that cannot be reasonably anticipated or controlled (Merriam-Webster.com), and 3) an unexpected and disruptive event that may operate to excuse a party from a contract (Dictionary.com).  To me, Quota would seem to fall under these (again, without being privy to specific content of any prior conversations with Cardinal regarding the intent behind our contract clause).

Bottom line, it appears to me that there is enough language in the contract to justify Quota as valid reason to deny per Force Majeure.  But if Cardinal continues to disagree, how willing are we to continue to fight for it?

Brent

When DEA implemented the requirement for customer specific DEA registration numbers on quota requests, they indicated that the information became necessary due to innovations in the manufacturing supply chain such as external manufacturers, 3rd party manufacturers, joint ventures. DEA establishes production limits for painkillers, with some drugs set for big increases

In a U.S. Federal Register notice, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration released a list of dozens of schedule I and II controlled substances that will be subject to production quotas in 2015. Regulatory Focus reported 22 of the drugs will see an increase in their quotas next year, and 10 will see a decrease in their allowed production limits. Several painkiller drugs including codeine for sale, oripavine and oxymorphone for conversion will see large increases in 2015. The article said phenylacetone, thebaine and codeine for conversation will see large decreases in 2015.

Regulatory Focus (09/5/2014), Read the Federal Register notice (09/8/2014)

The issue is that the sample is not check-weighed, or if it is, no sample transfer form is filled out by bldg. 5.  This causes an issue when there is a weight discrepancy and this has happened at least twice in the last year.  The complaint from Jonathan is that Bldg. 5 insists that the person delivering a sample to them verifies and records the weights, but bldg. 5 will not do the same when a sample is being received from them.  The sample has been handled and compromised before it gets to the end building.
*       DEA Compliance group met with HSE representatives at Webster, St. Louis and Hazelwood to complete next steps for List 1 controls in the labs.  We cannot proceed with storage and cabinet requirements until HSE tells us which chemicals can be stored together since there are flammables, liquids, corrosives and acids on the list.

For those of you who haven’t been present on recent Tri-Team calls but plan to attend, a big welcome and a note on the dynamic behind this Assessment.  

 

For the Metrics team, it may help to contrast this with the prescriber survey, where we found smart people, told them what FDA required of us and provided additional guidance, and paid them to do it.  We need to tread more delicately with the CE community, especially since providers are not all contractually obligated to field the survey with their completers. 

 

For the CE team, it may be helpful to note that FDA just provided 20 detailed comments to the patient survey protocol with expectations that we revise appropriately and may do the same with the LTE survey instrument.  The fact that the CE community typically operates at a distance from industry does not automatically relax “Metrics-oriented” FDA expectations/requirements.

 

In general, we are aiming to strike an appropriate balance and to convince the CE stakeholders that our preferred collaboration model is agreeable.  They may offer helpful input and it may be important to be flexible in some places (no FDA requirement) and firm in others (FDA requirement).

Subject: FDA, EU Likely to Increase Use of Special Designations to Speed Approvals in 2013, Tufts Says
From: Drug Daily Bulletin <enewsletters@fdanews.com>
Date: Thu, 10 Jan 2013 01:12:43 -0600
To: ginger.collier@covidien.com


If you are having trouble viewing this email, click here.
  

 

{Home} {Free eNewsletters} {Contact Us}
 

Vol. 10, No. 7
 Thursday, Jan. 10, 2013 


Biopharmaceutical Good Distribution Practices Summit, March 18-20, 2013, Bethesda, MD   If one syringe goes missing in your distribution chain, you could be facing a total recall.  Or, if your product exceeds its maximum allowed temperature by a fraction of one degree, the whole lot might have to be destroyed. Welcome to the emerging   and risk filled   world of good distribution practice compliance. Inspectors are requiring manufacturers to prove they have adequate risk management controls in place AND provide detailed records and test results that assure temperature stability of past shipments. The truth is, you re in for more headaches and complications.  But there s help close at hand. Register today.

 

In this issue...
    

FDA, EU Likely to Increase Use of Special Designations to Speed Approvals in 2013, Tufts Says
Court Dismisses Endo Suit, Opens Door to Generic Opana ER
Pharma Codevelopment Soaring, FDA Guidance Stalling
Drug World Daily
Pharma Blog Watch


-----
FDA, EU Likely to Increase Use of Special Designations to Speed Approvals in 2013, Tufts Says
U.S. and EU regulators hope to increase the use of special designations, such as fast track, priority review and accelerated approval, to speed approvals of drugs for non-cancer diseases that are rare and/or life-threatening, according to a new Tufts report. Regulators want to approve these products at the same levels oncology drugs enjoyed between 2007 and 2011.
Drug Industry Daily

Court Dismisses Endo Suit, Opens Door to Generic Opana ER
A Washington, D.C., district court judge has thrown out Endo Pharmaceuticals  bid to prevent generic companies from producing the opioid drug Opana ER. In March, the company pulled its oxymorphone extended-release drug off the shelves and replaced it with a new formulation it says is crush-resistant and harder to snort.
Generic Line

Pharma Codevelopment Soaring, FDA Guidance Stalling
A new report by healthcare investment bank Leerink Swann trumpets the benefits of codevelopment partnerships and acquisitions (P&A): improved market performance, reduced R&D inefficiencies and healthy product pipelines. The number of biopharma acquisitions in 2012 (nine) surpassed 2011 (six) and that trend is likely to continue as companies have spent less in aggregate on P&A over time, the report states.
Washington Drug Letter


-----
FREE WEBINAR ON DEMAND   CAPA & Clinical Trials: CAPA programs that employ Root Cause Analysis are key to providing quality practices within the clinical research process.  A solid CAPA system will not only identify problem trends, but help drive the highest quality of research. Learn how. Download today.

 




-----


Free White Paper: Insider's Guide to Selecting a Quality Management Software System
Learn the best practices for selecting a software vendor, some pitfalls to avoid, and the technical considerations for ensuring the software system is a good fit for your business. We will also make the business case for each of these considerations and describe a few of the key technological points to look for in a software system. Download Your Free Copy Now

 


-----


FDA Quietly Steps in to Inspect a Second Massachusetts Pharmacy
Federal regulators have quietly stepped in to inspect another Massachusetts pharmacy similar to New England Compounding Center, the Framingham compounding company blamed for the national fungal meningitis outbreak that has sickened more than 660 people and killed 40.
Boston Globe

Teva Seeks Women s Health-Care Market Beyond Fertility
Teva Pharmaceutical plans to boost work in women s health beyond fertility as it narrows its branded-drug focus amid competition to its best-selling medicine, CEO Jeremy Levin said.
Bloomberg

Indonesia s Pharmaceutical Industry Estimates Slight Decline in Growth
The growth of Indonesia s pharmaceutical industry in 2013 is projected to be not as strong as in last year due to expected rise in production cost, an industry leader said.
Global Times

China to Cut Prices of More Than 400 Drugs From February
China will cut prices of about 400 drugs for respiratory diseases, fever and pain by up to 20 percent from February, in a move to make medicines, including some products from Pfizer, GlaxoSmithKline and Novartis, more affordable.
Reuters

Malaysia an Asian Hub for Indian Pharmaceutical Companies
Malaysia is fast emerging as a major manufacturing hub for Indian pharmaceutical companies, especially for exports to South-East Asian countries.
The Star

UK-Based Pharmaceutical Company to Purchase Egypt s EPCI
Hikma Pharmaceutical plans to acquire the Egyptian Company for Pharmaceuticals & Chemical Industries (EPCI).
Ahram Online


-----
Guide to FDA Pharma GMP Regulations   For drugmakers, complying with FDA current GMP requirements is job one. But putting your hands on all the regulations, guidances, notices and interpretations that   taken as a whole   make up the GMP requirements is a challenge. This guide is a compilation of pharmaceutical GMP regulations that puts all the authoritative information you need in one place. In it, you get the current text of the FDA s GMP regulations for drugs and biologics, with Federal Register announcements and background information, plus the guidance that helps you maintain compliance. Order your copy today.

 


-----
Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, Thursday, Jan. 17, 2013, 1:30 p.m. - 3:00 p.m. EST   Device and pharmaceutical compliance officers have, over the years, worried that their foreign employees might unwittingly trigger a multi-million dollar fine over a cup of coffee or an innocent cab ride. Last August, Pfizer agreed to pay $60 million for illegal payments made by its subsidiaries to foreign officials to obtain regulatory approvals, sales and prescriptions for its products. For the past two years, industry groups have called for a new detailed written Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) guidance. Heeding their calls, in November 2012 the DOJ and SEC released a 130-page resource guide. Register today.

 


-----


Digital Health Increasing (World of DTC Marketing Blog)
In digital and mobile health, policy is changing at the federal level, cultural attitudes about wellness are evolving and new forms of technology are transforming the way patients relate to their bodies and the way clinicians practice medicine, blogger Rich Meyer writes. Venture capital funding of digital health grew dramatically in 2012 with investors funneling 46 percent more money and making 56 percent more deals in healthcare.  This sharp incline contrasts with declining investment in traditional healthcare fields, like biotechnology, life sciences and medical devices,  Meyer adds.

Is there any way to determine whether IV APAP/OFIRMEV specifically was a part of this study? Are any of you familiar with it?

 

UVA slashes opioid use while improving pain scores, study finds
EurekAlert
18 January 2017
 
Strategy offers way to address opioid crisis afflicting country
 
UNIVERSITY OF VIRGINIA HEALTH SYSTEM
 
A study of more than 100,000 surgical cases at University of Virginia Health System found patients' pain scores improved even as doctors gave fewer opioids.
 
UVA anesthesiologists reviewed 101,484 surgeries between March 2011 and November 2015 where patients received general anesthesia. During that timeframe, the average amount of opioids given per surgery at UVA declined 37 percent. At the same time, surgical patients' self-rated average pain score on a 0-to-10 scale in a post-surgery recovery unit declined from 5.5 to 3.8 - a 31 percent improvement.
 
As health officials across the U.S. look for ways to combat a opioid addiction crisis, UVA researchers believe their findings highlight one way to address the problem.
 
"There is very clear evidence that people can become opioid dependent because of the drugs they get during and after surgery," said Marcel Durieux, MD, PhD, one of three UVA anesthesiologists who conducted the study. "I think that by substantially limiting opioids during surgery, we've made an important step in addressing that problem."
 
Keys to Improving Pain Scores
Durieux points to two factors in how UVA was able to cut patients' pain while using fewer opioids. One factor, he said, is that research has shown opioids make patients more sensitive to pain, though the reason why that occurs is unclear. So reducing the amount of opioids given to patients might by itself improve pain scores.
 
The second factor was a significant increase in the use of non-opioid pain medications, such as lidocaine and acetaminophen, which is commonly used in over-the-counter pain medications. Anesthesiologists at UVA have regularly shared data with their colleagues about the benefits of using fewer opioids, Durieux said; in 2013, UVA also began implementing the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery program, which includes limiting opioids, for colorectal surgery patients.
 
The average amount of non-opioid pain medications given per surgical case at UVA increased 120 percent during the study period. While the non-opioid medications have a lower risk for addiction, Durieux said, they cannot be used for all patients. For example, they can cause bleeding in some patients, and can cause kidney problems.
 
Findings Presented
The study's findings were presented in December at the PostGraduate Assembly in Anesthesiology in New York. The study was presented by Gregory A. Smith, MD; Durieux; and Bhiken I. Naik, MBBCh.

Ackman Was Right: Valeant Skimps on Washington Lobbyists (1)

·         Underinvesting in government relations a `meaningful mistake'

·         Drugmaker spent $60,000 on lobbying in third quarter of 2015

By Anna Edney | November 5, 2015 10:04AM ET

(Updates with trading in eighth paragraph.)

Bill Ackman was right: Valeant Pharmaceuticals International Inc. spends a fraction of what similar drugmakers do on lobbyists to represent the company in Washington and keep it abreast of sentiment on the industry in the nation’s capital.

Valeant, under fire for price hikes on older drugs and a now-terminated relationship with a mail-order pharmacy that helped boost insurer reimbursement, faces investigations in both houses of the U.S. Congress. Yet the drugmaker, valued at $32 billion, is using very little of its $8.26 billion in 2014 sales on government relations, according to data compiled by Bloomberg Government.

Ackman, whose Pershing Square Capital Management is a top Valeant shareholder, said last week that Valeant had underinvested in government relations, a “meaningful mistake.”

Shire Plc and Endo International Plc, the two specialty pharmaceutical companies closest to Valeant in market value, spent $320,000 and $260,000 during the third quarter on lobbying. Valeant spent $60,000 in the same period and didn’t even have its own internal lobbyist.

‘Vulnerable to Attack’

“Shareholders need to understand the business and the progress of the company and really need to hear about bad news pronto,” Ackman, whose Pershing Square Capital Management owns 5.7 percent stake in Valeant, said Oct. 30 on a call about the company. “Anything less than complete transparency makes the company vulnerable to attack, and Valeant’s had its share of critics over the years.”

Valeant’s $60,000 went to the firm Mehlman Castagnetti Rosen & Thomas, which lobbied on tax, investment and labor issues. On Sept. 30, Valeant terminated Jeffrey J. Kimbell & Associates, which lobbied on pharmaceutical issues, according to Bloomberg Government.

Those two lobbyist firms, along with Valeant, Endo and Shire, didn’t respond to requests for comment. An outside spokesman for Ackman said he had no further comment.

Valeant shares fell 8.1 percent to $84.51 at 9:58 a.m. in New York, the lowest intraday price since June 2013.

Mehlman Castagnetti’s disclosure form says it lobbies for Valeant on “corporate structure, treatment of international income, reforms targeting internationally acquired companies.” Valeant has its tax domicile in Laval, Quebec, and its principal executive offices in New Jersey.

Kimbell was used for “pharmaceuticals and general FDA issues,” the firm said in its filing, without specifying further.

Lobbyists aren’t required to register that they started work for a company for 45 days, so it’s unclear whether Valeant has hired any other firms to advocate for them on drug pricing.

Hill Intelligence

In addition to bending the ear of lawmakers, lobbyists “can also provide intelligence from the Hill so that, before a company adopts a policy, they can have the benefit of ‘This is how it’s going to look to X, Y, Z, who matter,”’ said Len Nichols, director of the Center for Health Policy Research and Ethics at George Mason University.

Valeant has spent $200,000 total on lobbying in the first three quarters of this year, compared with $970,000 for Shire and $1.1 million for Endo. Pfizer Inc., with a market value of $216 billion, spent $6.5 million on lobbying in the first three quarters, according to Bloomberg Government data.

Turing Pharmaceuticals AG, also taking heat for raising the price of an older drug, hired Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney on Sept. 29 to lobby on pharmacy issues.

Seeking Subpoenas

In the U.S. House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, Democrats are pushing for a vote on Nov. 17 to subpoena the chief executive officers of Valeant and Turing to hand over documents on price increases. The lawmakers also want Committee Chairman Jason Chaffetz to hold a hearing on the issue.

Valeant raised the prices of two heart drugs, Nitropress and Isuprel,by 212 percent and 525 percent the day the drugmaker acquired the rights to sell them. Closely held Turing bought a decades-old anti-parasitic treatment and increased the price to $750 a pill from $13.50.

In the Senate, the Special Committee on Aging sent letters to Valeant, Turing, Retrophin Inc. and Rodelis Therapeutics asking about why they raised prices on drugs. The committee’s leaders, Senator Susan Collins of Maine, a Republican, and Senator Claire McCaskill of Missouri, a Democrat, said they would hold a hearing on the issue Dec. 9.

Sent: Tuesday, June 20, 2017 8:51 AM
To: Webb, Kevin J
Subject: Aetna embraces medication to combat opioid crisis



 

Aetna is going all in on medication-assisted treatment in response to the opioid epidemic, according to a letter CEO Mark Bertolini is sending today to a handful of Democratic senators. Bertolini highlights three goals the insurer hopes to achieve by 2022:

Reduce inappropriate opioid prescriptions by 50%.
Increase by 50% the number of opioid addicts treated with medication-assisted treatment and other evidence-based treatments.
Increase the number of enrollees with chronic pain who use alternative pain treatments by 50%.

Go deeper: Aetna's embrace of medication-assisted treatment is a sharp contrast from some insurers' previous reluctance to cover the approach, which Bob Herman covered for Modern Healthcare. It also follows Tom Price's controversial comment saying medication-assisted treatment is "substituting one opioid for another."

But Aetna has already worked to make medication more available: Earlier this year, it removed all pre-authorization requirements for certain products and put them on a preventive medicine list that reduces cost-sharing for patients.

Title

Treating pain in preterm infants: Moving from opioids to acetaminophen. [References].

Year of Publication

2016

Language

English

Author

van den Anker, John N; Allegaert, Karel; .

Source

The Journal of Pediatrics. Vol.168 Jan 2016, pp. 13-15.

Abstract

Comments on an article by A. Harma et al. (see record 2015-58644-011). The article by Harma et al. is extremely timely and might help in the important discussion on the question whether the use of intravenous acetaminophen in preterm infants is already justified based on our current knowledge. The authors found that the need for morphine decreased significantly in preterm infants of less than 32 weeks after the introduction of acetaminophen. However, to reach a 2-fold reduction in morphine use, almost 17 doses of acetaminophen per patient were needed. Moreover, there were no differences in adverse events detected between the 2 groups. Based on the current available literature in adults, term, and preterm infants, it seems that indeed the use of intravenous acetaminophen will reduce the amount of morphine used in different clinical situations. However, the question remains if acetaminophen used to decrease morphine also improves the overall safety for the patients. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)

Sorry an update

 

From: Wessler, Michael
Sent: Thursday, September 11, 2014 8:50 AM
To: Horton, DJ
Subject: Script for rescheduling....let me know your thoughts....



 

Doctor, effective October 6, 2014, hydrocodone combination products will be rescheduled from Schedule III to Schedule II.

 

This rescheduling will affect your prescribing in a number of ways. Among them, call-in scripts will no longer be accepted, and some states will prohibit prescriptions from nurses or physician assistants. Additionally, no refills will be allowed without a new office visit and a new written script.

 

With the prescribing of hydrocodone combination products becoming less simple, it makes sense that you may be reevaluating your go-to medication for pain. But you want to ensure you are providing your patients with a product that can manage your patient s pain. The CII category offers many options, but only one is a combination opioid with both immediate- and extended-release analgesia approved for acute pain: XARTEMIS XR.

 

XARTEMIS XR provides fast-acting, long-lasting pain relief with predictable twice-daily dosing; this means control over your patients  daily number of pills and steady drug exposure. In contrast, hydrocodone combination products do not contain an extended-release component; therefore, they must be dosed more frequently and less predictably (as needed).

 

When choosing a CII pain treatment for a patient for whom you might normally prescribe a hydrocodone combination product, consider making a change that maximizes your control. Consider XARTEMIS XR.

Mallinckrodt Announces Agreement with Xanodyne to Purchase Roxicodone?

  HAZELWOOD, MO ? August 23, 2012 ? Mallinckrodt, the Pharmaceuticals business of Covidien (NYSE: COV), today announced that it has entered into an agreement with Xanodyne Pharmaceuticals to purchase Roxicodone? (oxycodone hydrochloride tablets USP) in 5, 15 and 30 mg dosage strengths. Roxicodone, currently marketed in the United States, is an immediate release formulation of oxycodone indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain where the use of an opioid analgesic is appropriate. With this agreement, Mallinckrodt acquires all rights to the Roxicodone New Drug Application (NDA).  No financial details were disclosed. 

 

"We are excited about this agreement as it complements our existing portfolio of opioids and leverages our pain management expertise,? said Mark Trudeau, President, Pharmaceuticals. ?More importantly, we are committed to safe and effective use of all of our products along with ensuring access for all patients in need of pain treatment.?

  Mallinckrodt is the largest U.S. supplier of opioid pain medications and among the top 10 generic pharmaceuticals manufacturers in the U.S., based on prescriptions.  Its branded portfolio includes EXALGO? (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) and PENNSAID? (diclofenac sodium topical solution) 1.5% w/w.  Mallinckrodt is also one of the world?s leading producers of bulk acetaminophen.

  Covidien announced last December that the Company planned to spin off Mallinckrodt into a stand-alone company, a process that is expected to be completed in mid-2013.

   IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

  About ROXICODONE

  Roxicodone tablets are contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to oxycodone, or in any situation where opioids are contraindicated. This includes patients with significant respiratory depression (in unmonitored settings or the absence of resuscitative equipment) and patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma or hypercarbia. Oxycodone hydrochloride tablets are contraindicated in any patient who has or is suspected of having paralytic ileus.

  Serious adverse reactions that may be associated with Roxicodone tablets therapy include: respiratory depression, respiratory arrest, circulatory depression, cardiac arrest, hypotension, and/or shock.  Common adverse events that may be associated with Roxicodone tablets therapy include:  nausea, constipation, vomiting, headache, pruritus, insomnia, dizziness, asthenia, and somnolence.

  About EXALGO

  INDICATION

  EXALGO? (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

  WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL, LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION,
and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

  EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient?s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

  Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

  Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

  Accidental Exposure

  Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.


  ?         EXALGO is contraindicated in:

-   Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.

-   Patients with significant respiratory depression

-   Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or in the absence of resuscitative equipment

-   Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

-   Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the gastrointestinal tract, or have ?blind loops? of the gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

-   Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications

  ?         Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.

  
  About PENNSAID

PENNSAID is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (?NSAID?) indicated for the treatment of signs and symptoms of osteoarthritis of the knee(s).

<?XML:NAMESPACE PREFIX = V /> 
WARNING: CARDIOVASCULAR AND GASTROINTESTINAL RISK

Cardiovascular Risk

? Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may cause an increased risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, which can be fatal. This risk may increase with duration of use. Patients with cardiovascular disease or risk factors for cardiovascular disease may be at greater risk.

? PENNSAID is contraindicated in the perioperative setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery.

Gastrointestinal Risk

? NSAIDs cause an increased risk of serious gastrointestinal adverse events including bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal. These events can occur at any time during use and without warning symptoms. Elderly patients are at greater risk for serious gastrointestinal events.

   PENNSAID is also contraindicated in patients:

?     With known hypersensitivity to diclofenac sodium or any other component of PENNSAID.

?     Who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic-type reactions after taking aspirin or other NSAIDs. Severe, rarely fatal, anaphylactic-like reactions have been reported in these patients.

  Anaphylactoid reactions may occur in patients without prior exposure to PENNSAID. NSAIDs can cause serious skin adverse events such as exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS), and toxic epidermal necrosis (TEN), which can be fatal.

The most common treatment-related adverse events in patients receiving PENNSAID were application site skin reactions including dry skin (32%), contact dermatitis characterized by skin erythema and induration (9%), contact dermatitis with vesicles (2%) and pruritus (4%). In a long term safety study, contact dermatitis occurred in 13% and contact dermatitis with vesicles in 10% of patients, generally within the first 6 months of exposure, leading to a withdrawal rate for an application site event of 14%. Other common adverse events greater than placebo include: dyspepsia (8%), abdominal pain (6%), flatulence (4%), diarrhea (4%) and nausea (4%).

  ABOUT COVIDIEN

  Covidien is a leading global healthcare products company that creates innovative medical solutions for better patient outcomes and delivers value through clinical leadership and excellence. Covidien manufactures, distributes and services a diverse range of industry-leading product lines in three segments: Medical Devices, Pharmaceuticals and Medical Supplies. With 2011 revenue of $11.6 billion, Covidien has 43,000 employees worldwide in more than 65 countries, and its products are sold in over 140 countries. Mallinckrodt, the Pharmaceuticals business of Covidien, manufactures active pharmaceutical ingredients, including bulk acetaminophen, opioid pain medications, nuclear and contrast media diagnostic agents. Sales in 2011 were $2.0 billion.  Please visit www.covidien.com to learn more about our business.

Subject: URGENT- finalize 2017 Sci Comm budgets
Importance: High



 

Team,

 

Please prioritize the action items in this memo. 

 

I realize, as well as any of you, how frustrating and time consuming the current budget discussions are.  I ask you to consider all this growing pains for MNK- this is all new to me; and, one way or another, that this current round will be resolved very soon (and we can all go back to Scientific Communications).  Our total budget, of $1.9 million, is based on what we spent last year.  I still maintain- there will be money for great ideas.  Don’t despair! 

 

I had a good discussion with Tunde around budgets for 2017.  He started the meeting by mentioning that he needs to save $9 million.  I know he is sincerely trying to do this without touching headcount- meaning, anything incremental to the $150 k/ brand we started with will only occur, if at all, after a debate.  He also said, what is not committed by July will be taken away.  (Interpret that as June, FYI- I’ve seen all this before).  Our ‘favorability’ in 2016 is a main source of these challenges.

 

In general:

·         We will prioritize projects that are ‘truly medical’, notable Medical Writing Grants (and Scientific Platform… And Review Articles… etc)

·         We will start to discuss, and build the case, that budgets for Company Sponsored Studies should come from R&D.  I will discuss Publication budgets for clinical trials, starting with Lawrence; I’m sure this discussion will get elevated to Steve’s level.  This will take some time; but it is now time to formalize this discussion. 

 

We can discuss the details, but here’s the bottom line:   I need to provide Christine and Tunde with a revised version of the attached, getting all brands down to $150K. David and Molly, a few specific action-item requests for you.  Chirag, you lucked out this time- but please note, we were $200K favorable for the Stub period- and that was mostly for ARD.  

 

Acthar: no action needed

 

Intrathecal: Max $150K.  David, please identify all committed spends here.  Tunde was very focused on IT during our meeting.  Knowing the IT Hydromorphone CSRs are due late in 2017…  but see above- is any of this ‘truly medical’?  We need to tease (at least identify) out what’s R&D… Needs to be discussed with Lawrence Hill

 

Ofirmev: Max $150K. 

·         David: We need to shift the ad board to Medical Affairs as discussed

·         ID budgets for R&D (PREA, UV Burn) and set aside as separate group Needs to be discussed with Lawrence Hill

·         Same with proposed Review Articles (2 for Randi in particular)

·         From this foundation, prioritize what we need to do but not yet budgeted- and then, how much is left?  And (if there is something) what do you recommend we do with it?

 

Hemostats: No action needed

 

Inomax: No action needed

 

Terlipressin:  According to Christine, this is 100% R&D budget (I believe the rationale is because it is not yet marketed).  Needs to be discussed with Lawrence Hill

 

Therakos: $150K. 

·         Molly­: please propose what you would suggest we do with a $150K budget.  Tunde is aware of the $143 grant proposals.  Let’s discuss if we want to keep all of them (I suggest not), and which to drop (if any… but I think we should). 

·         Consolidate MWG and ‘other’ costs into one budget

·         Identify what else we need

·         Thumbnail sketch of Publication Plans for clinical trials (Japan study, cGvHD)  Needs to be discussed with Lawrence Hill  

 

 

I think that’s everything, but please let me know if you have any questions or comments. 

 

Best regards,

John

However, as I mentioned, this specific issue is reflective of some larger concerns Lawrence and I share regarding commercial influence on scientific matters.  I’ve attached another correspondence that seems to reflect a similar concern.

John,

I mean, it may be that many of her points go beyond what you are trying to do here, but they are relevant for the larger issues facing Ofirmev.  What would be the best way to promulgate them?  This is your wheelhouse and I would trust your opinion on this.

Lawrence

(314) 654-3631 (desk)

(314) 239-8105 (mobile)


 

From: England, Christina

Subject: RE: APS Letter to the Editor re_Chou.docx



 

Hi John,

 

I had the opportunity to go through the letter.  I think it is a really really good start, but we can definitely make it stronger before sending.

 

Please see my comments in the attached.  These are all very critical points to include.  We should keep the letter focused on the evidence and point to their lack of consideration for patient safety and not ask rhetorical or emotional questions.  They cannot promote MMA, whose whole goal is to reduce opioids, and then in the same document disregard the evidence across 4 studies that show clinically meaningful difference in opioid consumption vs. oral APAP.  In doing this, they are disregarding the entire point of MMA, which is to maintain adequate analgesia by reducing opioids.  They are better off not making a recommendation on route of administration than making this one, it is in clear disregard for patient safety.   That should be our ask, to reverse their recommendations or at a minimum remove their comparative comment and leave it to the provider to decide route of administration.

 

Mike and Jen, please find time to review this and see if you have anything to add.

 

Thank you and please let me know if you have any questions related to my comments in the attached.

 

Christy

 

Christy England, MPH

9920 Pacific Heights Blvd, Suite 150

San Diego, CA 92121

Hi Christy,

 

I’ve attached the draft response to the APS Guidelines that is nearly finalized, as we discussed today.  You indicated there are pharmacodymanic data being used by the field directly comparing IV vs Oral in a the classic pharmacodynamics sense (ie, comparing pain control rather than a proxy measure such as reduced opioid consumption), and I mentioned that I have not seen this.  I’m copying in Bonni as the field representative, as well as Krishna and Lawrence, with whom I vetted this response, so we are all on the same page. 

 

We received an early draft of this Letter to the Editor based on the SRL, but neither the response nor the SRL had PD data.  The closest was the Bollinger study, but this is supportive of the argument in this reply: that reduced opioid consumption is a valid *proxy* for pharmacodynamics evidence of analgesia (rather than a SPID or other measure of pain, typically vs placebo).   This version of the reply goes considerably beyond the SRL, to focus on the argument sketched out above. 

 

If there are PD data comparing IV vs Oral acetaminophen, I have not seen it.  As I mentioned today, this was the specific challenge to me from Dr. DeLeon Cassasola and Dr. Viscusi.  I would be grateful if you could please direct me to those data, or if someone else can do so, I would most welcome it and we will revise the response to include this additional information. 

 

Thank you for your comments to help us make this the response the best it can be. 

 

Best regards,

 

John

Our takeaway: Sum-of-the-parts analysis supports $70 per share
In this note we have built out separate income statements and DCFs for Acthar ($56 per share), Other Brands ex-Acthar ($61), and Specialty Generics ($11), which supports our belief that the stock at current levels remains attractive. The key overhang for the stock remains the sustainability of Acthar, particularly from potential competition, but our base case assumes significant competition already. In fact, without competition we believe that Acthar would be worth at least $100 per share. Given the stock currently trades at $46 and assuming our valuations for the other pieces of the company, this would imply that the market is attributing only $32 per share of value to Acthar. This valuation implies that Acthar sales would decline 16% CAGR from 2018-2025 as Acthar retains only 25% share with competition, which seems very extreme to us.

Additional thoughts
Some observers have pointed to different types of transactions, which potentially could unlock value, but at the end of the day, management may not move down any of these paths. It may instead just continue to add long-duration assets to the in-line portfolio and/or pipeline, which is really how it has added most value in the past. We would like to see diversification away from Acthar to help change the discussion versus a share buyback, which would probably help the stock in the short-term but not really change the discussion.

Thoughts on the stock: A favorable/risk reward
About a month ago during the week of the UBS Healthcare Conference the stock had moved below $40, and management talked about a sense of urgency and open-mindedness to think  out of the box  to get the stock higher. Since that time the stock has rebounded to $46, and this sense of urgency from management has somewhat resonated with investors. Hi Majid,

 

Sending this as an FYI.  In case you’re not familiar with Oscar deLeon Cassasola, he is an important Thought Leader for our Opioid, Ofirmev and Intrathecal franchises.   Copying in Tim as an FYI (while noting this needs to be carefully executed to avoid any semblance of this survey as a marketing exercise). 

 

We have been working on getting this survey going with Dr. Cassasola for several months (initiated at his suggestion), and I plan to talk with him in the next few days about the best ways to optimize the responses.  He is also working on about a dozen patients receiving high dose (much higher than the 2012 Polyanalgesia Guidelines) IT hydromorphone for a number of years, which he plans to submit for publication in the not too distant future (I don’t have a date yet).  He does not want our support or involvement in this research or publication, to maximize its credibility.  However, he is very easy to talk to, participates freely in advisory boards, and would generally be open to collaborating with us. 

 

We can also tweak the cover letter and survey instruments.  We did need to send a sample (the attached) to AAPM in order for them to send us the mailing list.

John Decker, PhD

Mallinckrodt


 

From: Decker, John F
Sent: Tuesday, March 17, 2015 4:00 PM
To: DeLeon, Oscar (Oscar.DeLeon@RoswellPark.org)
Subject: FW: AAPM Letter



 

Hi Oscar,

 

We have the AAPM mailing list- it’s got several thousand names and addresses- and are getting ready to circulate the survey.  I’ve attached a DRAFT cover letter and survey instrument.  Both still need some work, but you can see where we are from these. 

 

We are trying to figure out how to maximize the response rate.  I believe we discussed the possibility of the survey coming from you, and that you preferred not to do so because of your leadership role with ASRA.  (Please correct me if this impression is incorrect).  One alternative we might consider, if you are interested, could be for you to apply for an unrestricted grant from Mallinckrodt to support your sending the survey and compiling the results via your staff or a third party.   Our default position (for now) is that the letter would get sent under my name.  We will likely consult with a graphic designer for suggestions, but I tend to like a very simple, businesslike approach.  I don’t think we want anything too “designy”, which again may imply marketing. 

 

Response would be by return mail, as a default.  We could also (potentially) develop a simple website to allow for online survey response. 

 

Another thought I have is to get a bit into our plans for publishing these data once they are collected.  We do assure the recipient we will not use these data for non-scientific purposes.  We are not offering any compensation (which I think would really make this look like a marketing piece).  I do think it appropriate to say we plan to submit our results to a peer-reviewed journal.  From here, we could also offer to send any interested participants a copy of the article once it is published. 

 

Those are some of the things I’d like to discuss with you.  In the meanwhile, we can keep in touch by email.  I will be at AAPM, leaving tomorrow afternoon and returning Friday evening.  If you’d like to talk while I’m there, my schedule will be pretty flexible.

 

I look forward to talking with you soon.

 

Best regards,

John

Good Afternoon Scott-

Attached are mine and Gina’s comments on draft 1 of the dossier – there are quite a few, but many of them are regarding consistency of the document as a whole.

 

Regarding the BIM, I do not think that Xcenda made any errors in transcribing the model to Section 4 of the dossier. I think it just comes down to whether or not we are comfortable using Elia 2005 and Marret 2005 to support the 1:1 correlation presented in the BIM.

 

The BIM states:

·         “The default value for ADE reduction is 10%, and thus, the default set-up for the correlation is “a 10% reduction in opioid use would result in a 10% reduction in ADEs,” which was estimated based on two systemic review publications (Source: Elia 2005 and Marret 2005; full citations found on the “References” screen).

 

Information from these references:

·         Elia N, Lysakowski C, Tramèr MR. Does multimodal analgesia with acetaminophen, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, or selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors and patient-controlled analgesia morphine offer advantages over morphine alone? Meta-analyses of randomized trials. Anesthesiology. 2005;103(6):1296-304.

o   http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16306743

o   Article attached

o   IV APAP was associated with a 24 h morphine consumption decrease by 8.3 mg but was not associated with a significant decrease in incidence of respiratory depression, combined NV, urinary retention, or sedation

·         Marret E, Kurdi O, Zufferey P, Bonnet F. Effects of nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs on patient-controlled analgesia morphine side effects: meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Anesthesiology. 2005 Jun;102(6):1249-60.

o   http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15915040

o   Article attached

o   Of note, this article examined NSAIDs (not IV apap) so I think it could be a typo – maybe they meant to reference Remy 2005 (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15681586; article attached)

o   NSAIDs were associated with a significant decrease in PONV by 30%, nausea alone by 12%, vomiting alone by 32% and sedation by 29%. A linear relation was documented between the incidence of postoperative nausea (r=0.61; p=0.007) and vomiting (r=0.51; p=0.02) and morphine consumption in the postoperative period. For each milligram of morphine spared by NSAIDs, the incidences of postoperative nausea and vomiting decreased by 0.9% and 0.3%, respectively.

§  Perhaps this bolded part is where the BIM creators got the 1:1 assumption from, though I think it’s a stretch since this study evaluated NSAIDs and the 0.9:1 correlation was only observed in postoperative nausea (not all ADEs)

The use of intravenous acetaminophen for acute pain in the emergency department
 
Billy Sin, Mabel Wai, Tamara Tatunchak, Sergey M Motov
 
Academic Emergency Medicine: Official Journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine 2016 January 29
 
OBJECTIVES: Acetaminophen is a mainstay for pain management worldwide. The intravenous (IV) formulation has been widely used in Europe for more than 20 years in adults and children. In the United States, IV acetaminophen (APAP) obtained full approval from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2010. There is emerging literature to suggest the use of IV APAP for pain reduction in the Emergency Department (ED). This evidence-based review examines the evidence pertaining to the use of IV APAP for acute pain control in the ED.
 
METHODS: The MEDLINE and EMBASE databases were searched. Randomized controlled trials (RCT) that described or evaluated the use of IV APAP for acute pain in the ED were included. Duplicate articles, unpublished reports, abstracts, review articles, and non-English literature were excluded. The primary outcome of interest in this review was the difference in pain score between IV APAP and active comparator or placebo from baseline to a cutoff time specified in the original trials. Secondary outcome measures were the incidence of adverse events and reduction in the amount of adjuvant analgesics consumed by patients who received IV APAP. Methodological quality of the trials was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation criteria.
 
RESULTS: Fourteen randomized controlled trials (RCT) with various methodological flaws which enrolled a total of 1472 patients met the inclusion criteria. The level of evidence for the individual trials ranged from very low to moderate. In three of the fourteen trials, a significant reduction in pain scores was observed in patients who received IV APAP. The first trial found a significant reduction in mean pain scores when IV APAP was compared to IV morphine at 30 minutes after drug administration (4.7±2.3 vs. 2.9±2.2). In the second trial, patients who received IV APAP reported of lower pain scores (31.7mm+18, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 8.2-25.2) compared to those who received IV morphine (48.3mm+14.1, 95%CI: 8.2-25.2), 15 minutes after drug administration. A third trial found a significant reduction (p=0.005) in the mean pain scores when IV APAP was compared to intramuscular piroxicam at 90 minutes after drug administration. In the remaining 8 trials, pain scores were not statistically different when IV APAP was compared to other pain medications. The incidence of side effects associated with IV APAP was very low.
 
CONCLUSION: Fourteen randomized controlled trials with various methodological flaws provided limited evidence to support the use of IV APAP as the primary analgesic for acute pain control in patients who presents to the ED. This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
