Pharmacotherapy. 2012 Jun;32(6):559-79. doi: 10.1002/j.1875-9114.2011.01085.x. Epub 2012 May 8.

Clinical and economic evidence for intravenous acetaminophen.

Yeh YC, Reddy P.

Author information:

   Center for Drug Policy, Partners Healthcare, 115 Fourth Avenue, Needham, MA 02494, USA. yyeh@partners.org

Comment in

Authors' reply. [Pharmacotherapy. 2013]

Authors' reply.Yeh YC, Reddy P. Pharmacotherapy. 2013 May; 33(5):e84. Epub 2012 Oct 12.

Additional economic and pharmacokinetic considerations of intravenous acetaminophen in acutely ill patients. [Pharmacotherapy. 2013]

Additional economic and pharmacokinetic considerations of intravenous acetaminophen in acutely ill patients.Dasta JF, Kane-Gill S. Pharmacotherapy. 2013 May; 33(5):e83-4. Epub 2012 Oct 12.

Abstract

Intravenous acetaminophen received United States Food and Drug Administration approval in November 2010 for the management of mild-to-moderate pain, management of moderate-to-severe pain with adjunctive opioid analgesics, and reduction of fever. Although intravenous acetaminophen generally improved pain relief and demonstrated opioid-sparing effects compared with placebo, it did not consistently reduce the frequency of opioid-related adverse events (e.g., postoperative nausea and vomiting). The safety and efficacy of intravenous acetaminophen as an antipyretic agent have been documented in adults and children; however, its cost is several-fold higher than that of the oral and rectal formulations. Although use of intravenous acetaminophen has reduced other postoperative resource utilization (e.g., hospital length of stay) in some studies outside the United States in patients undergoing abdominal surgery, a full economic evaluation in the United States has yet to be undertaken. In addition, its administration time (15-min infusion) and packaging (glass, single-use vial) have the potential to adversely affect patient flow in the postanesthesia care unit, create burden on patient care units, and lead to drug waste. Furthermore, 1 g of intravenous acetaminophen is formulated in 100 ml of solution, which may be an issue for patients with fluid restrictions. Given the clinical and economic evidence currently available, intravenous acetaminophen should not replace oral or rectal acetaminophen, but its use may be considered in a limited number of patients who cannot receive drugs orally and rectally and who cannot tolerate other parenteral nonopioid analgesic or antipyretic agents.

  2012 Pharmacotherapy Publications, Inc.

 
PMID: 22570116 [PubMed - indexed for MEDLINE]

 
{Description: Icon for John Wiley & Sons, Inc.}

 
1.

 Am J Ther. 2013 Mar-Apr;20(2):189-99. doi: 10.1097/MJT.0b013e31828900cb.

Intravenous acetaminophen: a review of pharmacoeconomic science for perioperative use.

Jahr JS, Filocamo P, Singh S.

Author information:

   Department of Anesthesiology, David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center, Los Angeles, CA 90095, USA. JSJahr@mednet.ucla.edu

Erratum in

Am J Ther. 2013 Jul-Aug;20(4):458.

Abstract

Hospitals are subject to more economic pressures than ever before. On the one hand, cost containment or cost reduction is paramount, particularly in relation to costly branded pharmaceuticals. On the other hand, quality measures and value-based reimbursement penalizes poor patient care. Multimodal analgesia sits squarely in this quandary, since its very nature requires use of multiple drugs with their associated costs, though this approach has the potential to improve quality of care. We undertook a comprehensive review of the pharmacoeconomics of IV acetaminophen, a new drug useful as part of a multimodal analgesic approach. While this new branded drug adds to direct drug costs, there is clear potential for IV acetaminophen to reduce the incidence of opioid-related adverse events and, in so doing, result in net hospital savings. This review describes many clinical studies showing significant improvements in postoperative nausea and vomiting, excessive sedation and pruritus. In addition, we describe studies demonstrating faster recovery times in the post-anesthesia care unit, intensive care unit and total hospital length of stay. Lastly, we summarize many studies demonstrating the robust effect of IV acetaminophen on patient satisfaction. A holistic view of total hospital performance should be adopted when reviewing drugs rather than a silo mentality within the pharmacy. While IV acetaminophen adds to drug costs, the body of evidence indicates this drug has the potential to improve outcomes and hospital efficiency.

 
 PMID: 23466620 [PubMed - indexed for MEDLINE]

 
  
    

 

Paediatr Anaesth. 2013 Jun;23(6):475-95. doi: 10.1111/pan.12163. Epub 2013 Apr 9.

Opioid-sparing effects of perioperative paracetamol and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) in children.

Wong I, St John-Green C, Walker SM.

Author information:

   Department of Anaesthesia, Great Ormond St Hospital for Children NHS Foundation Trust, London, UK.

Abstract

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES:

Perioperative pain in children can be effectively managed with systemic opioids, but addition of paracetamol or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may reduce opioid requirements and potentially improve analgesia and/or reduce adverse effects.

METHODS:

A systematic literature search was conducted to identify trials evaluating postoperative opioid requirements in children and comparing NSAID and/or paracetamol with placebo. Studies were stratified according to design: continuous availability of intravenous opioid (PCA/NCA) vs intermittent 'as needed' bolus; and single vs multiple dose paracetamol/NSAIDs. Primary outcome data were extracted, and the percentage decrease in mean opioid consumption was calculated for statistically significant reductions compared with placebo. Secondary outcomes included differences in pain intensity, adverse effects (sedation, respiratory depression, postoperative nausea and vomiting, pruritus, urinary retention, bleeding), and patient/parent satisfaction.

RESULTS:

Thirty-one randomized controlled studies, with 48 active treatment arms compared with placebo, were included. Significant opioid sparing was reported in 38 of 48 active treatment arms, across 21 of the 31 studies. Benefit was most consistently reported when multiple doses of study drug were administered, and 24 h PCA or NCA opioid requirements were assessed. The proportion of positive studies was less with paracetamol, but was influenced by dose and route of administration. Despite availability of opioid for titration, a reduction in pain intensity by NSAIDs and/or paracetamol was reported in 16 of 29 studies. Evidence for clinically significant reductions in opioid-related adverse effects was less robust.

CONCLUSION:

This systematic review supports addition of NSAIDs and/or paracetamol to systemic opioid for perioperative pain management in children.

  2013 Blackwell Publishing Ltd.

MNK-795 File Accepted for Priority Review

<image009.jpg>Today we announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has accepted the New Drug Application for MNK-795 and granted it Priority Review.  As you are aware, MNK-795 is an important component of our growth story at Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals and today marks a significant milestone for all of us.

 

MNK-795 is controlled-release oral formulation of oxycodone and acetaminophen that has been studied for the management of moderate to severe acute pain where the use of an opioid analgesic is appropriate and will be part our Brands product line.  MNK-795 was developed by our Research and Development (R&D) team using two known compounds and incorporates technology designed to provide abuse deterrence and tamper resistance.

 

Based on certain qualities of MNK-795, the FDA granted a Priority Review, a designation given to drugs that, if approved, offer significant improvements in the safety or effectiveness of the treatment when compared to standard applications.  As a result of this classification, the product will be reviewed faster than a Standard Review, and if approved could allow us to bring this product to market earlier to help treat patients in pain.

 

The successful filing acceptance and Priority Review are a result of the hard work and dedication of employees across the organization, specifically in the R&D, Regulatory, Commercial, Operations, Legal, and Medical Affairs teams.  Thank you to all employees who got us to this point.

 

Our next milestone as an organization will be at PAINWeek September 4-7, where we will share our clinical data for MNK-795 with attending healthcare providers.  This will be a great opportunity for us to share the clinical story of our exciting product.

 

Look for more information on our @work intranet as we approach the FDA decision date and (if approved) launch to learn more about the teams working across the organization supporting this important product.

 

?   PLEASE CLICK HERE OR READ BELOW FOR THE FULL PRESS RELEASE.

 

 

 
MALLINCKRODT NEW DRUG APPLICATION GRANTED PRIORITY REVIEW BY FDA

 

Mallinckrodt s MNK-795   controlled-release oxycodone/acetaminophen combination

accepted for filing by U.S. Food and Drug Administration

 

 

Hazelwood, MO   July 29, 2013   Mallinckrodt (NYSE: MNK) today announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has accepted for filing the New Drug Application (NDA) for MNK-795 and granted priority review. MNK-795 is a controlled-release oral formulation of oxycodone and acetaminophen that has been studied for the management of moderate to severe acute pain where the use of an opioid analgesic is appropriate. FDA priority review is a defined NDA review process used for drugs that, if approved, offer significant improvements in the safety or effectiveness of the treatment when compared to standard applications. 

 

If approved, MNK-795 would be a controlled-release oxycodone and acetaminophen combination medication that has immediate and extended release components. The dosage form was designed using Depomed s advanced Acuform  drug delivery technology with tamper-resistant properties.

 

 Despite the number of available pain medications, patients continue to experience unresolved pain and lack treatment options that offer fast-acting and long-lasting relief. We are pleased the FDA granted priority review designation,  said Mark Trudeau, President and Chief Executive Officer, Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals.   Mallinckrodt has unique capabilities in complex formulations such as MNK-795 and this marks an important milestone for us as our first NDA acceptance as an independent specialty pharmaceutical company.     

 

Mallinckrodt s submission is based on data from a comprehensive clinical trial program for MNK-795 that included 14 clinical studies with 1,281 patients. The studies evaluated pharmacokinetics, efficacy, safety and abuse liability. 

 

 

About Mallinckrodt

Mallinckrodt is a leading global specialty pharmaceuticals business that develops, manufactures, markets and distributes specialty pharmaceutical products and medical imaging agents. The company s Specialty Pharmaceuticals segment includes branded and generic drugs, and the Global Medical Imaging segment includes contrast media and nuclear imaging agents. Mallinckrodt has approximately 5,500 employees worldwide with direct sales in roughly 50 countries and distribution in approximately 40 countries. The company s 2012 revenue totaled $2.1 billion. Mallinckrodt Announces Agreement with Xanodyne to Purchase Roxicodone(r)


[cid:image005.jpg@01CD8137.15700660]As part of our ongoing effort to grow the business through acquisitions, licensing and co-promotion activities, I am delighted to announce that Mallinckrodt has acquired Roxicodone(r) (oxycodone hydrochloride tablets (USP) in 5, 15 and 30 mg dosage strengths.  Roxicodone is an immediate release formulation of oxycodone indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain where the use of opioid analgesic is appropriate.



In our agreement with Xanodyne Pharmaceuticals, we acquired all the rights to the Roxicodone New Drug Application (NDA).  This acquisition complements our existing portfolio of opioids and leverages our pain management experience.  We will immediately begin the sale and distribution of Roxicodone.



Congratulations to the teams who worked to make this opportunity possible.


READ FURTHER FOR COVIDIEN'S PRESS RELEASE ANNOUNCEMENT.





Mallinckrodt Announces Agreement with Xanodyne to Purchase Roxicodone(r)


HAZELWOOD, MO - August 23, 2012 - Mallinckrodt, the Pharmaceuticals business of Covidien<http://www.covidien.com/> (NYSE: COV), today announced that it has entered into an agreement with Xanodyne Pharmaceuticals to purchase Roxicodone(r) (oxycodone hydrochloride tablets USP) in 5, 15 and 30 mg dosage strengths. Roxicodone, currently marketed in the United States, is an immediate release formulation of oxycodone indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain where the use of an opioid analgesic is appropriate. With this agreement, Mallinckrodt acquires all rights to the Roxicodone New Drug Application (NDA).  No financial details were disclosed.



"We are excited about this agreement as it complements our existing portfolio of opioids and leverages our pain management expertise," said Mark Trudeau, President, Pharmaceuticals. "More importantly, we are committed to safe and effective use of all of our products along with ensuring access for all patients in need of pain treatment."



Mallinckrodt is the largest U.S. supplier of opioid pain medications and among the top 10 generic pharmaceuticals manufacturers in the U.S., based on prescriptions.  Its branded portfolio includes EXALGO(r) (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) and PENNSAID(r) (diclofenac sodium topical solution) 1.5% w/w.  Mallinckrodt is also one of the world's leading producers of bulk acetaminophen.



Covidien announced last December that the Company planned to spin off Mallinckrodt into a stand-alone company, a process that is expected to be completed in mid-2013.



IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION



About ROXICODONE


Roxicodone tablets are contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to oxycodone, or in any situation where opioids are contraindicated. This includes patients with significant respiratory depression (in unmonitored settings or the absence of resuscitative equipment) and patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma or hypercarbia. Oxycodone hydrochloride tablets are contraindicated in any patient who has or is suspected of having paralytic ileus.


Serious adverse reactions that may be associated with Roxicodone tablets therapy include: respiratory depression, respiratory arrest, circulatory depression, cardiac arrest, hypotension, and/or shock.  Common adverse events that may be associated with Roxicodone tablets therapy include:  nausea, constipation, vomiting, headache, pruritus, insomnia, dizziness, asthenia, and somnolence.


About EXALGO


INDICATION

EXALGO(r) (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL, LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION,
and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE
Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient's risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



*         EXALGO is contraindicated in:

-   Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.

-   Patients with significant respiratory depression

-   Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or in the absence of resuscitative equipment

-   Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

-   Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the gastrointestinal tract, or have "blind loops" of the gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

-   Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications



*         Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.





About PENNSAID

PENNSAID is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug ("NSAID") indicated for the treatment of signs and symptoms of osteoarthritis of the knee(s).

[cid:image015.png@01CD8100.AE9006B0]


WARNING: CARDIOVASCULAR AND GASTROINTESTINAL RISK

Cardiovascular Risk

* Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may cause an increased risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, which can be fatal. This risk may increase with duration of use. Patients with cardiovascular disease or risk factors for cardiovascular disease may be at greater risk.

* PENNSAID is contraindicated in the perioperative setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery.

Gastrointestinal Risk

* NSAIDs cause an increased risk of serious gastrointestinal adverse events including bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal. These events can occur at any time during use and without warning symptoms. Elderly patients are at greater risk for serious gastrointestinal events.





PENNSAID is also contraindicated in patients:

-     With known hypersensitivity to diclofenac sodium or any other component of PENNSAID.

-     Who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic-type reactions after taking aspirin or other NSAIDs. Severe, rarely fatal, anaphylactic-like reactions have been reported in these patients.



Anaphylactoid reactions may occur in patients without prior exposure to PENNSAID. NSAIDs can cause serious skin adverse events such as exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS), and toxic epidermal necrosis (TEN), which can be fatal.

The most common treatment-related adverse events in patients receiving PENNSAID were application site skin reactions including dry skin (32%), contact dermatitis characterized by skin erythema and induration (9%), contact dermatitis with vesicles (2%) and pruritus (4%). In a long term safety study, contact dermatitis occurred in 13% and contact dermatitis with vesicles in 10% of patients, generally within the first 6 months of exposure, leading to a withdrawal rate for an application site event of 14%. Other common adverse events greater than placebo include: dyspepsia (8%), abdominal pain (6%), flatulence (4%), diarrhea (4%) and nausea (4%).


ABOUT COVIDIEN



Covidien is a leading global healthcare products company that creates innovative medical solutions for better patient outcomes and delivers value through clinical leadership and excellence. Covidien manufactures, distributes and services a diverse range of industry-leading product lines in three segments: Medical Devices, Pharmaceuticals and Medical Supplies. With 2011 revenue of $11.6 billion, Covidien has 43,000 employees worldwide in more than 65 countries, and its products are sold in over 140 countries. Mallinckrodt, the Pharmaceuticals business of Covidien, manufactures active pharmaceutical ingredients, including bulk acetaminophen, opioid pain medications, nuclear and contrast media diagnostic agents. Sales in 2011 were $2.0 billion.  Please visit www.covidien.com<http://www.covidien.com/> to learn more about our business.



EXALGO is a registered trademark of Mallinckrodt LLC.  PENNSAID is a registered trademark of Nuvo Research Inc.  Roxicodone is a registered trademark of Xanodyne Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

Cc: "Tyndall, Mark" <Mark.Tyndall@mallinckrodt.com>, "Long, Erika" <Erika.Long@mallinckrodt.com>, "Naten, Derek" <Derek.Naten@mallinckrodt.com>, "Gouveia, Staci" <Staci.Gouveia@mallinckrodt.com>, "Stauder, Nancy R" <Nancy.Stauder@mallinckrodt.com>
Subject: Mary Bono, CADCA CEO author Op-Ed in USA Today / When painkillers kill



Please see below for awareness.

 

http://www.usatoday.com/story/opinion/2015/06/10/painkillers-opioids-abuse-prevention-column/28466747/

 

When painkillers kill: Column

Mary Bono, Arthur T. Dean and Jeffrey Levi 9:36 a.m. EDT June 10, 2015

With opioid abuse and fatalities on the rise, it's time for a truly collaborative effort.

{635690197948435724-AX219-294A-9}

Students at Chad's Hope, a Christian drug addiction treatment center in Kentucky, pray before eating dinner. Kentucky sued Purdue Pharma, the makers of OxyContin, a few years ago for misrepresenting the addictiveness of its painkiller. 2015.(Photo: Luke Sharrett, Freelance)

 

The faces that represent today's opioid abuse epidemic are startling. So often, they are people with familiar stories of jobs, of families, of college or even of high school and the unbridled optimism of a life ahead. As this epidemic has spread throughout America, it's disturbing to note that {http://www.cdc.gov/drugoverdose/data/overdose.html} more Americans died in 2013 from a drug overdose than from any other form of injury. Half of these overdose deaths involved prescription drugs, just over two-thirds of which were opioids.

 

Thankfully, this situation is beginning to change.

 

The American public, media, and policymakers are learning about the true nature of this crisis. Earlier this spring, for example, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services launched a multi-faceted {http://www.hhs.gov/news/press/2015pres/03/20150326a.html} initiative to reduce deaths from prescription opioids and related substances. With a {http://www.cdc.gov/drugoverdose/data/index.html} quadrupling of fatalities related to this abuse between 1999 and 2013, these actions could not come soon enough.

 

A Complex Problem

Preventing abuse of prescription painkillers is a particularly challenging problem because the medicines that are {http://www.drugabuse.gov/drugs-abuse/prescription-drugs-cold-medicines} most widely abused are those that also help relieve pain and suffering for so many patients. They must remain accessible, for patients who need them and have been prescribed by a health care professional. Efforts to curb prescription drug abuse contrast sharply with campaigns to combat the misuse of other substances where any use is illegal and where zero tolerance is justifiable.

 

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), nearly {http://www.cdc.gov/media/releases/2014/p0701-opioid-painkiller.html} 260 million prescriptions for opioids were written in 2012. This represents a significant {http://www.drugabuse.gov/about-nida/legislative-activities/testimony-to-congress/2014/americas-addiction-to-opioids-heroin-prescription-drug-abuse} increase over the previous two decades. Some of this trend has questionable clinical benefit. Inappropriate prescribing of opioids — intentional or unintentional — must be addressed through a combination of patient and provider education and enforcement actions against rogue actors.

 

This challenge also is partly about advancements in medicine that have resulted in {http://www.agencymeddirectors.wa.gov/Files/GuidelineMaster041615ForPubComment.pdf} more effective therapies to help people manage pain, the causes of which can stem from chronic illness, injuries, or other {http://www.researchgate.net/profile/Javad_Parvizi2/publication/51203945_Multimodal_pain_management_after_total_joint_arthroplasty/links/0deec53567418a0f06000000.pdf} medical procedures. In some cases, newer therapies help patients not only manage their pain, but allow for the restoration of function that can also allow them to live more fulfilling and active lives.Our response must encourage innovation in how we treat people with pain therapies, while not limiting legitimate access to those who need it.



An effective response to the prescription drug abuse epidemic requires stakeholders from all perspectives to rally around a comprehensive plan. We at the {http://cepoponline.org/}Collaborative for Effective Prescription Opioid Policies (CEPOP) call on patients, healthcare providers, pharmacists, law enforcement, public health, treatment centers, health plans, distributors and manufacturers to join us in this collaborative effort. Our approach supports strategies like greater access to medication monitoring that aids in preventing abuse, education for providers about the many dimensions of the problem, access to evidence-based treatment and recovery services, increased development of abuse-deterrent pain therapies and community-based prevention and education efforts. Together, we must seize this opportunity to promote the most effective government and private sector solutions. Far too many lives hang in the balance.

 

Mary Bono was a member of the U.S. House of Representatives from California for 15 years and is now a principal at {http://www.faegrebdc.com/}FaegreBD Consulting. Retired Major General Arthur T. Dean is CEO of {http://www.cadca.org/}Community Anti-Drug Coalitions of America (CADCA). Jeffrey Levi is executive director of the {http://healthyamericans.org/pages/?id=29} Trust for America's Health.

 

In addition to its own editorials, USA TODAY publishes diverse opinions from outside writers, including our {http://www.usatoday.com/reporters/boc.html} Board of Contributors. To read more columns like this, go to the {http://www.usatoday.com/opinion/} Opinion front page.

Cc: Otulana, Tunde; Hill, Lawrence; Cortes, Robert
Subject: RE: IT Hydromorpone Investigator concerns



 

Thank you, John.

During my meeting this morning with Dr Saulino, he articulated, in order of importance, the following frustrations around our Hydromorphone study:

1)      There appears to me no leadership for this study….no point person.  “Who is running this study.”  He would like to have a single, identified individual with whom he can interface as needed. I’m confused by this since the protocol has the contact individuals listed.  Who do you think he means?

2)      There have been no investigator meetings in 3 years and there have been no conference calls in 2 years.  What do you think his expectation is regarding this?  I mean, except for the oncology trial we have conducted that had a data safety monitoring board with some of the lead investigators, we do not normally have regular conference calls with the investigators.  Our communication channel is typically between the in-house clinical trial manager and the site’s study coordinator.  Communication with the actual investigator occurs on an as-needed basis, usually because of a safety incident.

3)      There have been no abstracts for this study.  Yes, that is correct.  There have been no publication efforts for this program.  As you know, this is driven primarily by the med affairs strategic agenda.  

4)      There is no consistency of protocol.  He has had 8 study monitors and each seems to bring in their own set of protocols.  For example:  Patient required pump replacement secondary to end of life pump.  Was told by one study monitor that this was okay and not a documentable adverse event and then was told after the surgery by another study monitor that this was indeed a documentable adverse event.  I can understand this concern.

5)      Just yesterday, Dr Saulino met with his institution and was told, due to the volume of issues with this study, that the IRB may significantly restrict his investigator status resulting in a loss of other, unrelated studies he is currently involved with.  This he indicated he feels he can mitigate.  This is a serious comment.  Did he happen to mention what issues are of concern to the IRB? 

6)      In conclusion, Dr Saulino indicated that if this study is going to be discontinued, then discontinue it.  If it’s going to be modified, then stop this study and start over.  Just don’t let it keep limping along as it is.  The study has been enrolling relatively steadily; I’m confused why he characterizes it as limping along.  The last patient visit will occur in about April of next year and then the submission will go in.

 

I do think the next step from us would be someone reaching out to Dr Saulino.  He indicated that email will be the best course for this action.  Please, let me know if you would like his email address.  Yes, reaching out to him is clearly necessary. 

 

Thank you,

 

Holt Miller

Market Development Manager

Gablofen

Mallinckrodt Intrathecal Therapies

St. Louis, MO

M: 224-234-7978

www.Gablofen.com

Cc: Otulana, Tunde <Tunde.Otulana@mallinckrodt.com>; Hill, Lawrence <Lawrence.Hill@mallinckrodt.com>; Miller, Holt W <Holt.Miller@mallinckrodt.com>; Cortes, Robert <Robert.Cortes@mallinckrodt.com>
Subject: IT Hydromorpone Investigator concerns



 

Hi Domingo,

 

I got a call from Holt, who just met with Dr. Saulino, one of our IT-H investigators. Holt let me know that Dr. Saulino is very upset with the way that Mallinckrodt is managing this clinical trial and related communications.  Holt, can you please share some of Dr. Saulino’s concerns that he shared with you?

 

I spoke with Tunde and Lawrence, so they are aware, and both wanted me to share this with you.

 

I’d also like to mention that we (several folks from MNK, including Tunde) will be meeting with another IT-H investigator, Dr. Oscar deLeon Cassasola, at ASRA.  Krishna will be presenting our phase 1 Ofirmev data there.  Oscar is the outgoing president of ASRA (being followed by Gene Viscusi).   They were both authors on the recent APS guidelines, which were very unfavorable to Ofirmev.  My point is that our Investigators are also very influential KOLs and Authors, and not necessarily for one brand.   Oscar specializes in cancer pain, and is a passionate supporter of intrathecal hydromorphone.  Ofirmev is only of passing interest to him- but he can be very influential in how others perceive it, and Mallinckrodt.

 

I realize there are many factors at play, and I know I don’t see all the pieces.  I’m simply passing along a message, and letting you know of the potential implications from my perspective.  And I’d really like to know if there is something I can do to help.

 

Lawrence indicated you would be in the office next week, and I will be out on PTO from Oct 22 to Nov 9- so I wanted to share this information, and open this channel of communication promptly.

 

Best regards,

John

Subject: FOR REVIEW: DRAFT EC EMAIL: Part D and Medicare Advantage 2019 Proposed Rule Released



 

The Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) released an advance copy of a proposed rule yesterday, proposing changes to Medicare Part D and Medicare Advantage (MA) plans for the 2019 contract year.  While we re still reviewing the rule, a few items to highlight include proposals such as:

 

 

           Manufacturer Rebates and Pharmacy Price Concessions to Point of Sale.  The proposed rule includes a Request for Information soliciting comments on potential policy approaches for applying some manufacturer rebates and all pharmacy price concessions to the price of a drug at the point of sale.  CMS states that they would use ideas and comments provided in response to the Request for Information to evaluate and consider proposals for rulemaking, but no proposals are currently included in the rule.  MNK Impact:  The idea of passing on rebates and other price concessions to consumers is being widely discussed, and would put pressure on Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) and insurers [KEVIN: we also may significant concessions/rebates to the distributors/wholesalers, so not aware if they re getting the same level of scrutiny as the PBMs, but they should be included], who may very likely oppose these ideas.  For patients, this could increase adherence and minimize patient abandonment rates and for pharmaceutical manufacturers, this would shine a brighter light on the ways in which PBMs and health plans utilize rebates and discounts. I would include whether MNK plans on commenting (I think we are, right? KEVIN: agree, we should comment) and whether we think this is neutral or positive or too soon to tell based on the information.

 

           Implementation of the Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act (CARA).  The proposal seeks to implement provisions of CARA by allowing Part D sponsors to establish a drug management program for  at risk beneficiaries.   Under such a program, Part D sponsors can limit access to frequently abused drugs, such as opioids, to a selected prescriber(s) and/or network pharmac(ies), sometimes also known as  lock in.   Specifically, Part D sponsors would be able to limit an at risk beneficiary s access to coverage of opioids beginning 2019 through a point-of-sale (POS) claim edit and/or by requiring the beneficiary to obtain opioids from a selected pharmacy(ies) and/or prescriber(s) after case management and notice to the beneficiary.  MNK Impact:  This will be an opportunity to highlight our view that opioids should be used sparingly, and that a balanced, multi-modal approach to pain management must be the preferred standard of care.  Restricting access to certain pharmacies or prescribers could negatively impact patient access to these medicines and negatively impact the specialty generics business. I would put this sentence first.[Kevin: Agree this should be first sentence.  What s not being said in the CMS document is what the sponsor is required to do if they limit access to medications. Our comments should state that the sponsor, if opioids are limited/withheld, would be required to provide the patient an alternative form of pain management, such as MMA]

 

           All opioids are proposed to be designated as  frequently abused drugs,  except for buprenorphine for medication-assisted treatment and injectables [Kevin: another example of CMS shifting market to buprenorphine and Vivitrol (injectable).  If they re going to call out MAT, they should say  all FDA approved MAT s].  MNK Impact:  Designating all opioids as  frequently abused  heightens the stigma around these medicine, and could be cause for concern.  Could also have a negative impact on MNK s methadone business.

 

           Mid-Year Formulary Changes.  Current regulations prohibit Part D sponsors and MA organizations from removing a covered Part D drug from a formulary or changing the preferred or tiered cost-sharing status of a covered Part D drug between the beginning of the annual election period and 60 days subsequent to the beginning of the contract year associated with that annual election period.  In the proposed rule, CMS would permit Part D sponsors to immediately remove brand name drugs (or to make changes in their preferred or tiered cost-sharing status), when those Part D sponsors replace the brand name drugs with (or add to their formularies) therapeutically equivalent newly approved generics--rather than having to wait until the direct notice and formulary change request requirements have been met.   MNK Impact:  Neutral.  The proposed mid-year formulary changes are concerning, as are proposals to change cost-sharing status for beneficiaries. This could cause patients to abandon medications if a change causes their cost sharing to increase mid-year.  If a therapeutically equivalent generic version of Acthar is approved in 2019, it could have a negative impact. Agree

 

           Any Willing Pharmacy Standard.  The proposed rule seeks to clarify Part D rules and CMS expectations regarding the statutorily required Any Willing Pharmacy provisions, and proposes to add a clarifying definition of mail-order pharmacy and revise the definition of retail pharmacy, among other changes.  Specifically, Part D sponsors are required to contract with any pharmacy that meets the Part D sponsor s standard terms and conditions for network participation.  In the proposed rule, CMS clarifies that the any willing pharmacy requirement applies to all pharmacies, regardless of how they have organized one or more lines of pharmacy business.  MNK Impact:  Neutral.  The proposed change would not apply to  at risk beneficiaries  and  frequently abused drugs  as described above.

 

           Biosimilar Payments.  CMS proposes to treat lower-cost  biosimilar  versions of biologic products like other generic drugs when determining how much certain beneficiaries pay for drugs out of pocket under Medicare Part D. This change seeks to encourage the availability of lower-cost alternatives for Medicare beneficiaries. MNK Impact:  Neutral.

 

The proposed rule is expected to be published on November 28, with comments due on January 8, 2018.  We will continue to review and engage with BIO and others as we prepare comments on behalf of MNK.

 

Please let us know if you have any questions.

 

Best,

Kendra

Subject: Good Morning


To all

I hope that each of you had a tremendous week and are prepared to recharge this weekend. As I am sitting in the Dublin Airport awaiting my flight back home, I thought it would be beneficial to recap the Strategic Plan Board presentation:

1. The overall feedback from the board was complimentary on not only the aspiration of our plan but also the amount of progress we have made over our last twelve months.

2. There was robust conversation regarding the future expansion of the business beyond Questcor and ultimately there was agreement about the potential external opportunities necessary to deliver the plan.

3. A large degree of time was dedicated to capabilities throughout the organization. While there was recognition of the positive steps we have made as a company, the challenge ahead for all of us is to be extremely rigorous in our approach to building the capabilities required for us to be successful now and throughout the plan. This will require us to be courageous in our approach to performance management in order to ensure that our teams reach their full potential while upgrading talent where appropriate.

4. As it relates to the commercial review, the Board was supportive of the plan but challenged me to ensure that we are realistic and prepared in our responses to the needs of the market. As you recall, the US Spec Pharma plan delivers a 10% CAGR on the top line and a 12% CAGR on the bottom line across the entire 5 year landing period. To deliver these results will require the commercial team to embrace the idea of continuos improvement across all facets of our organization. We cannot allow ourselves to be content with our current skills and capabilities. We have to build customer intimacy in order to ensure impact and value for our teams. We must build the voice of the customer into our plans earlier in the process while challenging our assumptions of what will be necessary to succeed. Finally, we have to embrace the business acumen required to ensure our investments deliver the required return for the company.

5. Finally, the Board confirmed what we have been saying all along, this plan will require Mallinckrodt to become a Commercial Excellent organization. All facets of the broader company must be focused on what will be required to win in the marketplace. It was clear to the Board as it has been to us, the future of Mallinckrodt lies squarely in the hands of the commercial organization.

I couldn't be more thankful to each of you for the amount of dedication and effort that you bring to your job everyday. Leadership is not easy and it requires not only vision but also collaboration and trust. It is up to each of us to work together, to let go of whatever personal agendas might exist and focus on the greater good of the organization. We must learn to work together, to push each other, to trust each other and finally, to support each other. These are the characteristics of great teams.

There is no doubt that we have our work cut for us, including:

1. The stabilization and return to growth for Ofirmev
2. The correction of the Xartemis XR launch curve
3. Improving the effectiveness and impact of our customer facing teams
4. Building our commercial excellence capabilities
5. Continuing to feed the growth of our multi source business through both internal and external opportunities
6. Successfully preparing the market and the launch of MNK-155
7. Strengthening our Market Access presence and impact for the entire portfolio
8. Integrating Acthar Gel and other external opportunities as they occur

This team has the chance to deliver the future for Mallinckrodt. I hope that each of you are excited as I am about this rare opportunity.

Thanks and have a great weekend. I will be in NJ moving next week but I will be available by phone, text or email so please don't hesitate to reach out.

All the best

Hugh

Foundation for Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation and Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals Announce New Grant Partnership

 
 

ROSEMONT, Ill., March 31, 2014 /PRNewswire-USNewswire/ -- The Foundation for Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation (FPM&R) and Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals are partnering in the development of a new research grant. The Mallinckrodt Acute Pain Management Research Grant will offer up to three grants of $10,000 each in 2014 for research on the use of acute opioids by physiatrists in physical medicine and rehabilitation, with special consideration given to outcomes research. Applications are being accepted through May 01, 2014. The FPM&R Awards and Grants Review Committee will independently score all proposals and recommend a winner to the FPM&R Board of Directors. The award will be presented at the 2014 Annual Assembly of the American Academy of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, November 2014.

Phyllis Anderson, MA, Executive Director of the FPM&R stated: "Every year, the Foundation receives up to six times as many qualified research grant applications than we are able to fund. We established a Pain Management and Spine Care Fund in 2013 to address a great need for evidence and outcomes research in this area. Many thanks to Mallinckrodt for joining us in support of this research grant we are offering specifically for acute pain management."

"This research grant underscores our commitment to developing and providing new treatment options for the millions of patients who suffer from pain," said Dr. Mario Saltarelli, Senior Vice President and Chief Science Officer, Mallinckrodt. "As experts in the development of complex products to help manage pain, Mallinckrodt is proud to partner with the FPM&R in this important long-term effort."

About The Foundation for Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation:

The Foundation for Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization, strives to restore health, improve function, minimize pain and enhance quality of life for individuals with disability through research and education in the field of physical medicine and rehabilitation. For more information, visit www.foundationforpmr.org.

About Mallinckrodt

Mallinckrodt is a global specialty pharmaceutical business that develops, manufactures, markets and distributes specialty pharmaceutical products and medical imaging agents. The company's Specialty Pharmaceuticals segment includes branded and generic drugs and active pharmaceutical ingredients, and the Global Medical Imaging segment includes contrast media and nuclear imaging agents. Mallinckrodt has approximately 5,500 employees worldwide and commercial presence in roughly 70 countries. The company's fiscal 2013 revenue totaled $2.2 billion. To learn more about Mallinckrodt, visit www.mallinckrodt.com.

Subject: Hungry and Smart!!!



 

West Region Sales Team:

 

I appreciate you all getting on our call yesterday.  Please take the time to read this email and review our 5 Cultural Hallmarks.  It s important that we are all on the same page and driving in the same direction! 

 

I hope that you all agree that we have unique opportunity to help Mallinckrodt realize our vision of becoming a Top Quartile Specialty Pharmaceutical Company!  A quality company with 5 Cultural Hallmarks (Attached) that I believe in and will transform who we are!  I want you all to know that I am committed to do my best in this position and to help in any way that I can.

 

Our Region has started off in 3rd place.  Our vision is to be the #1 Region!  At this point our selling execution is at a C+.  Our/your opportunity is to improve selling effectiveness, which will directly and quickly improve our selling execution and sales results!  And I m confident that we can do accomplish great things together!  I d like to recognize our top Region performers:

 

Top West Region XARTEMIS XR Performers:

1.       71 - Brett Nichols (Boise, ID)

2.       62   Franco Castaldo (Las Vegas South, NV)

3.       27   Patrick Day (Santa Rosa, CA)

4.       23   Tina Bethia (San Jose, CA)

5.       21   Jeff Sandys (Anchorage, AK)

6.       20   Kimberly Gallegos (Albuquerque, NM)

7.       19   Maricela Chaidez (Sacramento East, CA)

7.       19   Lynda Namba (Salt Lake City, UT)

9.       16   Ross Couples (Phoenix North, AZ)

9.       16   Rossalyn Lopez (Temecula, CA)

9.       16   Dayami Nickel (Thousand Oaks, CA)

9.       16   Kent Vinson (Berkley, CA)

 

Top West Regions Districts:

1.       Portland led by John Kelly at 156

2.       Salt Lake City led by Sean Wilmert at 114

3.       San Francisco led by Nels Fiksdal at 91 

 

2 Critical Success Factors:

          #1 TARGETS   Maniacal Focus on the Right Targets with the Right Frequency!  It s important that you identify your most important targets and influence them to write XARTEMIS XR!  Use your current Target list, your territory knowledge, and other prescribing analytics to select your biggest Oxy/APAP writers/accounts.  With focus on those who are surgeons (Ortho, Podiatrists, Plastics, Oral, General, etc.), Family Practice, and select pain/physical med and rehab HCPs.  Understand that with your surgeons the prescribing influencers will likely be a mid-levels, nurses, clinical nurses, MAs, etc.  It s important for you to target and treat those influential customers as the prescribers when selling!  Total Office Call is not just something we say here at Mallinckrodt.  It s a way of life for us!

          #2 SELLING EFFECTIVENSS - Highly Effective Sales Messaging.  The goal is meaningful action taken by Targets, Mid Levels, or staff in your territory.  Meaningful action is defined in the West as WRITING XARTEMIS XR and PENNSAID 2% consistently!  This means that you have to have the skill and will to be the BEST Sale Professional that you can be!  Engage customers, ask great questions, deliver a selling message with impact, use all of your available resources, etc.  That you are professionally persistent and unwavering in your goal to close your customer and then to  close the loop  as soon as you get any buying signs   If you don t ask you won t get and you have to be able and willing to routinely ask your customers to do things!

 

The most successful sales professionals possess two main traits and is what s expected in the West!!!

o    Hungry    The do what it takes to see (access) their customers enough times to sell them.  They make more calls   use more resources   They are true business owners   They are accountable and always wanting more   Love a challenge   Push for more   They are in offices at 5:00am and stay out  till 7:00pm if necessary.  They wait in the parking lot for their customers to arrive in the morning and stay late to see them when they go home.  They see customers when it s convenient for the customer   Not when it s convenient for them!  They ask for prescriptions today!  Not tomorrow   Not next week   Not next month   TODAY.  RELENTLESS!!!

o    Smart    Strategic smart   They know who their most valuable customers are and see them frequently.  They provide value to get repeat appointments and opportunities to sell them.  They work on and deliver selling messages that are impactful and drive/change prescribing behavior   They really know their customers   If they belong to important associations, hold regular meetings, work at other facilities, etc.  Always looking for opportunities to partner with their customers.  Looking to fill customer needs with XARTEMIS XR and finding  win-win  situations.

 

For a number of you being successful in the West Region at Mallinckrodt today is going to require you to look at things differently and to change your selling approach and behavior.  Assume that what you did before to be successful won t work anymore.  Why?  1) This industry has changed and will continue to change and 2) You may be selling an acute pain med for the first time in your career and selling to surgeons!  This requires a different approach.  Assume that every Monday you have 0 sales!  You have to be relentless and consistent in asking for more business.  More patients!  Because the ones you got last week aren t taking the drug anymore.  You may have to significantly change your  mindset! 

 

As I said on the call, please take the time to internalize and access your last 90 days   Review our cultural Hallmarks   Make sure that you agree with the hallmarks and get energized by them.  And that you understand, buy into, and fully support our Vision:

          Top Quartile Specialty Pharmaceutical Company

          West Region to be #1 at Mallinckrodt in Sales and Sales Execution

I realize that everything isn t perfect and that we ve had to adjust and change since launch.  And I feel that you have everything you need to be successful today!  The bus has left the station and isn t coming back.  Change is required to change our sales trajectory. 

 

Thanks to all of you for dealing with the call-in number confusion.  It won t happen again!  And thanks to Brett and Franco for sharing what s working for you and what we need to do to have success selling to surgeons. 

 

I m confident that we can get to #1 if we all work together.  Your managers and I are here to help in any way that we can.  I truly look forward to watching our team climb from 3rd to 1st by the end of the fiscal year!

 

Christian H. Kampfl | West Region Sales Director, US Specialty Sales

[RxNews] Pharmacists Blame Patient Fears on DEA

Pharmacists Blame Patient Fears on DEA
March 12th, 2014 by Pat Anson, Editor
Pharmacists and patient advocates say the results of a survey by the National Pain Foundationshow that a crackdown on
prescription painkillers by the Drug Enforcement Administration is causing fear and confusion in the pain community.
In the survey of of over 300 pain patients, over half (52%) said that they are worried that "I may be viewed as a drug
addict" and 29% were concerned that they might be "embarrassed" by their pharmacist while trying to get a prescription
filled. Many patients also complained they were unfairly denied pain medication by a pharmacist.
I

"These survey results are not really surprising considering the DEA's
aggressive efforts attempting to stem the tide of prescription drug abuse," theNational Community Pharmacists
Association (NCPA) said in a statement to National Pain Report.
"Their crackdown efforts, while well intentioned, have put medication wholesalers into a defensive crouch where
pharmacies that don't fit into the standard dispensing patterns for controlled substances, such as pharmacies serving
hospice patients or located near a surgery center, could have their supplies limited or cut off, thus greatly affecting
patients with legitimate pain issues."
NCPA represents over 23,000 independent pharmacies across the U.S. In January, NCPA said many of its members had
their shipments of controlled substances abruptly cut off by drug wholesalers, which it blamed on the "perceived pressure,
intimidation or a lack of clear guidance" from the Drug Enforcement Administration.
"We believe the root cause of the prescription drug abuse crisis is a small handful of prescribers writing hundreds or even
thousands of prescriptions that find their way into the hands of substance abusers," NCPA said in its statement.
"As the DEA further refines their policies much of the apprehension that some patients feel will hopefully be addressed,
and be replaced with the positive attitude that most patients have towards pharmacists, especially independent
community pharmacists at whose pharmacies patients are a name and not a number."

THE NATIONAL
PAIN FOUNDATION
While the survey by the National Pain Foundation did find that many patients
were worried about how they were perceived by pharmacists, nearly two-thirds (62%) said they were treated "well" or
"very well" by their pharmacist.

MNKOI 0004183495

 "I think that it would be interesting if these patients that are happy with their pharmacist to determine if there was a higher
level of satisfaction with independent pharmacies over chains. The chain pharmacists get paid if they fill zero controls
(controlled substance prescriptions) or 100 controls. Not so much for the independently owned pharmacy," says Steve
Ariens, a retired pharmacist and patient advocate who has a blog called Pha€racist Steve.
"I am aware of three pharmacies, one in Arizona and two in California, that had a lot of chronic pain patients in their
practice and they were both completely cut off from getting opiates from their wholesalers because the wholesalers were
told by the DEA that they had to establish some arbitrary limits of ratio of controls to the rest of their purchases," Ariens
said in an email toNational Pain Report.
"My understanding is that other pharmacies when their shipments hit this arbitrary monthly limit they are just cut off for the
rest of the month. Patients that need their medication after that point are out of luck."
The DEA has denied trying to limit or ration access to opioid painkillers. A DEA spokesman toldNational Pain
Report "nothing should stand in the way" of a patient getting a legitimate prescription for pain medication filled.
"We do look at distributors and what they're selling. And typically what we look for are patterns, like abrupt changes. So if
we see that a distributor sells "X" amount that's pretty steady and then all of sudden there's a significant spike, we might
want to ask questions why," said DEA spokesman Rusty Payne.

"We look for patterns. We take action on egregious violations. And CVS and
Walgreens would be good examples of that," said Payne, referring to enforcement actions taken against the drug store
chains, which were fined tens of millions of dollars for violating rules and regulations for dispensing controlled substances.
The Los Angeles Times reported this week that CVS pharmacies could face additional fines for allegedly losing track of
37,000 prescription painkillers at four of its California stores. Many may have been sold on the black market.
In addition to their fear of being perceived as drug addicts, the National Pain Foundation survey also revealed that many
pain patients go from doctor to doctor before finally finding one to treat their pain.
A large majority (82%) said they had stopped seeing a doctor because they were treated poorly. Many patients (71%) had
seen four or more physicians to treat their pain and 20% had gone to ten or more doctors.
Only about half (53%) said they were treated "well" or "very well" by their current pain physician during appointments.
"What I personally get from these results is the proof of why we, as patients must stop adding our emotions and fears into
the mix. They are being used against us as a way of focusing the blame on us and keep the `old school' doctors hanging
around longer," said Dennis Kinch, a patient advocate and chronic pain sufferer.
"These results show the patient fears and perceptions of care contrasted with the actualities of treatment. It also shows a
large inconsistency in the professional ranks with over 80% of patients changing doctors due to poor treatment, yet better
than half finding good treatment with the next doctor, or at least the third. How much of this is a personality clash or the
doctor thinking poorly of the patient and treating them thus, the survey doesn't tell. In my experience it is the latter."

Cc: Wessler, Michael; Sarah Showalter
Subject: RE: Question re Sunshine Act Interpretation



 

Apologies for the delay but I was ill.  The question is not whether the fee is reportable or not but whether this is one we wish to have in our database   and it is.  Our policy requires that we capture all spend or transfers of value (non-sales related) involving a hospital or an HCP.  At the appropriate time, we filter all hospital spends or transfers of value to determine whether the hospital is  reportable   or not.  I understand that this hospital is not on the current reportable list, but we are so early in this process I cannot be sure that it is not going to change.

 

To put it more broadly, we would rather that you not think about what is Sunshine Act reportable, and what isn t, but instead think about what we wish to have reported, and what we do not, so that we can make the best call about what gets reported and what doesn t at the appropriate time. 

 

Does this clarify?

Subject: Question re Sunshine Act Interpretation



 

Hi Brian   quick question for you.

 

We have identified a hospital that is willing to rent us an area to film the video segments for the XARTEMIS XR content we are developing. According the guidelines laid out by CMS for Sunshine Act reporting the amount of the rental fee (in this case, $500) is only reportable if the hospital is qualified as a  teaching hospital.  We have confirmed that this hospital is NOT a teaching hospital according to the definition provided by CMS below (in blue); however, we wanted double check that MNK doesn t have any reporting rules above and beyond what has been outlined out by CMS.

 

Can you confirm that this fee would not be reportable? We will be able to move forward with solidifying plans for filming as soon as we hear from you.

 

Thanks,

Kristie

 

For the purposes of this program, teaching hospitals are defined as hospitals that received a payment under a Medicare direct graduate medical education (GME), inpatient hospital prospective payment system (IPPS) indirect medical education (IME), or psychiatric hospital IME programs during the last calendar year for which such information is available.)

 

Applicable Manufacturers are Required to Report to CMS

Applicable manufacturers of at least one covered drug, device, biological, or medical supply must report all payments or other transfers of value provided to covered recipients, regardless of whether any particular payment or other transfer of value was related to a covered drug, device, biological, or medi cal supply. Applicable manufacturers will be required to categorize all reportable payments as falling within one of the following natures of payment:

                Consulting fees

                Compensation for services other than consulting, including serving as faculty or as a speaker at an event other than a continuing education program

                Honoraria

                Gifts

                Entertainment

                Food and beverage

                Travel and lodging

                Education

                Research

                Charitable contributions

                Royalty or license

                Current or prospective ownership or investment interest

                Compensation for serving as faculty or as a speaker for an unaccredited and non-certified continu ing education program

                Compensation for serving as faculty or as a speaker for an accredited or certified continuing educa tion program

                Grants

                Space rental or facility fees (teaching hospital only)

 

(http://www.cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Legislation/National-Physician-Payment-Transparency-Program/Downloads/Physician-fact-sheet.pdf)

I explained in detail that this was an effort in due diligence and in no way would Mallinckrodt authorize/approve or give the impression of authorization as to their individual SOM programs, that it was simply another step in our process to ensure that our products were being handled appropriately all throughout the supply chain.

DI White reviewed the difference between excessive orders/purchase reports which were required by DEA in the past and a suspicious order.  Stated that excessive order reports are no longer required by DEA and that if an order is determined to be suspicious, we are not permitted to ship.  I stated that Mallinckrodt understood the difference and asked for an elaboration on what is considered "suspicious" of which her comment was 100,000 doses of Oxycodone to Florida in one month she would consider "suspicious", she did comment any further.

DI White gave indication that she was going to make some phone calls to her colleagues in the Cincinnati and St. Louis field division offices regarding the recent DEA initiative of "know you're customer's customer"


Should DI White contact me regarding this subject, I will be sure to keep you informed.
 
Regards,
 
Eileen

Subject: FW: Follow up from AfBPM Summit Meeting (Nov 12-13)
From: "Webb, Kevin J" <kevin.webb@mallinckrodt.com>
Date: Fri, 11 Dec 2015 18:14:02 +0000
To: pdantonio@geron.org


Tricia,


FYI.  Message I sent to Debra Pasko at ASHP. 

 

I believe you had invited her based on your previous work experience.  Hopefully Debra will join our little band as we continue to drive access and patient safety forward.

Kevin

 

From: Webb, Kevin J
Sent: Friday, December 11, 2015 12:08 PM
To: 'dpasko@ashp.org'
Subject: Follow up from AfBPM Summit Meeting (Nov 12-13)



 

Debra,

 

On behalf of the Alliance for Balanced Pain Management (AfBPM), I would like to thank you for attending our recent Summit meeting held November 12-13 in Washington, DC.  Many of the points you raised during the work shop discussions were spot on regarding need to balance access to appropriate pain management with patient safety across the health care continuum, and the hospital/health system setting is of particular importance.

 

As you were leaving you had mentioned that the AfBPM would be a good fit with the ASHP.  The sole purpose of the AfBPM is to advance aligned coordination, singularity of message, and continuity in educating and empowering all stakeholders regarding responsible pain management. This includes the safe use, storage and disposal of pain medications.  The ASHP and the health-system pharmacist is crucial to this success, and we would be honored to have you as a member of the Alliance.

 

Attached is a brief slide deck that provides an overview, mission and structure of the Alliance for Balanced Pain Management.  After reviewing, let me know if you have any questions, or if would like to discuss in further detail.

 

For full disclosure I also wanted to make you aware that after the first of the year, management of the AfBPM will transition from Green Room Communications to a third-party, non-profit organization called the Alliance for Patient Access (AfPA).  This is a better long-term fit for the strategic direction and needs of the AfBPM, as the AfPA has the capabilities and capacity to guide the AfBPM to realize its full potential.  Over the next week I will be sending an announcement out the full membership, which I will copy you on, but I wanted to be completely transparent with you as you consider your decision.

 

Again, it was a pleasure meeting you, and look forward to your favorable reply.


Best regards,

Kevin

Subject:RE: Oxycodone
Attachments:Chargebacks by Customers.xlsx
Ginger,

Please find below information on Oxy as requested. There are a lot of moving parts, but let me know if you would like to discuss
the below further.

 Backorders were low in June.
o  Have some orders kicked out of the system for being on backorder too long?Yes , there have been a total of
297 orders to date that have been cancelled due to expired 222 forms, in which the customer had to
re-order. The value of the lost sales is ~$8.8M (based on June ASP), assuming that the order was not
placed again (which it most likely was).

Item Description Cancelled Orders
OXYCODONE HCL 5MG TABS
055201 73
USP
OXYCODONE HCL 5MG TABS
055262 38
USP
OXYCODONE HCL 15MG TABS
851501 77
USP
OXYCODONE HCL 30MG TABS
853001 109
USP
Total  297

o  Was this partly due to timing of product shipped to wholesalers being too late to sell to pharmacies? This was
due to us allocating product to priority customers while on backorder as well as those customers that
were cut off but still ordering product. Only 10 of these cancelled orders were direct ship priority
customers; the rest were wholesalers and distributors (mainly distributors).
 Are we shipping everything we get in stock?Yes , however, we keep minimal inventory on hand for direct ship
customers depending on the next expected release date.
 Are the chargebacks dropping? Yes, it appears that within the past several months (starting in Jan), the 3 month
average has been slowly decreasing by ~4%. Oxy 15 and 30 are driving the decrease, Oxy 5 remains steady.

o  What end customers drove this?McKesson  OneStop is contributing a lot to the decrease in chargebacks
on the 15 and 30mg. The attached file shows the breakdown of key drivers based on past 3 month
average compared to the previous 3 month avg. Rite Aid is driving a lot of the inconsistency of OneStop
demand. For example, for the 30mg, during the months of Oct - Dec, they ordered ~15K bottles/month
through OneStop and for the past few months they are back to 0.


o  Is it any particular wholesaler at issue more than others?McKesson  OneStop as mentioned above.
o  Are we supplying distributors all that they need?No , we are still not supplying Optisource fully. Once we
start supplying all of the distributors, the wholesaler demand may slow. This would also increase our
distribution in hopes to regain the end users back. However, we are still allocating product to
distributors when we are in a safe inventory position until the next release.
 I keep hearing we will have ongoing issues
o  Is that based on forecast which is above demand? I think we are still playing catch-up for the most part
along with trying to fully understand the increase in wholesaler's demand (whether it  is true demand or
not). According to the chargebacks we have lost business at the end user due to backorders. The
Kroger compliance report is a perfect example of how Cardinal has substituted our product for a
competitors because of backorders. Kroger is very compliant, so I do not think it will be very difficult to
regain that business back quickly.
o  Have we permanently lost any customers?I  am not aware of losing any business from our backorders. The
feedback that I have received is that other suppliers are having issues as well and that all of our
customers (especially distributors) want our product back to 100% of their demand as soon as we can
supply.

Thank you,
Lisa

Subject: e-MD /alert: New tablet strength FDA approved
From: e-MD/alert <emdalert@alertmarketingmail.com>
Date: Thu, 27 Sep 2012 10:45:53 -0500
To: melissa.falcone@covidien.com


View this e-mail in a browser   |   Forward to a friend   |   Printer Friendly Version


{e-M.D./alert } 
{e-M.D./alert  Providing important information to healthcare professionals since 1976} {e-M.D./alert } 
{e-M.D./alert } 

The FDA has approved the EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) 32 mg tablet for use inappropriate
opioid-tolerant chronic pain patients. With the addition of the 32 mg tablet, along with the already approved 8, 12, and 16 mg dosing strengths, you now have greater dosing flexibility.

Learn more about EXALGO.

The features of the added EXALGO 32 mg tablet include:

 

 Dosing flexibility. EXALGO 32 mg complements the already approved 8, 12, and 16 mg tablets.1

 
 

 Proven efficacy. EXALGO 32 mg was the median effective dose in the pivotal trial.*2

 
 

 Robust patient exposure. EXALGO 32 mg has been thoroughly tested in 14 clinical trials conducted in 2474 patients, with 1483 of these patients exposed to a dose of 32 mg or greater.3

 

* Mean effective dose was 37.8 mg.1

Additional EXALGO information available.

P.S. Learn about proper dosing and titration with
once-daily EXALGO.

REFERENCES: 1. EXALGO  Prescribing Information. 2. Hale M, Khan A, Kutch M, Li S. Once-daily OROS hydromorphone ER compared with placebo in opioid-tolerant patients with chronic low back pain. Curr Med Res Opin. 2010;26(6):1505-1518. 3. Data on file. Mallinckrodt Inc.

800-778-7898 | www.EXALGO.com

COVIDIEN, COVIDIEN with logo and Covidien logo are U.S. and internationally
registered trademarks of Covidien AG.
EXALGO is a registered trademark of Mallinckrodt LLC.
  2012 Mallinckrodt LLC, a Covidien company.  MK20158 September 2012

 

  

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION,
and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

 

 

 EXALGO is contraindicated in:

- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 
 

 EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.



 
 

 EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.

 
 

 Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.

 
 

 Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.

 
 

 Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.

 
 

 Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.

 
 

 Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.

 
 

 Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.

 
 

 Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


 

See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information and Medication Guide.

    There is a listing of INCB estimates on the DEA website. Anyone has access to the website.  I have asked Lisa Edelen (DEA) in the past if she has information that we do not see.  She said no.  The only information that someone has access to that we do not is the total amount used by any given country at any given time. 

 

    I am willing to ask again, but even if she agrees to "pre-approve" the estimate, and taking into consideration how slow they are, we would probably have week or two for them to approve the estimate before sending  in the application.  There would then be another  two or three weeks more for the permit to arrive.  I think we would end up taking more time for the pre-approval.

Either way, they would know to go back to their contact and ask for more. Wendy Slaby
