From: "Terifay, Terry W" <terry.terifay@covidien.com>
Date: Thu, 05 Jul 2012 10:40:20 -0500
To: "Hasse, Debra C" <debra.hasse@covidien.com>,
    "Duarte, Joe A" <joe.duarte@covidien.com>


FYI.

From: Littlejohn, Stephen E
Sent: Thursday, July 05, 2012 10:17 AM
To: Berry, Tom E; Cano, David J (Human Resources); Edwards, Peter G; Giuliani, Michael; Harbaugh, Matthew; Harrell, Jamie; Haynes, Elaine E; Mannebach, Mark; Missey, Tim; Silver, David; Smith, Thomas; Stevens, Dirk E; Trudeau, Mark C; Von Rohr, Dawn M; Wirth, Christian
Cc: Schooler, JoAnna S; Phillips, Lynn; Kim, Stuart K.; Lohman, Donald A; Patrick, Jeffrey; Elsbernd, Brian D; Brendel, Diane; Terifay, Terry W; Wuestner, Joe A; Swartz, Betty Jean (BJ); Stauder, Nancy R; Saake, Lisa M; Gillies, John V; Stamer, Jeremy; Collier, Ginger L; Williams, Jane L
Subject: WSJ -- Methadone and Suboxone Abuse

This story (pasted below) comes immediately after the CDC story<http://healthland.time.com/2012/07/03/methadone-a-major-driver-of-prescription-painkiller-overdose-deaths/> earlier this week regarding methadone related deaths.  Notably, it illustrates how a small outfit like Titan can get attention for an apparently "abuse deterrent" innovation, even before filing for FDA approval.  Titan has been working on this product for a number of years and announced<http://www.drugs.com/clinical_trials/titan-pharm-announces-positive-ph-3-probuphine-opioid-results-5184.html> Phase III results in 2008.

More important for Mallinckrodt is the role managed care is playing in promoting use of methadone for pain treatment due to lower cost, despite safety concerns - as noted in this article and articles about the CDC report.  Not in these stories but very pertinent is the recent announcement<http://www.kaiserhealthnews.org/Features/Insuring-Your-Health/2012/BCBS-painkiller-abuse-Michelle-Andrews-061212.aspx> by Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Massachusetts that it will be limiting reimbursement for opioid pain medications.   Also related is another recent story<http://www.nytimes.com/2012/06/03/health/painkillers-add-costs-and-delays-to-workplace-injuries.html?pagewanted=all> reporting extra workers comp costs associated with opioid use, to which states and insurers are responding by limiting prescribing.  Clearly, managed care needs help with appropriately integrating cost, safety and therapeutic considerations.

BJ Swartz and Lisa Saake are all over this, having introduced several managed care plans to C.A.R.E.S..  I'm wondering whether we can extend our data based approach to breaking down the abuse/misuse problem into high value (in terms of solving the problem) hittable targets, using data-validated solutions that work.  It's how David Silver, Don Lohman and their respective teams are tackling the suspicious order monitoring challenge, as well as hydrocodone rescheduling through the task force Tom Smith has pulled together.  In addition, at last week's C.A.R.E.S. summit, Lisa and team ensured the challenge of getting better data, e.g. death certificates, ICD coding, etc. was a major part of the agenda with several speakers including one from CDC.

In the long run, such a data based approach applied end-to-end across the abuse/misuse/appropriate use issue will position Mallinckrodt extremely well as a credible go-to problem solver with important audiences, especially government agencies, policy makers and managed care.  We are well equipped to do so, given the strength of the analytics capabilities in David Silver's team.    Explicitly adopting such a strategy, creating a strategic plan and funding would be among next steps.

Concluding note:  Years ago, when Express Scripts was just getting started, it decided to invest in a research function to track drug utilization patterns.  The reports emerging from that function provided the basis for the company's highly regarded Drug Trend Reports and Outcomes Conferences.    As the expert, go-to source for information unavailable anywhere else, ESI used the data to support policy and benefit designs that helped address (in the eyes of its clients and the government) high drug costs in ways that were advantageous to its bottom line.  We can do the same.

Wall Street Journal

Addicts Misusing Drug Treatments

  *   July 4, 2012, 7:54 p.m. ET
By TIMOTHY W. MARTIN<http://online.wsj.com/search/term.html?KEYWORDS=TIMOTHY+W.+MARTIN&bylinesearch=true>
In the latest sign of how entrenched the nation's epidemic of painkiller misuse has become, people are also abusing treatments meant to cure their addiction.
Titan Pharmaceuticals Inc. plans to file for Food and Drug Administration approval in September for a matchstick-size implant of buprenorphine, a drug that eases withdrawal symptoms. Current versions of the drug normally come in a pill or strip, but many are being diverted to the black market and taken to get high, because they contain small amounts of opioids, or used more heavily by addicts than they should be to relieve withdrawal symptoms, according to Titan as well as law enforcement officials.
Enlarge Image
[Description: image]
Close

Buprenorphine is abused by injecting or snorting crushed tablets, according to the Center for Substance Abuse Research at the University of Maryland, the same methods addicts use to get high from oxycodone or any other powerful painkiller.
The San Francisco-based biopharmaceutical company is hoping to cut down on abuse of buprenorphine by offering the implant-called Probuphine-which is inserted just under the skin in the upper arm and releases continuous, small doses of the drug over a six-month period. "You cannot easily remove these implants from the arm," said Katherine L. Beebe, a senior vice president with Titan.
Drugs like buprenorphine are on the market in ever greater quantities to help combat a growing epidemic of painkiller abuse. Pharmacies dispensed enough painkillers last year to keep every American adult medicated around the clock for a month, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. An estimated two million Americans are addicted to the prescription opioids. Of that number, 800,000 are currently receiving treatment, Titan said.
Methadone, another drug used to treat addiction, now causes 30% of prescription painkiller deaths, putting it second behind painkilling drugs containing oxycodone, according to the CDC.
Doctors normally use the slow-release drugs to wean addicts off heroin or powerful narcotic painkillers. Use of methadone is heavily restricted and the drug is commonly dispensed on-site at treatment centers in daily doses. But some doctors are now also prescribing methadone, which contains small amounts of opioids, to treat chronic problems like back pain, a practice that has made the drug more widely available and helped it make its way onto the black market.
Some health plans rate methadone as a preferred drug over oxycodone for treating some chronic pain because it is often just a quarter of the cost for other extended-relief painkillers.
"Today in the U.S., there are probably more people who receive prescriptions for methadone for pain than there are people who receive methadone as part of a drug-treatment program," CDC Director Thomas Frieden<http://topics.wsj.com/person/f/thomas-frieden/1587> said in a conference call with reporters Tuesday. "There has really been an overuse of methadone for pain."
Methadone can be deadly because unlike painkilling drugs like OxyContin its contents tend to build up in the body, Dr. Frieden said. Taking the drug more than three times a day can dangerously slow breathing, according to the CDC.
Addiction doctors say that buprenorphine is bought off the black market just as commonly for legitimate needs as it is for nonmedical use. Stuart Gitlow, acting president of the American Society of Addiction Medicine, said that in order to prescribe Suboxone, the brand name for the best-selling version of buprenorphine, he is limited by Drug Enforcement Administration rules to treating 100 patients, even though he has a waiting list for the drug about the same size.
The high demand is partly filled by people selling Suboxone pills or patches on the black market, Dr. Gitlow and law enforcement officials say.
"The number of patients coming in who are new to Suboxone is very low now. Most everybody has started it on the street," said Dr. Gitlow, whose practice is in Woonsocket, R.I.
Titan Pharmaceuticals said its aim is to help fill the demand for legitimate need of buprenorphine that the current supplies of pills and patches cannot meet. The company published the results of its clinical study of its implant in the Journal of the American Medical Association in 2010. The 163-patient trial found that users of the implant had "significantly" less illicit opioid use and fewer symptoms of withdrawal and craving. "There are just a lot more people who need treatment than who are getting access now," said Titan President Sunil Bhonsle.
Suboxone, made by U.K.-based Reckitt Benckiser Group<http://online.wsj.com/public/quotes/main.html?type=djn&symbol=RB.LN> RB.LN -0.14%<http://online.wsj.com/public/quotes/main.html?type=djn&symbol=RB.LN?mod=inlineTicker>PLC, was approved by the FDA in 2002. It was the first narcotic drug doctors were able to prescribe from their offices for opioid addiction. Sales rose 18% in 2011 to $1.3 billion from $1.1 billion in 2010, according to IMS Health Inc., which tracks prescription drug sales.
Reckitt Benckiser declined to make an executive available for comment Tuesday or Wednesday.
In Kentucky, law enforcement and community groups say the number of Suboxone investigations are approaching those for oxycodone or hydrocodone.
The estimated number of drugs or paraphernalia containing buprenorphine analyzed by state and local forensic law enforcement jumped to 10,537 in 2010 from 90 in 2003, according to an April report by the Center for Substance Abuse Research.

To: Romer, Peter M; Williams, Jane L
Cc: Lasker, Karen L
Subject: McKesson VIP proposal


Pete & Jane,

Attached is the revised McKesson VIP model and a separate file containing just the summary of the latest proposal (without all the data and calculations).  This takes the model that Karen reviewed and approved over the weekend and makes minor modifications as we discussed yesterday, including:

1.      Removal of APAP/Codeine from the compliance tiers.  Due to our supply issues, they have not been coming anywhere close to the original trend, and it is likely that we've even lost a portion of the volume.  Growth is pretty unrealistic at this point.
2.      Inclusion of a column showing current run rate for the compliance families.  This allows a comparison to where they were trending based upon March data (pulled for the original model), and shows that they've already achieved about half of the growth we are targeting in total.
3.      A modification of the compliance targets to provide two levels, which they had asked for in June.  The first level is clearly within reach and has lower payouts than the previous version, and the upper level has higher targets and, in some cases, slightly higher payouts.  The full analysis (on the "7-9-12 Level 1" and "7-9-12 Level 2" tabs) shows that both of these two options now give us 40% or more in standard margin, up from the 39.5% we had in the one-level version we started with yesterday.  And, the first level gives McKesson an 18.2% overall payout, while the second level (still attainable, I think) gives 19.5%, right in the middle of where they wanted to be.

Pete, I did not include sales by product family for the last VIP period anywhere...I can't remember if you said you did want that for sure, but if you do, I can send that to you separately.

I am copying Karen on this since there are minor tweaks since yesterday, but I hope those won't be a problem since we are now better off in terms of margin for both new compliance target levels.  Karen, please advise if you do have concerns.

Thanks, and let me know if you have questions.
Kevin

The American Telemedicine Association has identified a valid access to care issue for patients who suffer with chronic
pain who require ongoing opiate therapy.
Instead of Telemedicine, we have our stable pain patients examined, monitored and medically maintained by a
Prescribing Pharmacist who is more accessible/local to the patient than his Pain Management specialist. At VeraPharm,
we think our solution to this problem is safer for both the patient and his community. (VeraPharm.biz)
Under a strict protocol from a pain management specialist, VeraPharm pharmacists may prescribe pain medications to
stable patients for whom access to their Pain Management Specialist is problematic. This system helps protect the
patient, his community, and his prescriber from the potential issues that may arise with chronic pain. Under the
protocol, patients may be seen by their local VeraPharm pharmacist if:
*The patient has an intractable pain diagnosis
*the patient has been stable on medication and therapy for at least a year
*the patient has not shown aberrant behaviors
*the patient's condition has not changed
*the patient is not ill from other causes
*the patient has a significant other who can monitor their daily functionality and medication use and report
responsibly
If any of the above conditions change, the Pain Management: specialist is immediately contacted.
At a monthly, IN-PERSON office visit, the Prescribing Pharmacist examines and interviews both patient and significant
other, The pharmacist: monitors for aberrant behaviors, checks for ADE. and other functionality, and may make minor

MNKOI 0004243891

 changes to the pain patient's medication regime. Patients are not pre--warned about toxicology screening. The patient's
chart: information is then sent to the Pain Management specialist who reviews it in a timely manner per legal
requirements. Both the physician and pharmacist have full access to the patient's chart at all times,
At VeraPharm, patients get a hands-on visit with a qualified pharmacist. Telemedicine may be the best choice for some
pain patients, but, where possible, and in-person visit with a VeraPharm pharmacist is often a better choice.
VeraPharm.biz

Subject: [RxNews] N Engl J Med    From 2010 through 2013,	there was a notable downturn in abuse of prescription opioids and a	coincident increase in abuse of heroin in the United States
From: Coolidge <coolidge@dakota2k.net>
Date: Thu, 12 Nov 2015 01:33:44 +0000
To: NADDI <rxnews@listserve.com>


http://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMc1505541



Correspondence

Shifting Patterns of Prescription Opioid and Heroin Abuse in the United States

N Engl J Med 2015; 373:1789-1790October 29, 2015DOI: 10.1056/NEJMc1505541

Share:
{Facebook}
{Tweet}
{Google+}
{LinkedIn}




Article
To the Editor:

From 2010 through 2013, there was a notable downturn in abuse of prescription opioids and a coincident increase in abuse of heroin in the United States.1 Given that there is some evidence of a relationship between the two trends (e.g., some persons who abuse prescription opioids switch to heroin for a number of reasons and drug interchangeability has been observed),2-4 we sought to examine this relationship more closely, including the validity of reports suggesting regional differences in the balance between prescription opioid and heroin abuse.5

Data on opioid abuse in the previous month were collected quarterly from January 1, 2008, through September 31, 2014, with the use of self-administered surveys that were completed anonymously by independent cohorts of 15,227 patients with opioid dependence, as defined by the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th edition, who were entering nonmethadone-maintenance treatment programs throughout the United States. Of these patients, 267 agreed to online interviews to gather qualitative information in order to amplify and interpret findings from the structured national survey.

Figure 1Figure 1National Rates of Abuse of Opioids in the Previous Month among 15,227 Respondents. shows the unadjusted rates of abuse of prescription opioids only, abuse of prescription opioids and heroin, or abuse of heroin only among respondents who reported such abuse in the previous month from 2008 through 2014. Rates of exclusive prescription opioid abuse remained stable from 2008 through 2010, at 70%, but then decreased steadily, with an average annual reduction of 6.1%, to less than 50% in 2014. Conversely, concurrent abuse of both heroin and prescription opioids in the previous month increased, with an average annual increase of 10.3%, from 23.6% in 2008 to 41.8% in 2014. Although the exclusive use of heroin was low in this population, it more than doubled from 2008 through 2014 (from 4.3% to 9.0%).

The national data obscure important regional differences (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix, available with the full text of this letter at NEJM.org). The Northeast showed the most striking shifts in patterns of abuse. The West followed closely behind, with concurrent heroin and prescription opioid abuse surpassing exclusive prescription opioid abuse in 2014. The Midwest and South followed similar trends, with the latter showing exclusive prescription opioid abuse to be more prevalent than in any other region.

These findings suggest that as prescription opioid use has waned, concurrent heroin abuse has increased, with important, distinct regional variations. The factors contributing to these evolving changes are not well established. However, in our exploratory qualitative online survey of a subgroup of 267 patients, among the 129 respondents who reported abusing prescription opioids prior to heroin use, 73.0% (92 of 126 respondents) primarily cited practical factors, such as accessibility and cost, when explaining their transition to heroin. Three of the 129 respondents did not provide an explanation for their transition to heroin.


Theodore J. Cicero, Ph.D.
Matthew S. Ellis, M.P.E.
Jessie Harney, M.S.
Washington University, St. Louis, MO
cicerot@wustl.edu

Subject: Endo Pharmaceutals Fails in Maneuver to Have Own Drug Called Unsafe
From: Anne Marie White <awhite@fingerpaintmarketing.com>
Date: Fri, 21 Dec 2012 15:36:38 -0600
To: Michael Wessler <michael.wessler@covidien.com>,
    Jennifer Lierman <jennifer.lierman@covidien.com>,
    Kevin Webb <kevin.webb@covidien.com>,
    Ryan Rausch <ryan.rausch@covidien.com>






Endo Pharmaceutals Fails in Maneuver to Have Own Drug Called Unsafe



Endo Pharmaceutals Fails in Maneuver to Have Own Drug Called Unsafe [the Philadelphia Inquirer]





From Philadelphia Inquirer (PA) (December 21, 2012)

Dec. 21--Perhaps only in the strange business of pharmaceuticals would a company sue to have a federal agency declare that one of its products was unsafe and then be disappointed when it lost the suit.

But that s what happened with Endo Pharmaceuticals Inc., a subsidiary of Endo Health Solutions Inc., of Chadds Ford.

The drug in question is Opana ER, first approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2006. It is an opioid painkiller, a group of medicines that are controversial because of deadly overdoses by abusers.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recently said misuse of prescription painkillers was a "deadly epidemic" and caused more deaths by overdose than cocaine and heroin combined. Some addicts reportedly cut or crushed the drug and snorted or smoked it.

With officials from several agencies and branches of government looking at the overdose problem, Endo created what it says is a crush-resistant version of the drug, and put the last of the dosages of the new version into the market in June of this year. Then Endo employed legal and regulatory tactics to try to delay generic competitors from taking revenue from its second best-selling product.

The hope was that if the old version was declared unsafe, generic versions would have to be pulled from the market or prohibited from entering.

In August, Endo filed two citizens  petitions with the FDA seeking to have its crushable version declared unsafe compared with the newer noncrushable version, and have generic versions -- the crushable variety -- declared null. Under the normal timeline, the FDA would need to answer those petitions by May 2013.

But on Nov. 30, Endo filed suit in U.S. District Court in Washington hoping to force a decision by Dec. 31 -- one day before a generic competitor is scheduled to enter the market.

In a statement, Endo said it argued in the suit that "the FDA failed to meet its legal obligation to determine in a timely manner whether the original formulation of Opana ER was withdrawn from the market for reasons of safety."

On Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Reggie B. Walton dismissed Endo s suit, saying the FDA was operating in a timely manner.

In its court filing, the FDA indicated it was not convinced Endo was only concerned with the potential for overdoses, since Endo had not recalled the original formulation of Opana ER. It simply stopped marketing it after the crush-resistent version was on the market.

The FDA also argued that Endo s insistence on a decision by Dec. 31 was less a safety concern than a tactic to delay a generics company from entering the market on Jan. 1.

One generic version is already on the market -- Endo is suing that company -- and others are to start in 2013. Impax Pharmaceuticals will start selling its version of the medicine Jan. 1.

Impax, like other generic companies, negotiated a settlement of a patent-infringement suit with Endo in 2010, allowing it to enter the market Jan. 1. Such arrangements are examples of the pay-to-delay settlements between the makers of brand-name drugs and the makers of generics of the same medicines that the Supreme Court will hear arguments on in 2013.

"The Dec. 31  deadline  reflects only Endo s commercial concern that, as a result of a settlement agreement it made with another manufacturer, it will face additional generic competition beginning Jan. 1, 2013," the FDA attorneys wrote in a memo submitted as part of their objection to the suit and request for an injunction. "Endo s self-inflicted timeline does not trump the statute and does not justify the emergency relief it seeks."

Dave Holveck, president and chief executive officer of Endo Health Solutions, announced last week that he was retiring and that the company was lowering its financial expectations. Opana ER s sales fell from $97.8 million in the third quarter of 2011 to $62.2 million in the same period of 2012. The generic competition in 2013 will further hurt sales.

Holveck said in a statement that the company was "extremely disappointed" by the judge s decision.

From: Kelly A. Ryan
Sent: Tuesday, October 02, 2012 4:48 PM

Subject: Pharmacy Advisory Committee meeting summary

Hi all  

I covered the Medicaid Pharmacy Advisory Committee meeting today.  As is often the case, much of the meeting was either a reiteration of updates we are already aware of or discussion of issues from a very pharmacist-specific perspective, but there are always a few helpful tidbits that come out of the meetings.  Today was no exception here is a quick rundown, let me know if you have any questions or need more detail on any of the below (or anything else on the attached agenda):

BNE I-STOP update:

-          Some schedule changes from I-STOP will be effective on Nov 25 (these include the changes that were already made on the federal level and were just incorporated into state statute via I-STOP).  The biggies, hydrocodone to schedule II and tramadol to schedule IV, are effective February 23, 2013.  There will be further information and a set of Q&As posted on the BNE site shortly   I will monitor and circulate when this pops up.

o   One interesting point   when hydrocodone moves to schedule II, all outstanding refills will be immediately void, there is no transition time for existing scripts.

-          Members have been appointed to the I-STOP workgroup (I caught a couple of names only because Larry Mokhiber mentioned them during his separate update).  It is expected that the first workgroup meeting will be scheduled very shortly.  I caught the BNE representative off line and asked if the meetings will be public   her first response was no and then she said she didn t know.  It sounds like at least some members are representatives of state agencies so I m surprised it s not a public body   not sure if it s really our fight, but it would certainly be nice to monitor policy discussions that are going to directly impact regs and I-STOP implementation.

-          An interactive map re Rx disposal sites is up on the BNE website.  Further action on this item is on hold pending federal regulations (currently in progress) re drug disposal

Board of Pharmacy update:

-          Regs re pharmacists giving shingles vaccine will be published on an emergency basis tomorrow

-          Public sessions regarding the Limited English Proficiency Rx labeling law are being held (Albany on 10/11, NYC on 10/25)

Ride-booking bill in Albany still stuck in roadblock over insurance

Buffalo News

Though its plans to expand into New York have been watered down, the ride-hailing industry is leveling an all-out push for approval of the taxi-alternative transportation to upstate. The Senate and Assembly, however, are still apart over a key sticking point: how much insurance liability ride-hailing drivers must carry. Time is running out with next week’s scheduled end of session. It is a matter that has attracted the interest of transportation companies, trial lawyers, insurance firms, unions and disability groups. Here is the conflict: • Ride-hailing companies, led by giants Uber and Lyft, say consumers crave their services, and that the upstate economy and transportation choices will be bolstered by their presence. • Opponents, including upstate taxi companies, say job-creation claims are bloated, consumers will have fewer protections and cab companies will go out of business. http://goo.gl/5eYYVu

 

COR's big score: Why did a juicy job from NY state draw just one bidder?

Syracuse News

There's something odd about the way COR Development Co. faced no competition for a lucrative state contract to develop Central New York's nanotech projects. The contract was advertised and approved in a hurry. Other developers that might have fought for the job never knew about it. Instead, COR --€“ a major contributor to Gov. Andrew Cuomo's campaign -- was the only bidder. The deal has already brought the company $75 million in work funded by state taxpayers, with the potential for more. COR was selected in late 2013 as the state university's "strategic partner'' to develop and build high-tech economic development projects in Central New York. The five-year deal, which can be extended to 10 years, makes COR the preferred developer for all relevant projects. "That's a heck of a deal,'' said Michael P. Falcone, chairman and CEO of the Pioneer Companies, another prominent developer. "I kind of wish I had seen that ad.'' But the opportunity went unnoticed by Falcone and other leading Syracuse developers. The request for proposals was publicized less widely than many state procurement offers worth far less money. http://goo.gl/QP7Ejg

 

Cuomo releases recommendations to combat heroin, opioid abuse

Times Union

The Governor’s Heroin and Opioids Task Force, created last month, issued a report Thursday with 25 recommendations for combating the abuse of the illicit and prescription drugs in New York. The report follows a statewide listening tour by the Task Force, co-chaired by Lt. Gov. Kathy Hochul and state Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services Commissioner Arlene González-Sánchez. It comes as the legislative session is winding down to its final days. The Task Force was created in response to an epidemic of heroin and opioid abuse that has resulted in a rising number of deaths in recent years. A separate report released Thursday by state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli showed deaths from heroin and prescription narcotic overdoses reached record highs statewide in 2014, and rose faster over the previous decade than in most other states in the nation. About 2,300 New Yorkers died in 2014 due to drug overdose. http://goo.gl/cJlN2W

 

Belmont Stakes Is Backdrop for Battle Over Racing

WSJ

The Belmont Stakes is set to anchor a festive day Saturday even as a fight brews in Albany for control of the New York Racing Association, the operator of the state’s top thoroughbred venues. For one day at least, the political battle may seem far off the radar at Belmont Park, where positive signs abound. In the clubhouse, most luxury seating areas have sold out. On the far side of the track, a new dormitory will improve living conditions for backstretch workers. And while Saturday’s crowd isn't expected to be as large as in years when a Triple Crown was possible, about 10,000 general-admission tickets were sold before consumers knew whether history was possible. These improvements have come about since 2012, when state lawmakers, in agreement with Gov. Andrew Cuomo, passed legislation that put the state in control of the racing association for three years. The goal was to make changes and tighten oversight before returning the organization to its previous status as a private nonprofit. Mr. Cuomo then secured a one-year extension of that control. http://goo.gl/LhSOgI

 

New York state Assembly plans on taking up child-sex abuse victims bill ‘next week’ before legislative session ends

Daily News

Despite criticism from those on both sides of the issue, the state Assembly still intends to take up a bill dealing with child sex abuse victims.“The plan is still to do the bill next week,” Assembly Democratic spokesman Michael Whyland said Thursday. “Nothing has changed.” Introduced Tuesday night, the bill designed to make it easier for victims to bring lawsuits was assailed by survivors for not going far enough while the Catholic Church opposes a provision that would allow for old cases to be revived. Whyland said he doesn’t expect any changes to the Assembly bill unless a deal on the issue is reached with Gov. Cuomo and the state Senate. “We’ll see how things progress,” he said. Whyland defended the bill. “It is a step forward and allows victims of sexual abuse to seek justice,” he said. Under the legislation, the five-year statute of limitation on felony criminal child sex abuse cases would start at age 23, up from 18. For civil cases, a person would have until their 28th birthday to bring a lawsuit against a predator, up from the current 23. The bill would also do away with a requirement that those abused in a public institution like a school must file a notice of intent to sue within 90 days of the incident. Instead, a person would have until their 28th birthday to bring cases regardless of whether the abuse occurred in a private or public institution. http://goo.gl/uMyKu6

Subject: FW: FYI from Pharmalot - "Walgreens And A Secret Checklist For Pain Reliever Prescriptions"
From: "Harper, Karen" <karen.harper@mallinckrodt.com>
Date: Thu, 10 Oct 2013 19:19:26 -0500
To: "Brian Rucker (brian.rucker@ipcrx.com)" <brian.rucker@ipcrx.com>


 

 

 

Karen Harper  |  Sr. Manager, Controlled Substances Compliance Group

Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals

675 McDonnell Blvd.

Hazelwood, MO 63042

T: 314.654.1868  |  M: 314.401.1573

karen.harper@mallinckrodt.com  |  www.mallinckrodt.com

 

This information may be confidential and/or privileged.  Use of this information by anyone other than the intended recipient is prohibited.  If you receive this in error, please inform the sender and remove any record of this message.

 

 

 

 

http://www.pharmalive.com/walgreens-and-a-secret-checklist-for-pain-reliever-prescriptions

As regulators, legislators and physicians grapple with ways to mitigate the ongoing abuse and misuse of prescription painkillers, there are unintended consequences   some patients are having a harder time obtaining needed medications. The latest indication is a secret check list that the Walgreens pharmacy chain is requiring its pharmacists to use to weed out prescriptions that may be suspect, according to a report by WTHR, an Indianapolis television station.

Called the Good Faith Dispensing Policy (here it is), the effort comes shortly after the drug-store chain agreed to pay a record $80 million in civil penalties for violating its license and the rules that govern how prescription painkillers are distributed (back story). The deal stemmed from an investigation that began at a Walgreen s warehouse and pharmacies in Florida and extended to other locations around the country.

The settlement prompted some other large pharmacy chains to tighten their oversight of prescribing practices over concerns that federal officials will widen their probes. CVS, for instance, scoured a database to identify questionable prescribing (read this). The Walgreen s policy also arrives as the FDA announced plans to require class-wide safety labeling changes and new post-market study requirements for all extended-release and long-acting opioid analgesics (look here).

These moves are designed to thwart what many public health and law enforcement officials describe as an epidemic of deaths and accidental addictions due to the rising use of these medicines. Three years ago, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention noted that the increase in overdose deaths in the US paralleled a 300 percent increase since 1999 in the sale of prescription painkillers (read this).

Consequently, the US Senate Finance Committee last year began a probe into the promotional efforts by drugmakers (read here). Meanwhile, a recent study found that the use of opioid painkillers may have rocketed over the years, but the beneficial effect these controversial prescription drugs have actually had on pain treatment appears to have been inconsequential. And the use of safer alternatives   specifically, non-opioid analgesic painkillers that do not include opioids   was essentially flat (more here).

For its part, Walgreen s is not discussing its policy with customers. But its pharmacists are required to use a checklist each time a customer presents a prescription for one of several powerful narcotics, including Oxycodone, Fentanyl and Opana, among others, according to WTHR. But some customers are finding it difficult to obtain a prescription.

In response the American Medical Association and the American Academy of Pain Management tell WTHR that they have begun tracking consumer complaints. Consider one woman who asked not to be named. She was Oxycodone for blood clots in her legs, but was turned away by a Walgreens (WAG) pharmacist without providing an explanation, other than to say he was following the new policy.

 He said,  We suggest you take it to CVS. At this point, we re just feeding an addiction.  He was very loud and it was right in the open when he basically called me an addict. At that point, I was just so upset I left,  she tells WTHR.  I ve been going to the same Walgreens for eight years. All I wanted was the same medication from the same doctor for the same medical condition, and they refused with no warning. 

The practice angers Deborah Peel, who founded the Patient Privacy Rights Foundation.  This is really outrageous,  she tells the TV station.  It s simply wrong for people not to know they are being evaluated in this fashion. If Walgreens wants to really offend its customers and prescribing physicians, this is the way to do it: have a secret policy and force people to comply with it and not tell them what it is  Everyone who has a pain prescription is being treated as a suspected criminal. We need programs that target the abusers, that don t treat everyone as an abuser. 

Meanwhile, Jackie Rowles, a certified registered nurse anesthetist at Meridian Pain Group in Carmel, Indiana, says the questions that Walgreens pharmacists may ask healthcare providers can be problematic. For instance, the expected length of treatment may be unknown and a particular drug may not be within the standard of care if prescribed off-label.

But the new policy does not surprise former Walgreens pharmacy technician Maryanne Ryan, who tells WTHR that the practices that led to the $80 million in penalties was not confined to Florida.  In our store, no prescriptions were ever turned down. We had a reputation that we were the store that would  fill anything,  so we saw suspicious prescriptions all the time. Even when we d raise red flags, our pharmacy managed didn t care. He told us to fill them anyway. 

  I saw very few things changes when this came out, other than people were being inconvenienced. The truth is a lot of bad prescriptions still get approved because the pharmacy manager s bonus is based on the amount of scripts that get filled,  she tells WTHR. And she adds that the policy is applied inconsistently, depending upon the decisions of the pharmacy staff on duty.

As for Walgreens, the chain issued a statement to WTHR that says, in part:  Our policy does not require prescriber contact for every prescription. We firmly believe that addressing prescription drug abuse will require all parties   including leading the community, physicians, pharmacies, distributors and regulators   to play a role in finding practical solutions to combating abuse while balancing patient access to critical medication.  You can read the rest of the statement at the bottom of theWTHR story.

STORY ENDS HERE

 



Sent from my iPad

Subject:

Amendment offered on Mandatory Training and expected on the Floor to CARA

Opioid Abuse Bills Advance as Democrats Complain About
Funding
The Senate Judiciary Committee on Thursday advanced a pair of bills intended to address the prescription drug abuse epidemic
as Democrats complained that money to fund the response won't be included. Some suggested the legislation was an anemic,
response to a crisis that in 2014 claimed nearly 30,000 lives due to overdoses.
"We passed larger bills to address swine flu and Ebola, even though we did not have Ebola in the United States," said
Sen. Patrick J. Leahy,
th.e committee's ranking member. "This, we do have in the United States, every community
does."
One measure (S 524), by Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.1., and Rob Portman, R-Ohio, would provide financial assistance to state
efforts including such as prescription drug monitoring programs. The bill would also increase access to drugs that can
counteract the effect of opioids and prevent overdoses, as well as expand prevention and treatment efforts.
A second bill (S 483), by Orrin G. Hatch, R-Utah, would instruct the Drug Enforcement Agency and the Department of Health
and Human Services to collaborate ou strategies to prevent prescription drug abuse while ensuring that patients who
legitimately need the drugs can still access them.
Both bills were cleared. by voice vote and will likely be taken up by the full Senate after the President's Day recess. A.ntonia
Ferrier, a spokesperson for Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-IKy., said the senator "is very pleased with the Judiciary
committee's action on such a critical, bipartisan piece of legislation."
Despite an abundance of Democratic support for the bill by Whitehouse and Portman, some expressed frustration that the bill
only authorizes new funding and doesn't actually allocate the funds.
"We have to walk the walk, not talk the talk. To just authorize money and not actually put money to spend will do nothing to
resolve the crisis," said Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.
When the measures reach the floor Democrats are expected to make a push to include legislation, introduced byjearme
Shaheen, D-N.H., that would provide $600 million in emergency supplemental funding to address heroin and opioid abuse.
Following the Judiciary markup, Schumer, Shaheen and other Democratic senators expressed support for the intent of the
V,Whitehouse-Portman bill and elaborated on the need for more funding.
"We're glad that passed, but that's not the whole answer, because what's really needed are he .resources,"Shaheen said.

MNKOI 0001640076

 Schumer declined to say whether Democrats would filibuster the bill when it comes to the floor. "We're going to fight hard to
get the funding on the floor, and we'll cross that bridge when we come to it," he said.
Two other ❑emocrats, Edward J. Markey of Massachusetts and Joe Manchin HI of West Virginia, have placed holds on the
nomination of Robert Califf to lead the Food and Drug Administration over that agency's approvals of prescription opioid
drugs.
Last week the FDA announced plans to overhaul its opioid approval policies, including requiring independent advisory
committee to evaluate those drugs that aren't manufactured to prevent abuse. Markey believes drugs with abuse-deterrent
formulations must also receive the extra scrutiny from an advisory committee,
"Abuse-deterrent opioids is an oxymoron," Markey said. "Whether an opioid is abuse-deterrent or not hasn't prevented tens of
thousands of people who have had their wisdom teeth removed or experienced lower back pain from getting addicted to these
painkillers. nn
During the markup, Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., tried to offer an amendment to the Portman-Whitehouse bill that would
require prescribers of opioid. painkillers and other controlled substances to undergo mandatory training in safe practices. He
was told such a requirement fell outside of the committee's jurisdiction.
Markey hopes to revive the provision during floor debate, "We have to have the debate on that amendment, on the floor of the
United States Senate, on prescriber education," he said.

MNKOI 0001640077

Subject:
Thank you and follow-up on C.A.R.E.S. Alliance Fall Summit
Attachments: Fall Summit Survey_FINAL_11.3.11.doc

Sent on behalf of Dr. Herb Neuman and Art Morelli

Dear Paul,
Thank you for joining us at the C.A.R.E.S. Alliance Fall Summit and for participating in the robust, action-oriented discussion.
The purpose of the C.A.R.E.S. Alliance is to reduce prescription drug abuse and misuse through collaboration — and the
conversation and action items that came out of the Summit will help to guide our collective efforts moving forward. Below are
a few potential opportunities discussed at the Summit:
•

•
•

The AAPM prescriber education event at the end of February in Palm Springs. This will include an innovative and
practical PCP-targeted education session on opioids and PMPs, a state-of-the-art drug take-back event and associated
patient education kiosks, media, etc. Several organizations — Project Lazarus, American Pain Foundation, American
Chronic Pain Foundation, in particular — expressed an interest in helping AAPM and the C.A.R.E.S. Alliance see this
through.
The Partnership at Drugfree.org's strong proposal on educating parents and their children via a proven media
approach.
Take-back days as standalone or embedded opportunities that continue to promote safe use and prevent abuse and
misuse.

This is just the beginning and we hope all attending organizations will get involved in the collaborative spirit. If you have
additional thoughts that did not get shared yesterday, we'd love to hear from you right away.
We will also be sharing full details on the Fall Summit with organizations that were not able to attend to increase awareness
and participation beyond those who were at the meeting.
As we discussed at the Summit, there is a need for increased communication to enable planning and enhance awareness of
what the C.A.R.E.S. Alliance is doing and also what all the participant organizations are doing. In the coming days, you will
receive further post-Summit communications from us with full notes from the day and an action plan for next steps. We
would like to share the master deck of everyone's presentations as well as all attendees' email addresses, please let us know
by early next week if you do not want us to share either of these pieces of information. Over the coming months we will be
communicating with you more regularly. Please share with us any activities or initiatives that you would like us to distribute to
all the participants in the C.A.R.E.S. Alliance.
For those who did not complete the survey distributed at the end of the Summit, it is attached to this email. Your feedback is
important, as it informs future Summits. Thank you in advance for taking the time to reply.
On behalf of the entire Covidien team, we send our sincerest thanks for attending the Summit and for helping us to shape the
future of the C.A.R.E.S. Alliance. We thought it was an incredibly productive discussion and hope you share our enthusiasm for
what we will build together in 2012 and beyond.
Best regards,
Herb Neuman, MD

Rod and Terri:

 

Re:  PENNSAID shift from 1.5% to 2%

 

Please take a look at the attached   the shift from 1.5% ~10K TRx s/month to 2% ~2K TRx s/month presents significant issues for SICP:  to prevent absolute IC $ from declining due to PENNSAID mix shift, IC $ / TRx must increase while moderating for the issue created in previous SICP plans:  compensating same $ payout / TRx for low volume territories same as high volume territories.

 

We need to land on methodology today   please review/discuss with Travis any questions you have.  We will need to circulate to IC Governance Committee ASAP to generate goals   due to field 2/18.

 

Thanks

Stacy

 

From: Moore, Travis
Sent: Monday, February 10, 2014 7:09 PM
To: Chick, Stacy A
Cc: McDaniel, Neal O; Meyer, Jay E
Subject: IC Proposals



 

Stacy,

 

The attached slide deck illustrates a few comp plans that we worked with ZS to model. Slide 1 shows a comparison between a $50/$100 graduated commission above goal (which we looked at Friday), as well as the straight $100 commission rate above goal (proposed today). Looking at the comparison, the payouts are slightly better, but still shows a bias towards lower payment for lower volume territories.

 

Neal and I had an opportunity to discuss this with Jay today and came up with an alternative plan that would pay the current payout curve up to 125%, at which point a $100 commission rate per TRx would kick in. By extending the payout curve to 125% instead of 100%, we are able to help provide a little additional value for the first couple scripts above goal to the lower volume territories. This approach helps reduce the bias created by a straight commission rate at 100%.

 

Additionally, ZS has come up with a plan that pays out according to the current payout curve, but applies a soft cap of  no more than $150 per TRx . According to this methodology, the value per percentage point will be normalized to $150/TRx if the value were otherwise greater. This plan is very similar to the plan outlined above, except that the point at which a commission will kick in is variable depending on the size of the goal. If the goal is small (37 or less, which will likely be the majority of territories for 2%), the commission will kick in at the first incremental script above goal. If the goal is larger than 37, the rep will earn a lower amount per script until the commission kicks in.

 

The approaches are very similar. Looking at the analysis on the attached slides (slide 2), the variance between the methods is small. The first approach provides a little more value up front, while the second approach spreads it out a bit. If we adjust the commission rate and the soft cap to be the same, the variation above 150% in the second model (goal of 16) would be even less.

 

Please review the slides and information and let me know if you have any questions or comments. If you re still available in the morning, we can touch base on the phone to discuss these options.

Not rendering correctly? View this email as a web page here.

 

 

 

        Volume 7 Issue 9                                                                                                        July 6, 2017

 In This Issue:

Lawsuits against pharma effective weapons

Michigan’s PDMP to merge into record systems
Ohio coroner warns of fentanyl-laced marijuana, cocaine




 

 
Summit Spotlight

 

 

 
Just Over 1 Month Left to Submit a Presentation for the 
2018 National Rx Drug Abuse & Heroin Summit!


 

 



 


 

 
April 2 – 5, 2018 | Hyatt Regency Atlanta

Deadline to Submit: Monday, August 7, 2017

Don't miss your chance to present at the largest national collaboration of those impacted by Rx drug abuse and heroin use. Join professionals from local, state and federal agencies, businesses, academia, clinicians, treatment providers, counselors, educators, state and national leaders, and advocates at the 2018 National Rx Drug Abuse & Heroin Summit in Atlanta.

{  Call for Presentations }


 

 
Top Stories in the News Disclaimer: Articles and links within articles do not necessarily reflect the views or opinions of the National Rx Drug Abuse & Heroin Summit or Operation UNITE.



 

 

 
Lawsuits against pharmaceuticals effective weapon in war
against prescription opioids
David Whiting, The Orange County Register This nation’s billion-dollar opioid industry is finally starting to crack thanks to a series of successful lawsuits aimed at curtailing the ever-spiraling epidemic of pharmaceutical drug addiction. After Orange and Santa Clara counties led the charge three years ago, a series of counties, states and the Drug Enforcement Administration followed with numerous lawsuits against manufacturers and distributors of opioids alleging lax security, deceptive marketing and failing to check suspicious orders.

{Read More}
-----
Opioid costs push struggling states to dust off tobacco strategy
Jef Feeley and John Laureman, Bloomberg News State and local leaders fighting a worsening opioid-abuse epidemic are studying tactics used in the tobacco lawsuits of the 1990s, as they try to claw back billions from the companies who make and sell the powerful painkillers. More than 20 U.S. states, counties and cities have sued firms in the past year, claiming they fueled a public-health crisis with misleading marketing and aggressive distribution of opioids. It’s a strategy cigarette manufacturers will recognize: Two decades ago, they faced similar allegations as states and local governments sued, saying they’d shouldered huge costs for treating diseases blamed on tobacco.

{Read More}
-----
Michigan’s PDMP to merge into hospital, physician record systems
Jay Greene, Crain’s Detroit Business Michigan state officials have partnered with health systems, physician organizations and pharmacies to merge provider electronic medical record systems into the state's newly improved online prescription drug reporting and tracking system. At Henry Ford Health System corporate headquarters in Detroit on Monday, Lt. Gov. Brian Calley, Henry Ford officials and the state's vendor, Appriss Health, announced that about $2.1 million in state and federal funding will be used to connect the state's Michigan Automated Prescription System with existing patient data systems such as Henry Ford's Epic Systems Corp. electronic medical record.

{Read More}
-----
Ohio coroner warns of fentanyl-laced marijuana, cocaine
WLWT TV-5, Cincinnati Synthetic opiates like fentanyl have been found in marijuana, Hamilton County Coroner Dr. Lakshmi Sammarco said Monday, June 19. Fentanyl, a drug 50 to 100 times more powerful than morphine, has been linked to a surge of fatal overdoses across the county. It has been showing up in other drugs across the area.

{Read More}

Hi Mike & DJ - 


Hope this note finds you well. Attached, please find a VERY ROUGH draft of the sales force training slides for the patient experience program. The team from PI provided the templated content and I just went through and cleaned it up very quickly to drop in our program name, the brand name, and a couple of other details. Please note that there are still some placeholders in here that I've highlighted in red that we are waiting on. I would like for our team to take another pass at cleaning this up once we get through the big push for our PARC submissions, but I didn't want to delay any more in getting this over to you. 


Additionally, here are some additional details that PI has provided for the role playing exercise. Please have a look and let me know if this will work for your needs or if you would like us to make any adjustments. If you are good with this text below, then we will use this as a foundation to the Sales Force Instruction Sheet that will accompany the delivery of the program materials when they are shipped to the representatives. 


The Patient Prescription Insights program provides feedback about XARTEMIS XR to doctors, through the voice of their own patients.

 

Key points:

1.       A great way to get quick feedback on how your patients feel about this new treatment option

2.       Patients value both the copay savings as well as the opportunity to give you feedback

3.       [Referring to sample report] This is an example of the kind of input you ll get from your own patients

4.       No extra work is required   simply give your patients the Kit with the prescription and we take care of the rest

 

Steps:

Introduce the Program by closing your detail with an introduction of the XARTEMIS XR Patient Prescription Insights Program and drop off <5?> patient kits.
Gain Commitment from the doctor and office staff to participate in the program and invite eligible patients to enroll in the Program.
Return <One Week> Later and encourage the doctor to give a patient kit to patients who receive a script for XARTEMIS XR.
Return again and continue to encourage the doctor to give the patient kits to patients who receive a script for XARTEMIS XR.

 

How it works:

         At the end of your sales call, you will introduce the program to your Healthcare Professional and drop off the kits

         Doctors will be automatically enrolled in the program via a data feed from your <SFA> system after you drop off the kits.

         Doctors will receive a welcome letter with a sample report to remind them about the program.

         The patient is provided the XARTEMIS XR Starter Kit along with their script. It contains specific enrollment directions

         Patients enroll in the survey and complete the survey online or on the phone. Surveys assess treatment experience and satisfaction

         Doctors receive a report of their patient s responses to the surveys

Benefits for you:

         Positively impacts your sales by establishing your credibility and interest in promoting patient education and communication between patient and Healthcare Professional

         Provides an effective tool to impact prescribing behavior among Healthcare Professionals in your territory by creating brand impressions even when you aren t detailing them

         Creates an opportunity to reach Healthcare Professionals and encourage them to prescribe XARTEMIS XR and see what their patients  experiences are.

Your role:

         Close your detail with the program flashcard, and leave it with the office.

         Encourage Healthcare Professionals to give their patients a XARTEMIS XR Starter Kit that s all they have to do

         Follow up with offices to keep the program top of mind!

Benefits for Healthcare Professionals:

         Increases confidence in writing XARTEMIS XR by allowing Healthcare Professionals to receive feedback from patients who have had a positive experience on it

         Personalized feedback reports help Healthcare Professionals keep track of patients  unique treatment experiences

         Encourages helpful dialogue during follow-up appointments

Tips for making the program a success:

 
          Highlight the sample report on the flashcard so that Healthcare Professionals see the value of the information they will receive

          Remind Healthcare Professionals that the program is easy:  The Healthcare Professional hands a starter kit (with enclosed program invitation) to a patient

          The patient enrolls online or by phone and takes a brief survey about their experience with XARTEMIS XR

          Healthcare Professionals receive confidential, individualized reports showing how the patient is doing with treatment

o   Assure Healthcare Professionals that the program is strictly confidential patients  personal information and reports will not be shared with anyone but them

          Engage the nurse or medical assistant show them the kits, explain the program and its benefits, ask for their assistance in getting patients to enroll

Increase your credibility and value by offering a service Healthcare Professionals truly value and appreciate.





 



 I hope this helps. Please let me know if you have any questions or if you'd like to jump on a quick call to review/discuss. 
Thanks,

FDA's CDER Unveils Plans for 2016 Guidance ➢ocuments
Regulatory Focus
By Zachary Brennan
1/22/2016
http://www. raps.org/Regul atoryFocus/News/2016/01/22/23952/FDA%E2%80%99s-CDER-Unveils-Plans-for2016-Guidance-Documents/
The guidance agenda for the next fiscal year from the US Food and Drug
Administration's (FDA) Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER)
reveals a lot of new advice on generics, pharmaceutical quality, off-label
communications and other recommendations carried over from 2015, particularly
on the implementation of the Drug Supply Chain Security Act (DSCSA).
The 15 categories of guidance documents planned for 2016 range from
advertising (including a potentially controversial one on communications on
unapproved, unlicensed or uncleared uses of approved, licensed or cleared human
drugs, biologics, animal drugs and medical devices) to clinical (meta-analysis on
randomized controlled trials) to safety (new guidance on post-market reporting for
biologics and vaccines).
The total of 102 planned guidance documents is slightly higher than the 90 CDER
planned to release in 2015 and considerably more than what was planned
for 2014 and 2013.
And included on both 2015 and 2016 lists: The same three biosimilar guidance
documents (on interchangeability, labeling and statistical approaches for
evaluating similarity data), one on Internet, social media and promotional
labeling, one on pregnant women in clinical trials and one on multiple endpoints
in clinical trials, among others.
As for generic drug companies, FDA will release new draft guidance on: "General
Principles for Evaluating Abuse-Deterrent Properties of Generic Solid Oral
Opioid Drug Products," "Three-Year Exclusivity Determinations for Drug

MNKOI 0001644104

 Products," and "Updating ANDA Labeling After the Marketing Application for
the Reference Listed Drug Has Been Withdrawn."
Also included in this year's list are new guidance plans for different types of
treatment, including those for ulcerative colitis (also included in 2015's list),
revised guidance on allergic rhinitis products and exocrine pancreatic
insufficiency drugs.
On the DSCSA implementation front, which has already begun, FDA plans six
guidance documents, all except one (Field Alert Submissions) of which were
included in 201.5's list:
-Annual Reporting by Prescription Drug Wholesale Distributors and Third-Party
Logistics Providers;
-Products Eligible for Grandfather Status;
-Standards for the Interoperable Exchange of Information for Tracing Certain
Human, Finished Prescription Drugs;
-The Product Identifier for Human, Finished, Prescription Drugs;
-Verification Systems for Prescription Drugs;
-Waivers, Exceptions and Exemptions from Product Tracing Requirements; and
-Field Alert Report Submissions.

Below are my initial thoughts.  It may be helpful to discuss some of
this live. 

If I understand the project correctly, the intent is to provide a
decision support tool / algorithm that can drive appropriate opioid
selection, by providing education on important pharmacologic differences
in opioid agents.  While I agree fully with a simplified approach, we
can't assume that prescribers understand the basic principles and thus,
it is important to not oversimplify the tool.   I think this can be a
valuable tool for opioid prescribers and believe that we should include
the level of detail that will have the greatest impact. 

In its current format, the algorithm may be confusing to prescribers.
Consider adding additional information to clarify 'when and why' an
alternative opioid may be appropriate.  For example, a patient may be a
"partial responder" to a specific medication and/or have unacceptable
adverse effects, at which point a change in therapy would be
appropriate.  Additionally, the patient may be a "partial responder"
with no adverse effects and a change in therapy may also be appropriate,
but for a different reason.  On the other hand, the "partial response"
could be the result of a subtherapeutic dose, at which point an increase
in dose on the current therapy may be sufficient.  The only perspective
reflected in the current algorithm (on the hydrocodone side) is that a
"partial response" is the result of inferior potency (designated by the
X) and the solution is hydromorphone.  

Adding a few key decision points will help provide a more useful tool to
providers.  In its current format, the algorithm doesn't provide enough
information or decision points to explain why, for example, a "partial
responder" would be best transitioned to "specific named opioid".  As I
stated above,  a partial response could be the result of many things
(subtherapeutic dose, drug -drug interaction, receptor variability, etc)
all of which have a different solution.  Likewise, I would suggest the
same level of detail for "responder" and "non-responder"
recommendations.  Responsible clinicians should not and typically will
not select or prescribe a specific opioid, based on limited guidance
such as "partial response" or "no response".  I think we have to modify
the algorithm to align with what a clinician should and typically will
consider in making an opioid selection decision.  With those additional
decision points, the algorithm can become a useful tool to providers.

Additional points to consider about the current diagram:  
*	Consider adding information to clarify why we have only included
the opioids listed.  I believe you are focusing on a transition from the
available short-acting combination products (e.g., HC/APAP and OC/APAP).

*	There is a triangle in the key that is followed by the statement
"Oxymorphone makes very little contribution to analgesic activity;
oxycodone produces most of the analgesic effect".  As written, this
statement is incorrect as oxymorphone produces most of the analgesia
associated with oxycodone (e.g., a non-responder / partial responder to
oxycodone may not be fully metabolizing oxycodone to its more active
metabolite).  In that case a dose increase (if no intolerable side
effects) or a change in therapy may be appropriate.  
*	The left side of the diagram (hydrocodone) has an option for
"responder" but the right side does not.  This could be perceived as
bias towards hydromorphone.  A "responder" on SA oxycodone (e.g.,
Percocet) would likely be transitioned to "oxycontin" first if an ER
formulation is appropriate.  
*	The left side of the diagram indicates that if a patient does
not respond to HM then oxymorphone is the appropriate treatment choice
(dotted line) .  It would be more appropriate to state "consider
different opioid" - oxymorphone may or may not be the next appropriate
choice.   For example, if the patient has liver dysfunction, oxymorphone
may be the least appropriate choice.  Same for the other said - if "does
not respond" to oxymorphone, hydromorphone may or may not be the next
appropriate choice.

Narcotics bureau set to host symposium on methadone
Staff reports
Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics is hosting a "Methadone Symposium" for law enforcement investigators, prosecutors,
health care professionals, civic leaders and legislators at the end of the month.
OBN spokesman Mark Woodward said prescription drug deaths have increased 73 percent over the past decade, and the
synthetic opioid, methadone, has been linked to significant number of those deaths.
"In recent years, methadone has been used in the management of chronic pain, and justifiably, because it is long acting
and the cost is very low," Woodward said in a release. "Thus, as the increased use of methadone continues in our society,
it is imperative that we have an increased knowledge about this drug."
The symposium will be at Lake Murray Lodge in Ardmore and will feature experts such as Mark Parrino, M.P.A. president,
American Association for the Treatment of Opioid Dependence; Lisa McElhaney, secretary, National Association of Drug
Diversion Investigators and sergeant at the Broward County Sheriff's Office; and Dr. John W. Nelson, M.D., a pain
management physician.
"These individuals have extensive knowledge about methadone and will provide in-depth presentations on the use, abuse
and trends of methadone," Woodward said.
Methadone is a synthetic opioid that was developed in Germany in 1937.
The drug is used primarily in narcotic treatment programs for the treatment of opioid dependence because it, although
chemically unlike morphine or heroin, also acts on opioid receptors.
Deaths related to drug overdose in Oklahoma has increased by 73 percent in the last eight years. Of these drugs
overdose deaths, 87 percent in 2008 were directly related to pharmaceutical drugs.
The symposium is sponsored by Regional Organization Crime Information Center and National Association Drug
Diversion Investigators. Registration cost for the event is $25.

Subject: Alert: Pharma. Law & Industry Report: Highlights
From: Bloomberg Government <alerts@bgov.com>
Date: Thu, 07 Dec 2017 15:00:34 +0000
To: derek.naten@mallinckrodt.com


{Bloomberg Government}  

 

 

Pharma. Law & Industry Report: Highlights

December 7, 2017 10:00AM ET | Bloomberg BNA


 

 

 

 

HIGHLIGHTS AND CONTENTS

1. Pharma Exec Prosecuted in Off-Label Case Won't Get New Trial

A pharmaceutical company founder's conviction for promoting off-label uses stands, as a federal appeals court found no error in his trial. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

2. Teamsters Health Plan Sues Opioid Manufacturers, Distributors

Opioid manufacturers and distributors are facing yet another suit over their marketing of the painkillers, this time from a Springfield, Mass.-based union health benefit plan. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

3. SCOTUS Seeks Government View in Fosamax Case

The U.S. Supreme Court asked the government Dec. 4 to weigh in on whether it should review a federal appeals court decision reviving some 500 Fosamax product liability suits against Merck & Co. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

4. Opioid Marketing Suits Sent to Federal Court in Ohio

Suits by states and local governments alleging Purdue Pharma LP and other makers of opioid painkillers contributed to an epidemic were sent to federal court in Ohio for consolidated proceedings. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

5. Court Won't Decide Perrigo Prilosec Generic Exclusivity Question

Perrigo Research & Development Co. lost a bid to have a court decide, after the FDA wouldn't, whether it needed to market a generic version of Prilosec now to avoid forfeiting a potentially lucrative exclusivity period. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

6. J&J, Bayer Ordered to Pay $28 Million in First Xarelto Loss

Johnson & Johnson and Bayer AG are responsible for a woman's injuries tied to the blood-thinning drug Xarelto and must pay almost $28 million in damages, jurors concluded in the companies’ first loss at a trial over the medicine. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

7. Compounding Pharmacy Fails to Boot False Claims Lawsuit

A compounding pharmacy the government says deliberately overcharged the federal health-care system for active duty military service members failed to end a lawsuit against it. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

8. Janssen Shielded by Mich. Law Despite Off-Label Risperdal Use

Michigan law immunizes Janssen Pharmaceuticals Inc. from liability in thirteen cases over side effects from the antipsychotic Risperdal, a Pennsylvania appellate court ruled. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

9. Aventis Wins Dismissal in Clomid Birth Defect Suit

Aventis Inc. won dismissal in federal district court of a birth defect suit linked to the prescription fertility drug Clomid. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

10. Opioid Lawyers Warned by Judge Cases Face ‘Serious’ Hurdles

States and local governments suing Purdue Pharma and other makers of opioid painkillers face “serious” legal hurdles that can derail their bids to reap a multibillion-dollar payout to cover the costs of a burgeoning drug epidemic, a federal judge said. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

11. Government Should Negotiate Drug Prices, Science Academy Says

The federal government should negotiate drug prices and allow for more flexible drug formularies, a national scientific organization said Nov. 30. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

12. Revisions to Anti-Bribery Law Enforcement Could Prove Significant

Recent revisions to the Justice Department's enforcement policy on the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act could be significant for companies deciding whether to voluntarily disclose wrongdoing under the anti-bribery statute. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

13. FDA Signals Review of Company Executive Liability Approach

The FDA wants to clarify when corporate officers should be held criminally responsible for company wrongdoing, the agency's top lawyer said. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

14. Growth of U.S. Health Spending Slows as Drug Prices Decelerate

Total U.S. health spending increased in 2016 but slowed compared with prior years, as Americans shelled out less on prescription drugs and the initial effects of increased Obamacare enrollment dwindled. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

15. FDA Seeks to Speed Approvals of Generic Drug-Device Combos

New FDA guidance will make it easier for generic companies to get drug-device combination products approved. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

16. More Money Needed to Tackle Opioid Crisis, Lawmakers Told

Federal agencies need funding through appropriations to address aspects of the opioid crisis such as research of alternative medication and oversight of insurance company compliance, witnesses said at a hearing on preventing, treating, and recovering from opioid abuse. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

17. States Want Continued Federal Funds to Fight Opioid Epidemic

States are providing more access to addiction treatment and putting more resources into prevention to fight the opioid epidemic, state officials testified before Congress Nov. 30. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

18. Lawmakers Open to New Ideas to Spur Drug, Device Innovation

Members of a key House panel indicated they're open to additional legislative action if necessary to speed new medicines to patients. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

19. Once-Monthly Opioid Addiction Injection Cleared for U.S. Sales

Efforts to combat the opioid epidemic killing thousands of Americans each year got a boost from U.S. regulators with the approval of a first-of-its-kind monthly treatment for addiction to opiates including pills and heroin. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

20. Forget Amazon. Health Companies Really Want to Be UnitedHealth

As the specter of Amazon.com Inc. looms over the health-care industry, it's easy to see the tech giant's threat as a major factor behind the megadeal between CVS Health Corp. and Aetna Inc. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

21. Who's Next? CVS-Aetna Deal Could Start a Health Takeover Run

CVS Health Corp.’s deal to buy insurer Aetna Inc. for about $67.5 billion could be just the start of a new wave of health-care takeovers. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

22. Pharmacy Making Intravenous Drugs Hit With FDA Warning

A New Jersey compounding pharmacy making intravenous drug products received an FDA warning letter for problems that included insanitary manufacturing conditions. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

23. CVS to Buy Aetna for $67.5 Billion, Remaking Health Care Sector

CVS Health Corp. will buy Aetna Inc. for about $67.5 billion, creating a health-care giant that will have a hand in everything from insurance to the corner drugstore. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

24. Newer Birth Control Pills Don't Lower the Risk of Breast Cancer

Newer birth control drugs developed to replace those tied to cancer risk were thought to improve safety for the women who took them. It turns out they didn't, according to a massive new study. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

25. Express Scripts CEO Open to Insurer Deal, Ties with Amazon

Express Scripts Holding Co.’s chief executive said he's open to a deal with a health insurer or partnering with Amazon.com Inc. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

26. U.S. Drug Approval Helps Push Biocon Shares to Fresh Record

Shares of Biocon Ltd. extended a record after U.S. regulators approved its competing version of Roche Holding AG's blockbuster breast cancer drug Herceptin. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

27. Frayed Gasket Delaying Astra's ZS-9 Shows Pharma M&A Perils

When AstraZeneca Plc paid $2.7 billion for an experimental drugmaker in 2015, it had its sights set on a potential blockbuster medicine. Instead, it got a Texas factory riddled with defects and two scathing reviews from U.S. regulators rejecting the treatment. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

28. Biotech Eyes Tax Revamp as Next Chance to Shake Its Recent Woes

Biotechnology investors who saw their portfolios stumble after a late-summer bull run may refocus on a key reason that the group took off: the U.S. tax overhaul and repatriation. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

29. Bayer's Ready to Spend on Its Transformation to Cancer Company

Bayer AG is ready to spend more money on deals and research that will help make it into a cancer company as the company's blockbuster blood-thinner Xarelto nears the final years of its patent life. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

30. CVS Said to Near $65 Billion-Plus Deal for Insurer Aetna

CVS Health Corp. is nearing an agreement to acquire health insurer Aetna Inc. for more than $65 billion, according to a person familiar with the negotiations, in a deal that could reshape the pharmacy and health insurance industries. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

31. A Deadly Drug Cocktail Shines a Light on an AstraZeneca Blockbuster

The last time John Nebinger spoke to his son Bradley was about thirty minutes after midnight on March 15, 2010. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

32. Minnesota Mulls Per-Pill Fee to Counter Opioid Abuse

Pharmaceutical companies would have to pay fees to sell opioids in Minnesota under a bill expected to be introduced in 2018. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

33. This Company Is Ready to Flood the U.S. with Cheap HIV Drugs

Among the coconut plantations and beaches of South India, a factory the size of 35 football fields is preparing to churn out billions of generic pills for HIV patients and flood the U.S. market with the low-cost copycat medicines. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

34. Canada Proposes Tougher Reviews of New Drug Prices

Canada proposed changes to its pricing controls for patented medicines that are projected to lower net drug costs for provincial health plans by C$1.8 billion ($1.2 billion) per year. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

35. Drug Companies from Glaxo to J&J Pledge to Make U.K. Investments

GlaxoSmithKline Plc, Johnson & Johnson, Merck & Co., and AstraZeneca Plc are among more than two dozen global pharmaceutical companies pledging to invest funds in the U.K. as part of a multi-billion-pound effort to spur the country's health-care industry. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

36. European Drug Regulator's Brexit Move Sparks Concern at Genmab

The Brexit-induced relocation of the European medicines regulator to Amsterdam may slow product approvals, hurting some drugmakers, Genmab A/S Chief Executive Officer Jan van de Winkel said. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

37. Richter Falls as Liver Cases Prompt Review of Flagship Product

Shares in Gedeon Richter Nyrt., eastern Europe's largest drugmaker, plunged after cases of serious liver injuries prompted the review of one of its flagship products. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

38. 50,000 New Drug Tests Among Brexit Worries for Pharma Companies

Global drugmakers from Johnson & Johnson to AstraZeneca Plc warned that potential trade and regulatory hurdles may burden them with a host of additional costs after Britain leaves the European Union. {Link to Story}(Story Link)
