Press Release: Mallinckrodt Receives Patent from U.S. Patent and Trademark Office
(Dow Jones and Company, Inc.) Feb 25 08:30 AM EST

Mallinckrodt Receives Patent from U.S. Patent and Trademark Office

U.S. Patent covers the release profile of XARTEMIS(TM) XR (oxycodone hydrochloride and acetaminophen) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) DUBLIN--(BUSINESS WIRE)--February 25, 2014--

Mallinckrodt (NYSE: MNK) today announced that it was granted a patent from the United States Patent and Trademark Office which contains composition claims directed to unique design, formulation, pharmacokinetic, and release characteristics of XARTEMIS(TM) XR. XARTEMIS XR (formerly known as MNK-795) is an investigational extended-release oral formulation of oxycodone and acetaminophen that has been studied with twice daily dosing for the management of acute pain in a post-surgical model. If approved, XARTEMIS XR will be the first oxycodone and acetaminophen combination medication specifically designed with immediate- and extended-release components. The patent, U.S. Patent Number 8,658,631, was issued on February 25, 2014.

The release profile of XARTEMIS XR combines Mallinckrodt-proprietary technology and Depomed's advanced Acuform(R) drug delivery technology. Between the Mallinckrodt and Depomed patent families, Mallinckrodt believes XARTEMIS XR will have strong patent protection for its novel features.

"XARTEMIS XR, a key driver in our near-term pipeline, represents an important component of our strategy to unlock continued potential and grow our branded specialty pharmaceutical portfolio," said Mark Trudeau, President and Chief Executive Officer, Mallinckrodt. "Mallinckrodt's patent, which includes the product's release profile, underscores our ability to effectively leverage our core formulation capabilities and partnerships."

Acuform is a registered trademark of Depomed.

ABOUT MALLINCKRODT:

Mallinckrodt is a leading global specialty pharmaceuticals business that develops, manufactures, markets and distributes specialty pharmaceutical products and medical imaging agents. The company's Specialty Pharmaceuticals segment includes branded and specialty generic drugs, and the Global Medical Imaging segment includes contrast media and nuclear imaging agents. Mallinckrodt has approximately 5,500 employees worldwide with sales in roughly 70 countries. The company's fiscal 2013 revenue totaled $2.2 billion. To learn more about Mallinckrodt, visit www.mallinckrodt.com.

MANCHESTER, N.H.  Distressing new numbers show the scope and toll of the heroin epidemic in New Hampshire.

 


The state medical examiner said there are 60 potential deadly drug overdoses from 2016 alone, three of which are confirmed.

It comes after a record 420 people died of drug overdoses last year in 2015.

Manchester AMR said February could be the deadliest month for drug overdoses in the city's history.

They say they respond to an average of two heroin or fentanyl overdoses each day.

A Manchester recovery specialist said she doesn't know what the solution is, but people need to pay attention.

"Oh my God, he was a great kid, he was funny, he got into some trouble," said Kelly Riley, with Hope for NH Recovery.

In 2007, Riley's son Richie fell into the wrong group of friends, tried cocaine, then someone suggested to him taking an oxycontin, and he just went to sleep, Riley said.

Riley then became a counselor at Hope for NH Recovery in Manchester to give other addicts a place to go.

But last week, seven of her recovering addicts died, by likely overdosing on opioids.

"It's very challenging as a person who has been through this and seen so many lives devastated by this," Riley said.

She continued: "Once my son died, then what happens, it's a whole ripple effect to the family. I lost my house, I got divorced, my daughter had to change schools, just so many things happened."

Manchester American Medical Response has responded to 51 suspected drug overdoses in February alone, 12 of them deadly.

If these deaths are confirmed by the medical examiner, February will be tied for the deadliest opioid overdose month in Queen City history.

Rocco Caprarello, AMR Manchester station manager, compares that to last February, when AMR responded to 38 overdoses and lost five people.

"And we see that the trend is, the amount of narcan that we're giving patients, we're thinking that it's something more than heroin," Caprarello said.

Riley said her center needs more funding for more beds for kids addicted to heroin and fentanyl.

"It's heartbreaking, you know?" Riley said. "You see moms with their kids, and they're desperate. They want their kid to live. And it's almost like you can't let them out of your sight.

Hope for NH Recovery is now trying to open 13 centers.

Barb,

 

The unit code has to be filled out every time a “**” NDC code is issued.  The unit field is a number between 1 and 6 and represents the measurement or unit such as Kilo, Gram, Milligram, Liters, Milliliters. This is for most of the items from the St. Louis Plant.  The exception of this rule would be when fentanyl lozenges are shipped from StL Plant to Hobart.  Then the unit field would be blank.

 

Mary

Sent: Monday, November 04, 2013 1:21 PM
To: Grass, Barbara J; Lewis, Mary

In the Hobart distributor system, blank is all that is ever used.  The “7”, “8” is used when the ** Packaging code is used.  When dosage finished goods are reported, the field is blank.  So long answer, yes blank is valid.

 

Eileen

Subject: RE: NDA 21217 S-004 Labeling Information Request 09jul12

Dear All,
In regard to FDA's recommendation for the Exalgo bottle labels, that we use either 'bolding' or 'a different font color such as red' for the statement on swallowing the tablets whole, without chewing, crushing or breaking, we would like to recommend keeping the black font with bolding of the statement.  Does the team have a preference for using a different font color for that statement on the bottle labels or is bolding the current black font acceptable?

Also we would like to inform FDA that we will incorporate their recommendation for the currently approved bottle labels at next printing.  Do we have the team's agreement for the Exalgo 8mg, 12mg and 16 mg bottle labels change?

If needed, I'll be happy to schedule a meeting to discuss FDA's recommendation for the bottle labels.
Kind regards,
Linda

From: Noa, Linda
Sent: Monday, July 09, 2012 10:34 AM
To: Ziemba, Robert J.; Durham, Katherine; Bonfanti, Mike D; Carroll, Jerilynn; Wessler, Michael; Novak, Rod P; Terifay, Terry W; Patrick, Jeffrey; Fuller, Philip; Wang, Jennie L; Saake, Lisa M; Mitchell, Brian R; Devarakonda, Krishna; Blumberg, Alan L; Weidman, Jennifer R
Subject: FW: NDA 21217 S-004 Labeling Information Request 09jul12

Dear All,
Please find attached approval letter for Exalgo class REMS.  Yes!!

In addition, please find recommendation from DMEPA for the Exalgo bottle labels, in conjunction with the review of the 32mg but also requested to be implemented at next printing for the 8, 12 and 16mg bottle labels.  We will need to respond to FDA as to whether we intend to comply with their request to revise all the bottle labels for Exalgo.

Since DMEPA recommendations for labeling changes will be required for Exalgo 32mg, it makes sense to make the change for all the strengths, even though the current bottle labels were included in the class REMS approval issued today.

Look like FDA is requesting only the bolding of the statement "Swallow tablets whole. Do not break, crush or chew tablet" but no other changes for the 32mg and also requested for the other strengths at next printing.

Kind regards,
Linda

From: Walker, Diana [mailto:Diana.Walker@fda.hhs.gov]
Sent: Monday, July 09, 2012 9:46 AM
To: Noa, Linda
Subject: NDA 21217 S-004 Labeling Information Request 09jul12


Dear Linda,

I have received the following comment from the Division of Medication Errors Prevention and Analysis (DMEPA) concerning your proposed carton and container labels for Exalgo S-004.  Please respond to the following comment/recommendation regarding your container label:

Postmarketing review identified 3 domestic cases where patients reported cutting their Exalgo tablets in half and experienced adverse events including
respiratory arrest. Due to the potential severity of the outcome from cutting Exalgo tablets, we recommend bolding or highlighting the statement "Swallow tablets whole. Do not break, crush or chew tablet" on the side panel by utilizing a different color font such as red. Also, consider revising this statement in a similar manner on the 8 mg, 12 mg and 16 mg container labels at the next printing.


Please note that labeling comments for your proposed Package Insert label for this supplement are still in progress and will be sent at a later date.

Kind regards,

Diana

Sent: Monday, June 09, 2014 5:50 PM
To: Lynda
Cc: Chick, Stacy A; Wessler, Michael
Subject: FW: Unaided Message Recall Verbatim_XXR Launch-to-Date



 

Hi Lynda,

 

I went back to Pelin for the exact verbatims from the message recall.  I was concerned that what we see as  long acting Percocet  may just be a function of the verbiage used for coding of responses.  In the attachment you will see that there certainly mentions of Percocet, but not to the degree that we saw in the summated data.  Rather, the summated data reflects improper verbiage and coding. 

 

Generally, I do see a trend that the long acting component is being recalled to a greater extent than the immediate release component.  I think we should reinforce the balanced approach   both the IR and ER components are important (and the consequences to the patient).

Please find all verbatim on unaided message recall as in the attached.

Please note that since this is a text analysis to categorize verbatim into buckets, not every verbatim will state exactly  long-acting Percocet/Oxy-APAP  per say; text around long acting MOA with oxy/APAP or Percocet in it appears to be rolled into this bucket.

I ve noticed a few that did not necessarily make sense to be put in the long acting category and I ve instructed the vendor to comb through this for the next reporting. However, having said that, a few misses probably wouldn t make much of a difference in overall unaided message recall percentages.

In the attached, Column H will be unedited text, and Column I is indexing it for  long acting Percocet . One thing I noticed is that long-acting message recall pattern mitigated as weeks progressed; this could be an issue in the early weeks post-launch.

Subject: Hydrocodone Scheduling - Financial risk to the Strategic Plan Forecasts

We have been asked to provide some guidance to management on the potential financial impact of the rescheduling of hydrocodone.
We can see three potential areas

1.       API hydrocodone sales/income

2.       Generic hydrocodone/APAP sales/income

3.       Zircon

What do we know:

1.       FDA has scheduled an advisory cmte meeting on October 29-30th

2.       20% of hydrocodone/APAP TRx are refilled prescriptions

3.       9% of hydrocodone/APAP TRx are written by physicians who do not write CII products

What do we suspect timing around re-scheduling based on advisory cmte action

1.       Advisory cmtes have taken between 6-9 months to come to a conclusion/report

2.       Further add DEA action and time to implement   would not expect rescheduling to occur before June 2013 and most likely January 2014

What will be the issues:

1.        Number on logistical issue will be sufficient vault space and the time it takes to acquire/build vault space   could also impact manufacturers

2.       Warehousing chains and other direct purchasers of CIII products will most likely not have vault capacity or insufficient vault capacity and will require wholesalers to provide on a just in time basis.

3.       Retail pharmacies will have insufficient vault space and will either be out of stock more often

Based on the above would like to get some sense of downsides and potential upsides (codeine sales for instance)

Need to get this by end of the week
Have met with the API and Generics folks to start process
Brands   let me know how I can facilitate
David

Opioids: The Roots of Patient Confusion View this email in your browser

 

Visit our website

 

 

 

 
 

 

 

 
Study Illustrates Need for Better Patient/Provider Communications on Opioid Therapy

A new study published online in the Annals of Emergency Medicine found that patients seen in the emergency department for acute pain expressed a desire for better communication from physicians about their pain management options, along with discussion of the risks of opioid dependence. The study was conducted via semi-structured open-ended telephone interviews of patients discharged from the emergency department at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania during a 4 month period in 2014. The subjects revealed several themes related to opioid dependence including 1) fear of developing dependence or addition; 2) worries about following prescribed dosing preventing the possibility of addiction; 3) relying on media and other individuals as a source of information about opioids; and 4) awareness of physicians  need to balance patients  pain management needs and safe opioid prescribing guidelines.

Subject: FW: Exalgo PI FDA version sent 2-21-12

Dear All,
Please find attached latest FDA version of the EXALGO labeling.  We have several wins and a few losses.  And it looks like FDFA has tracked both their deleted and added text making for ease of review.

As to the additional text proposed for the geriatric sections based on the previously submitted but unlabeled results from the pop-pk study, FDA has requested more time to review.  Their note recommends that we resubmit the proposed text separate from the class REMS and in conjunction with the pending supplement to add the 32mg.

A major win is for the abbreviated boxed warning FDA's agreement to delete their proposed statement on 'instructing patients on proper administration' and adding our text:

Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

An anticipated loss is our attempt to introduce a 75% dose conversion factor.  However, FDA has proposed to move our text on withdrawal to prominence in the bullets associated with the conversion Table 1.

*         Monitor patients for signs or symptoms of opioid withdrawal when converting patients to EXALGO.

Also rejected was our effort to replace dose reductions of 25% with 'a reduced dose', with FDA indicating the statement was not helpful to prescribers and that their proposed reduction was based on PK (albeit IR) data.

Please review closely and let me know if you'd like to meet to discuss.  I'd like to get back to FDA on Friday if at all possible.
Kind regards,
Linda

I’m looking at the model, and I think I agree with your thinking and tier proposals, if I’m reading them correctly (current run-rate, with Exalgo AG, of $20.4M and tiers starting at $21M, and starting them lower than last year at 1%).  However, how you got to that number confuses me.  You have 12 month actual net sales of about $64M, less $34M of methylphenidate ER sales to get to $29M.  It looks to me like their net sales for 12 months are actually over $100M, less methyl ER of $63M, or something close to $40M of eligible sales.  This lines up well with Laurin’s calc’s, projecting $39M.  Part of it is the profit model…”net” on the profit model is too low as it takes out all the fees we pay Cardinal, too, which shouldn’t come out.  However, even if you use that, the $64 and $34 don’t tie to anything.

{HDA Weekly Digest: A Newsletter for HDA Members} 
{A Newsletter for HDA Members} October 10, 2017 
{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d} {http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

HDA to Testify before Senate HELP Committee on Drug Pricing

The Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) has called upon representatives from pharmaceutical supply chain organizations to testify at an October 17 hearing entitled, "The Cost of Prescription Drugs: How the Drug Delivery System Affects What Patients Pay, Part II." HDA Senior Vice President, Government Affairs and General Counsel, Liz Gallenagh, will testify on the role of distributors in the pharmaceutical supply chain. The hearing will take place at 10:00 a.m. in 430 Dirksen Senate Office Building. 

A full list of scheduled witnesses includes: 

Lori M. Reilly, Executive Vice President, Policy, Research & Membership, Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, Washington, D.C. 
Chester "Chip" Davis, Jr., President and Chief Executive Officer, Association for Accessible Medicines, Washington, D.C.
Elizabeth A. Gallenagh, Senior Vice President Government Affairs and General Counsel, Healthcare Distribution Alliance, Arlington, Va. 
Mark Merritt, President and Chief Executive Officer, Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, Washington, D.C. 
Thomas E. Menighan, BSPharm, MBA, ScD(Hon.), FAPhA, Executive Director and Chief Executive Officer, American Pharmacists Association, Washington, D.C.

For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}


One Month Remains to Register for the 2017 Blockchain Pre-Seminar Workshop and the Traceability Seminar

A short time remains to register for the November 8 Blockchain Pre-Seminar Workshop (hosted in partnership with IEEE) and HDA’s 2017 Traceability Seminar (November 8–10) in Washington, D.C. The pre-seminar workshop will provide attendees a look in to blockchain technology and how it can be applied to traceability in the pharmaceutical supply chain, while the Traceability Seminar will educate registrants on a variety of traceability topics and how they relate to DSCSA implementation efforts.

Register for the seminar and the workshop. For registration help or questions, contact HDA’s Meetings and Conferences at (703) 885-0278.  

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

Congressional Hearings on the Opioid Crisis

Senate HELP Committee Discusses Federal Response to the Opioid Crisis

The Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee held a hearing last week (October 5) on "The Federal Response to the Opioid Crisis."  There were a range of questions about treatment, research, prescribing issues, concerns with illicit fentanyl and funding for addressing opioids, among others. It was noted that this is the first in a series of hearings on opioids. The next hearing will be in November (no date has been announced); the hearing will focus on state and local perspectives, exploring the challenges they face and the successes they have had in addressing the epidemic.

House Energy and Commerce Committee to Host Hearing on Opioids

The Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee is holding a "Member Day" tomorrow, Wednesday, October 11 at 10:15 a.m. to allow members both on and off the committee the opportunity to testify about the opioid epidemic.  

For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

Administration Names Acting DEA Administrator

Robert Patterson has been named Acting Administrator of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). Patterson is a career DEA Special Agent, having served with the agency since 1988. He had been serving, in effect, as Acting Deputy Administrator since late last year. An acting deputy administrator has not been named.

For more information, contact Ruth Miller.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

New Member Spotlight: Domino Amjet, Inc.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}     HDA recently welcomed Domino Amjet, Inc. as a service provider member. Based in Gurnee, Ill., Domino has become the global solution provider for all product identification needs — including UDI and track and trace — for the most significant brands in the life science sector. Whether it’s serialized or variable printing, product marking or date coding, Domino Amjet and its products are a proven solution.

 

For more information, visit the company’s website or contact Paul Hammond, President.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

USP Announces Intent to Delay Chapter on Handling Hazardous Drugs

The United States Pharmacopeia (USP) has announced that it intends to delay the effective date of its General Chapter <800> Hazardous Drugs—Handling in Healthcare Settings until Dec. 1, 2019. The chapter, which relates to drugs identified by NIOSH as hazardous, describes standards that healthcare personnel, pharmacies, hospitals, physicians’ offices, and veterinarians should use to promote patient safety, worker safety, and environmental protection. Several states have discussed adopting the chapter into their requirements. The chapter does not impose requirements on wholesale distributors.

For more information, contact Ruth Miller.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

What’s Included in Your HDA Membership?

Make the most of your HDA membership by building close business relationships with wholesale distributor, manufacturers and service provider colleagues, while benefiting from their expertise with industry-created resources.

HDA’s website is full of information; you can search our online membership directory and access the service provider search, which gives you a list of HDA service provider members and the services they provide. Additionally, one of your many member benefits is access to HDA’s free educational publications, guidelines and forms.

To log in, your username is your email address; click on "forgot password" to create a password of your choosing. For more information about your member benefits or accessing the HDA website, contact Lisa Gallagher at (703) 885-0251.

DEA Releases 2013 Drug Threat Assessment Summary

Posted: 20 Nov 2013 08:10 PM PST

By Karla L. Palmer – 

On Monday, November 18, 2013, DEA released the 2013 National Drug Threat Assessment Summary, which provides an assessment of the threat posed to the United States by trafficking and abuse of illicit substances and non-medical use of controlled prescription drugs.  The Summary also provides an analysis of the domestic drug situation during 2012 based on available law enforcement, intelligence, and public health data.  DEA took over responsibility for preparation of the Summary in June 2012 as a result of the closure of the National Drug Intelligence Center.  DEA considered both quantitative data from various sources (seizures, investigations, arrests, drug purity or potency, and drug prices; law enforcement surveys; laboratory analyses; and interagency production and cultivation estimates) and qualitative information (subjective views of individual agencies on drug availability, information on smuggling and transportation trends, and indicators of changes in smuggling and transportation methods). 

Highlights include the following:

§ The trafficking and abuse of illicit drugs continue to constitute a “dynamic and challenging” threat to the United States.

§ Controlled prescription drug abuse continues to be the United States’ fastest growing drug problem.  The rate of abuse of controlled prescription drugs remains high; abuse remains at a higher rate than any illicit drug except marijuana.  Pain relievers are the most common type of abused prescription drug, and are most commonly involved in overdose incidents. 

§ The availability of heroin continued to increase in 2012, likely due to high levels of heroin production in Mexico, and Mexican traffickers expanding into in the eastern and midwestern United States.  Some metropolitan areas observed an increase in heroin overdose deaths.  Reports reveal that many prescription opioid users have turned to heroin as a cheaper and/or more easily obtained alternative to prescription drugs. 

§ The trend of lower cocaine availability in the United States that began in 2007 continued through 2012.  

§ Methamphetamine availability is likely increasing because of sustained production in Mexico (the primary foreign source for the United States market) and continuing small-scale domestic production. 

§ Marijuana availability appears to be increasing because of sustained high levels of production in Mexico (the primary foreign source of United States supply) and increased domestic cultivation. 

§ The abuse of synthetic designer drugs has emerged as a serious problem in the United States.  The abuse of synthetic cannabinoids, such as “K2” and “Spice,” and synthetic cathinones, like “bath salts,” increased over the past few years, and “abusers have suffered severe consequences.”  Both state legislation and national scheduling of these drugs have helped to “mitigate the threat.”  DEA noted that the threat posed by synthetics most likely will continue to increase, in part because the chemical make-up of these drugs often differs by only one compound.  Thus as DEA exercises its scheduling authority to control certain substances, producers quickly change the chemical component of the newly banned substance to create a new one 

§ MDMA (ecstasy) is available in markets throughout the United States.  However, data suggest availability and abuse of the drug may have peaked.

From: "morelli, art "

    "schooler, joanna s"


Ok thanks. We discovered that Perdue has provided funding for this program.
Just one factor in our eval of potential programs.




-----
From: Connel, Greg <greg.connel@fleishman.com>
To: Morelli, Art ; Schooler, JoAnna S
Sent: Fri Jul 23 09:20:29 2010
Subject: FW: Project Lazerus
Hi Art:

 

Per the discussion at the break, below is a top line summary of Project Lazarus. We interviewed one of its founders as part of an awareness effort we’re developing Ohio Department of Health.

 

Please let us know if you’d like us to help with a deeper dive on this initiative or how it can be integrated into the CARES Alliance.

 

Thanks,

 

Greg

 

Project Lazarus in Wilkes County, N.C., is another example of a program designed with heavy emphasis on the community. According to Fred Wells Brason, the first objective of Project Lazarus was to raise awareness of the prescription drug abuse problem in the community so that residents understand the extent of the problem and the various contributing factors. To achieve this objective, his team identified the stakeholders within the community – schools, medical centers, civic organizations, the business community/Chamber of Commerce, law enforcement, etc. – and brought them to the table with the goal being that each of those stakeholders would then build awareness within their sphere of influence. Fred noted that the awareness-building process was underway for more than two years and that providing resources for the various stakeholders was critical to enable them to implement the work within the community.

 

Physician education and training was a central component of Project Lazarus in Wilkes County, N.C. Experts met with county physicians to provide training on pain and addiction, management of chronic pain patients, proper prescribing methods, identifying diversion and forged materials and protecting prescriptions. Project administrators also worked closely with hospitals in the county to encourage them to change their policies on narcotics dispensing. Because of the low population and rural setting of the county, pharmacies weren’t open past 11 p.m. as recently as two years ago. As a result, people with addiction issues would show up at the ER late at night to get prescription pain medications. In part because of the efforts of Project Lazarus, most hospitals in the county changed their policies and now refer patients to a primary-care doctor or a specialist if they have chronic pain. If they do dispense drugs, they give a small number of pills, typically enough for only two days. Because of these changes, people who are abusing now understand that the hospitals are not a source of prescription opiates.

 

Fred Wells Brason acknowledged that it took some convincing to get the hospitals on board with the new policies, mainly due to the oversight agencies’ evaluations based on measureable excellence scales. Although the potential exists for disgruntled patients to complain about not receiving the medications they felt they needed, the hospitals understand that prescription drug abuse is a community problem and view the policy shifts as a way that they can contribute to the solution.

 

While complete data on the impact of Project Lazarus should be available later this year, it’s worth noting that Wilkes County dropped from being the heaviest dispenser of prescription opiates in 2007 to eighth in the state in 2009. Fred views this as an indicator that the efforts to educate physicians and hospitals have resulted in more appropriate prescribing practices and more careful scrutiny of individuals trying to access prescription drugs for illicit use.

 

 

Fred was adamant that the type of campaign being implemented in Ohio needs to be built up from the community level. He feels that the paradigm and mindset of the entire community needs to shift in order for true changes to be made. In fact, he attributes much of Project Lazarus’ success to its focus on working the problem at the community level, looking at the dynamics of the community and dissecting them to see how they could make a difference. He described the approach as very logical rather than scientific and said that interestingly, state and Medicaid officials are now reaching out to the project organizers for guidance on how to replicate the model throughout the state.

To:  'rxnews@listserve.com'
Subject:  [RxNews] 498-count indictment was unsealed today charging 53 defendants in a multimillion dollar drug conspiracy
Attach:  ATT1780851.txt

Included in the indictment are Dr. Norman Werther, of Horsham, pharmacist Ihsanullah

 Sean  Maaf, of Northeast Pharmacy in Philadelphia, and alleged drug trafficker William

Stukes, of Philadelphia. According to the indictment, Stukes and his alleged drug trafficking

organization recruited large numbers of pseudo patients and then transported them to Dr.

Werther s medical office for fake examinations. These  patients  paid an office visit fee, usually

$150, to the office staff and Werther would write prescriptions for those  patients  to obtain

oxycodone-based drugs without there being a medical need for the prescription. The  patients

were then driven to various pharmacies to have their prescriptions filled, including Northeast

Pharmacy where Maaf would fill the prescription. The drugs were then turned over to Stukes or

his drivers. Stukes and his organization would allegedly sell the narcotics to numerous drug

dealers, who are also named in the indictment, who would also then resell the drugs on the street.

It is estimated that between September 2009 and July 2011, the Stukes drug trafficking

organization earned more than $5 million through these illegal prescriptions and that the

defendants unlawfully acquired and distributed over 200,000 pills containing oxycodone.


The complete press release can be accessed here:


http://www.justice.gov/usao/pae/News/2011/Aug/werther_release.pdf


Kim

All the best,

Laura

Apologies for the delayed response; we have a draft 30 second that I'd previously passed along (I may have just sent it initially to Lucy, I will check!), and are working on the draft 60 second script.  Hope to have for your review / consideration over next day or two.  Will that work?

Derek Naten

202-257-5904 (m)


 


Sent from my iPhone

Hi Derek and Kendra,

 

We are excited to be working with you to record PSAs at the Healthcare Summit!  We will be recording 30-second and 60-second evergreen scripts that can be played year-round on radio stations, and I wanted to check in with you to see whether you would like to have a 30-second and 60-second script focused on an awareness day, week, or month.  Please let me know, and we will be happy to work with you on drafting these scripts.

Laura

Subject: RE: Women In Government DC Conference- Speakers



 

Hi Lucy,

We’re all set!  We’re prepared to move forward with this proposal for both the PSA recording as well as the panel extension.  We’ve confirmed that there are two leading opinion leaders in this space, both from Duke University, that can present.  They have presented together before on this topic and from what I understand, really rock it!

http://anesthesiology.duke.edu/?portfolio=timothy-e-miller-md

 

https://surgery.duke.edu/faculty/julie-k-marosky-thacker-md  *Julie is also the President of the American Society for Enhanced Recovery (ASER)

 

Further, we’re working on a few draft PSA scripts, for your review.  A draft 30-second below:

 

Women in Government PSA

 

30 second

 

Did you know that millions of people prescribed opioid pills for surgery pain are at risk for addiction? Hi, I’m [Name] from [District/State]. A recent study found many people take prescription opioids long after they’ve recovered from surgery.[i] Misusing prescription opioids can lead to addiction, and in some cases overdose or death.[ii] There are other pain management options. Before surgery, ask your doctor about the option that’s best for your needs. 

 

Is there a way we could get a little more granularity on the proposal around the PSA’s… I was speaking with the team on the document you sent, but I think it would be helpful just to understand how all of this is operationalized and how they are distributed.  We may wish to do a call with them as well on it.  Also, might you be able to send a few sample PSA’s that have been done in the past?  (I know we did the rare disease day one with y’all early this year, and there are many more).  That would be helpful.

 

Might be good to, regardless, hop on the phone just to discuss everything.  Let me know what you think.  But, in short, we’re good to go!

 

Thanks,

 

Derek

We’ll keep a close eye on the schedule to see if anything opens up.

 

Lucy

Derek

Title


Effect of i.v. acetaminophen on total hip or knee replacement surgery: A case-matched evaluation of a national patient database.


Source


American Journal of Health-System Pharmacy. 72(22):1961-8, 2015 Nov 15.


Country of Publication


United States


Abstract


PURPOSE: The effects of i.v. acetaminophen on adverse events, hospital length of stay (LOS), and overall hospital costs for total hip or knee replacements were evaluated.
METHODS: We conducted a matched-pairs analysis of adult inpatients who underwent elective total hip arthroplasty or total knee arthroplasty in hospitals participating in the Premier Healthcare Alliance from January 1, 2011, to November 30, 2012. Each case who received i.v. acetaminophen on the day of surgery was matched to a control who did not receive i.v. acetaminophen within the same hospital. Treatment groups were analyzed for differences in the rate of adverse effects, LOS, and hospital resource utilization.
RESULTS: A total of 22,146 cases and controls were similar in terms of age, race, sex, marital status, insurance status, and preoperative comorbidities. Overall adverse events were significantly lower with i.v. acetaminophen (24.3%) than with controls (26.3%, p < 0.001), numerically less frequent in all subgroups, and significantly less frequent for renal, infectious, and miscellaneous adverse events (all p < 0.05). I.V. acetaminophen was also associated with a shorter LOS, with 1 out of 11 patients discharged one day earlier (p < 0.001) and lower average hospital costs: $16,381 for cases compared with $16,927 for controls (p < 0.001). Cost savings estimated by structural equation modeling of $547 per patient were due to $325 from direct effects and $222 from indirect effects, the latter mediated through adverse events and reduced LOS.
CONCLUSION: In this retrospective cohort study of case-matched patients who underwent total hip or knee replacement surgery, multimodal analgesia with i.v. acetaminophen was associated with improved clinical outcomes in terms of fewer adverse events, shortened LOS, and reduced total hospital resources compared with patients who did not receive i.v. acetaminophen.Copyright © 2015 by the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists, Inc. Title


Comparison of preoperative oral acetazolamide and intraperitoneal normal saline irrigation for reduction of postoperative pain after laparoscopic cholecystectomy.


Source


Journal of Laparoendoscopic & Advanced Surgical Techniques. Part A. 25(4):285-90, 2015 Apr.


Country of Publication


United States


Abstract


PURPOSE: Visceral and shoulder tip pain following laparoscopic cholecystectomy is mainly due to carbon dioxide (CO2) insufflation. Various methods have been adopted to eliminate residual CO2. We compared the postoperative analgesic efficacy of intraperitoneal normal saline (30mL/kg) irrigation with preoperative oral acetazolamide administration in patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: Sixty patients between 20 and 60 years of age were included in this prospective, randomized, double-blind study. Patients in Group I received placebo, Group II patients received preoperative oral acetazolamide (5mg/kg), and Group III patients received intraperitoneal irrigation with 30mL/kg of normal saline. Intravenous paracetamol (1g) was administered every 6 hours for postoperative analgesia. Parietal and visceral pain scores at rest, on movement, and on coughing and shoulder tip pain were recorded using a visual analog scale after arrival in the postanesthesia care unit, at 1, 2, 4, 6, 12, and 24 hours after surgery. Rescue analgesia was provided with an intravenous fentanyl (1mug/kg) bolus whenever the visual analog scale score was >4.

RESULTS: Compared with Group I, Group III patients had significantly lower visceral pain scores at all time intervals except at 12 hours. Group III patients also recorded significantly lower visceral pain scores than Group II from 2 to 24 hours. There was no significant difference in shoulder tip pain. The total dose of fentanyl used was significantly less in Group III.

CONCLUSIONS: Intraperitoneal normal saline irrigation is more effective than acetazolamide in reducing postoperative visceral pain after laparoscopic cholecystectomy and has significant opioid-sparing effect. However, its effect on shoulder pain is comparable to that of acetazolamide.

"Message from Mark" is a monthly series that features business topics of particular interest and importance to Pharmaceuticals President Mark Trudeau. This month's topic focuses on Pharmaceuticals' portfolio of businesses.

[Mark_Trudeau_FP.jpg]One of the reasons I found the opportunity to become the President of Pharmaceuticals so compelling is its strong and broad portfolio of businesses. Each of our businesses - Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients, Specialty Generics, Specialty Pharmaceuticals, and the Nuclear Medicine and Contrast Media arms of Imaging - complement each other and play an important role in the growth strategy for the new Mallinckrodt.

Once we're an independent company, our investors will ask how we intend to grow. They will want to know both our short-term goals and what we have in the pipeline to potentially ensure a return on their investments in the future. This is why being a portfolio of businesses puts us in a position of strength. We have the right balance of businesses that generate cash for short-term expectations and others that have the potential to meet investors' expectations for generating long-term growth.

It's no secret the Nuclear Medicine and Contrast Media businesses produce a lot of cash. Investors will expect us to use that cash for growth investments, but this doesn't mean we will look to Imaging only to generate cash. Instead, we're looking for growth in all of our businesses:


*         Contrast Media & Delivery Systems (CMDS) is one of the world's leaders in prefilled syringes and it also provides us a global footprint in high growth markets.



*         Nuclear has opportunities with its unique distribution, vertical integration and enhanced customer recognition programs to grow its Technetium-99m generator business in the U.S and Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA).  We can also explore opportunities with other radiopharmaceuticals.



*         Specialty Pharmaceuticals' two key branded pain products, EXALGO(r) (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release Tablets, (CII) and PENNSAID(r) (diclofenac sodium topical solution) 1.5% w/w, directly support our growth by laying the foundation for future products in the space.


*         Specialty Generics submitted six Abbreviated New Drug Applications (ANDAs) last fiscal year to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and we're actively looking to submit more to generate value. We believe the business' exceptional reformulation and vertical integration capabilities will continue to open opportunities for future growth.



*         API grew last year and continues to generate value, especially as we execute on Project Pinnacle at the St. Louis plant. Customers value our stable supply of controlled raw material and our quality in a highly regulated environment. API products operate in intensely competitive markets where this is a differentiator.

Our short-term growth opportunities are evident. Now we need to focus on our long-term plans to ensure our investors trust we're going to have healthy, sustainable, ongoing business growth. It's a challenging, but wonderful, opportunity to focus on building our product pipeline and expand into new markets. This is an exciting time in the history of this company, and our continued success will depend on the active engagement of each and every one of us.

To: Webb, Kevin J; Novak, Rod P
Cc: Neuman, Herbert R; Darton Jr., Eddie L
Subject: FW: PENNSAID and heat question



 
Hi Kevin and Rod:
 
I emailed Dr Galer about the question of application of heat to a PENNSAID treated knee.  Anything with a transdermal delivery would have more rapid and increased penetration with the application of heat (this is a known way to abuse fentanyl patches).  He did state that he had no reports of skin reactions, so that makes me feel a little more comfortable that it would not cause a burn or blistering.  I will contact Dr. Riccardo with this information.  I will not be able to give her a clear-cut yes/no answer, but present her with this information from one of the physician's from Nuvo.  I will email the sales representative to inform him of my contact with Dr. Riccardo too.  If there is anything else I can do, please let me know.  Thank you so much!
 
Phil
 
PS  If you would like I will apply heat to my knees this weekend and see what happens.  My middle name IS Sprague-Dawley (HA, that was a little bit of medical rodent humor:-)  Yeah I know I will never cut it at stand-up!)

Phil

Subject:        2011 Procurement forecasts

Dave,

I mentioned this in conversation last week, but wanted to get it written down.

As far as I know, the basic premis for JDA is the same as BPCS.  For demand out several years, ending inventory defaults to minimum + 1 run.  For example, Oxycodone 886599 minimum is 1200 Kg. and 887399 is 700 Kg.  Inventory is added in 1500 Kg increments, so forecasted inventory will be between 1900 and 4900 Kg (with both items forecasting below minimum) with all the intermediates defaulting to zero.  In fact oxycodone inventory runs much higher and this is one of the products with intermediates on hand 12/31.

How do I get target inventories for December 31, 2011? 
Should I ignore JDA and get the numbers by hand from planning?
Should I assume constant inventories?

I do think we need to forecast demand better than plus or minus 3,000 kg.

{Current medical research and opinion.}Curr Med Res Opin. 2014 Jan;30(1):149-60. doi: 10.1185/03007995.2013.860019. Epub 2013 Nov 15.

Incidence, patient satisfaction, and perceptions of post-surgical pain: results from a US national survey.

Gan TJ, Habib AS, Miller TE, White W, Apfelbaum JL.

{Open/close author information list}Author information

         Duke University Medical Center , Durham, NC , USA.

Abstract

Abstract Objective: During the past two decades, professional associations, accrediting bodies, and payors have made post-surgical pain treatment a high priority. In light of the disappointing findings in previous surveys, a survey was conducted to assess patient perceptions and characterize patient experiences/levels of satisfaction with post-surgical pain management. Research design and methods: Survey included a random sample of US adults who had undergone surgery within 5 years from the survey date. Participants were asked about their concerns before surgery, severity of perioperative pain, pain treatments, perceptions about post-surgical pain and pain medications, and satisfaction with treatments they received. Results: Of the 300 participants, ?86% experienced pain after surgery; of these, 75% had moderate/extreme pain during the immediate post-surgical period, with 74% still experiencing these levels of pain after discharge. Post-surgical pain was the most prominent pre-surgical patient concern, and nearly half reported they had high/very high anxiety levels about pain before surgery. Approximately 88% received analgesic medications to manage pain; of these, 80% experienced adverse effects and 39% reported moderate/severe pain even after receiving their first dose. Study limitations: Key study limitations include the relatively small population size, potential for recall bias associated with the 14-month average time delay from surgery date to survey date, and the inability to account for influences of type of surgery and intraoperative anesthetic/analgesic use on survey results. Conclusions: Despite heightened awareness and clinical advancements in pain management, there has been little improvement in post-surgical analgesia as measured by this survey of post-surgical patients.

Hi Stacy and Team,

Stacy, thanks for your comments.  I agree with them and that further analysis is needed to understand the proposed changes and additional filters which need to be evaluated.  You came to the same conclusion which we came to today.  After much discussion we landed on:
1) Taking a closer look at the HCPs being removed.  We need to be able to better characterize them (i.e., the quantity of HCPs which are recommended for removal based upon the Texas market dynamics).  We also need to assess the magnitude of disruption for the higher producing territories vs the lower producing territories.

2) Not sending out a target list tomorrow.  We need to better understand the changes and make sure we apply filters, like the ones you indicate below.

3) Once we agree that the target list is in a shape where we all agree to the methodology, filters and magnitude of disruption we think that the RSDs and a few DMs should have the opportunity to view the list and provide commentary on the impact.  We should do this before rolling out to all of the DMs.  We want to be able to catch any major issues before distributing to the rest of the DM team for inspection.  We also need to take a look at the PENNSAID contribution with our colleagues as it appears much lower than expected. 

4) We need to package the revised targeting along with the other initiatives to change our course (i.e. call planning guidance and any other changes).  Clarion is coming to STL on Wed to work through this with a small team.  We want to be sure that all the course corrections are done at the same time.  Our desire is to have this package ready for Monday next week so we can finalize as a team.  Ideally, we would like to have the package for the Tues RSD meeting.

We hope you are having a good vacation and will continue with the analysis in earnest this week.

Best regards,

Melissa

Summit Spotlight

 

 

 
Register Now for the 2018 National Rx Drug Abuse & Heroin Summit! Lowest Rates Now Available!


 

 



 


 

 
April 2   5, 2018 | Hyatt Regency Atlanta


The National Rx Drug Abuse & Heroin Summit is where solutions are formulated, stakeholders convene, and change begins. It is the annual gathering for stakeholders to discuss what s working in prevention and treatment. Notable speakers in past years have included President Barack Obama in 2016 and U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price in 2017. Be part of the international discussion on addressing the opioid crisis by attending the 2018 National Rx Drug Abuse & Heroin Summit in Atlanta.

{     Register Now     }




 

 
Top Stories in the News Disclaimer: Articles and links within articles do not necessarily reflect the views or opinions of the National Rx Drug Abuse & Heroin Summit or Operation UNITE.



 

 

 
At least 17 states enacting limit on length of painkiller prescriptions
Katie Zezima, The Washington Post States are enacting strict limits on the number of powerful prescription painkillers doctors can prescribe, a move that many believe will help fight the opioid crisis but has raised alarms among some physicians. At least 17 states have enacted rules to curb the number of painkillers doctors can prescribe. Some, including Arizona, Connecticut, Delaware, Massachusetts, New Jersey and Ohio, have passed laws limiting the duration of initial opioid prescriptions to five or seven days. Others are passing dosage limits. In Kentucky, a law went into effect last month capping opioid prescriptions for acute pain to three days.


{Read More}
-----
7-fold spike seen in opioid-linked fatal car crashes
Steven Reinberg, HealthDay News In yet another sign of just how deadly the U.S. opioid epidemic has become, researchers report a sevenfold increase in the number of drivers killed in car crashes while under the influence of prescription painkillers. Prescriptions for drugs such as oxycodone (OxyContin), hydrocodone (Vicoprofen) and morphine have quadrupled, from 76 million in 1991 to nearly 300 million in 2014, so it's no surprise these medications are playing a growing role in highway deaths, the Columbia University researchers said.

{Read More}
-----
Opioid overdose ICU admissions, death rate increasing
Salynn Boyles, MedPage Today Deaths associated with opioid overdoses in hospital intensive care units nearly doubled over a seven-year period from 2009 and 2015, and the costs of treating overdose victims in the ICU has skyrocketed, researchers report. The average cost of caring for an opioid overdose patient in the ICU increased by 58% from $58,500 to $92,400, according to a retrospective analysis of hospital billing records from 162 hospitals in 44 states. Admissions to ICUs linked to opioid overdoses increased by 34% at the hospitals from January of 2009 to September 2015, according to the analysis appearing online in Annals of the American Thoracic Society.

{Read More}
-----
Police try out new database for documenting opioid overdoses
Jennifer McDermott, Associated Press Police in Massachusetts are testing a new database for documenting opioid overdoses they hope will help departments share information in real time and get people into treatment. It works like this: When a department is called to an overdose, it's recorded in the system. The system then alerts the department to do a follow-up outreach visit. Within 24 hours of a nonfatal overdose, a non-uniformed officer and recovery coach will go to the person's house to discuss treatment and offer resources to their family.

{Read More}

Yesterday the U.S. Senate passed the historic 21st Century CURES Act, a bipartisan bill that includes $1 billion for states to fight the opioid epidemic and related areas of addiction.

As a member of the Recovery Movement, YOU helped spearhead this historical and comprehensive effort, which includes key addiction, mental health, as well as criminal justice reform.

This bill will also reinforce key principles in the Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act (CARA) and authorize additional funding for our communities.

There is a lack of recovery specific funding in the 21st Century CURES Act, which will require continued legislative education and advocacy efforts from our end.

Memorandum 
 
To:           David Moody 
 
CC:          Jim Meyer; Hal Harrison 
 
From:     Tom Readling 
 
Date:      6/9/2009 
 
Re:          Receipt of Tampered Shipment: Mallinckdrot Oxycodone W/APAP 7.5/325 mg 
 
On Monday, June 8, 2009 at approximately 11:00 AM a shipment was received from Mallinckrodt via FedEx. The shipment was signed for and the driver released before the shipment was checked. 
 
The items were delivered in a cardboard box which had been secured with strapping tape. The contents of the box were shrink wrapped in blue plastic.  
 
Gene Thompson checked the shipment in, which included 82 cases of Oxycodone w/apap 10/325 in 100 count bottles (SKU 609-826) and 11 cases of oxycodone w/apap 7.5/325 mg in 100 count bottles (SKU 609-842). During the process Thompson noticed one of the cases of the Oxycodone w/apap 7.5/325 mg had been opened and was missing three (3) bottles. The case in question contained nine (9) bottles instead of the usual twelve (12).  
 
Thompson notified David Thompson who in turn contacted writer. Writer observed the box and noted that the tape securing the box appeared to have been cut and the case was missing three bottles. The case was subsequently photographed by Phuong Ho and the photographs will be maintained. 
 
The shipment noted above was order number 7726533, PO# S48986, and the FedEx tracking number was 9864 7326 9667. The FedEx shipment was made 2-day freight and appears to have originated in Hobart, NY. 
 
Individuals in receiving have indicated that it is FedEx policy that a Mutual employee must sign for the shipment before it can be opened. The driver will subsequently note any problems with the shipment. 
 
The associates in receiving have been instructed to inspect all shipments received from FedEx and to ask for assistance if the inspection requires it. The driver from FedEx is to remain until the shipment has been inspected for tampering.

I just received the e mail information below which highlights and confirms that our Fentanyl Lozenge is listed on the FDA website. According to our reimbursement group, CMS expects to update the list one time in December 2010 with deletions for new listings on the FDA NDC Directory since October 2010.  We will use the updated December list to establish new edits beginning on or around January 1, 2011 that will reject prescription drug event (PDE) submissions from Part D sponsors for NDCs identified. Subject: [RxNews] Senate approves lock in amendment now goes to the house
From: Coolidge <coolidge@dakota2k.net>
Date: Mon, 07 Mar 2016 18:58:39 -0600
To: NADDI <rxnews@listserve.com>


 


Senate approves Medicare 'lock-in' amendment on opioid abuse
Drug Store News (03/04/16) Johnsen, Michael

The U.S. Senate approved an amendment on March 2 that gives Medicare Part D plans the authority to require at-risk beneficiaries to use a single prescriber and pharmacy for frequently abused drugs. The Medicare "lock-in" provision is part of a larger prescription drug abuse bill which aims to curb the opioid abuse epidemic through enhanced grant programs and other efforts. "As the pharmacy community is well aware, prescription drug abuse and dependency have been on the rise in America for several years," said Thomas Menighan, APhA EVP and CEO. "This epidemic is a major issue for our nation due to the devastating impact it is has had on individuals, families and communities. We have made this a central theme for APhA2016. As we inform and educate pharmacy professionals, they will be able to help their communities." APhA supports the passing of the lock-in amendment and believes that solutions to curb opioid and prescription drug abuse "will take everyone working together, including health care professionals, patients, and federal, state and local governments," said Jenna Ventresca, APhA associate director, health policy. The organization supports a multifaceted approach that balances legitimate patient access to prescription drugs with the need to protect individuals from misusing and abusing such medications. The Senate still has to vote on the broader comprehensive bill before it moves to the U.S. House of Representatives for review.

text:
Subject: GOP Spending Talks Meet Resistance; Tax Talks May Focus on AMT
From: BGOV Congress Tracker <alerts@bgov.com>
Date: Tue, 05 Dec 2017 20:20:54 +0000
To: derek.naten@mallinckrodt.com


{Bloomberg Government}  

 

 

GOP Spending Talks Meet Resistance; Tax Talks May Focus on AMT

By Zachary Sherwood | December 5, 2017 03:17PM ET | Bloomberg Government


House Republicans leaders face resistance to their stopgap funding plan, tax talks may focus on the alternative minimum tax, the nominee for next Federal Reserve chairman advances out of committee.

Here’s what Bloomberg Government is tracking in Congress so far today.

Year-End Spending Talks

Republican leaders’ plan to avoid a federal shutdown by funding the government past Friday has been thrown into disarray as House conservatives push back over the timing of a stopgap spending measure. 

The rift within the Republican ranks forced the Rules Committee to postpone its meeting scheduled for today on setting parameters of debate for the continuing resolution. Rules now plans to meet tomorrow.

House Republican leaders told their rank and file this morning they intend to pass a two-week CR through Dec. 22, Reps. Lamar Smith (R-Texas) and Mike Bost (R-Ill.) told reporters. The current stopgap bill runs through Friday. Members of the conservative House Freedom Caucus want the temporary patch to extend through Dec. 30.

House Speaker Paul Ryan (Wis.) wouldn’t say whether the continuing resolution would go until Dec. 22 or Dec. 30. "You’ll see when we bring the vote to the floor," he said at a press conference this morning. Read more from Jack Fitzpatrick in today’s budget and appropriations update.

Chief Senate Tax Writers Prefer AMT Repeal

Two influential GOP senators -- Rob Portman (Ohio), one of the chamber’s main tax writers, along with Orrin Hatch (Utah), chairman of the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee -- said their preference is to repeal the corporate AMT.

“I’m not a big AMT fan,” said Portman, who also wants to repeal the individual AMT. “I’d like to end up there, but we’ve got to do the back and forth with the House.” Hatch added: “I’d like to get rid of it.”

In a last-minute change, the Senate bill preserved the corporate AMT at its current 20 percent rate, along with a modified version of the individual AMT. The House legislation repeals both levies.

Sen. David Perdue (R-Ga.), said he too would like to see the AMT eliminated for corporations and individuals by the House-Senate conference committee that’s expected to begin working out compromise legislation this week. “We couldn’t go all the way because we needed the revenue,” Perdue said, referring to the corporate AMT. Repealing it would have cost about $40 billion over a decade -- which shows just how close tax writers were to hitting the $1.5 trillion deficit limit set by their budget resolution.

House Ways and Means Chairman Kevin Brady (R-Texas), who’s overseeing the conference committee, said repealing the corporate AMT is “one of the priorities” for the conference.

Also, the repeal of the individual mandate requirement that’s part of the 2010 Affordable Care Act -- a feature of the Senate bill, but not the House legislation -- is still under discussion, but is likely to have strong support among House Republicans, Brady said.

Other negotiations will center on the temporary nature of the individual tax cuts in the Senate plan, with Brady acknowledging “we can’t achieve permanency in everything.” Catch up on all of today’s tax talk here.

PUBLIC OPINION: Opinion polls suggest a majority of voters aren’t happy with what they’ve seen. Fifty-three percent of U.S. voters disapprove of the Republican overhaul plan, and 64 percent say it favors the wealthy, according to a Quinnipiac University poll released today. The poll was conducted from Nov. 29 to Dec. 4.

DEMOCRATS’ OPPOSITION: The tax overhaul bill is likely to pass, but Congress will revisit parts of it in January and February, Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.), the House Ways and Means Committee’s top Democrat, said. “This is more about a need for a political victory than it is for tax reform,” he said at a breakfast meeting of the New England Council, a regional group of business leaders. “We will revisit a lot of these items next year. You accountants and attorneys, you are going to be busy.”

Neal, the ranking Democrat on the conference committee, said he goes into the process with an open mind. Members who go into conference announcing that they are opposed to the bill are marginalized, he said. That said, he doesn’t expect any Democrats to vote in favor of the bill. “It’s a tax cut, let’s call it what it is. I think when people find out who’s going to pay for these cuts, I’m not sure they will be so enthusiastic,” he said. Read more from Aaron Nicodemus.

More Legislation to Watch

IMMIGRATION: A group of House Republicans are seeking legislation that would allow undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children to stay under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program. “Reaching across the aisle to protect DACA recipients before the holidays is the right thing to do,” Reps. Scott Taylor (R-Va.), Dan Newhouse (R-Wash.), Mia Love (R-Utah) and Mark Amodei (R-Nev.) said in a letter to Ryan signed by 30 other House Republicans.

Meanwhile, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) was encouraged by bipartisan talks on immigration and border security. "We think we’re moving in the right direction there," Schumer told reporters of efforts to bolster border security, and find a way to shield "dreamers" from deportation.

BIODIESEL CREDIT: Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) said he has a promise from fellow senators to reinstate a lapsed $1-per-gallon biodiesel tax credit that expired at the end of 2016. That doesn’t include a promise to convert it into a producers credit, Grassley said in a conference call with reporters. Critics say the change is needed as historic structure of biodiesel tax incentive as blender’s credit subsidizes foreign production. Read more from Jennifer A. Dlouhy.

SECRET SERVICE OT: Secret Service agents would be eligible for additional overtime this year and next under legislation the House passed today. The Secret Service Recruitment and Retention Act (H.R. 3731) would raise the current cap on agents’ salaries, including overtime, from about $162,000 to $187,000 this year. The cap would rise again in calendar 2018 based on the salary in effect for federal employees at Level 2 of the Executive Schedule. Read more from Louis C. LaBrecque.

D.C. METRO BILL: A bill to overhaul the board of Washington’s public transit agency offers a 50 percent increase in federal funding but only if there are substantial reductions in spending on the union workforce. The bill (H.R. 4534) would take the Washington Area Metropolitan Transit Authority from a 16-member board to a five-member board. It was introduced yesterday by Rep. Barbara Comstock (R-Va.), whose constituents live in the Washington suburbs served by the Metro subway and bus lines. Read more from Mara Lee. 

Nominations Watch

FED CHAIRMAN: Federal Reserve Governor Jerome Powell, facing a Senate committee vote on his nomination to become the central bank’s chairman, won strong bipartisan support that suggests he’ll sail through the full Senate. The Senate Banking Committee voted 22-1 today in favor of Powell’s nomination. The lone no vote was from Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who voiced concern before the tally was taken that he’d weaken financial regulations. Read more from Randall Woods.

DHS CHIEF: The Senate plans to vote at 4 p.m. on President Donald Trump’s nomination of Kirstjen Nielsen to serve as head of the Department of Homeland Security, Cornyn’s office said in a statement. If confirmed, Nielsen would fill the slot left vacant when John Kelly became White House chief of staff.

ENERGY RESEARCH: Linda Capuano, the nominee to be administrator of the Energy Information Administration, told lawmakers today she isn’t taking a position on climate change: “For me to take a position would introduce a bias.” Capuano faced questions on her position on climate change from Democrats during her Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee confirmation hearing. Capuano is Trump’s pick to be head of the independent statistical research arm of the Energy Department.

“The EIA provides unbiased data to inform those kinds of discussions. They’re very complex and the environment is very important,” Capuano said. “As the administrator of EIA, if I am appointed, it would not be wise for me to take a position on any particular issue, but to make sure that accurate and credible data is provided so that those issues can be debated and discussed.” Read more from Rebecca Kern.

What Else to Know Today

OPIOID FUNDING: Federal agencies need funding through appropriations to address aspects of the opioid crisis such as research of alternative medication and oversight of insurance company compliance, witnesses said at a hearing on preventing, treating, and recovering from opioid abuse. Democratic senators and witnesses from federal agencies also urged President Trump to take decisive actions to identify resources to reduce opioid misuse and to declare the crisis a national emergency rather than a public health emergency. They spoke at a Senate Appropriations Labor, Health and Human Services, Education and Related Agencies subcommittee hearing. Read more from Sara Merken.

CONYERS RESIGNS: Rep. John Conyers (D-Mich.), the longest serving House member, announced today that he’s leaving Congress immediately amid allegations that he sexually harassed members of his staff. "I am retiring today," said Conyers, who was also the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee. Conyers made the announcement in an interview with a Detroit radio station. Last week, House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) and other Democratic leaders called for his resignation because of the accusations he abused staff members.

He said he’s endorsing his son, John Conyers III, to replace him in the safe Democratic seat, where a special election will be held. "I want you to know my legacy will continue through my children," he said. But there could be a family feud developing. Ian Conyers, a Michigan state senator and the congressman’s grand-nephew, told the New York Times that he plans to run for the Detroit-area seat. Read more from Billy House and Jackie Edwards.

MOORE PROBE: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) said today that Alabama’s Republican Senate Candidate, Roy Moore, could face a Senate Ethics Committee probe if he wins next week’s special election. "If he were to be elected I think he would immediately have an issue with the ethics committee which they would take up," McConnell told reporters. "We’ll see what happens after that," McConnell said.

text:
Subject: Mallinckrodt Request for Meeting with DEA Quota Unit to Discuss Hydrocodone Market
From: "Harper, Karen" <karen.harper@covidien.com>
Date: Fri, 15 Jun 2012 10:43:17 -0500
To: "Sannerud, Christine A" <chris.a.sannerud@usdoj.gov>
Cc: "Lohman, Donald A" <donald.lohman@covidien.com>


Dr. Sannerud,

Confirming voicemail to you this morning, I am writing to request a face-to-face meeting with you to shine some light on a situation impacting the hydrocodone/APAP market that, if not addressed, we  believe will result in a significant disruption of the hydrocodone market.  Mallinckrodt participated in the at the recent DEA/FDA meetings concerning drug shortages and the purpose of this meeting request is in the same spirit of those meetings - we want to avoid a significant market disruption.

The magnitude of the disruption cannot be overstated.  Hydrocodone/APAP products are the most prescribed medicines in the U.S. and Mallinckrodt is a very large player in both the API and generic markets.  Mallinckrodt has its own generic hydrocodone/APAP products and supplies hydrocodone API to other dosage manufacturers.  Mallinckrodt and one of its largest customers have a combined market share of 75% or more in 9 of the 12 hydrocodone/APAP strengths and essentially 100% market share in a couple of strengths.

Mallinckrodt has pending procurement and manufacturing hydrocodone quota requests, which, if not granted, will result in us running out in 4 weeks.  Our manufacturing will be interrupted, workers will be furloughed and, most important, legitimate patients, including a large number of veterans, ultimately will be deprived of this product.

We are trying to understand why our hydrocodone quota requests have not been granted.  We are concerned that perhaps DEA has been informed that Abbott's plans to switch Vicodin to 300 mg of APAP will, in effect, "re-brand" a significant portion of the market.  We do not believe that significant re-branding will occur and we would like to share what we know on this situation.  We believe the market disruption will be far more significant if DEA fails to grant our quota requests in the next few weeks.

We have also requested a meeting with John Partridge.  We would like to meet with you in person next week as well to share this information to insure that legitimate pain patients are not deprived of this important medicine.

As you know, Mallinckrodt rarely requests meetings with DEA related to quota, but we view this as extremely important.  The meeting will not take long, but we believe it is very significant.

Thank you.



Karen Harper
Mallinckrodt/Covidien Pharmaceuticals
Sr. Manager, Controlled Substances Compliance Group
Legal Division

cellular (314) 401-1573

08/23/10

Safety Update:   

Primary Directive:  NO ONE GETS HURT

OSHA inspector has rescheduled for tomorrow (8/24/10). 
Please return comments regarding the combined LOTO/Line breaking to Steve Goewert.
Be patient and aware in the plant.  If you are uncertain of your task, please stop and ask someone for assistance.  We are a team and here to help each other.          




People & Plant Highlights:

A bake sale and Amighetti’s sale to benefit Karen House and Worth Industries is being held this week.  Please see special section below.  Take the opportunity to get involved and help make a regular day special for someone.  



By the Numbers:

19:  Number of replacement employees starting today.  Background clearances late last week allowed us to start 5 more than anticipated.

 

HSE/Security/HR:

OSHA will return on Tuesday, August 24.
Interview for HR Manager candidate tomorrow.  Two more next week.
Issue with wage people showing up in the SPT should be remedied although the names may still show up in the tool.

·        Annual electrical PM scheduled for 9/17 - 9/19. Please review maintenance requests and bring them to planning meetings to assist with preparation and scheduling.

·        Standby TOX taken down today for annual maintenance work so no backup is available. 

·        Issue with the back-up TOX not lighting over the weekend should be resolved with the PM work on the peepers.

·        Utility group proposed a new procedure for cleaning the cooling towers which should avoid the reduced cooling water flow that caused the weekend incident.

·        MMR ASR submitted for bar code scanning to issue and receive materials
 

Financials/OpEx:



 

Narcotics:

          Bldg 6:

·        Building restarting from weekend shutdown.

·        Parzone samples will be going to the lab this week.   

 

            Bldg 235:

·        Train 1: Running Taz Thebaine Bitartrate to Alkaloid.

·        Train 2: Running Glaxo Thebaine.

·        Train 3: First batch of step III Methylphenidate complete with reaction.

Bldg 250:

·        Running Hydrocodone 2X for Crystallization trials.

Bldg 97/97Tech:

·        Tech Center is on the 3rd batch of the new Nalbuphine process.

 

Bldg 5/OTFC:

·        Short on Milling/Blending/Packaging resources this week. John Spatz is on vacation and Brooke Lacey will be out until further notice.

·        Milling Morphine Sulfate.

·        Air booster compressor was rebuilt successfully over the weekend for OTFC.  All systems running.

 

Imaging:

> Jay, listed below is what we are trying to do to grow our business in a challenging  manage care environment in the Pittsburgh and surrounding areas.
> 
> 1. Planning and preparation - Focus on physician offices that have favorable manage care coverage for our products - Highmark (open lives 70%) / Caremark  -  We will review our IMS Data and our Physician Map Tool  ( we utilize our IMS data more often). We steer away from UPMC and Gessinger physician offices that have a large percentage of their patients with these manage care companies. We spend a lot of time reviewing our IMS data, so we can build an effective call routing action plan for our territories.
> 
> 
> 2. Territory & Time management - These are key ingredient toward success - we need to make sure that we are effectively and efficiently working our territories, so we are getting quality face time with or key targets that have favorable manage care coverage for our products. When we are reviewing our IMS data together, the reps are amazed of the potential and opportunity there is in their territories for XXR and Pennsaid, even though UPMC makes up for about 31% of their Percocet and Hydrocodone combos meds prescribed in their territories!!! We try to look for the positives in each territory - we focus on where we can grow our business daily.
> 
> 3.Confirmation - once we do our due diligence with the data, we will confirm the information at the physician offices with the key insurance person in the office, not the physician!!!! Once we have confirm our fact finding adventure (positive / negative - leave the building), we will move forward influencing the physician to prescribe our products to their patients focusing on their Highmark / Caremark patients. We will emphasize that UPMC and Gessinger will not pay for XXR and Pennsaid unless you complete a step/edit or PA. Then we will repeat it again about UPMC to the physician & staff, but sure enough the first patient they prescribe XXR or Pennsaid for, is a UPMC patient.
> 
> 4.Educating the physician & Office staff - when we convinced our providers to prescribe our products, we need to educate them on In Network and Out of Network pharmacies for Highmark and UPMC. If a Highmark patient tries to fill their prescription at a CVS pharmacy which is Out of Network for Highmark, the pharmacist will charge the patient cash price for our products, but if they would go across the street to a Rite-Aid, Giant Eagle, Wal-Mart or Sam's Club they would pay the around $10.00 or $20.00 co-pay!!!!Additionally, we supply the physicians /staff, what pharmacies (addresses and telephone numbers) that are currently stocking XXR in their area.
