To: Wickline, Ronald P; Novak, Rod P
Cc: Neuman, Herbert R; Meyer, Jay E; McGowan, Gavin J; Kisinger, Connie ; Wessler, Michael
Subject: FW: Label Language - Converting to Exalgo



Sales and Marketing Colleagues,

 

Please see the email I sent to Herb following a discussion we had on potential educational needs for physicians on issues surrounding the conversion process of patients on other opioids to Exalgo. The Exalgo label excerpts that I included below provide treating physicians with information that is pertinent to the management of the opioid rotation process to Exalgo, however, there are questions regarding physicians awareness of these additional elements of the label, as they are located somewhat deeper in the label and there is likelihood that physicians may not have thoroughly read these elements as a result.

 

We believe that some, if not many, physicians may be utilizing only part of the conversion recommendations (the general recommendation for dose reduction of 50%) and they may not necessarily be implementing other elements as described in the label to ensure the process is managed thoroughly and safely. There may be educational needs for the physicians on the aspect of the opiate deficit that is created by the employing the recommended dose reduction which can lead to withdrawal symptoms, which is why it may be important to utilize other steps that are described in the label language, such as monitoring rescue medication usage. Additionally, the importance of understanding the pharmacokinetics of Exalgo is pertinent to the conversion and titration aspect, which may result in the requirement of supportive rescue medication and physician evaluation of patients  response and side effects, until the patient is at steady-state on Exalgo. Finally, as the label language suggests, there is no single fixed conversion ratio that will suitably address the needs of all patients and physicians might benefit by being apprised of alternative conversion options, such as that employed in the pivotal 301 study published by Hale et al, which utilized a 25% dose reduction and the proceeded with titration.  

 

An idea we had was to consider developing a leave-behind educational card, with  Considerations for Conversion to Exalgo  that would utilize the label language elements on conversion and titration (such as those included below) and provide physicians with a succinct review of the FDA recommendations for the process of conversion to and titration of Exalgo. However, if the sales force already cover these elements or have an educational piece of this nature, there is no need to be redundant.

 

We look forward to your thoughts and input on this subject.

 

Thank you.

 

jtp

 

From: Patrick, Jeffrey
Sent: Wednesday, December 08, 2010 6:38 PM
To: Neuman, Herbert R
Cc: Patrick, Jeffrey
Subject: Label Language - Converting to Exalgo



 

Herb,


 


Appropriately, the FDA wrote the label language to aid and direct physicians in their efforts to convert patients to Exalgo. However, they did not suggest that there is one fixed process that will satisfy all patients converted. The following EXALGO label excerpts point to the need for the prescribing physician to utilize their clinical judgement as well as close communication to best manage patients in the conversion process:


 


In the selection of the initial dose of EXALGO, give attention to the following:

? the daily dose, potency, and specific characteristics of the opioid the patient has been taking previously;

? the reliability of the relative potency estimate used to calculate the equivalent hydromorphone dose needed;

? the patient's degree of opioid tolerance;

? the age, general condition, and medical status of the patient;

? concurrent non-opioid analgesics and other medications, such as those with Central Nervous System (CNS) activity [see Drug Interactions (7)];

? the type and severity of the patient's pain;

? the balance between pain control and adverse effects;

? risk factors for abuse, addiction, or diversion, including a prior history of abuse, addiction, or diversion

 

In general, start EXALGO therapy by administering 50% of the calculated total daily dose of EXALGO (see conversion ratio table below) every 24 hours. The initial dose of EXALGO can be titrated until adequate pain relief with  tolerable side effects has been achieved. The following table provides approximate equivalent doses, which may be used as a guideline for conversion.

? The conversion ratios and approximate equivalent doses in this conversion table (Table 1) are only to be used for the conversion from current oral opioid therapy to EXALGO. No fixed conversion ratio is likely to be satisfactory in all patients, especially in patients receiving large opioid doses.

Individualization of Dosage

? Once therapy is initiated, assess pain relief and other opioid adverse reactions frequently.

? Titrate patients to adequate analgesia with dose increases not more often than every 3 to 4 days, in order to attain steady-state plasma concentrations of hydromorphone at each dose.

? As a guideline, consider dosage increases of 25% to 50% of the current daily dose of EXALGO for each titration step.

? If more than two doses of rescue medication are needed within a 24 hour period for two consecutive days, the dose of EXALGO may need to be titrated upward.

? Administer EXALGO no more frequently than every 24 hours.

During periods of changing analgesic requirements, including initial titration, maintain frequent contact between physician, other members of the healthcare team, the patient and the caregiver/family.

 

I believe these are educational points for all discussions related to patients who have Exalgo prescribed for them.

 

jtp

Nearly all of the comments are consistent with our original submission but represent slight modifications of the labeling to be more consistent with embeda.  This is great news, as it means the recommended changes should be easy to accept and implement.  

In the Medication Guide the majority of changes are 1) changing  doctor  to  healthcare provider , 2) moving language from one section to another [the information in the Most important increases] 3) taking out Exalgo Alliance language, or 4) modifying our proposed language slightly to be consistent with embeda. The boxed warning has minimal recommended changes to language (and highlights the importance of  Proper Patient Selection )
The Indication (remove  intended for once-daily administration )
The indication is substantially smaller than our proposed indication and highlights opioid tolerance and not intended for prn analgesia. This removes contraindication for acute and post-operative pain and the should not be used to treat mild or short term pain (although this is elsewhere)
The agency requested to change the dosage range from 12-64mg to 8-64mg
The 5:1 potency ratio is kept

The have recommended a caution for medication errors between the 8 mg IR and 8mg EXALGO dosages

Subject: Exalgo mentioned by Dr. Webster in Medscape article
From: "Littlejohn, Stephen E" <stephen.littlejohn@covidien.com>
Date: Thu, 05 Apr 2012 16:18:01 -0500
To: "Bozzini, Alfredo" <alfredo.bozzini@covidien.com>,
    "Patrick, Jeffrey" <jeffrey.patrick@covidien.com>,
    "Saake, Lisa M" <lisa.saake@covidien.com>,
    "Harrell, Jamie" <jamie.harrell@covidien.com>,
    "Terifay, Terry W" <terry.terifay@covidien.com>,
    "Novak, Rod P" <rod.novak@covidien.com>,
    "Wessler, Michael" <michael.wessler@covidien.com>,
    "Brendel, Diane" <diane.brendel@covidien.com>




Opioid Rotation Practices Linked to Fatalities
Pauline Anderson
April 5, 2012 - Opioid rotation - switching from one opioid drug or route of administration to another to improve the outcome - is largely to blame for the growing number of unintentional deaths related to opioids, a new review suggests.
The review cites evidence of a link between opioid-related deaths and common opioid rotation practices, including the use of dose-conversion ratios published in equianalgesic tables.
Opioid rotation is flawed, said study coauthor Lynn R. Webster, MD, president elect of the American Academy of Pain Medicine and medical director and founder of Lifetree Clinical Research, Salt Lake City, Utah. Although using conversion tables is harmless in most cases, "this is an area where the harm has such devastating consequences - death - that we cannot accept even a 1% error," said Dr. Webster.
Along with his coauthor, Perry G. Fine, MD, Pain Research Center and Pain Management Center, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Dr. Webster reviewed the literature and found several case reports of opioid-related deaths or "near misses."
The review was published online<http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1526-4637.2012.01357.x/abstract> March 28 in Pain Medicine, the official journal of the American Academy of Pain Medicine.
In an accompanying article<http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1526-4637.2012.01356.x/abstract> published at the same time in the same journal, Dr. Webster and Dr. Fine suggest a slower and potentially safer method for switching opioids.
Painkiller Overdoses
Almost 15,000 people die every year as a result of overdoses involving prescription painkillers, with that number exceeding deaths from heroine and cocaine combined, according to a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention<http://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/752700> report. The US Food and Drug Administration<http://archinte.ama-assn.org/cgi/content/abstract/167/16/1752> (FDA) found that opioids, including oxycodone, fentanyl, morphine, methadone, and acetaminophen/hydrocodone, accounted for 5 of the 15 drugs most frequently named in fatal outcomes.
According to the new review, most proposed protocols for opioid rotation involve the use of equianalgesic dosing tables to convert the dose of the original opioid to a putative equivalent dose of morphine. That dose is then converted to that for the new opioid, with a safety margin incorporated.
One of the problems is that the most widely accepted guideline for opioid rotation was developed many years ago. At the time, experts believed that the relative strength of one opioid compared with that of another in the chronic state would be the same as that in the acute state, said Dr. Webster. "In other words, we didn't take into account that people would develop a tolerance, and certainly until just recently, we never knew about the genetic issues."
Not only did most studies use a single dose or a limited range of doses, they also investigated only a specific route. Thus, the findings aren't generalizable to other routes. Further, the studies didn't account for responses based on ethnicity, advanced age, concomitant medication use, or comorbid conditions.
"The key issue is that every human being has a different sensitivity to every different opioid molecule," said Dr. Webster. "So the way you respond to morphine will be different to the way that I respond to morphine, even in the acute state."
The rotation protocol has never been formally validated for safety or efficacy, added Dr. Webster. "There has never been an attempt to determine what is an equal analgesic of 1 opioid over another for chronic use - for example, after someone has been on a drug for 6 months or a year or 2. There is no research that has demonstrated consistently, across the board, that these tables have any validity."
Relying on tables derived from single-dose studies is especially problematic with repeated dosing of methadone. The authors noted the FDA's public health advisory on deaths and life-threatening changes in breathing and heart rate in patients newly started on methadone.
Although prescribing a new pain reliever might be necessary because of loss of effectiveness or side effects, in many cases the switch is called for because an insurer no longer covers a particular drug, said Dr. Webster. "So doctors have been forced to move to less costly drugs, and the least costly is usually methadone."
Gambling With Life?
Contributing to the problem is that published equianalgesic tables have inconsistent and variable conversion ratios. In addition, dose conversion guidelines found in package inserts for opioids, particularly the newer extended-release opioids, are inconsistent and potentially dangerous, said Dr. Webster.
He used the example of hydromorphone (Exalgo, Mallinckrodt/Covidien); the language of the insert is such that the conversion would result in 1 of 3 options, he said: an underestimate of the amount of extended-release hydromorphone necessary for adequate analgesia, an overestimate of the necessary amount that could increase the risk for overdose, or a dose within a reasonable window.
This, said Dr. Webster, boils down to "guessing" or "gambling" on the part of the clinician. "When we're dealing with a life, we should not be gambling."
Prescribing competence is "shockingly inadequate," said the authors. Errors can stem from inadequate education, lack of attention to detail, and calculation errors.
Confusion can also contribute to the problem. A survey of 406 non-pain specialist physicians found that 59% had difficulty calculating opioid dosages when rotating. When asked to convert a daily dose of 60 mg oxycodone to the dose for a fentanyl patch, 41% of clinical specialists, 28% of general practitioners, and 17% of geriatric care physicians said they "don't know" how to do that.
Physicians may be lulled into believing that conversion tables are safe and appropriate. "We like to have things structured in medicine," said Dr. Webster. "These tables were established to some degree to provide some security and safety and guidance toward rotating, but the irony is that they've actually made it unsafe."
Research suggests that 50% to 80% of patients with chronic pain who respond poorly to one opioid improve after being rotated to another opioid.
In their second report, a clinical case also published in Pain Medicine, Dr. Webster and Dr. Fine suggest an alternative to using opioid-rotation tables.
The best approach, they suggest, is to decrease the first drug by 25% to 30% per week while introducing the new drug at a dose that would be given to an opioid-naive patient, increasing the dose according to the clinical response, said Dr. Webster. "In many instances, it may take 3 to 4 weeks to rotate from one opioid to another," he said.
If patients are experiencing pain during the switch, physicians should give an immediate-release opioid to help "bridge" inadequate dosing.
He cautioned that some patients may be sensitive to the new drug. "A new molecule may be highly effective at a very low dose."
Hold Next Dose
Seddon Savage, MD, medical director, Chronic Pain and Addiction Program, Silver Hill Hospital, New Canaan, Connecticut, and president of the American Pain Society, agrees with this slow rotation protocol.
She added that patients should be told that if they feel sedated they should hold their next opioid dose and call their physician.
Dr. Savage commented that the review paper does a good job of pointing out and documenting the problems related to opioid rotation and of making physicians more aware of the limitations of conversion tables.
"One of the points that the authors make is that there is a lot of variability in response to different opioids. If you take these opioid conversion tables as gospel, apply them indiscriminately to all people, and just do a mathematical conversion, you will end up with some people for whom the conversion aren't appropriate."
For a list of companies from which Dr. Webster has received funding, and for conflict of disclosures for Dr. Fine, please see original paper.
Pain Medicine. Both articles published online March 28, 2012. Abstract<http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1526-4637.2012.01357.x/abstract> Abstract<http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1526-4637.2012.01356.x/abstract>

Dear Lisa,

Please find attached Exalgo PI with FDA changes accepted and additional changes tracked.  Our global labeling group has edited the margins, spacing and footer to reflect the current revision, as well as replacing several instances of the infinity sign with a corrected symbol.  Two instances of EXALGO in all caps are also included as minor edits.

 

For the FDA comment to include increments in mg for dose increases, Mallinckrodt proposes to edit the revised text to replace 4 mg with 8 mg as the lowest available strength of EXALGO, for which multiples of the same strength could be prescribed until the patient was stabilized on a dose.  The rationale comment from the labeling is copied into this email for ease of reading.

 

               Comment as Rationale for Change from 4-mg to 8-mg Incremental Dose Increase:

The 4?mg dose increment is problematic from a prescription/patient instructions-logistics perspective, creating prescribing issues for physicians and safety issues for patients.  The concerns with this prescriptive approach are that it would not only hinder appropriate management of the opioid-tolerant patient s pain but could also result in safety issues due to patient confusion and the potential for medication errors when multiple tablet strengths were required to achieve a prescribed dose.  There is also the additional safety concern for patients attempting to split tablets to save money on the additional strength prescriptions.

 

This prescriptive approach is especially concerning combined with the removal of the proposed 25% dose reduction from previous opioid therapy, which was based on the EXALGO clinical trial (50% reductions were never studied).  Drastic dose reductions in this opioid tolerant population could lead to repeat, i.e., over-dosing due to inadequacy of the first dose and the 4 days that are required to achieve steady state for EXALGO.  Similarly, the minimal 4-mg dose increment could increase the rates of withdrawal symptoms in the opioid-tolerant patients who would be prescribed EXALGO.

 

Mallinckrodt recommends initiation at 8, 12, 16, 24, or 32 mg followed by an 8-mg titrating dose for EXALGO until stabilized. 

 

Thank you for your efforts to finalize this class labeling for EXALGO.

Linda

FDA approves 32 mg Why stock the 32 mg tablet?

 

 EXALGO 32 mg was the median effective dose in the pivotal trial.*1

 
 

 You may already be distributing multiple 16 mg tablets to patients.

 
*

 Mean effective dose was 37.8 mg.2

 

EXALGO TABLET STRENGTHS2

Tablets shown are not actual size.

START STOCKING EXALGO 32 MG TODAY!

REFERENCES: 1. Hale M, Khan A, Kutch M, Li S. Once-daily OROS hydromorphone ER compared with placebo in opioid-tolerant patients with chronic low back pain. Curr Med Res Opin. 2010;26(6):1505-1518.
2. EXALGO  Prescribing Information.

800-778-7898 | www.EXALGO.com

COVIDIEN, COVIDIEN with logo and Covidien logo are U.S. and internationally
registered trademarks of Covidien AG.
EXALGO is a registered trademark of Mallinckrodt LLC.
  2012 Mallinckrodt LLC, a Covidien company.  MK20164 September 2012

To ensure that you receive future email from EXALGO, add us to your address book.
If you no longer wish to receive email from EXALGO, unsubscribe now.

 INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

 

 

 EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications



 
 

 EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.



 
 

 EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.



 
 

 Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.



 
 

 Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.



 
 

 Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.



 
 

 Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.



 
 

 Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.

 Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase.
Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to

EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

FYI
FDA NEWS RELEASE

FDA approves abuse-deterrent labeling for reformulated OxyContin
Agency will not approve generics to original OxyContin
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved updated labeling for Purdue Pharma L.P.'s
reformulated OxyContin (oxycodone hydrochloride controlled-release) tablets. The new labeling indicates
that the product has physical and chemical properties that are expected to make abuse via injection
difficult and to reduce abuse via the intranasal route (snorting).
Additionally, because original OxyContin provides the same therapeutic benefits as reformulated
OxyContin, but poses an increased potential for certain types of abuse, the FDA has determined that the
benefits of original OxyContin no longer outweigh its risks and that original OxyContin was withdrawn
from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness. Accordingly, the agency will not accept or approve any
abbreviated new drug applications (generics) that rely upon the approval of original OxyContin.
The FDA approved the original formulation of OxyContin in Dec. 1995. The product was abused, often
following manipulation intended to defeat its extended -release properties. Such manipulation causes the
drug to be released more rapidly, which increases the risk of serious adverse events, including overdose
and death. In April 2010, the FDA approved a reformulated version of OxyContin, which was designed to be
more difficult to manipulate for purposes of misuse or abuse. Purdue stopped shipping original OxyContin
to pharmacies in August 2010.
"The development of abuse-deterrent opioid analgesics is a public health priority for the FDA," said
Douglas Throckmorton, M.D., deputy director for regulatory programs in the FDA's Center for Drug
Evaluation and Research. "while both original and reformulated oxycontin are subject to abuse and misuse,
the FDA has determined that reformulated OxyContin can be expected to make abuse by injection difficult
and expected to reduce abuse by snorting compared to original OxyContin."
The FDA has determined that the reformulated product has abuse-deterrent properties. The tablet is more
difficult to crush, break, or dissolve. It also forms a viscous hydrogel and cannot be easily prepared
for injection. The agency has determined that the physical and chemical properties of the reformulated
product are expected to make the product difficult to inject and to reduce abuse via snorting. However,
abuse of OxyContin by these routes, as well as the oral route, is still possible. The reformulated
product also may reduce incidents of therapeutic misuse, such as crushing the product to sprinkle it onto
food or to administer it through a gastric tube. When FDA finds that a new formulation has abuse
deterrent properties, the agency has the authority to require generics to have abuse-deterrent properties
also
The agency review of this issue included an analysis of the following:
*
Citizen petitions requesting that the agency determine whether original OxyContin was voluntarily
withdrawn from sale for reasons other than safety or effectiveness;
*
Comments submitted to the public dockets associated with these petitions;
•
Information concerning original and reformulated OxyContin and the withdrawal of original OxyContin;
Clinical data, peer-reviewed literature, and other information concerning postmarketing adverse
events associated with original OxyContin, reformulated OxyContin, and other extended -release oxycodone
products.
Postmarketing assessments of the impact of reformulated OxyContin on abuse are ongoing, and the FDA will
update its evaluation of the effects of reformulated OxyContin on abuse as new data become available.
The FDA, together with other public health agencies, continues to encourage the development of abusedeterrent formulations of opioids and believes that such products will help reduce prescription drug
abuse. At the same time, the FDA remains committed to ensuring that patients with pain have appropriate
access to opioid analgesics.

Hi Herb,

Everything you say makes sense and I completely agree with the time of 60 minutes. I just checked other recent Ad
Comms and Remoxy, Embeda and Oxycontin used only 45 min for sponsor presentations, and 60 min for Fentora.

MNKOI 0002959075

 do need to supply our list of presenters and the timeframe (either 60 min or 90...or I guess 75 is an option) by

Also, I recalled that I had received a 'piece' of FDA's agenda (although draft I'm sure at the time) as an example of what I

Cc: Stauder, Nancy R; Schooler, JoAnna S; Kim, Stuart K.
Subject: My thoughts after MOCK B
I have finally gotten a chance to gather my thoughts after Mock B. I suggest a significantly narrower focus. Specifically:
No changes to the RA and PK portions
For the clinical experience, we take the FDA's apparent ceding of efficacy and build on it. My version of the talk would
follow this track
•
Describe the history of hydromorphone immediate release (IRHM), when approved, number dispensed, etc
•
Note sales are increasing in the US without sales/marketing efforts as proof of demand or need of the HM moeity
•
Really punch up the European 17 million patient days as proof of both safety and efficacy for the 98% of US patients
who will use this drug properly
•
Review the 301 study only in the context of a successful conclusion to the SPA.
The medical need portion should be truncated.
•
All references to abuse and diversion removed.
•
Present 3-4 real patient scenarios of patients Lynn has seen that required IRHM to relieve suffering
•
Talk about the pain/sleeplessness associated with the troughs in IRHM
•
Clear, factual statement Exalgo is needed in a subset of patients and to deny the product is to prolong their suffering
Annette's portion of REMS
•
•
•

Limit the discussion to matching the a priori risks we identified to the resulting tool in the alliance.
Have very solid back ups that explain the ABC's of the Alliance (enrollment, etc) to use if needed
The REMS is designed to assist in abuse, misuse, inadvertent overdose, and certain types of diversion (involving
an uninformed patient). It is not a panacea for drug diversion in this country

My portion

MNKOI 0002959076

 •
•
•
•
•

We will be good stewards of this product
Detailed review of our sales and marketing plans, including sales compensation, targeting, advertising, etc.
The REMS is a living document and is focused on appropriate patient use (note: the 98% who need it and will use
it appropriately, not diversion, intentional misuses, etc)
The REMS is moldable and adaptable as new information evolves or a class-wide REMS is enacted
The REMS has teeth and miscreants can be subject to termination, reporting to DEA, reporting to state licensing
boards or state law enforcement officials.

We should be done in 60 minutes. My goal is to avoid the traps we fell into on Mock B. I do not want to get bogged down
into confidence intervals of a non-inferiority design, how we will stop people from recreationally abusing opiods, prove you
are better than other LA opiods, and what nefarious sales and marketing schemes do you have planned. If these issues
come up, we should give a 10 word or less answer and move back to one or more of the following:
HM is safe and effective. We successfully fulfilled the SPA. It is truly needed by a subset of patients. We will
responsibly market it. We have a robust yet flexible REMS to help assure use only by educated and informed
patients in the indicated population
I am re-working my slides along the above lines. I recognize this is late in the day, but would be happy to discuss any time
this weekend. My cell is 314-409-6363 or I will respond to emails as soon as possible. Please forward if I left anyone out

Subject: Payer Trends - 60 Ct Patient Unit of Use Bottles
From: "Hasse, Debra C" <debra.hasse@covidien.com>
Date: Mon, 23 Apr 2012 15:27:24 -0500
To: "Terifay, Terry W" <terry.terifay@covidien.com>


Terry,

I have been thinking about the 60 count patient unit of use bottle.  This MCO trend lines up well with this package size (15 DOT).  If we considered $6.00/day WAC with 25% discount, gets net price down to $4.50-$5.00/day costing the MCO $67.50 - $75.00/script.  If Tier 3 co-pay ranges from $40-$60/TRx, the difference in price to MCO may be similar or a bit more than what they pay for generic.  Also addresses the concern regarding over prescribing opioids to acute pain/opioid na ve patients. Benefits include potential to improve adherence and offers abuse deterrent formulations (safety) benefits over IR's without paying much for it.

If we want to stick with $8.00/day WAC with 30% discount...maybe we should consider 10/DOT - 50 count bottle to neutralize cost to MCO.  Problem with this approach is that patients may have to get more refills and costs will increase to them. OK, let's level set here:

First, as far as I know OPDP NEVER approves promotional material.  They provide advisory comments.  If you take those comments and operate within them you have a safe harbor, at least until they tell you that they have changed their minds, which they sometimes do. Even in cases like accelerated review (I think this is the CFR type) where pre-submission of launch marketing materials is required, you don't get an approval or clearance, you just get advisory comments that you have to interpret.

The standard misnomer is that FDA "approves" or gives "pre-clearance" to marketing materials that are submitted to them.  That is very common with non-regulatory types and a basic mistake made in interpretation of what advisory comments mean.  I have even seen this mistake made when materials are just routinely submitted at time of first use.  In the latter case, people who don't know any better think that if you don't hear anything it means that FDA has 'approved' your material.  Even the terminology "pre-clearance" which people often use, is not appropriate.  So, Tammy's bullet below is probably just some executive mis-speaking.

Second, PARC has continued to encourage Marketing to submit materials for advisory comment.  In that regard we would like these materials to be PARC-approved so that we stand the best chance to make a good impression with OPDP.    Marketing has not been willing to do this but PARC constantly tries to get them to change their mind.

Third, we don't know what was in their marketing materials that OPDP reviewed.  If it is a simple statement of physical properties that might have gotten through OPDP.  If they tried to link those to treatment benefit or safety (read: abuse deterrence or overdose avoidance), I doubt that would have gotten through.

Fourth, PARC's position has been that if language is REMOVED from the draft PI during FDA review division review of the application, it would be difficult to market to that information.  There are many examples where physical properties of drugs have been marketed to where those properties or comparisons to other drugs properties, are not specifically called out in our labeling without ever having been removed in labeling negotiations.  You generally can't claim safety or efficacy benefits of these physical properties if they are not addressed in your PI but you can generally list those attributes and allow the reader to digest and interpret the meaning for themselves.  The comment below that Tammy put together is most likely that situation, i.e., that they are just listing the properties.  Note that we already list physical properties, some in comparison to other drugs where that data exists, for a lot of our products including EXALGO, Optiray and Optimark.  Doing this for Ruby or Zircon should not present any issues as long as it is done correctly and in the correct context.

From what I have read below I don't see anything new to consider.  If Debra thinks there is, I would be happy to have a meeting to discuss this.

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information<http://lists.jobson.com/t?r=4&c=0&l=3818&ctl=54A3B:B41DB4189704864061FB1363A448C720&> and Medication Guide<http://lists.jobson.com/t?r=4&c=0&l=3818&ctl=54A3C:B41DB4189704864061FB1363A448C720&>.

•
> FDA NEWS RELEASE

•> For Immediate Release: April 16, 2013
> Media Inquiries: Morgan Liscinsky, 301-796-0397;
morgan.liscinsky@fda.hhs.gov<mailto:morgan.liscinsky@fda.hhs.gov>
> Consumer Inquiries: 888-INFO-FDA
•> FDA approves abuse-deterrent labeling for reformulated OxyContin
> Agency will not approve generics to original OxyContin
•> The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved updated labeling for Purdue Pharma L.P.'s
reformulated OxyContin (oxycodone hydrochloride controlled-release) tablets. The new labeling indicates
that the product has physical and chemical properties that are expected to make abuse via injection
difficult and to reduce abuse via the intranasal route (snorting).
•> Additionally, because original OxyContin provides the same therapeutic benefits as reformulated
OxyContin, but poses an increased potential for certain types of abuse, the FDA has determined that the
benefits of original OxyContin no longer outweigh its risks and that original OxyContin was withdrawn
from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness. Accordingly, the agency will not accept or approve any
abbreviated new drug applications (generics) that rely upon the approval of original OxyContin.
•> The FDA approved the original formulation of OxyContin in Dec. 1995. The product was abused, often
following manipulation intended to defeat its extended -release properties. Such manipulation causes the
drug to be released more rapidly, which increases the risk of serious adverse events, including overdose
and death. In April 2010, the FDA approved a reformulated version of OxyContin, which was designed to be
more difficult to manipulate for purposes of misuse or abuse. Purdue stopped shipping original OxyContin
to pharmacies in August 2010.
•> "The development of abuse-deterrent opioid analgesics is a public health priority for the FDA," said
Douglas Throckmorton, M.D., deputy director for regulatory programs in the FDA's Center for Drug
Evaluation and Research. "While both original and reformulated OxyContin are subject to abuse and misuse,
the FDA has determined that reformulated OxyContin can be expected to make abuse by injection difficult
and expected to reduce abuse by snorting compared to original OxyContin."
•> The FDA has determined that the reformulated product has abuse-deterrent properties. The tablet is more
difficult to crush, break, or dissolve. It also forms a viscous hydrogel and cannot be easily prepared
for injection. The agency has determined that the physical and chemical properties of the reformulated
product are expected to make the product difficult to inject and to reduce abuse via snorting. However,
abuse of oxycontin by these routes, as well as the oral route, is still possible. The reformulated
product also may reduce incidents of therapeutic misuse, such as crushing the product to sprinkle it onto
food or to administer it through a gastric tube. When FDA finds that a new formulation has abuse
deterrent properties, the agency has the authority to require generics to have abuse-deterrent properties
also
•> The agency review of this issue included an analysis of the following:
•> *
Citizen petitions requesting that the agency determine whether original OxyContin was voluntarily
withdrawn from sale for reasons other than safety or effectiveness;
> •
Comments submitted to the public dockets associated with these petitions;
> *
Information concerning original and reformulated OxyContin and the withdrawal of original
OxyContin;
> *
Clinical data, peer-reviewed literature, and other information concerning postmarketing adverse
events associated with original OxyContin, reformulated OxyContin, and other extended -release oxycodone
products.

MNKOI 0000602323

 > Postmarketing assessments of the impact of reformulated OxyContin on abuse are ongoing, and the FDA
will update its evaluation of the effects of reformulated OxyContin on abuse as new data become
available.
•> The FDA, together with other public health agencies, continues to encourage the development of abusedeterrent formulations of opioids and believes that such products will help reduce prescription drug
abuse. At the same time, the FDA remains committed to ensuring that patients with pain have appropriate
access to opioid analgesics.

To: "Duarte, Joe A" <joe.duarte@covidien.com>


Dear Valued Retailer:

Mallinckrodt LLC, the Pharmaceuticals business of Covidien, is pleased to announce the approval of the 32 mg strength of EXALGO(r) (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release Tablets (CII).

Please find the attached documents:

-       EXALGO New Product Announcement letter

-       HDMA Form

-       MSDS

-       Package Insert

-       Copy of EXALGO label
**Product specs were sent to Pricing Data Banks on August 27, 2012.

PLEASE SEE IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION, INCLUDING BOXED WARNING BELOW.
SEE FULL PACKAGE INSERT FOR FULL PRESCRIBING INFORMATION.

INDICATION
EXALGO(r) (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL, LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION,
and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE
Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient's risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



*   EXALGO is contraindicated in:

- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or in the absence of resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the gastrointestinal tract, or have "blind loops" of the gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications

*   EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.

*   EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.

*   Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.

*   Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.

*   Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison's disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.

*   Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.

*   Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.

*   Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.

*   Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

See Full Prescribing Information and Medication Guide enclosed.

Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

 

 

 EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications



 
 

 EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.



 
 

 EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.



 
 

 Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.



 
 

 Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.



 
 

 Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.



 
 

 Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.



 
 

 Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.



 
 

 Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.

               Comment as Rationale for Change from 4-mg to 8-mg Incremental Dose Increase:

The 4?mg dose increment is problematic from a prescription/patient instructions-logistics perspective, creating prescribing issues for physicians and safety issues for patients.  The concerns with this prescriptive approach are that it would not only hinder appropriate management of the opioid-tolerant patient s pain but could also result in safety issues due to patient confusion and the potential for medication errors when multiple tablet strengths were required to achieve a prescribed dose.  There is also the additional safety concern for patients attempting to split tablets to save money on the additional strength prescriptions.

 

This prescriptive approach is especially concerning combined with the removal of the proposed 25% dose reduction from previous opioid therapy, which was based on the EXALGO clinical trial (50% reductions were never studied).     - Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications

* EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.

* EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.

* Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.

* Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.

* Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison's disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.

* Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.

* Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness. Post marketing events include hypersensitivity reactions, angioedema and urticaria.

* Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.

* Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

See Full Prescribing Information (http://ad.doubleclick.net/ddm/clk/278353412;105507703;y?http://exalgo.com/media/pdf/EXALGO_FullPrescribingInformation.pdf) and Medication Guide (http://ad.doubleclick.net/ddm/clk/278353410;105507703;w?http://www.exalgo.com/hcp/medication-guide.aspx?utm_source=Pain_Live&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=EXALGO-Flight1-we-will-help-you-make-the-switch).

   INDICATION
EXALGO (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION 

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL, LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE
Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.
Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone. 

  
   EXALGO is contraindicated in: 
  - Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant. 
  - Patients with significant respiratory depression 
  - Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or in the absence of resuscitative equipment 
  - Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus 
  - Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction 
  - Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications 
   EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer. 
   EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist. 
   Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery. 
   Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO. 
   Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment. 
   Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO. 
   Serious adverse events could also include
hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest
from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal.
Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in
clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation
(31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence,
headache, asthenia and dizziness. Post
marketing events include hypersensitivity
reactions, angioedema and urticaria. 
   Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention. 
   Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

{EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII)}   
 

 
{What is your next step for your OxyContin  patient experiencing adverse events or escalating doses with inadequate analgesia?} 
{4 REASONS to CONSIDER EXALGO  as a NEXT STEP} 
 

{1} True once-daily dosing with smooth and steady delivery over 24 hours. (Steady state is achieved 3 to 4 days after initiation.)1 
{2} May reduce pill burden for patients taking OxyContin  20 mg or 40 mg tablets.1 
{3} No CYP450 drug interactions. (Concomitant use of opioids such as EXALGO with other CNS depressants can have additive effects.)1-3 
{4} In a pivotal trial, EXALGO reduced pain intensity scores by 50% (6.4 to 3.2) from stable state in successfully converted patients.*4 
  *In a double-blind, placebo-controlled withdrawal study, 447 opioid-tolerant patients with low back pain enrolled and 268 were randomized; 66 [49%] EXALGO patients and 44 [31%] placebo patients completed the study. Both arms were allowed limited supplemental IR hydromorphone as rescue medication during all phases of the study.1 


For these reasons and more, consider EXALGO for your opioid-tolerant chronic pain patients. 
  
And to make switching easier, download a FREE Opioid Conversion Calculator for iPhone  or iPad .

References: 1. EXALGO  Prescribing Information. 2. Pergolizzi JV Jr, Labhsetwar SA, Puenpatom RA, Joo S, Ben-Joseph R, Summers KH. Exposure to potential CYP450 pharmacokinetic drug-drug interactions among osteoarthritis patients: incremental risk of multiple prescriptions. Pain Pract. 2011;11(4):325-336. 3. Smith HS. Opioid metabolism. Mayo Clin Proc. 2009;84(7):613-624. 4. Hale M, Khan A, Kutch M, Li S. Once-daily OROS hydromorphone ER compared with placebo in opioid-tolerant patients with chronic low back pain. Curr Med Res Opin. 2010;26(6):1505-1518.

To ensure that you receive future email from EXALGO, add us to your address book. 
  
If you no longer wish to receive email from EXALGO, unsubscribe now. 

   INDICATION
EXALGO (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION 

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL, LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE
Abuse Potential
EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.
Life-threatening Respiratory Depression
Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.
Accidental Exposure
Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone. 

  
   EXALGO is contraindicated in: 
  - Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant. 
  - Patients with significant respiratory depression 
  - Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or in the absence of resuscitative equipment 
  - Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus 
  - Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction 
  - Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications 
   EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer. 
   EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist. 
   Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery. 
   Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO. 
   Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment. 
   Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO. 
   Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness. Post marketing events include hypersensitivity reactions, angioedema and urticaria. 
   Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention. 
   Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

Dealing with pain while  EXALGOTM is reaching effective levels

EXALGO is an extended-release medication.  It usually takes 6 to 8 hours for you to begin to feel pain relief.  Since the active ingredient (hydromorphone) in EXALGO is slowly released into the bloodstream, it may take up to 3-4 days for EXALGO to reach maximum effectiveness.  At that point, the medicine in EXALGO should remain at a constant and effective level.  Your doctor will help you manage any pain during this time.  Do not take another dose of EXALGO within 24 hours unless your doctor tells you.  Taking a second dose within 24 hours may cause you to overdose. An overdose can cause death.

Only take EXALGO if . . .

You have moderate to severe chronic pain.
You have been taking an opioid medicine up until the time you were prescribed EXALGO, so your body is used to taking these medicines.
You need to be on a pain relief medicine for a long time. Ask your doctor if you are unsure you are taking an opioid medicine.

  You  need management of mild pain or pain that is not expected to continue for a long time

  You are having an asthma attack or have severe asthma, trouble breathing, or certain other lung problems

  You have narrowing  of the stomach or intestines or have bowel blockage

  You have a history of surgery in your stomach or intestines.

  You are allergic to any of the ingredients in EXALGO, including hydromorphone or sulfites.

Before taking EXALGOTM, tell your doctor . . .

Subject: Response to Phil's discussion about PARC
From: "nosco, dennis l"
Date: Wed, 17 Mar 2010 23:24:06 +0000
To: "neuman, herbert r"


Herb,

Phil said you wanted me to respond to his detailed description that he sent you last night.  The reason for the volatility of the meeting centered around Marketing's misunderstanding that I had told them that they could  put the study results they considered pertinent on the reprint carriers of the PENNSAID articles and then have the sales force present all these results to customers.  My understanding is that these included all the secondary endpoints and the AE data from the studies, very similar to what was presented in the various training modules that they submitted for our review.  As I remember, each time we reviewed these modules I expressed my concern about this data because it was not in the PI and, at the last review, said I wouldn't find it acceptable from a regulatory point of view to have this type of information in the reprint carriers.  I also remember us eliminating the sales manager section where the reps would be quizzed on points from these studies not in the PI there were covered twice before.  All the time we were being told that this was just for sales rep knowledge in case they were asked by the doctor.  Clearly, when I started this process with Kevin I went over the five pivotals with him and told him that I didn't see anything in any of them that would keep me from approving them as disseminated leave behinds.  I said that some of them would not be able to be detailed and some of them would have to have reprint carriers which limited what the reps said about them.  Specifically, I allowed for the reprint carrier for the Simon article to contain, in the reprint carrier, the methodology for the entire study (summary of all the comparators) but only speak in the results section about the three placebo/vehicle vs PENNSAID arms.  We also had some language in place, I thought, that said if the customer asked about the other two arms, the sales rep would direct them to Medical Affairs or that the customer could choose to read the paper themselves.  I have been unwavering from that position all along and, frankly, don't understand how I could possibly be misunderstood as I said the same thing all along.

Based on our conversations (you and me) and those of PARC, we acknowledged that presenting the study results in the physician's slide deck in a peer-to-peer presentation would make more palatable the presentation of all the study results, including the secondary endpoints.  We still did not want to see it in any sales aid and, obviously, Kevin and Caroline have a different idea about how much of it we should allow the sales reps to present and put in the reprint carriers.  So, Phil is incorrect in his statement regarding the negative endpoint.  In the slide deck Marketing mentioned all the efficacy variables that Pennsaid was positive for but failed to mention one it was not positive for, stiffness.  So I asked for that endpoint to be mentioned for fair balance.  FYI, subsequently PARC agreed not to have summary slides for any of the clinical studies.  He is also incorrect in his statements about the results of the Simon study in the two arms with oral diclofenac.  We want no mention in sales materials, including the reprint carriers.  Personally, I also want no mention of the individual study AE data in the reprint carrier, which I will discuss below.

My main disagreement with Marketing centers around the reprint carriers in terms of what can be in them.  I don't want the AE data or secondary endpoint results.  Marketing thinks I told them that they could put them there.  I have, again, been completely consistent and rock solid on this from day 1 and the AE data was NEVER addressed.

Our main disagreement among all members was on how the individual study AE data should be presented, if at all, in the speaker slide deck.  To me, its presentation is difficult and becomes even more so if it is presented where it might make scientific sense, with efficacy results and AE data from the study together.  My suggestion, that I thought Kevin took, was to present the AE data from the PI and then the AE data from the individual studies.  While that may not the most sense scientifically I have seen enough clinical study presentations to know that this has been done and that most doctors are interested in the efficacy of the drug and its overall safety profile, not the safety profile in one study.  Thus, creating one AE section that talks about the overall AE data (PI) and those from the individual studies, with results but little or no discussion, save maybe a summary slide that is approved by PARC.

We can talk more about the reasons that I hold this position relative to AE data from individual studies if you would like.

Regarding EXALGO and cancer, we HAVE reached agreement on this.  Similar to what we did for the unbranded Tofranil webinar, we allow it but only where it is important to describe the study.  Where it isn't important, we leave it out. 

Finally, the only person who is fighting for the two color PENNSAID logo not being a claim is Caroline.  PARC is unanimous on this and, to me, the point is moot as we are beyond 'reminder' ads with this product, although it does pop up every once in a while as Marketing doesn't like the compromise of a one color logo on pieces that they don't want the boxed warning and IRI on.  Also, Marketing kind of screwed themselves on this issue as the refused my suggestion to just send a reminder ad to DDMAC for comment to see if DDMAC considered the two colored logo a claim.  Now they are trying to revisit it.

Regarding personalities, to me this is a non-issue.  We have personality clashes in every group in this company.  We are working our way through them on PARC as we do every time they creep up.  Will they always be there?  Yeah, maybe.  But they are clearly workable.
